headline: Israel admits that it fired on vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 16:50 BST | Last update: 8 hours 8 min ago
article_body: Israel ’s military has for the first time admitted that it opened fire on a vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and her family in Gaza City two-and-a-half years ago. The military said it would open a criminal investigation into the killing of nine people on 29 January 2024, including Hind. On that date, the Palestinian girl initially survived an Israeli attack on a vehicle which killed several members of her family. Following the Israeli shelling, Hind answered a phone call from the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS), during which she told medics to come and save her. After coordination with the Israeli army, an ambulance was sent to rescue her. That ambulance was shelled by Israeli forces, killing paramedics Yousef Zeino and Ahmed al-Madhoun. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Twelve days after the attack, the bodies of Hind, six members of her family and the two paramedics were found. PRCS accused Israeli forces of "deliberately targeting the ambulance upon its arrival at the scene" despite prior coordination to facilitate the rescue mission. Her mother, Wissam Rajab, told Middle East Eye at the time that the family was separated when they tried to flee the area, which was under intense Israeli attacks. Due to poor weather, Wissam had put her daughter in the vehicle along with her uncle, his wife and their children, while the rest of the family fled on foot. After hearing gunfire in the area, the family called the Red Crescent to tell them the car was getting shot at. Initially, Wissam thought everyone in the car was killed until she got a call from Layan Hamadeh, her 15-year-old cousin, saying: "Hind and I are wounded, and all my family is dead, I don't want to die. Please call an ambulance to save us. I'm scared. The tanks are 500 metres away from me." The line went dead, and Wissam thought they had both been killed. But when she called again, Hind answered and said: "I'm alive, but Layan was martyred. Mum, I'm afraid, they are all dead. Come and get me." The PRCS dispatched Zeino and Madhoun, the two paramedics, to rescue Hind. The medics said they were 15 minutes away and that they were looking for her, but then the line cut off and the crew lost contact. PRCS released an audio recording of the last phone call with Hind, during which her final pleas can be heard amid the rattle of gunfire. "I'm scared of the dark, come get me," she said. According to Rajab, Hind said: "Don't leave me, I'm cold, hungry, and afraid." Israel says 'no criminal misconduct' in three other cases Hind’s death sparked widespread condemnation, and her name circulated in headlines around the world. "Due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division," the Israeli military said on Wednesday. It said that the investigation would be led by Israel's Military Police Criminal Investigation Division - the main body that investigates allegations of wrongdoing by the military. Dozens of Israeli soldiers identified in ICC complaint on killing of Hind Rajab Read More » At the time of the killings, Israel’s military said it was not in the Tel al-Hawa area of Gaza City where the deaths took place. However, multiple media reports identified Israeli tanks in the area. At the time that the car and ambulance were found, the Israeli military had stated that it "conducted raids on terror targets" in areas including Tel al-Hawa. It later deleted that press release from its website. A film about the killing, The Voice of Hind Rajab , was nominated for an Oscar this year. The Israeli military also announced it was opening a criminal investigation into the death of 15 aid workers in Tel al-Sultan, in southern Gaza, in March 2025. However, in three other cases, the military said there was "no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct". That included the Israeli killing of two Doctors Without Borders (MSF) employees in November 2023, the killing of two other MSF workers in February 2024, and the killing of seven World Central Kitchen employees in April 2024. Since October 2023, when Israel's genocide in Gaza began, Israeli forces have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and wounded over 174,000 others. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: US mulls shrinking military footprint in Gulf as a result of war on Iran: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 19:34 BST | Last update: 1 day 6 hours ago
article_body: The Trump administration is examining whether to pull troops out of the Gulf as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran , with the Pentagon weighing the risks facing large US bases in the region that have come under Iranian drone and missile attack. The evaluation is being led by the Department of War’s policy office, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday, saying the war was viewed as “a once-in-a-generation chance for the Pentagon to reconsider its presence in the region”. The report said that the US has already signalled that it might not rebuild its bases attacked by Iran to pre-war status. The Washington Post corroborates Middle East Eye’s June report that cited current and former US officials as saying that a reckoning with the US’s old basing framework was expected as a result of the war. Former senior US officials have raised the prospect of a drawdown for months. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “The truth is that we are not as inclined to occupy these bases now that we have seen what the Iranians can throw at them,” David Petraeus, a former director of the CIA and head of Centcom, which oversees all military forces in the Middle East, told Bloomberg in May. “This is much more than when I was commander at Central Command,” he added. Another former head of Centcom, General Frank McKenzie, said in July that the US needs to relocate its bases in the Gulf to Israel and neighbouring countries to better protect its assets from Iran’s missiles and drones. 'Vulnerability exposed': War on Iran will change how the US bases troops in Gulf Read More » “No one in their right mind would ever put the Centcom forward headquarters, you know, 100 miles away from Iran, [in Qatar], yet that’s where it is,” he told the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, referring to al-Udeid military base. McKenzie said that the current US basing system in the Middle East has become an “artefact”, describing it as a legacy of the Cold War, when the US was concerned about a potential Soviet invasion of the oil-rich Arab Gulf states and later, the counter-insurgencies the US waged in Iraq and Afghanistan. “[The US] strategy does not match the reality on the ground,” he added. The Washington Post reported that US Admiral Bradley Cooper, the current head of Centcom, has supported discussions about potentially moving US troops westward from the Gulf. Iran has already effectively forced the US away from the Gulf coast. The Islamic Republic has targeted Bahrain, home to the US’s Fifth Fleet; Qatar, home to US Central Command’s headquarters; and air bases in Kuwait and the UAE. The US’s presence in small Gulf states close to Iran, such as Kuwait and Bahrain, has been exposed as particularly vulnerable. The US already relocated west during the war. MEE was the first to report that the US gained access to Taif Air Base in Saudi Arabia in March after Iran pummelled Prince Sultan Air Base, southeast of Riyadh. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: US elections: Progressive Democrat scores shock win in Florida
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 22:21 BST | Last update: 2 hours 42 min ago
article_body: Voters headed to the polls in three US states on Tuesday for a series of Democratic and Republican primaries. The verdict in Alaska, Florida, and Wyoming testified to a Democratic Party split along establishment lines and progressives critical of US support for Israel and the war on Iran. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) played a key role in several races. Aipac showered funds on candidates on both sides of the aisle to defeat opponents critical of the US's interventions in the Middle East. Meanwhile, some challengers sought to tie voters' concerns about the cost of living to the cost of the US-Israeli war on Iran. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Overall, the results underscored the establishment's hold on the states. Florida: Progressive Democrat has surprise win In Florida, State Representative Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialist and former union organiser, defeated Alexander Vindman, a retired army lieutenant colonel and national security council aide, in the Democratic primary race for governor. The margin and the financial disparity were formidable, as Nixon raised less than $1m , while Vindman raised more than $16m. Nixon's campaign emphasised an anti-war stance alongside Medicare for All and affordable housing. On the Republican side, Congressman Bryon Donalds won the primary against a field of candidates. Donalds was endorsed by US President Donald Trump and came under intense criticism from challenger James Fishback for his closeness to Aipac. Fishback, who was endorsed by far-right podcaster Nick Fuentes, campaigned critically against US support for Israel and the war on Iran. He was also endorsed by podcaster Tucker Carlson. Florida has become a solidly red state in recent elections, and Donalds is widely expected to win the November general election and succeed Governor Ron DeSantis. Trump-backed Congressman Cory Mills lost his Florida primary after months of controversy and a House Ethics Committee investigation involving allegations of campaign finance violations and sexual misconduct. Alaska and Wyoming: Aipac candidates unchallenged Alaska’s primaries cemented the hold of establishment parties endorsed by Aipac on both sides of the aisle. Former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola and Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan both advanced in the state’s nonpartisan Senate primary. Peltola’s campaign focused on Alaskan fisheries and the energy sector. She received more than $96,546 from Aipac and limited her criticism of the US war on Iran to the issue of more stringent congressional oversight. Wyoming offered little evidence of a Democratic reckoning. Republicans maintained their dominance of the state, nominating Harriet Hageman for the Senate seat being vacated by Senator Cynthia Lummis and Chuck Gray for Hageman’s House seat. Hageman is an ally of Trump and has vocally supported the US war on Iran and military aid for Israel. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Former UAE presidential aide's post mocking Pakistan exposes unease over Mecca pact
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 16 August 2026 08:19 BST | Last update: 3 days 14 hours ago
article_body: A prominent Emirati political analyst and former aide to UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed has sparked backlash after mocking Pakistan over its economic and social challenges while also questioning its role in defending Saudi Arabia under a new regional security arrangement. Abdulkhaleq Abdulla wrote on X on Friday that it was “one of the paradoxes of time” that a country where “a quarter of its population is poor” and “a third” is illiterate could “opportunistically” position itself to defend a country among the world's 20 largest economies. The Emirati political analyst also referred to Pakistan's estimated national income and nuclear arsenal, arguing that the country had endured decades of internal instability and military rule while presenting its nuclear capability as its principal strategic qualification. Abdulla said Pakistan had “suffered from corrupt military rule since its founding, chronic internal unrest and wars with its closest neighbours”, adding that the country’s main qualification was its “170 nuclear bombs”. The former presidential aide was apparently referring to the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, signed on 17 September 2025, which treats any act of aggression against one as an act against both. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters However, his post, which has since garnered more than 1 million views, also indicates the anxieties that the broader Mecca Joint Defence Agreement among Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia has triggered in his native United Arab Emirates. Abdulla’s disparaging remarks about Pakistan - where nearly 1.6 million Pakistanis reside in the UAE and remain a major source of remittance flows to their country - have sparked a backlash, with one user commenting: “Comparing poverty and the size of the economy with the political stance is misleading." من مفارقة الزمان ان دولة ربع سكانها فقراء وثلث سكانها لا يعرف القراءة والكتابة ودخلها القومي 400 مليار $ وتعاني من حكم عسكري فاسد منذ تأسيسها واضطرابات داخلية مزمنة وحروب مع اقرب جيرانها وكل مؤهلاتها 170 قنبلة نووية، تتنطع بشكل انتهازي للدفاع عن دولة ضمن 20 اكبر اقتصاد في العالم — Abdulkhaleq Abdulla (@Abdulkhaleq_UAE) August 15, 2026 "Pakistan is a sovereign state with interests and alliances, and its eligibility for international positions is not conditioned on its wealth. Moreover, reducing its qualifications to nuclear weapons ignores its demographic and geopolitical weight and its economy, which has exceeded $400bn,” the user added. Several users posted his older remarks to point out contradictions in his stances over relations with Pakistan and Israel, including the one in which he wrote: “Damn every Gulf Arab tweep who calls for normalisation with the Israeli enemy.” Another X user posted Abdulla's 2015 comments on the military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in Yemen, in which he said : “Gulf and Saudi diplomacy should have moved with force and weight, been convincing, and utilised all its capabilities to win the vote for Pakistan's participation in Operation Decisive Storm.” Abdulla had previously questioned the logic of the new agreement. Saudi defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan sparks UAE backlash Read More » "Congratulations on the establishment of this alliance, but strengthening Gulf military and political cooperation and unifying the Gulf house is far more important than investing in regional military and political cooperation that includes countries whose credibility and ability to confront the Iranian-Israeli threat are not taken seriously," Abdulla wrote in one of several posts on the matter on 7 August, the day the Mecca agreement was signed. "One of the conditions for the success of any alliance is identifying the common enemy. So who is the enemy for the countries of this alliance?" Abdulaziz Altwaijri, former head of the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (Isesco), the OIC's Rabat-based cultural and educational body, had replied to the post on X by hinting at the UAE's ties with Israel, stating: "Anyone who betrays and collaborates with the Zionists will never find security." Reacting to Abdulla's Pakistan post on X, Altwaijri wrote : "It seems that the Mecca Agreement syndrome has left you dizzy." Rivalry spills into regional alliances The recent exchange points to a deeper rift as relations between the UAE, the first Gulf country to officially recognise Israel, and Saudi Arabia, which has refused to recognise Israel despite American pressure, have soured over Abu Dhabi’s support for southern Yemeni separatist groups. Analysts also see the Mecca agreement as a counter to UAE-Israel military cooperation, which remains unpopular outside Israeli and American circles. Theodore Singer, a former US intelligence officer, told Middle East Eye: "At first glance, the UAE-Israel bloc delivers more tangible gains for both parties, but the Mecca pact may ultimately resonate more broadly and less transactionally.” In May, after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that he visited the UAE at the height of the war on Iran, Abu Dhabi moved to deny the official statement. In contrast, the Mecca pact was celebrated in public. It was announced that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan attended Friday prayers together in Islam's holiest city. Why Egypt held back from joining Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan's defence pact Read More » Some analysts say that the very fact that three countries have publicly codified their agreement gives it room to grow, potentially in ways the UAE-Israel alliance cannot. The UAE-Saudi rivalry that appears to underpin Abdulla's remarks is also evident in the debate over who was left out of the pact, as Riyadh has grown increasingly wary of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's alignment with Abu Dhabi. Saudi Arabia reportedly opposed Egypt’s entry into the new defence pact, citing growing unease over Cairo's "subordination" to the UAE. Egypt sent air defence systems and fighter jets to Abu Dhabi in response to Iranian attacks, while Sisi visited Mohammed bin Zayed more than once during the war. No such steps were taken towards Saudi Arabia. Riyadh sees several Emirati policies as running against Egypt's own strategic interests, including the UAE’s involvement in the breakaway state of Somaliland and its strategic relationship with Israel. Other points of contention include Abu Dhabi's support for Ethiopia during disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and its backing of the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary in Sudan. According to earlier MEE reporting , Egypt does not want to choose sides between emerging blocs comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on one side, and Israel, the UAE and India on the other. Egypt also has a defence treaty with Abu Dhabi and deployed Rafale fighter jets in response to Iranian strikes against the UAE in May, leading Saudi Arabia to view Egypt as unreliable. headline: 'Playing with fire': Israel's Syria strike tests Turkey after Mecca defence pact
author: Ragip Soylu Levent Kemal
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 14:30 BST | Last update: 10 hours 33 min ago
article_body: Turkey has sought to downplay Tuesday’s Israeli strikes on the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northern Syria, about 70km from the Turkish border, viewing them as an election stunt by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Netanyahu has recently portrayed Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani as enemies of Israel in his election campaign materials. However, the attack - which immediately followed the signing of the Mecca defence agreement between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan - suggests that Israel may be seeking to undermine Ankara's credibility as an ally in Syria. The Syrian government condemned the attack, saying eight strikes hit the runway of the defunct airbase early in the morning. Anonymous Israeli officials initially offered contradictory explanations, first accusing Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa of backing proxy forces before the official rhetoric shifted. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Israeli prime minister’s office said in a statement that Israel and Syria had agreed to maintain the security status quo, “which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo”. Reports alleged that the strikes occurred as Turkey was preparing to take control of the base and that they were carried out shortly after a Turkish official delegation had left the site. However, Syrian officials told Middle East Eye that a Turkish technical team had been tasked with repairing the runway and control tower and that there was no military presence at the base. “The last team tasked with reconstructing the base was there two days beforehand,” one official said. The officials added that Turkey had been helping the Syrian army build bases across the country, without any specific plans directed at Israel. Ankara, they said, wants to rebuild a robust Syrian military capable of defending the country. “Turkey doesn’t take over every base,” one official added. MEE Osint Track and ACLED data shows 1,722 incidents deduplicated by place and time Ankara has, in fact, closed many smaller military outposts in northern Syria and already operates several established bases in the area. A potential Turkish presence at Abu al-Duhur would not alter the aerial balance, as some Israeli officials have claimed, because the base is already very close to the Turkish border. Turkish officials told MEE that Israel had not used the hotline established between the two countries last year to prevent military accidents, raising the risk of escalation. Thomas Barrack, the US envoy to Turkey and Syria, told an Israeli outlet that the strikes “carried a real risk of rapid escalation into a direct military confrontation between Israel and Turkey as well as Syria”. “Turkish forces were not aware that the Israeli aircraft were en route to that specific Syrian base, nor of their intended purpose, and therefore could potentially have been inclined to scramble their own jets in the belief that they themselves were under attack,” Barrack said on Wednesday. 'Playing with fire' In numerical terms, the strike was entirely consistent with Israel’s broader campaign. Incident data compiled from Telegram reports and independently coded events from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) include 1,722 verified and deduplicated records between January 2025 and 18 August 2026, showing that the campaign has not let up since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government. Why the Mecca Agreement has given the UAE-Israel alliance the jitters Read More » Turkish officials responded to Israel’s messaging through the Turkish presidency’s communications office, which said Netanyahu intended to continue his expansionist and destabilising regional policies “ahead of elections in Israel”. In two separate interviews, Barrack said a new deconfliction mechanism involving Syria, Israel and Turkey needed to be activated. However, Israel’s failure to use the existing military hotline suggests that it wanted to provoke Turkey rather than proceed cautiously. “It is clear that they wanted to intimidate Ankara,” one Turkish official said on condition of anonymity. “They are playing with fire.” A Turkish source familiar with the operational readiness of the Turkish armed forces said Ankara had radar capabilities that could monitor Israeli aerial activity as far away as Jordan and had not been caught off guard by the strikes. The source speculated that US officials may also have warned Turkey of the impending attack. A message to Erdogan Two Ankara insiders with ties to the Turkish government, speaking anonymously, said they believed that the strikes were intended not only as an election stunt but also to undermine the credibility of Turkish support for Syria. “The Mecca Accords with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which Israel has presented as a new Sunni axis, put Netanyahu in a difficult position domestically,” one of the insiders said. 'It is a way of telling Erdogan that they won’t let him feel comfortable in Syria' - Turkish insider “So Israel is basically saying: We don’t care about the new security architecture being built by Turkey, and we will continue to strike wherever and whenever we want.” The insider added that Israel was also testing the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has backed Sharaa's government. Trump welcomed the Mecca Accords earlier this week. The second insider said Israel had now officially confirmed that it regarded Turkey’s presence in Syria as a threat. “Israel may have elections, but Turkey also has elections in 2028. These tensions could deepen and lead to a repeat of the 2015 incident in which Ankara shot down a Russian fighter jet,” the insider warned. He added that the attack could also have been an attempt to send a direct message to Erdogan. Over the weekend, Erdogan revealed that he was planning to visit Damascus later this year - his first visit since the fall of Assad. “It is a way of telling Erdogan that they won’t let him feel comfortable in Syria,” the insider said. headline: Trump envoy 'deeply concerned' by Israeli strikes on Syrian air base
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 20:03 BST | Last update: 1 day 5 hours ago
article_body: US special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack defended the Syrian government on Tuesday after Israeli air strikes targeted the Abu al-Duhur military air base in northern Syria, calling it an "unnecessary escalation". "The Al-Sharaa government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces. It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel," he wrote on X. "We are deeply concerned," he added. "[This] does not advance regional stability." Israel has not confirmed it was behind the attack, but Barrack said it was responsible. His comments followed a meeting with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani in Istanbul, Turkey, one day earlier. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Syrian government condemned the attack and said eight strikes hit the runway of the defunct air base in the early morning hours of Tuesday, local time. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the strikes followed a visit by a Turkish military delegation to the airfield in recent days "as part of efforts to reactivate it". Since former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia in December 2024, Israel has consistently targeted sites along Syria's western border and its north, focusing on degrading the Syrian air force. It has also sent ground troops into a United Nations-operated buffer zone between the two countries. But talks have also been held between the two sides, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa confirmed last year. 'We want to rebuild Syria' Syria and Israel do not have formal relations. In 1967, Israel seized the Golan Heights from Syria and illegally annexed the territory. However, under the rule of Hafez al-Assad, they signed a disengagement agreement that established a security regime on their border. “Because we want to rebuild Syria, we didn’t respond to these aggressions,” Sharaa previously told The Washington Post of the thousands of Israeli air strikes in his country. Syria says missing chess champion’s six children likely killed under Assad Read More » He added that Israel’s claim that it was targeting Shia militants with ties to Iran was false, noting that "we are the ones who expelled those forces out of Syria". “The advances that Israel made into Syria are not coming from [their] security concerns but are coming from their expansionist ambitions,” he said. Last month, Shaibani condemned "the continuation of Israeli military actions" and warned that "the unlawful occupation of our land beyond the 1974 line is a direct threat to the security of the region". Israeli officials, as recently as last week, said they planned to keep troops in Syria. "The United States has in the past, and will continue in the future, to host discussions to encourage diplomatic cadence over kinetic frustration for both nations," Barrack said on Tuesday. "The United States continues to believe that restraint and engagement offer the more constructive course. We encourage all parties to prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents." headline: Palestinian ‘doctor of the poor’ says he faces abuse, medical neglect in Israeli prison
author: Bilge Kotan
publication_date: Published date: 2 August 2026 21:09 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: Dr Mazen Rantisi, a 71-year-old Palestinian physician popularly described as the “doctor of the poor”, says he has suffered physical abuse and medical neglect since Israeli authorities detained him more than a month ago, Haaretz reported on Sunday. The doctor, known for often waiving fees, supplying medicines and operating a clinic that serves as a refuge for low-income Palestinians, was detained in a pre-dawn raid on his home in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank on 21 June. Prosecutors later indicted him for serving as chairman of the board of the Union of Health Work Committees, a Palestinian non-profit that provides medical care to thousands of Palestinians each year. According to the report, Rantisi told a lawyer from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel that prison authorities withheld his regular medication for the first 10 days in Ofer prison and are still denying him one of his medicines. His requests to see a doctor went unanswered, and a medic checked his pulse only once through a small opening in the cell door. Rantisi also reported physical violence, saying that said the prison units raided his cell several times a week and beat detainees. “The younger prisoners surround me to protect me, taking the beatings themselves,” Rantisi said, adding that the guards sprayed tear gas into the cell during one raid, leaving him struggling to breathe. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Saja Misherqi Baransi, the first lawyer to see Rantisi face to face since his arrest, said the physician has rapidly lost weight after receiving tiny portions of food that he described as unfit for human consumption, including mouldy bread, almost-rotten tomatoes, uncooked hummus and foul-smelling rice. He also said ten prisoners share his six-bed cell, with four taking turns sleeping on mattresses on the floor. Prisoners receive no cleaning supplies and share one piece of soap for washing themselves and their clothes, while wet mattresses have developed mould and the hot cell is infested with pests. The Israel Prison Service rejected the physician’s account, saying that it held all prisoners in accordance with the law, the Haaretz report said. The physician’s account, however, echoes accounts from other Palestinian detainees and prisoners. A Public Defender’s Office report published on 1 July last year said there had been “a significant deterioration in prison conditions in Israel” and “an unprecedented violation of the rights of detainees and prisoners.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Jury refuses to convict seven Palestine Action defendants over Elbit raid
author: Katherine Hearst
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 13:15 BST | Last update: 8 hours 52 mins ago
article_body: Jurors at a London court were discharged after being unable to reach verdicts for seven Palestine Action defendants accused of coordinating a raid on an Israeli-owned arms factory. One person who could not be named for legal reasons was convicted by a majority of 9-1 of criminal damage in relation to the incident. The defendants- Hannah Davidson, 53, Ian Sanders, 47, Aleksandra Herbich, 41, Teuta Hoxha, 30, William Plastow, 35, Julija Brigadirova, 33, Sean Middlebrough, 33, and Madeleine Norman, 31- were accused of criminal damage and violent disorder in connection with a break-in to an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol in August 2024. But on Wednesday, following an eight-week trial and around 37 hours of deliberations at the Old Bailey, jurors could not reach verdicts for seven of the defendants. They could face a retrial. Plastow had previously been acquitted of violent disorder due to a lack of evidence. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters All eight defendants are accused of coordinating the break-in by carrying out reconnaissance and purchasing equipment, but were not alleged to have gone into the factory premises during the action. Prosecutors said that they encouraged and assisted other groups of activists - known as the “red team” - who broke into the site itself and destroyed weapons and equipment - and the “black team”, whose role it was to distract the security guards outside the factory. All eight defendants deny the charges. Initially, the jury had been directed by the presiding Judge Patrick Field to deliver a unanimous verdict. But on Tuesday, he told jurors he would consider majority verdicts on the different counts. Outside the court, the defendants were greeted by chanting supporters. They wept as they were embraced by family and friends. ‘Invisible coordinator’ The eight were charged under the joint enterprise doctrine, meaning that, while they are not alleged to have committed the offences themselves, they faced the same allegations as the defendants who broke into the site. The prosecution accused them of coordinating the raid, pointing to their involvement in a number of signal groups which they said were connected to organising the break-in. Representing Brigadirova, lawyer Tom Copeland reminded jurors last week that they had not seen any evidence of financial transactions made by the defendant linked to the Filton raid, nor any messages sent from her Signal handles related to planning the action. “If the prosecution is right, perhaps she should be called the invisible coordinator,” Copeland said. 'We didn’t know how an action could turn into a terrorism case. We were all terrorist prisoners' - Teuta Hoxha, Palestine Action defendant He told jurors that, in the weeks prior to the action when the coordination was alleged to have taken place, Brigadirova had attempted to take her own life. Copeland noted that the prosecution had “glossed over” the information about Brigadirova's mental health at the time, by describing the defendant as suffering from “low mood”. Representing Herbich, lawyer Emma Fenn told jurors in her closing speech that the evidence showed that her client's role in the raid was primarily limited to purchasing food and cooking. Co-defendant Norman told jurors that, before the action, at an Airbnb "safe house" rented by the activists in Bristol, Herbich had been "cooking a lot of pasta. That’s all I saw her doing”. Fenn emphasised that “cooking doesn’t even come close” to qualifying as an “intentional act” assisting or encouraging the offences of violent disorder and criminal damage. “There is nothing to connect her with tools or weapons,” Fenn said, describing Herbich as “someone doing the cleaning at most and the cooking at least”. Plastow, who was the only defendant not alleged to have travelled to Bristol at the time of the raid, told jurors that he had no knowledge of the Filton site prior to the action. He said that the first he had heard of it was via an X post on the morning after the raid. 'This isn't the Britain I grew up in': The activists raided by police over Palestine Action videos Read More » Jurors heard that forensic analysis of Plastow’s phone and laptop found no evidence of access to an encrypted document allegedly used to plan the action at Filton, and no history of him accepting group calls via the Signal app. They also heard that the analysis found no history of internet searches, communications, documents or notes referencing the Filton site before 6 August 2024. Plastow admitted to purchasing items for Palestine Action and handing them over to co-defendant Charlotte Head. But he said that he thought the equipment was intended for use in a general store for future actions. His lawyer, Alex Rose, urged jurors that they must be sure his client supplied the equipment to Head with the intention that "Elbit’s property would be destroyed or damaged in accordance with the plan in which Charlotte Head and others were engaged”. Each of the defendants denied that they knew the raid would involve violence against security guards. When giving evidence, Hoxha said: "Given that behind the scenes lobbying groups [were] lobbying the government, it wouldn’t be in [the] interests of Palestine Action to be violent." 'Terrorist prisoners' During the trial, jurors heard that the defendants had been arrested by counter-terrorism police. Hoxha said when giving evidence that they were all "terrified" upon arrest. "We didn’t know how an action could turn into a terrorism case," she said. "We were all terrorist prisoners." Plastow told jurors that he was arrested by “about 20” counter-terrorism police days after the raid and then held for six days “in a little white room with no windows and lights that didn’t go off”, like "Hannibal Lecter”. Chaos at London court as over 1,500 Palestine Action cases listed in one day Read More » Davidson wept while she was on the stand, saying that she and her co-defendants “still have PTSD” following their arrests. All seven defendants were held in prison on remand for up to 18 months, in excess of standard UK custody time limits. Hoxha was among several prisoners who launched hunger strikes over their detention conditions during their imprisonment. The court heard that Plastow "missed the last year" of his mother's life, who died of terminal cancer while he was in prison. He was briefly granted bail to sit by her deathbed, before being remanded back to prison. The six members of the "red team" previously faced a months-long trial which concluded in May, with four of them being convicted of criminal damage, one of committing grievous bodily harm without intent, and two acquitted of all charges. Following an initial trial which ended in February, the six were acquitted of aggravated burglary charges, with the jury hung on criminal damage and grievous bodily harm charges. Jurors also acquitted three of the defendants of violent disorder charges, and failed to return verdicts on the same charge for the remaining three. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Israeli soldier visiting India accused of war crimes in Gaza's Khan Younis
author: Azad Essa
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 17:57 BST | Last update: 7 hours 50 mins ago
article_body: The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a war crimes complaint in India against an Israeli soldier accused of deliberately demolishing civilian property in Gaza. The complaint, filed on Tuesday , is the second brought by the HRF against an Israeli soldier visiting India. In June, the organisation filed a complaint against Eitan Gilboa, a soldier with Israel's 271st Combat Engineering Battalion. Gilboa had shared images of his battalion "turning entire neighbourhoods in Gaza into ash and dust" and video of himself celebrating the demolitions. The Indian government took no action, and Gilboa subsequently left the country. HRF said its case against the second soldier - whom it has not publicly named - stems from his alleged direct involvement in the unlawful destruction of civilian property in Abasan al-Saghira, in the Khan Younis Governorate, between March and April 2024. HRF said his actions may amount to war crimes, crimes against humanity, and acts of genocide. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The lawyer who filed the case on behalf of HRF in India told Middle East Eye that India had obligations under the Geneva Conventions and international law that it had to uphold. "India cannot become a 'second home' where Israeli soldiers accused of grave international crimes travel with impunity, and come to cleanse themselves of accountability after participating in the destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza," the lawyer, who asked not to be named, said. "The obligation is clear: where there are credible allegations of grave breaches of international humanitarian law, India must act," the lawyer added. Destruction of civilian infrastructure Since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, around 250,000 Palestinians have been killed or injured in Israel's genocide in Gaza. Around 82 percent of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged, while 90 percent of its energy infrastructure has been demolished. In its submission, HRF said it used satellite imagery, social media footage, and other open-source intelligence to reconstruct the sequence of events surrounding the demolition of the area in Khan Younis. It said the evidence showed that the buildings were deliberately demolished rather than destroyed during active warfare. The organisation said the pattern aligned with Amnesty International’s independent findings regarding the “buffer zone” destruction along Gaza’s eastern perimeter. It said the demolitions also reflected the continuing expansion of the “Yellow Line” into Gaza. Tens of thousands of Israelis travel to India each year after completing their mandatory service. Many of these former conscripts follow what is commonly known as the “hummus trail”, which passes through several towns and states across the country. "HRF exists to ensure that no one who participates in genocide escapes justice," Dyab Abou Jahjah, general director at HRF, said in a statement. The Israeli government, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli diplomats, has repeatedly praised India’s support over the past two-and-a-half years. India has not backed South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. It has also not joined calls for an arms embargo on Israel, while Indian companies have continued to supply Israel with military components. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Iran issues warning against Arab states aiding US, as UAE cuts economic ties
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 13:51 BST | Last update: 11 hours 56 mins ago
article_body: Iran has warned Gulf states against aiding the US , hours after the UAE said it was cutting economic ties with Tehran. Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of the Iranian armed forces, warned on Wednesday that "any assistance or facilitation provided to the aggressor US military amounts to participation in the US military operation", as reported by Iran’s Mehr news agency. "It seems unlikely that such a large number of military aircraft, particularly refuelling aircraft, could be present at regional bases without knowledge of host countries," said Abdollahi. He added that Gulf countries "should know that we are fully aware of the situation". Some media reports have suggested that Saudi Arabia , the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain have hit targets in Iran in response to attacks on the Gulf, but the countries have mostly denied such reporting. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Several Gulf states host US military bases and installations, including the UAE, which said on Tuesday that Iran had fired two ballistic missiles at vessels along its coast. Abu Dhabi said both missiles fell in the sea, adding that one of them was within the UAE's territorial waters. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei "categorically rejected the United Arab Emirates' claim that Iran had launched a missile towards that country". On Tuesday, the UAE announced that it was suspending all economic dealings with Iran. "In light of regional escalations... all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice," foreign ministry official Afra al-Hameli said. The UAE is home to a large Iranian community, and had been a major trading partner for US-sanctioned Iran before the war . Since the war broke out, however, the UAE has taken several measures against Iran, including recalling its ambassador and closing Iran-linked schools and a hospital. In the early months of the war, which erupted in late February after the US and Israel launched heavy attacks on Iran, Tehran heavily struck sites across the Emirates. US mulling troop withdrawal from Gulf The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that US President Donald Trump's administration was examining whether to pull troops out of the Gulf as a result of the war on Iran, with the Pentagon weighing the risks facing large US bases in the region that have come under Iranian drone and missile attack. The evaluation is being led by the Department of War’s policy office, which said the war was viewed as "a once-in-a-generation chance for the Pentagon to reconsider its presence in the region". The report said that the US has already signalled that it might not rebuild its bases attacked by Iran to pre-war status. Iran warns enemies to 'anticipate strategic surprises' as it shifts from a defensive stance Read More » The Washington Post corroborates Middle East Eye’s June report that cited current and former US officials as saying that a reckoning with the US’s old basing framework was expected as a result of the war. Former senior US officials have raised the prospect of a drawdown for months. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump posted an image on social media labelling the Strait of Hormuz as "NEW U.S. Territory". The map of the strategic waterway - through which a fifth of the globe's oil and liquefied natural gas passes - was posted on his Truth Social account. Iran’s secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, ridiculed the post. "The gap between America’s inability to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and its claim to own it is greater than the 7,000-mile [11,265km] distance between Washington and the Strait itself," he wrote in a post on X. "Welcome to the post-American order in the Persian Gulf." Iran’s top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in a speech on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US "commitments stipulated in the memorandum of understanding... are implemented", including lifting its naval blockade. Meanwhile, South Korea's foreign minister said on Wednesday that Trump's ordering of the scaling back of joint military drills appeared to include pressure on Seoul to become involved in the war on Iran. "I think President Trump's message ​includes pressure over several pending issues concerning the South ​Korean government, as well as a message to North ⁠Korea and an intention by the United States to break ​a stalemate in the Iran war," Cho Hyun said. Cho indicated that neither South Korean nor US officials had prior knowledge of Trump’s order to reduce joint military exercises. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli finance minister calls for building settlements near Gaza amid ongoing offensive
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 2 August 2026 14:35 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 3 days ago
article_body: Israel 's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich on Sunday called for the construction of three new Israeli settlements along the northern fence of Gaza. The statement comes as Israeli military attacks continue in Gaza and the occupied West Bank despite a ceasefire agreement announced in October. Smotrich, who heads Israel's Settlements Administration, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to approve the plan in a post on X. "The Settlements Administration under my leadership is prepared to establish 3 settlements in the northern sector of the Gaza Strip, and I call on the Prime Minister to give the green light to the move," he wrote. Israelis are "returning" to settlements evacuated in 2005, Smotrich said, adding that Israel would establish additional settlements in the occupied West Bank. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Alongside the four settlements to which we are returning, we will establish a long line of new settlements in northern Samaria. On Mount Ebal, in the Dothan Valley, and in more than 10 additional points, we will strengthen and fortify the settlement," he said. Israel withdrew its settlers and military installations from Gaza in 2005 under then-Prime Minister Ariel Sharon's unilateral disengagement plan, dismantling all settlements in the enclave as well as four settlements in the occupied West Bank. Earlier today, the Palestinian health ministry in Gaza said six Palestinians were killed and 23 wounded in Israeli attacks over the last 24 hours. The ministry said at least 73,356 Palestinians have been killed and 174,185 wounded since Israel began its genocidal war in October 2023. It added that 1,230 people have been killed and 4,076 injured since the ceasefire took effect last year. However, according to Al Jazeera Arabic, nine Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza since dawn, including three children. And local media reported that the number of people killed in Israeli attacks had risen to at least 11 after an air strike hit a vehicle in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. The Israeli military said it killed Salem Jamal Abdelrahman Abu Labad, whom it identified as a commander in Hamas's Nukhba special forces, in an air strike in southern Gaza on Saturday. It said Abu Labad had participated in the October 2023 attack on Kibbutz Nir Oz. The 'Board of Peace' announced a Palestinian body will take Hamas weapons. That's not what Trump said Read More » The military also said it killed Muhammad Abdelnasser Muhammad Khatib, whom it identified as a commander in Hamas's Maghazi Battalion, in a separate strike in central Gaza on Friday. Meanwhile, Hamas said on Friday that any agreement on the "complete disarmament" of Palestinian factions in Gaza depends on Washington and Israel honouring commitments made under last year's ceasefire. The statement followed US President Donald Trump's announcement that the US-led Board of Peace had secured an agreement to disarm Hamas and every other armed group in Gaza. Former Israeli Ambassador Alon Pinkas told Al Jazeera that Israel was "absolutely not" satisfied with the arrangement. "Israel is presented with a situation where the US president says there's an agreement, but there isn't really an agreement, and so I am extraordinarily sceptical that this is going to work out," Pinkas said. He added that Netanyahu viewed the agreement as a "colossal failure" and said Israel had yet to implement measures expected under the deal, including withdrawing to the "Yellow Line" buffer zone, allowing unrestricted humanitarian aid into Gaza and halting military operations. Israeli media outlet Ynet has reported that the United States is expected to deploy about 10 additional aerial refuelling aircraft to Israel in the coming days, citing unnamed Israeli security officials. The report said the aircraft would join more than 30 US refuelling planes already stationed at Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport. In the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that Israeli forces detained five Palestinians during raids in Bethlehem and Nablus. The agency said Israeli troops also raided homes and posted threatening signs on the walls of the Salah al-Din Mosque in Bethlehem. The raids followed a week of intensified Israeli military and settler attacks, particularly around the village of Tal near Nablus, where four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed after armed settlers attacked Palestinian villages last week. Separately, Hamas said a delegation led by Zaher Jabarin met Palestinian Islamic Jihad leaders in Cairo on Saturday to discuss efforts to end Israel's attacks in Gaza and developments in the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem. The group said the two sides stressed the need to compel Israel to withdraw fully from Gaza and called for closer coordination between Palestinian factions. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Oil supertankers in Gulf are renting for $500,000 per day: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 21:45 BST | Last update: 4 hours 2 mins ago
article_body: Supertanker owners are getting paid $510,000 per day to bring crude oil from the Gulf to Asia, in a sign of high demand for vessels to transit the waterway as fighting rages in the region and alternative routes take supply from the market. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that earnings from the Middle East-to-China route have jumped to their highest level since June. The rising figure suggests that demand for vessels is high and some are risking the threat of war to take profits. “Right now, the strait is open. A lot of boats are coming through. People aren’t reporting that," US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday. One vessel, a very large crude carrier (VLCC), the Mongolia Prosperity, operated by South Korean shipowner Sinokor, is set to load crude from an unnamed Persian Gulf port for delivery to East Asia, with the voyage costing $31m, Bloomberg reported. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A ceasefire struck in April amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, and extended in June, is all but defunct in the Strait of Hormuz, with each side trying to impose its own blockade. The US military fired on a Panama-flagged container ship earlier this month that it said attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman to an Iranian port. Meanwhile, at least one sailor was killed this week in Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the water, the Joint Maritime Information Centre, a multinational organisation, said. But Gulf states are still trying to export millions of barrels of oil to customers in Asia. UAE's Adnoc announces $8bn gas expansion, as it mulls Hormuz bypass Read More » The fighting means that shipowners willing to brave the risk stand to make handsome profits with demand high and the supply of vessels low. The Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF (BWET), which allows investors to bet on the price of crude oil freight futures, is up a whopping 2,200 percent since the start of the year. BWET surged after the US and Israel attacked Iran in April, then fell when the ceasefire was declared. But it has soared in value over the summer as investors bet against an end to fighting in Hormuz. Yemen’s Houthis have restarted attacking vessels in the Red Sea. To avoid the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint, Saudi Arabia has had to send oil via the Sumed Pipeline to the Mediterranean, where it is loaded onto VLCC tankers. The vessels take a longer route around the tip of Africa, reducing the supply of ships available in the market and driving up prices. The Trump administration has insisted that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that more vessels are transiting the waterway than is being publicly reported. The UAE boosted oil production to an all-time high in June, pumping 4.1 million barrels per day, the International Energy Agency said in a July report. The UAE has taken a risk-prone approach to sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, with its ship-tracking signals turned off. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: 'We cried instead of celebrating': War and loss shadow Gaza's top students
author: Ahmed Dremly
publication_date: Published date: 1 August 2026 13:29 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 4 days ago
article_body: For most students, the General Secondary Education Certificate, known as Tawjihi in Palestine , marks the end of school and the start of a new chapter. It is usually a time of celebration, relief and hope for the future. In Gaza, nearly three years into Israel 's genocide, the milestone has taken on a different meaning. For thousands of Palestinian students, simply surviving long enough to sit the exams and see the results announced became an achievement in itself. For Saba Rabah, who topped Palestine's scientific stream with an average of 99.9 percent, the result fulfilled a childhood dream. But the moment she had imagined for years was overshadowed by the absence of her father, who was killed in an Israeli strike on a neighbouring building in al-Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Since childhood, Rabah's parents had encouraged her to excel at school and dreamt of her becoming one of Palestine's top students. "In my last conversation with my father, he told me he dreamed I would rank among the top students in the scientific stream and study medicine, just as I had always hoped," she told Middle East Eye. "He said he wanted to spend his retirement in my future clinic." Saba Rabah's last selfie with her father, taken during Eid al-Fitr on 10 April 2024, before he was killed (Courtesy of Saba Rabah) Like thousands of Tawjihi students across Gaza, Rabah studied under conditions that made even the most basic aspects of education a daily struggle. Days before her final exams, an Israeli strike damaged the family's rented shelter, forcing her to study in the only room left intact - a space where the family also cooked, slept and spent most of the day. "No words can describe the suffering of studying while starving or while fleeing," she said. She recalled having to choose, during repeated displacement, between carrying her books, her mother's heart and blood pressure medication, or helping her 25-year-old brother, Saeed, who has quadriplegia. 'We want to study like everyone else. We want to live in dignity.' - Saba Rabah, Palestinian student Textbooks, stationery and even paper have become scarce, while unreliable electricity and internet access have made it even harder to study. "It's hard for high school students to find even second-hand books because no new textbooks have entered Gaza for the past three years," she said. "Even A4 paper is expensive. Two hundred sheets cost around $150. Everything is expensive." But whenever she felt overwhelmed, her mother and siblings reminded her of her father's dream. "Every family in Gaza has experienced grief. We have lost fathers, mothers, siblings and sometimes entire families. We didn't choose to live through this genocide, but we keep trying to live and hold on to the small moments because that is our right. "The only solution is for the Israeli war to stop. We don't want to lose any more of our loved ones. We want to study like everyone else. We want to live in dignity." Wounded but determined Alongside repeated displacement, bombardment and loss, thousands of students sat their Tawjihi exams while recovering from injuries. For Maram Muqit, from northern Gaza, the exams came just four months after an Israeli bullet lodged in her spinal cord, leaving her with hemiplegia. "She was on her way back to the tent from a maths class when she was injured," her mother, Naheel, told Middle East Eye. "Doctors told us she might never walk again if she remains in Gaza because of the lack of medical supplies." Before she was wounded, Maram attended two makeshift schools despite the dangers of travelling across northern Gaza. "Her father and I begged her not to go because we feared for her safety," her mother said. "But she insisted she couldn't waste any opportunity to learn." When internet access was available, she downloaded lessons from YouTube and studied materials her teachers shared on WhatsApp. Before the war, Maram and her family lived in Beit Lahia, but their home was destroyed during the first month of the Israeli attacks, forcing them to flee from one place to another. They now live in a tent in al-Atatra neighbourhood in the north of Gaza. "She was like my right hand," her mother said. "She used to help me with cooking, fleeing and everything we had to do." Maram Muqit wears a graduation cap and sash from her hospital bed after completing her Tawjihi exams on 28 July (Provided) Maram is now undergoing rehabilitation at al-Wafa Hospital. "It was exhausting for her to balance treatment with studying, but she still achieved an outstanding 96.6 percent," her mother said. "When the results came out, we cried instead of celebrating. Her father and I tried to help her stand, but she still couldn't keep her balance." The hospital later allowed Maram to spend a day with her family at their displacement camp. "We had a small celebration with relatives and friends. When she returned to hospital, the doctors and other patients celebrated with her too. Some even brought her gifts." Despite her result, Maram says her future remains uncertain. 'I am happy I achieved the grades I needed. But I am sad that I may never walk again' - Maram Muqit, Palestinian student She dreams of studying dentistry, but fears her disability could prevent her from pursuing the career she has wanted since childhood. "I am happy I achieved the grades I needed," she said. "But I am sad that I may never walk again. "I hope I can get an electric wheelchair, travel abroad for treatment and go to university." According to the Palestinian Ministry of Education, Israeli forces have wounded at least 28,293 students since October 2023. Results never seen While some students celebrated their achievements, others never lived to see their results. Among them was Yahya Nasman, who scored 96.6 percent but was killed alongside five members of his family in an Israeli air strike on their home on al-Nasser Street in western Gaza City, a week before the results were announced in July. Two days before the attack, his uncle, Waleed, invited Yahya and another student from the family to celebrate the end of their exams. Waleed said that it had been an exhausting year for his nephew, who studied while helping his family fetch water, collect firewood and survive the war. 'He wanted to study architectural engineering so he could help rebuild the homes destroyed in Gaza' - Waleed Nasman, uncle of student killed in Israeli strike Over pizza, Yahya spoke confidently about his future. "He told me he was sure he would get high marks and wanted to study architectural engineering so he could help rebuild the homes destroyed in Gaza," Waleed said. He remembered him as the most caring member of the family. "Whenever anyone needed help, he was there. As soon as he finished, he went straight back to studying." The day before the strike, Yahya brought his six-year-old sister, Arwa, to play with Waleed's daughters. Waleed said he never imagined it would be the last time he would see them alive. The following day, another of Yahya's brothers, 12-year-old Ayham, returned home to find the family house reduced to rubble. He ran back to alert his relatives. "We rushed there hoping someone had survived," Waleed said. "My brother, his wife and their three children, including Yahya, were killed instantly. "The force of the explosion threw parts of their bodies hundreds of metres down the street. I collected the remains of my nephews and nieces from the road and the displacement camps before burying them." Yahya Nasman pictured at a restaurant in Gaza (Provided) Five days later, the family learned Yahya had achieved one of the highest Tawjihi scores in Gaza. What should have been a celebration became another funeral. His cousins, who had hoped to celebrate their success together, could not bring themselves to do so. "Yahya was one of thousands of students who tried to build a future despite everything happening around them," Waleed said. "We want people around the world to help stop the attacks on Gaza. Every day more people are killed." Despite a ceasefire agreed in October to pause the two-year genocide in Gaza, Israel has continued to bomb the strip on a near-daily basis. Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,200 people since the ceasefire began. Overall, the Israeli army has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians since October 2023. They include nearly 19,000 students and around 800 teachers and education workers, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Education. The ministry says Israeli attacks have also damaged or destroyed 279 schools, leaving Gaza's education system in ruins. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. subheadline: Some topped Palestine. Others were killed before their results were announced

headline: After Israel killed her three sons, she found hope in a newborn. Then he was killed too
author: Nada Nabil
publication_date: Published date: 1 August 2026 10:59 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 4 days ago
article_body: In a small room beside an open window, 15-month-old Zaid Nofal slept without a blanket, unable to escape Gaza's sweltering summer heat. At 3am, an Israeli air strike hit his family's home in al-Bureij refugee camp, burying his small body beneath the rubble. A few metres away, his 38-year-old Palestinian mother, Fatima Nofal, stood in shock. Covered in blood and dust as neighbours screamed around her, she faced a tragedy she had endured before: Zaid was the fourth son she had lost to Israeli attacks after three of his brothers were killed in 2023. Neighbours rushed to the family's home, which had already been partially destroyed, before it was rebuilt following the October 2025 ceasefire announcement. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "I still haven't processed what happened. I remain in a state of profound shock," Nofal told Middle East Eye. "All I remember is waking up just minutes before the strike. I moved to another spot because of the severe heat, leaving my little Zaid by the window so the breeze could help him sleep." 'Israel is intent on killing us' - Fatima Nofal, Palestinian mother Although wounded in the attack, Nofal refused to leave and called on neighbours to search for her son. "The room was filled with debris, and they began lifting the rubble to find him," she said. Zaid was eventually pulled from beneath the rubble, wrapped in a light blanket and taken to hospital. Three sons killed in 2023 His death reopened the trauma of 13 October 2023, when an Israeli air strike killed three of Nofal's sons. Only she and her two daughters survived. At the start of the war, Nofal and her family fled al-Bureij refugee camp, believing the al-Sawarha area in the coastal town of al-Zawaida would be safer. "We realised the gravity of the situation and decided to flee because we thought it would be safer than staying near the border," she said. "But we never imagined that the place we went to for safety would become where I'd witness the killing of my three sons and most of my husband's family." That strike killed her eldest son, 16-year-old Amin, 11-year-old Hamza, and Ahmed, her newborn son who was just 22 days old. Nofal and her two daughters were also wounded. Their shelter was destroyed, forcing them into repeated displacement. A small miracle Like almost all of Gaza's population, Nofal has endured months of displacement, loss and uncertainty since the war began in October 2023. Ten months after losing her three sons, a moment of hope entered her life when she discovered she was pregnant. Her happiness grew when she learned she was expecting a boy. Nofal gave birth to Zaid on 16 April 2025, amid the ongoing war on Gaza. She believed he had come to fill the void left by the children she had lost. 'His arrival brought immense joy to the whole family' - Fatima Nofal "Zaid's birth was the most significant event in our lives during the war," Nofal recalled. "His arrival brought immense joy to the whole family; everyone celebrated him as a small miracle that came to light up our lives after long months and nights of pain and tears." Relatives suggested naming him after one of his late brothers, but Nofal refused. "I wanted him to have his own name and his own destiny," she said. Over time, Zaid became the "joy of the home". His sisters grew especially attached to him. "Whenever I took him to the clinic for vaccinations or check-ups, his sisters would wait for him on the stairs. They could not bear being away from him, even for a few hours." Nofal spoke to MEE while recovering from burns to her feet. Her eldest daughter, Baraa, sustained minor injuries, while her youngest daughter, Lina, suffered head trauma. "Lina is still in hospital. When I visited her, the first thing she asked about was Zaid. I could not bring myself to tell her the truth while she was still wounded. I told her he was fine and waiting for her," Nofal said. "I don't know how I will tell her the truth when she is discharged." Zaid Nofal’s birth was a “miracle” for his family, his mother says (Provided) Nofal said her grief is deepened by the childhood Zaid never had. "On the day he was killed, he was restless in the afternoon and wanted to go outside. I told his sisters how much I wished I could take him out, but there are no places left for children to play." "He spent his whole life indoors. Even his cousins had been killed in Israeli air strikes, so he had no one to play with." Israel 'deliberately' targeting children Despite a ceasefire agreed last year to pause the two-year genocidal war on Gaza, Israel has continued to bomb the strip on a near-daily basis. Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,200 people since the ceasefire began nearly 10 months ago. Overall, the Israeli army has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians since October 2023. Children have not been spared from the mounting toll. The United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) said in June that around 260 children had been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began. Unicef spokesperson James Elder described the situation as a "cruel and deadly illusion of a ceasefire", saying that, on average, one child was being killed every day. After witnessing the deaths of her own children, Nofal believes Palestinian civilians, particularly women and children, have been deliberately targeted by Israel. "Since the war began, the vast majority of the casualties we've seen are women and children," she said. "Israel is intent on killing us, and it needs no justification to do so." The world must stop Israel's unprecedented assault on Palestinian children Read More » On the same day Zaid was killed in al-Bureij refugee camp, nine-year-old Ratil al-Abadla was also killed in an Israeli strike on her uncle's tent in al-Mawasi. Al-Abadla had been visiting her uncle with her mother and siblings two days earlier, in an attempt to give her a brief escape from the realities of war. A video of her father, Abdullah al-Abadla, holding her body and asking what his child had done to deserve such a fate spread widely online. For families across Gaza, the question has become familiar. The UN's independent commission of inquiry has said it found evidence that Israeli forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, describing such actions as part of conduct that contributed to its finding that Israel has committed genocidal acts. For Nofal, however, no report or statistic can bring back Zaid or the three sons she lost before him. As she sits beside her injured daughter in hospital, she faces a new struggle: finding a place to live and telling her child that her beloved little brother will not return. "The fire is burning in my chest, and I do not know who will extinguish it," she said. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Houthi missile barrage hits Mocha port as fighting escalates in Yemen
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 16 August 2026 11:57 BST | Last update: 3 days 12 hours ago
article_body: Yemen's Houthi movement launched fresh missile and drone attacks on the government-held city of Marib and the Red Sea port city of Mocha, wounding civilians, damaging property and forcing the suspension of commercial operations at the port, according to government officials and media reports. The latest escalation comes as fighting resumes across several Yemeni provinces after a relative lull that had largely held since April 2022. Yemen's Marib Governorate said the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles and launched four drones at residential neighbourhoods in the densely populated city on Saturday and Sunday. The attacks wounded at least four people and damaged homes, vehicles and other civilian property, according to the governorate's media office. One strike hit a bakery in al-Sharika north of Marib city, wounding one person. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The governorate said the continuing attacks threatened civilians and camps housing displaced people. It later reported that a sixth ballistic missile had struck the city, publishing photographs showing a crater and the wreckage of a damaged vehicle. The Marib media office called on the international community to “condemn these attacks and crimes targeting displacement camps, residential neighbourhoods and civilian facilities, and document them as violations of international humanitarian law”. The attacks followed earlier reports from Yemeni officials that several ballistic missiles and drones had targeted civilian infrastructure in Marib, causing explosions across the province. State-run Saba TV and government-aligned Aljoumhouria TV also reported missile strikes and explosions in the city. Fighting spreads across Yemen Meanwhile, repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks have forced commercial and maritime operations at Mocha port to stop, causing an estimated $16m in damages, according to Abdulmalik al-Sharabi, the port's director. Sharabi said the attacks had killed seven people, including four security personnel and three port employees, according to Yemen's state-run Saba news agency. He said the strategic port in southwestern Taiz province, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, had been struck by more than 25 missiles since 9 August, marking the first reported attacks on the facility since the 2022 truce. Houthi missile and drone attacks kill dozens of Yemeni government troops Read More » The attacks damaged six wooden vessels and a dredger being used for the port's expansion, Sharabi said, adding that the suspension of operations had left about 1,300 workers without income. On Friday, government-aligned National Resistance Forces had said that the Houthis had launched 40 ballistic missiles, 46 drones and explosive-laden boats targeting Mocha, its port and civilian sites in recent days. The Houthis, however, said they had targeted military gatherings, weapons depots and military boats in the areas around Mocha. The renewed violence has also spread to the southwestern province of Taiz, where the Yemeni military said three Houthi fighters were killed and several others, including field commanders, were wounded in drone strikes on Saturday. A military source told Saba TV that army drones targeted Houthi gatherings and vehicles on the Maqbanah front, west of Taiz city. Fighting has intensified in recent weeks across Marib, al-Jawf, al-Dhalea and Taiz, ending much of the relative calm that followed the April 2022 truce. Yemen's war began after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in September 2014. The conflict has since plunged Yemen into one of the world's most severe humanitarian and economic crises. The chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, warned that recent attacks on the port threatened shipping traffic and food and fuel supplies, potentially worsening Yemen's food crisis.
