headline: Five years of Taliban rule: A state has survived, but at what cost?
author: Zia Ur Rehman
publication_date: Published date: 15 August 2026 09:34 BST | Last update: 4 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Five years after the Taliban’s return to power on 15 August 2021, Afghanistan has transformed from a chaotic battlefield into a functioning but deeply authoritarian state. Foreign troops are gone, and fragmented opponents have failed to mount a significant challenge to Kabul’s centralised control. The movement has established a degree of internal security unimaginable under the previous government. However, this stability rests on systematic exclusion, most notably of women, leaving the nation economically fragile and politically isolated. While the Taliban have proven they can govern without western support, they remain an international pariah managing a historic humanitarian crisis. Afghanistan today is quieter than before 2021, but it is also poorer, more isolated, and severely repressive towards half its population. The regime’s primary achievement in its first five years was territorial consolidation. The next five will test whether it can survive mounting internal and external pressures. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Inside the Taliban’s administration The central story of the last five years is the patient, quiet accumulation of power by the Taliban’s reclusive supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, who operates from Kandahar. Since his appointment in 2016, Akhundzada has transitioned the movement from an insurgency to a rigid governing authority. Akhundzada has built a powerful network, ensuring key state positions, including the premiership, the central bank, and the chief justiceship, sit in Kandahari hands. This is reinforced by a massive patronage system of roughly 15,000 registered madrassas, in which students receive stipends and teachers receive graded salaries. This network secures the loyalty of the provincial clergy, the movement’s core constituency, by granting them both status and sustainable resources. 'Hardline elements within Taliban ranks view Pakistani militants as historical comrades-in-arms' - Taliban official in the interior ministry In Kabul, high-profile figures such as Mullah Abdul Ghani Baradar, Sirajuddin Haqqani, Maulvi Yaqoob, and Amir Khan Muttaqi manage daily governance, economic policy, and foreign diplomacy. However, real power resides in Kandahar, where a 119-article criminal procedure code was quietly approved in early 2026 to cement absolute obedience and criminalise public criticism. “Hibatullah’s influence reaches far beyond religious affairs: major political, judicial, and administrative decisions increasingly reflect the preferences of the Kandahar leadership,” Muhammad Israr Madani, an Islamabad-based analyst and co-author of a book on state-building in the Taliban-led Afghanistan , told Middle East Eye. This centralisation of power in Kandahar has “strengthened the Taliban’s ability to prevent internal fragmentation” while creating “resentment among commanders who believe that power is becoming excessively concentrated in one faction”, a mid-level Taliban leader who oversaw Khost told MEE in early 2024. Yet he emphasised that internal disagreement should not be mistaken for imminent collapse; top leaders recognise that unchecked conflict could cause the regime to crumble. Ultimately, the Taliban have learned a crucial state-building lesson: durable control requires more than military force - it depends on patronage, financial leverage, ideological alignment, and the institutional capacity to systematically reward loyalty. Economic void Afghanistan faces a multifaceted economic crisis defined by structural dependency and extreme isolation. Following the 2021 takeover, Afghanistan lost international grants that previously covered 75 percent of public expenditure. The financial void was exacerbated by the freezing of $7bn in central bank assets and the suspension of US humanitarian funding in early 2025, which previously accounted for about 45 percent of the country’s aid lifeline. While the Taliban have managed the economy better than many observers expected, expanding revenue collection through more effective customs duties and mining royalties, this has not translated into recovery for ordinary Afghans. Today, about 75 percent of Afghans cannot meet their basic needs. Economic expansion slowed from 2.3 percent in fiscal year 2023/2024 to 1.9 percent in 2024/2025, according to a May report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). Rapid population growth, fuelled by the expulsion of over five million Afghans from Iran and Pakistan since 2023, has outpaced these minimal gains. Consequently, real GDP per capita fell by an estimated 2.1 percent in 2025/2026, straining communities with scarce jobs and overstretched infrastructure, the UNDP added. Compounded by natural disasters, particularly earthquakes, diplomatic isolation, and severe international banking restrictions, Kabul remains cut off from World Bank and IMF support, locking the nation into an unsustainable cycle of forced self-reliance. Even the regime’s most touted achievement, an opium ban that reduced poppy cultivation by 95 percent, has functioned as economic self-immolation for the poor. While landowning farmers reaped capital gains from soaring prices on existing stockpiles, the ban decimated the livelihoods of land-poor rural households who relied on opium for their income. Women: the defining cost of Taliban rule The suppression of women and girls remains the most globally condemned aspect of Taliban rule, with international organisations such as Human Rights Watch framing the system as “gender apartheid” . A relentless succession of decrees from the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice has stripped women of fundamental freedoms, such as restrictions on movement, employment, and public life. Exclusive: ICC issued two secret arrest warrants for Taliban members for gender persecution Read More » Girls remain barred from secondary education, and women are prohibited from attending or teaching at universities. Enforcement has intensified sharply, with authorities detaining women for “improper hijab” or travelling without a male guardian. Reflecting this crisis, the International Criminal Court issued secret arrest warrants for Supreme Leader Akhundzada and Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani, citing gender-based persecution as a crime against humanity. Beyond its human toll, this policy represents severe economic self-sabotage. Barring women from the workforce deprives the nation of vital human capital while accelerating brain drain. The United Nations estimates that restricting female labour force participation costs Afghanistan up to $1bn annually, or nearly 6 percent of its GDP. The structural fallout, particularly acute shortages of female healthcare workers, teachers, and civil servants, has been “crippling basic health and education delivery for a generation,” said a Kabul-based humanitarian expert working for a UN body. By sacrificing half its population to enforce ideological purity, the regime is “dismantling the country’s prospects for sustainable economic recovery and long-term development”, he told MEE. The bitter divorce with Pakistan The relationship between the Taliban and their historical sponsor, Pakistan, has undergone a catastrophic collapse, shifting from strategic partnership to “open war” by early 2026. Initially, Islamabad celebrated the Taliban’s August 2021 return to power as a major geopolitical victory that would secure Pakistan’s western border and eliminate Indian influence. Then-Prime Minister Imran Khan declared that Afghans had broken “the shackles of slavery”, while current Defence Minister Khawaja Asif posted a photograph of a Taliban leader with former US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, captioned, “God is great.” However, that initial optimism quickly unravelled. The Taliban administration’s refusal to suppress the militant group, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), known colloquially as the "Pakistani Taliban", transformed the border between the countries into an active flashpoint. Why Pakistan and the Taliban are at war with each other Read More » Islamabad accused the Taliban administration of granting the TTP safe havens and access to abandoned US weaponry, driving a sharp escalation in cross-border attacks. A recent UN Security Council report reinforced these concerns, reiterating that the “terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan remained largely unchanged”, and warning that militant sanctuaries pose an enduring risk to neighbouring states and Central Asia. In response, Islamabad deployed aggressive coercive measures, deporting around 2.6 million Afghans since late 2023, repeatedly closing vital border crossings, and launching retaliatory air strikes inside Afghan territory. Publicly, Taliban officials reject allegations that they harbour TTP fighters, dismissing the violence as an internal Pakistani security crisis. Privately, however, managing the TTP has exposed deep ideological fractures within the regime. “Hardline elements within Taliban ranks view Pakistani militants as historical comrades-in-arms, making any forcible disarming politically unthinkable,” said a Taliban mid-level official now working with the interior ministry. He said that shielding the TTP is deepening Afghanistan’s international isolation, while taking aggressive action against it risks driving disaffected fighters directly into the ranks of Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). Minority marginalisation The fifth year of Taliban rule has accelerated the systematic exclusion of Afghanistan’s religious and ethnic minorities, particularly Shia and Hazara populations, who comprise 15 percent of the country. The Taliban 'are systematically working to remove our sect from the country’s legal and educational landscape' - Quetta-based Hazara Shia cleric Despite early promises of inclusivity, Shia jurisprudence has been erased from legal systems, universities, and schools, stripping away protections won under the former republic. Local Shia leaders highlighted a recent Taliban decree shuttering two vital cultural institutions, the Khatam al-Nabieen Educational Centre and Tamadon TV. Furthermore, Supreme Leader Akhundzada has excluded Shia scholars from new provincial ulema councils, even in Shia-majority provinces like Bamiyan and Daykundi. The Taliban "are systematically working to remove our sect from the country’s legal and educational landscape,” warned a Quetta-based Hazara Shia cleric connected to the Afghan Shia community, who chose to remain anonymous for safety concerns. Beyond the Shia population, the Taliban launched a sweeping crackdown on the Salafi minority under the guise of severing ISKP’s ideological pipeline, severely restricting access to mosques and seminaries. Analysts warn this heavy-handed repression risks alienating local communities and driving radicalised youth directly into ISKP’s ranks, exacerbating national instability. Outlook Five years after returning to power, the Taliban regime appears militarily entrenched yet structurally fragile. No organised opposition possesses the foreign backing, territory, or unified leadership needed to threaten Kabul. Armed groups like the National Resistance Front remain fragmented, incapable of challenging the regime’s centralised security apparatus. However, the regime’s greatest threat lies within its political architecture. Internal rifts continue to widen, prompting rare warnings from Akhundzada that discord could dismantle the government from within. While these political failures have not yet triggered a power crisis, an outright collapse would likely plunge Afghanistan into a civil war, devastating civilians and destabilising its neighbours. Demographics present an equally existential hurdle. With a stagnant economy and a population projected to double by 2050, long-term survival hinges on delivering livelihoods, food, and employment - a mandate current policies fail to meet. Internationally, pragmatic ties with Russia, China, and Central Asian neighbours provide economic lifelines without western recognition. Yet by governing through an extreme ideological police state, the leadership risks complete public alienation. The coming years will test whether the Taliban can transition from ruling through coercion to sustainable governance. Given their trajectory, this evolution remains improbable. Instead, persistent economic despair, social repression, and regional friction threaten to reignite systemic instability, preserving Afghanistan as an enduring catalyst for regional crises. headline: 'Mayfair means money': A walk through the Gulf elite's favourite part of London
author: Oscar Rickett
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 14:09 BST | Last update: 5 days 10 hours ago
article_body: It is 10am on Thursday, but the temperature on the streets of central London is already pushing beyond 30C, in what is set to be the UK ’s hottest summer on record. Outside Oxford Street’s Selfridges, the sun beats down on the pavement, a homeless man asks for change and a discarded free newspaper tells of yet more wildfires across the country. Inside, the air conditioning runs smoothly and a concession selling Arabic coffee promotes Saudi Arabia , whose Public Investment Fund now owns 40 percent of the famous department store. It was from Selfridges last weekend that Dubai’s ruler and the prime minister of the United Arab Emirates , Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, took a walk that saw him heckled on nearby North Audley Street over his country’s involvement in the Sudan war. A member of the ruler's sizeable entourage went up to the Sudanese man - who had shouted “UAE is killing people in my country, stop killing my people” from across the street - and called him a “Black bitch”. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Mohammed bin Rashid remains in London, where he has met with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and has been pictured in Chelsea, the now-affluent area once associated with London’s swinging 60s. It is Mayfair, though, that has become a real home away from home for wealthy Gulf citizens. The area, which includes North Audley Street, where Mohammed bin Rashid and his group were shouted at, is one of the richest in the world - full of upscale restaurants, luxury car dealerships and grand hotels. Visitors walk through Grosvenor Square in Mayfair, London, 13 August 2026 (Oscar Rickett/MEE) Inside Selfridges, 15-year-old Khaled and his uncle Mohammed, 53, are visiting from Dubai. “We come to London because we have a lot of investments here and we like to help them out,” the noticeably confident Khaled says. “Sudanese people are ignorant,” he tells Middle East Eye when asked about the incident with Dubai's ruler. “We are helping Sudan. We are sending humanitarian aid. It was disrespectful.” “Yes, you can have freedom of speech, but you can’t say that to a leader; it’s not respectful,” says Mohammed, whose father was a soldier and who remembers a “simpler, harder life” in Dubai before oil transformed the city. Today in the Emirates, he says, you can “get whatever you want within minutes. Someone will bring it to you. You don’t even have to get up”. The ruler of Dubai and prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Maktoum, has been confronted in central London over the UAE’s alleged involvement in Sudan’s ongoing war. A video posted on Sunday shows a Sudanese man confronting Mohammed bin Rashid and… pic.twitter.com/GPtQPXcaYj — Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) August 11, 2026 The family is staying in Mayfair for three weeks. It is a trip they make every August. They like the fact that London is awash with Emirati money, which helps the city feel familiar, as does the UAE’s historic connection to Britain and its empire, which they speak positively of. Khaled is planning to go to university in London. Mohammed bin Rashid, Mohammed bin Zayed and other Emirati leaders were educated or received military training in the UK. “I love it here. It’s not too hot,” says Khaled, on a day when even London at its hottest is still almost ten degrees cooler than Dubai, where life is air-conditioned. But although the family visit Oxford and Hampshire, London for this teenager from Dubai begins and ends in the affluent parts of the centre. 'We come to London because we have a lot of investments here and we like to help them out' - Khaled, visiting London from Dubai “We don’t go to the areas where there are roadmen and lots of migrants and stabbings,” he says, before getting out a map on his phone marked up with his favourite spots. The list, which does not stray far beyond Mayfair, is described by Khaled as a map of "prime khaleeji hangouts". It includes the restaurants Cipriani, Ivy Asia, Sexy Fish, Supernova and Nobu. Khaled’s fear of London outside its centre is echoed by one Saudi Arabian, who describes the reaction a teenager she knows has had to the British capital. Despite not being a member of the Saudi elite, this 15-year-old has come to London to attend a residential summer school for teenagers from the kingdom. Every day, he escapes the school to go to Harrods, the famous department store now owned by the state of Qatar . The boy has told the school he needs a bodyguard because “people here are so poor they will try and stab me for my Hermes”. “There’s a lot of things that remind us of back home and we see a lot of people from back home,” say two sisters from Bahrain , aged 15 and 17, in Selfridges. Both have bumped into school friends from Bahrain in Mayfair, as well as other girls they did not know would be in London. “When we go to Harrods we see people from the Gulf, we see friends and family… It’s not hot, it’s nothing compared to back home where we spend all the time with the AC on.” While Mayfair feels familiar to the sisters, other elements of London feel more alien. “We don’t really have or use public transport in Bahrain. The underground here is very crowded and chaotic. The architecture is different here too.” Influencers and jewellers Across the road from Selfridges, on North Audley Street, the first pint of the day arrives at the Marlborough pub, named after a 17th-century ancestor of Winston Churchill. The temperature rises. A toddler sitting on a tricycle screams as his father scrolls on his phone. Apart from the group drinking their pints, the street is almost entirely populated by visitors from the Gulf. Two Kuwaiti lifestyle and fashion influencers, Sarra and Elaf, are taking photos of each other. An elderly woman in pearls smiles as she steps around them. A Bugatti roars past. “We mainly spend our time here in Mayfair,” Sarra says. “We come for the weather, the people, the shopping. In our country we can’t find a lot of the brands you have here… For us, it’s good weather. We also come in November because we love the cold, and we love the Christmas vibes.” Sarra and Elaf, visiting Mayfair from Kuwait (Oscar Rickett/MEE) At Mayfair’s Grays Antique Market, which houses over 80 independent dealers, one jeweller tells MEE he never goes on holiday in August because that’s when wealthy visitors from the Gulf arrive. “They are an integral part of the business, especially in August; I can’t go away now.” Members of the royal families of Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the UAE have all been through the doors of the market. “A Thai princess came in last week,” the jeweller, who cannot be named, says. “She had 20 followers with her, which is less than her father the king, who has 100.” “Mayfair is the mecca of the Arab world in a way,” the jeweller says. “They love fine things. The men come here to buy silver jewellery, the women come here because they know they can get brands like Cartier, Tiffany and Bulgari at a steep discount. “Young girls from the Gulf will think nothing of spending £1,000 on a little charm. One lady from the Gulf didn’t blink when she bought something for £18,500. She knew she would have had to pay twice as much elsewhere.” Before the Ukraine war, London was known as Londongrad because of the number of Russians and the vast sums of Russian money in the city. “I used to deal with a lot of Russians, but they’ve all left like rats from a sinking ship,” the jeweller says. “The Russians still here don’t have any money.” 'Mayfair means money' Sitting in the heart of Mayfair, Grosvenor Square was home to the US diplomatic mission in Britain from 1785 until 2018. Now, the vast former embassy building is a luxury hotel containing a string of restaurants. These include the Qatari-owned Qinwan Cafe, another focal point for wealthy visitors from the Gulf. Three small chicken sandwiches cost £20. The same Palestinian dates available back home can be bought by tourists visiting London. Women in abayas and men in polo shirts scroll through their phones and post pictures of coffee on Instagram. Outside, sitting in his van, delivery driver Hash, from south London, waits for his next job. “Mayfair means money,” he says, looking out into the baking heat. There was a time six years ago, he says, when he could make £500 a day driving a delivery to Scotland and back. Now he says he is lucky to earn more than £100 a day. Beyond Grosvenor Square, a queue of tourists from the Gulf gently envelops Marchesi, the patisserie founded in 1824, while the Ferrari dealership shines in the sun on Berkeley Square. Inside Green Park Underground station, the temperature is approaching 40C. An announcement tells passengers that four lines are partially closed and that many more are experiencing severe delays. subheadline: In Mayfair, wealthy tourists from the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and elsewhere in the Gulf visit restaurants and department stores as London bakes in the heat

headline: Morale on US aircraft carrier enforcing Iran blockade plummets, as sailor jumps overboard: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 17:50 BST | Last update: 5 days 7 hours ago
article_body: The US is set to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier with the USS George Washington in the Middle East after reports of deteriorating conditions on the aircraft carrier enforcing a blockade of Iran . The Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days without a port call. At least one sailor jumped overboard the vessel, and another had to be restrained from doing so, according to media reports. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Lincoln will be rotated out of the theatre of operations and replaced with the USS George Washington. US lawmakers have raised concerns about the physical and mental health of sailors on board. The rotation comes after US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said that the blockade of Iran can be conducted “indefinitely”, as fighting continues to rage for control over the Strait of Hormuz with no return to a ceasefire in sight. "Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," Hegseth told reporters on Thursday. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Lincoln’s long deployment appears to have weighed on US Navy sailors. CNN reported on Thursday that a sailor wearing a life vest went overboard the ship earlier this month amid a mental health crisis on board as a result of the extended deployment. The sailor was rescued within an hour and transferred off the ship for treatment, CNN added. 'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance Read More » But the incident was not a one-off. US government-linked news sites, including Stars and Strips and The Navy Times, said that another crew member was prevented from jumping overboard amid exhaustion and declining morale on board the carrier. One woman told a town hall attended by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao that her husband aboard the ship “hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”, according to Stars and Strips. The US and Iran have been battling for control of the Strait of Hormuz for months. Iran has attacked vessels from Gulf states carrying oil and petroleum products outside the waterway, while the US has targeted vessels linked to Iran. The US fired two Hellfire missiles on a Panama-flagged ship that attempted to run the American blockade of Iranian ports early Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported. It’s not uncommon for an aircraft carrier to spend nine months at sea during wartime, but usually the vessel will make a port call every month in order to replenish supplies and give sailors an opportunity to rest. “We’ve just been turning and burning the whole time we’ve deployed,” one sailor told Stars and Strips. Nothing to really look forward to at this point. All we want is a date home.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. subheadline: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier will be replaced by the USS George Washington amid deteriorating conditions

headline: US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 18:22 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: The US has exhausted its stockpile of sophisticated long-range missiles during the war on Iran , suggesting that there are supply limits to President Donald Trump’s threat to subject the Islamic Republic to the "biggest attack" since World War II. The US has drained its supply of surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing two sources who said the US had used "virtually all" of these munitions. These long-range missiles are a critical part of the US’s arsenal, allowing it to accurately target foes from a distance without relying on warplanes that are vulnerable to air defence systems. Reuters reported that US Central Command - which oversees military operations in the Middle East - has had to replenish its stock of surface-to-surface missiles from other theatres of operation. The US and Israel first attacked Iran on 28 February. Fighting has flared throughout the summer despite a June ceasefire brokered through the Islamabad memorandum of understanding between the two sides. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The US pulled some air defence systems and troops from East Asia at the beginning of the war. Ukraine, which is battling a Russian invasion, has used US-supplied ATACMS to target Russia. Depleted defensive weapons The Trump administration boasted for months during the height of the war that Iran’s air defence systems have been obliterated, but Middle East Eye and other outlets reported that Iran has received new systems from China and Russia. An F-15E warplane was shot down over Iran in April, sparking a massive manhunt for the crew. If Iran had captured the pilot, it would have been a big bargaining chip in ceasefire talks. In addition to offensive munitions, the US was running low on missile and drone interceptors before the war. The shortage was a reflection of US efforts to defend Israel during a war in June 2025 that culminated in the US bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities. 'Suez moment': US missteps in Iran echo across East Asia to the Gulf and Europe Read More » Reuters reported that US military leaders have for weeks warned Trump that stockpiles of defensive weapons, including Patriot interceptors, were also dwindling. The report was seen as a vindication for critics of the war that the conflict is sapping the US’s military prestige and draining precious resources. “CENTCOM used everything they had before the war and have drawn down from rest of the world to critical levels,” Saagar Enjeti, a conservative commentator and host of Breaking Points, who has argued against foreign intervention, wrote on X. “Thank you FDD and UANI for the wonderful policies you have been advocating for. They have made America stronger!” Amir Handjani, a board member of the Quincy Institute think-tank in Washington, wrote on X, referring to the Foundation for Defence of Democracies and United Against Nuclear Iran, which critics say lobbied on behalf of the war. The report comes after Trump backtracked on a pledge to unleash massive new strikes against Iran. Trump said he planned to carry out “the biggest attack since World War II” on Iran last week. He backtracked on Monday, saying Gulf states asked him not to escalate the fight and claimed that a deal to return to the ceasefire is being negotiated. “I want to give them every last chance before decapitation,” Trump said Monday. Iran has denied it is in direct talks with the US. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Jack Letts appeals for repatriations from Iraq in 'out of the blue' phone call to parents
author: Simon Hooper
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 10:55 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: The parents of Jack Letts, a British-born Canadian man who travelled to Islamic State-controlled territory in Syria as a teenager in 2014, have described their shock, relief and frustration after being phoned “out of the blue” by their son from an Iraqi detention centre nine years after they were last able to speak to him. Sally Lane, Letts's mother, told Middle East Eye she hoped the unexpected phone call was a sign of mounting pressure by Baghdad to force the repatriation of foreign nationals held over alleged links to the Islamic State group (IS) for almost a decade in Syria until their transfer into Iraqi custody earlier this year. "It came completely out of the blue. It was just a random phone call and normally I wouldn’t answer. But I happened to recognise the Iraqi code so I answered it and Jack said 'Hello Mum'," said Lane. "It was very short and he said there were a million things he wanted to say to me. The good thing is he sounded perfectly sane and normal." Lane said she believed the phone call, which lasted just three minutes and took place last month, had been facilitated by Iraqi officials amid growing impatience about the continuing refusal of western nations including Canada and the UK to take responsibility for their own nationals. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "He said he needed to convey a message that an Iraqi lawyer had visited the Canadians a couple of days before," she said. "And he said to them that they needed to get a message out to the Canadian government that it needs to repatriate them before trial because the Iraqis don’t want them there." John Letts, Jack Letts's father, said his son had delivered the same message to him in a similar phone call. “He said: ‘The Iraqis don't want us here and the Iraqis are desperate to send us back',” said John Letts. Jack Letts, 30, was born and grew up in the UK and travelled to IS-controlled Iraq and Syria in 2014 aged 18. In 2017 he was stripped of his British citizenship, like many other British nationals who went to Syria during the country’s civil war. He was detained by Kurdish forces in northeastern Syria the same year amid the collapse of IS-held territory and has been held without charge among suspected IS fighters ever since. His parents were last able to communicate with him via voice messages shortly after he was captured, but for much of the past nine years they have only received scant and occasional updates about his whereabouts and well-being. In an interview in 2024, after he was located by a Canadian television crew in a Syrian prison, Letts denied he had ever been a member of IS but said there were things he could not say while he was still in prison. In January, Letts was among more than 5,000 prisoners previously held in northeastern Syria who were moved to Iraq in a US-led operation as part of the transfer of powers from regional Kurdish authorities to Syria’s central government. More than 3,500 of the detainees being held in Iraq are Syrian, according to Iraqi Ministry of Justice figures seen by MEE. They also include at least five Canadians, 10 Britons, 27 Germans and 13 Australians, with larger numbers from Arab countries, including Morocco (187), Egypt (116) and Saudi Arabia (68). Other countries with significant numbers of detainees include Russia (130) and Turkmenistan (165). 'They almost killed my child': Women in Syria's Roj camp describe night of gunfire and fear Read More » MEE understands that Letts is currently being held in a detention centre for foreign nationals controlled by Iraq’s Directorate for General Intelligence and Counter-Terrorism near Al-Karkh Central Prison, near Baghdad. While Canada has repatriated a number of women and children who had been held in Syria’s al-Hol and al-Roj camps, it has refused to do the same for male prisoners on national security grounds. Lane said Canadian embassy officials had visited Letts and other prisoners since their transfer to Iraq earlier this year and had passed on letters and photos. But she said Canada was continuing to reject calls from families to repatriate its remaining nationals and had advised them to hire local lawyers to represent their relatives. "The Canadian government has said that they can't interfere in the judicial affairs of another country," she said. "They've just said you need to get a lawyer, either somebody appointed by the Iraqi court, or an international lawyer who is approved by the Iraqi Bar Association." 'Legal nonsense' Legal experts and human rights organisations have raised concerns about the prospect of detainees being put on trial in Iraq for alleged offences committed in Syria after years being held in conditions widely criticised as amounting to unlawful detention. In February, Human Rights Watch warned that detainees transferred to Iraq were at risk of "enforced disappearance, unfair trials, torture, ill-treatment, and violations of the right to life" because of the country's "well-documented due process violations in counterterrorism proceedings". Clive Stafford Smith, a prominent human rights lawyer, told MEE it was "legal nonsense" to suggest that detainees held in Iraq should now be put on trial there for alleged offences that had not been committed in the country. He said that those accused of offences should face trial in their own countries, but noted that many had already spent the best part of a decade imprisoned "in pretty barbarous conditions". John Letts accused the Canadian government of "hiding behind words" since the detainees had been transferred to Iraq. In Syria, Canada had routinely refused to provide them or their families with consular assistance on the grounds that it did not have diplomatic representation in the country during the civil war. "In practical terms, nothing has actually changed. The Canadian position is still no repatriations," said John Letts. He said he had continuing concerns about how his son was being treated in detention since his transfer to Iraq. Despite having just three minutes, Jack Letts had given his father the names of two fellow detainees who he said needed help with finding lawyers. "We hardly had any time. I got the names of the two detainees and then the line went dead," said John Letts. "He sounded together, but the bittersweetness is that you know he’s had a terrible time and that terrible time is still continuing." Both of Letts's parents said they intended to travel to Iraq soon in the hope of visiting their son. MEE has contacted the Iraqi foreign ministry for comment. A spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada said: "The Government of Canada continues to assess developments related to Canadian citizens detained in Iraq. Canada cannot comment on specific consular cases." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Board of Peace caves to Netanyahu and rewrites Israeli withdrawal terms from Gaza
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 13:45 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: The US -backed Board of Peace has hardened the conditions for an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza after its senior officials met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The board linked any Israeli withdrawal beyond the Yellow Line, which divides Gaza into areas occupied by Israeli and Palestinian control, to the complete disarmament of Hamas, abandoning the phased approach it presented last week. “Contrary to inaccurate reports, we note that the withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators. This applies to light weapons, heavy weapons and the tunnels alike,” it said after Monday’s meeting. The Yellow Line was established following the so-called ceasefire of October 2025. Israel has since seized additional Palestinian territory and now controls more than 60 percent of the enclave, with Netanyahu even saying that the aim is to increase to around 70 percent. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Last week, a board official said Israel would initially withdraw to the Yellow Line under the disarmament plan. The proposal also tied phased Israeli withdrawals to the gradual decommissioning of Palestinian weapons. The board initially referred on Monday to the “full withdrawal of the IDF”, leaving open the possibility of earlier partial withdrawals. It removed the word “full” minutes later, bringing its position closer to Netanyahu’s demand that Israel retain its forces until Hamas has completely disarmed. Revision contradictions The revision also contradicted the board’s high representative, Nickolay Mladenov, who said last week: “Withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning.” Hamas says it will 'disarm when Israel keeps its word' Read More » Hamas accepted the original sequence, and the board’s retreat risks undermining that agreement while rewarding Israel’s refusal to halt its attacks or withdraw. Netanyahu told Mladenov that Israel would neither stop attacking Gaza nor pull back from the Yellow Line, Israel Hayom reported. According to reports Israel has also sought assurance that even after Hamas is disarmed it has the right to attack Gaza. Israel also objected to Turkish and Qatari participation in a committee monitoring disarmament and demanded the destruction, rather than storage, of Hamas weapons. Mladenov played down expectations after the talks. “This is the start of the hard phase and I have never pretended otherwise,” he wrote on X. “Not much of what we do now is dramatic. It is slow, grinding and technical work.” Hours after the meeting, an Israeli air strike killed two Palestinians in Gaza City’s Sheikh Ajlin neighbourhood. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Trump insists Iran talks under way, warns Tehran’s ‘last chance’ to secure deal
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 12:34 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump claims that direct negotiations with Iran are under way, and has warned that the latest round is Tehran’s “last chance” to secure a deal to end the war. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, denied that any direct negotiations with Washington were ongoing, nor any plans for meetings, as the talks over the management of the Strait of Hormuz remain mediated by Oman. According to sources who spoke to Anadolu, Pakistani and Qatari negotiators are working to secure a meeting date and venue. On Monday, Pakistan issued an urgent invitation to Iranian negotiators to Islamabad, in what appears to be a bid to renew stalled Iran-US talks. During a phone call, Pakistan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Mohammed Ishaq Dar invited Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to Islamabad “at his earliest convenience". New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Mohsen Rezaei, the top military adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, warned that American military vessels and forces will “face serious risks and casualties” if Washington’s naval blockade on Iranian ports continues. "The U.S. must change its behavior — or we will not tolerate this. We will never permit the opening of a second corridor in the Strait of Hormuz,” Rezaei said in a post on X . Iranian and US officials told the New York Times that Iran and Oman are close to finalising a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping traffic, handing Tehran near total control over the contested waterway. Reuters reported on Tuesday that a Liberian-flagged ship was struck by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait close to Oman’s coast. War on Iran: Rescuers search for survivors on Qeshm Island after US kills toddler and parents Read More » According to maritime sources, at least one seafarer remains missing after the crew abandoned the vessel. Meanwhile, Rezaei confirmed that a plan to conduct retaliatory strikes on three sites in Ukraine, following a Ukrainian attack on an Iranian ship, was scrapped after Kyiv issued an “apology”. In an interview with Iranian state television, Rezaei said that Tehran's armed forces had completed preparations for the strikes before the operation was aborted. The five month US-Iran conflict has sent oil giants’ profits soaring amid surging oil and gas prices, with BP reporting that its quarterly profits had more than doubled. Shell confirmed that it had doubled its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June, while Saudi-owned Aramco saw a 44 percent rise in net profits over the same period. Seventh round of peace talks Meanwhile, the seventh round of talks between Israel and Lebanon are under way in Rome. The three-day round of US-brokered negotiations will focus on continued Israeli violations of a conditional ceasefire struck in April, including land-clearing operations, explosions and the demolition of homes. A Lebanese official told Anadolu that their delegation will propose designating new pilot areas for Israeli withdrawal, with the second phase covering either Bint Jbeil or Khiam, both south of the Litani River in southern Lebanon. Turkey urges Iran to halt attacks on Kurdish groups Read More » Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said on Monday that the talks will bring "nothing but shame, humiliation, and successive compromises" for Lebanon. In a televised address, Qassem said Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun "has not acted as an arbiter, nor as a unifying figure, but has become biased and divisive, which is incompatible with his role and with Lebanon's strength". The renewed talks come amid ongoing Israeli attacks and demolitions targeting homes in several southern Lebanese towns. The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNFIL) said on Monday that it had continued to observe “daily Israeli violations of Lebanon’s airspace, roadblocks and activities in its territorial waters”. Peacekeepers reported 125 air violations, with the combined total overflight time exceeding 418 hours between Thursday and Sunday. “Peacekeepers also report extensive military activity on the ground in south Lebanon, including significant engineering works and active troop movements,” a UN deputy spokesperson said. Israel has killed over 4,300 people and wounded another 12,200 since it renewed its assault on Lebanon on 2 March. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: ‘De facto annexation’: Israel to shift civilian enforcement in West Bank from army to police
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 15:21 BST | Last update: 10 hours 17 mins ago
article_body: Israel is preparing to replace the army in the West Bank with civilian police forces, in a move seen as further advancing the annexation of the occupied Palestinian territory. Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Friday that he had instructed the military to draft a plan to transfer enforcement powers for civilian matters in the occupied West Bank from the army to the police. Under the plan, the police would “establish an appropriate force to handle and address civilian matters”, while the military would focus solely on “Palestinian terrorism” and protecting borders and communities, according to Katz’s office. Katz said it was appropriate for the police to oversee civilian affairs in the West Bank, arguing that the force performs that role “in every other place in the State of Israel”. The announcement was not coordinated with either the military or the police. However, Israel Hayom reported on Friday that the army welcomed the move and had been pushing for it for weeks. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The report also said National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, who oversees the police, had not been informed that the statement was being issued. Ben Gvir has yet to comment on the plan, but other settler leaders welcomed the announcement. Israel Ganz, head of the Regional Binyamin Council in the West Bank, said Katz’s statement should be followed by the cancellation of the Oslo Accords and the imposition of “full Israeli sovereignty” over the occupied territory. “The time has come to move from temporary management to the full application of Israeli law,” Ganz said. Request by the army According to Israeli news site Ynet, Friday’s announcement follows a request by army chief Eyal Zamir to reduce the military’s workload in the West Bank. Two weeks ago, Zamir told the Israeli cabinet that the army’s responsibilities in the Palestinian territory were continuing to expand, as “new settlements will soon be established”. “It’s untenable for IDF [Israeli army] soldiers to be chasing after a handful of people who are giving settlements a bad name,” Zamir reportedly told ministers, referring to settlers accused of terrorising Palestinian communities. Zamir said the army was “working in cooperation with the police”, but that it was appropriate for the Israeli army to stop handling such tasks. Israel pursuing ‘undeclared annexation’ of West Bank, Peace Now says Read More » A military spokesperson told Ynet on Friday that the army was conducting “internal and preliminary staff-level work” on the issue to examine “the division of authorities between the security bodies” in the West Bank. Katz’s statement referred to the entire West Bank, without distinguishing between Areas A and B, where the Palestinian Authority handles civilian affairs, and Area C, where Israel exercises civilian authority under the Oslo Accords. Israel has never formally annexed the West Bank, which has been under Israeli military occupation since 1967. However, the Israeli government has taken a series of steps over the past year that experts say amount to de facto annexation. These include expanding the role of civilian bodies in administering the West Bank while reducing the military’s role in areas traditionally under its control. Under Israeli and international law, the military is the occupying authority in the West Bank and holds enforcement powers there, including over civilian affairs. Rise in settler violence Katz’s statement comes amid a sharp rise in settler violence across the West Bank. Earlier this week, Israeli settlers besieged Palestinian homes in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus. Despite the army saying it was working to remove them, the settlers remained at the site on Friday. Last week, veteran Ynet military correspondent Ron Ben-Yishai said the Israeli army, police and Shin Bet were “unable to enforce the law”. A small group of extremist settlers had effectively become “the sovereign in the West Bank”, he said, adding that the army merely “secures it and its whims”. On Friday, Ben-Yishai said Katz’s announcement amounted to “de facto annexation”. He also questioned its legal basis and said the police lacked enough officers to assume civilian authority in the West Bank. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Deadly Israeli strikes kill nine in southern Lebanon as tensions escalate
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 15 August 2026 14:40 BST | Last update: 4 days 11 hours ago
article_body: At least nine people were killed and more than a dozen wounded after Israeli air strikes hit several towns and villages in southern Lebanon early Saturday, state media reported. Lebanon's National News Agency reported that an Israeli strike hit a house on the outskirts of Ansar in the Nabatieh district, killing seven people and wounding others. Another strike in Deir al-Zahrani killed at least two people and wounded several others, as the Israeli military intensified attacks across the Nabatieh region before dawn, according to local media reports . Lebanese media also reported artillery fire and other strikes in areas including Ali al-Taher Heights near Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Kfar Tebnit, Zawtar al-Sharqiya and other parts of southern Lebanon. The intensity of the overnight bombardment forced many residents to leave their homes, Lebanese media reports said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Al Jazeera reported that children and members of one family were among those killed in the Ansar strike, which "deepened fears among residents" as Israeli strikes and demolitions continued across southern Lebanon. “The attacks are escalating day by day,” the report said, adding that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce a significant change on the ground. The Israeli military said it struck "Hezbollah infrastructure" in the Nabatieh and Ansar areas, adding that the attacks came in response to "action against Israeli soldiers". Strikes test fragile agreement Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam rejected Israel's account and described the escalation in Nabatieh, Ansar, Deir al-Zahrani and surrounding villages as “extremely dangerous”, adding that it was undermining efforts to stabilise the region. “The seven people killed in the Israeli strike on Ansar are not ‘military infrastructure’, and the children and women killed in it are not military targets,” Salam said in a statement. He said responsibility for dealing with any military infrastructure on Lebanese territory, “if it exists”, rests exclusively with the Lebanese state through the army and other state institutions. “Its presence does not give Israel the right to violate Lebanese territory or put civilians at risk,” Salam said. Hezbollah said that Israeli attacks would be met with an "appropriate" response, urging authorities to halt "humiliating" negotiations with Israel. US-Iran peace deal: Six things we learned from the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding Read More » Israel "must clearly understand that its attacks, violations and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue, and will be met with an appropriate response", the group said in a statement, adding that Lebanese authorities "must not insist on continuing along the humiliating path of direct negotiations and providing the enemy with free concessions". Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has also condemned the attacks, saying the escalation in Nabatieh and surrounding areas amounted to repeated violations of the framework governing efforts to reduce hostilities and protect civilians. Aoun said the attack on Ansar had killed members of an entire family and described the escalation as “a clear message” to the negotiating process and US-led efforts to implement the agreement. The violence comes despite a reduction in hostilities following a US - Iran memorandum of understanding in June and a subsequent US-sponsored framework between Lebanon and Israel. The arrangement calls for Hezbollah's disarmament, the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the deployment of the Lebanese army in southern Lebanon. However, disagreements over its implementation have continued. On Thursday, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that Israel would not withdraw from territory it controls in Lebanon until Hezbollah was disarmed and what he described as the threat posed by the group was removed. On Friday, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem criticised Lebanese authorities over the implementation of the agreement, accusing them of placing pressure on the Lebanese army while Israeli attacks continued. “How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” Qassem said. The strike on Ansar was among the deadliest reported Israeli attacks in Lebanon since agreements reached in June led to a significant reduction in hostilities. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Israel: Court blocks prison crocodile plan for Palestinians out of concern for the reptiles
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 13:56 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: An Israeli court has blocked a plan by far right minister Itamar Ben Gvir to place crocodiles in moats encircling prisons where Palestinian prisoners are being held, Israeli media is reporting. Israeli authorities have reportedly already begun digging trenches around a section of Ketziot Prison in the Negev desert, in northern Israel. Under the plan spearheaded by Ben Gvir, and backed by his National Security Ministry and the Israel Prison Service (IPS), Nile crocodiles will be installed in the trenches. But Israeli broadcaster KAN reported that the Jerusalem District Court had issued a temporary injunction on Sunday, hours after an animal rights organisation filed a petition against Environmental Protection Minister Idit Silman, Ben Gvir and the IPS. The legal challenge – which was filed by Let the Animals Live – centres on concerns around the mistreatment of animals and the danger posed to prison staff, rather than over the escalating abuse of Palestinian prisoners. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In July 2025, Silman reclassified the Nile crocodile from a protected species to a “tended animal”, clearing the way for their introduction to prisons. The petition disputed the move, demanding that the animals be newly redesignated as a protected species, and arguing that Silman had ignored the opinions of legal advisers and the Nature and Parks Authority. Judge Abvraham Rubin said in his Sunday ruling that: “The claims regarding the expected harm to the crocodiles merit investigation and justify issuing an order prohibiting the transfer, or any action related to locating or preparing crocodiles for transfer.” Pro-Israel influencer and actor share a 'raped by Israeli dogs' joke Read More » He ordered that the temporary injunction will remain in place until a further ruling on the matter, giving Silman, Ben Gvir and the IPS until Wednesday to respond to the petition. Israel’s environmental bodies have long opposed Ben Gvir’s scheme, with the Environmental Protection Ministry and the Nature and Parks Authority arguing that Silman’s reclassification of the crocodiles has no scientific basis, and warning that the transfer of the animals could endanger prison staff. The plan is the latest in a series of measures proposed by Ben Gvir to make detention conditions for Palestinian prisoners even more unbearable, including visitation bans, food deprivation, medical neglect, torture and solitary confinement. On Sunday, footage circulated online of the far-right minister mocking a female Palestinian prisoner complaining of her poor detention conditions. According to Palestinian prisoner advocacy groups , over 9,600 Palestinians are held in Israeli custody, including 84 women and 350 children, where they are subject to mistreatment – including medical neglect, beatings and rape – tantamount to systematic torture. headline: Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 00:05 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Israeli political leaders have mocked and exploited the migration crisis engulfing Morocco , an Israeli ally, and Spain , whose relations with Israel have sharply deteriorated. Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, wrote on X last week with barely concealed glee: "Spain, which never misses an opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy." Spain did not declare a state of emergency in Ceuta . Danon's real grievance appears to be Madrid's forceful and consistent condemnation of Israel's genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, along with its refusal to back the US and Israel in their war against Iran. "The involvement of official Israeli channels and associated social media accounts in amplifying anti-Spanish rhetoric in the wake of the Ceuta crisis seeks to undermine Spanish strategic positions in the Middle East and North Africa region," Denis Cenusa, a geopolitical analyst and fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis, told Middle East Eye. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "This constitutes clear retaliation for Spain's firm stance on the Palestinian cause and the joint US-Israeli attacks against Iran," he added. More than 60,000 Moroccan migrants attempted to cross from Morocco into Ceuta , a Spanish enclave in North Africa. At least 70 drowned or were crushed in the attempt, a number expected to rise. 'Why did they open the doors' Among the dead was Moroccan footballer Faten Ben Omar El Azizi , who played for Moghreb Atletico Tetuan. "The youth are lost… Who opened the door the first time? Why did they open it so that our children could be killed?" her mother said in a video published by Al Ayoum 24, shortly before Faten was buried in a Tetouan cemetery. Beyond the grief inflicted on her family, El Azizi's death exposed an uncomfortable truth about the country she represented. Morocco has emerged as something of a footballing powerhouse in recent years: its men's national team ranks sixth in the world, and the state has poured millions of dollars into developing the women's game. El Azizi belonged to the generation that investment was supposed to benefit. Thousands make dramatic sea crossing into Ceuta from Morocco Read More » That investment into the country's human capital looks harder to square with what happened next. "There is certainly an image in this incident that contradicts official narratives and the fact that the incident took place right after the Throne Day speech adds to the overall reality about the gap," said Zine Ghebouli, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. According to several reports, the Moroccan state, headed by King Mohammed VI, opened the border gates into Ceuta, known in Morocco as Sabtah, last Thursday. The message to many Moroccans was unmistakable that the route out of the country and into Spanish territory was open. Madrid has so far avoided publicly blaming Rabat, but a source close to Spain's foreign ministry told MEE that officials privately believe the Moroccan state deliberately orchestrated the crisis. "Migration had already been a contentious topic for the past two decades but now, the need to secure borders and the narrative propagated about the "invasion of migrants" will push into more radical anti-migration speeches," said Ghebouli. "This will challenge European unity and governments like Spain where the approach has been rather focused on integrating all migrants," he added. Meanwhile Spanish authorities had received intelligence about a possible surge in crossings into Ceuta and Melilla ahead of Morocco's Throne Day but failed to act, the Spanish outlet The Objective reported on Saturday. Military and civilian intelligence sources told the outlet that officials repeatedly disregarded warnings, including alerts issued only days before the mass movement began. Observers had already recorded an unusual influx of buses into Fnideq, the Moroccan town closest to Ceuta, before thousands of people converged on the border and crossed into the enclave. 'Spain will pay a price' What Morocco has actually gained from all this remains unclear, beyond politically wounding Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, whose relationship with Washington has also deteriorated. Sanchez may well have believed he'd secured lasting peace with Rabat after a diplomatic rupture that ran from December 2020 to March 2022. Fifty years of plunder: How Morocco and its allies profit from Western Sahara Read More » In March 2022 he wrote to Mohammed VI endorsing Morocco's autonomy proposal for Western Sahara, a major shift in Spain's position on the decades-old dispute. A year later he helped bring Morocco into the joint Spanish-Portuguese bid to host the 2030 World Cup, and let the king unveil Morocco's inclusion through his own minister, Chakib Benmoussa. The alliance appears to have been jeopardised by Morocco for reasons no one has yet explained. Before many of the bodies had even been recovered from the sea, Israel's national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, offered his "congratulations" to Sanchez "for his profound commitment to welcoming immigration and 'human diversity'." He added: "As someone who demonstrates great concern for Hamas and the residents of Gaza, I call on you to translate words into actions: open the doors of Spain and grant refuge to the residents of Gaza who seek to emigrate." The intervention wasn't aimed at Spain alone. By turning dead Moroccans into ammunition against Madrid, Israeli officials also humiliated a government that normalised ties with Israel on 22 December 2020 and has treated that relationship as a source of diplomatic leverage ever since. Israel and the US have both started questioning Spain's hold over Ceuta and Melilla altogether. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, accused Sanchez's government of waging a "diplomatic war" and warned it would not be allowed to continue "without paying an immediate price." Spanish commentators accuse Israel and US of involvement in Ceuta crisis Read More » "Israel will not remain silent in the face of those who attack us," he said. Many analysts now suspect this was that price. "The Israeli ambassador to the UN and unofficial accounts on X have been amplifying anti-colonial rhetoric directed against Spain. Their emergence coincided with the height of the crisis, which could indicate a degree of coordination," geopolitical analyst Cenusa said. In Washington, a House Appropriations Committee report published on 30 April described Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish-controlled cities "located in Moroccan territory" and urged the secretary of state to push negotiations over their status. The wording appeared only in a report attached to the bill, not the bill itself, but it read as a signal to Spain, a Nato member. The House passed the legislation on 15 July; the Senate has not, and the president has not signed it. No hard evidence has emerged that Israel, the US and Morocco coordinated the crisis. However, with Israeli leaders openly gloating on social media, at least one member of Sanchez’s government has entertained the possibility. Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente shared a post stating: "Some in Washington, Tel Aviv, and Rabat... wanted images of our security forces and armed forces machine-gunning children on the beach." headline: Centcom chief visits US carrier enforcing Iran blockade amid reports of severe strain on crew
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 16 August 2026 16:17 BST | Last update: 3 days 9 hours ago
article_body: The head of the United States Central Command (Centcom), Admiral Bradley Cooper, has visited the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier in the Arabian Sea, which is enforcing the US blockade of Iran. His visit came amid reports of severe strain on the carrier's crew, including mental health concerns and supply shortages after an unusually long deployment. "History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era," Cooper said on Saturday. The Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days without a port call. CNN reported on Thursday that a sailor wearing a life vest went overboard the ship earlier this month. The sailor was rescued within an hour and transferred off the carrier for treatment. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The incident was not an isolated one. US military news outlets, including Stars and Stripes and Navy Times, have reported another case in which a crew member was prevented from jumping overboard amid growing exhaustion and declining morale. One woman told a town hall attended by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao that her husband aboard the ship “hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”, according to Stars and Stripes. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the Lincoln would be rotated out of the region and replaced by the USS George Washington. US lawmakers have also raised concerns about the physical and mental health of sailors aboard the carrier. The rotation comes after US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said the blockade of Iran could be maintained “indefinitely”, as fighting over control of the Strait of Hormuz continues with no return to a ceasefire in sight. Cooper also visited Israel, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates to meet political and military figures, Centcom said. The US and Iran have been battling for control of the Strait of Hormuz for months. Iran has attacked vessels from Gulf states carrying oil and petroleum products outside the waterway, while the US has targeted vessels linked to Iran. It is not uncommon for an aircraft carrier to spend nine months at sea during wartime, but such deployments typically include regular port calls to replenish supplies and allow sailors to rest. On Sunday, the general staff of Iran's armed forces pledged the "complete defeat" of the US and Israel in the region, saying the legacy of "resistance" has been passed to a new generation of Iranians. headline: Former Israeli soldier held captive in Gaza asks Ben Gvir to let him execute Palestinian prisoners
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 10:36 BST | Last update: 1 day 13 hours ago
article_body: A former Israeli soldier who was held captive in Gaza asked National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir to allow him to personally execute Palestinian prisoners during an interview published on Saturday, with the far-right minister responding that he would try to make it happen. Rom Braslavski, who was released from captivity in Gaza in October 2025, made the request while interviewing Ben Gvir in the first episode of his new podcast, October 8, according to footage from the programme and Israeli media reports. “I have a personal request,” Braslavski told Ben Gvir, asking the minister to let him be “the one who hangs them”, referring to Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli prisons. “I don't want a rope,” Braslavski said. “With my own hands I will execute every terrorist in the State of Israel.” "I promise you I'll try and turn the world upside down to make this happen," Ben Gvir replied positively to Braslavski's request, adding that it was one of his dreams to see the released captives executing Palestinians. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Braslavski was on leave from the Israeli military and working as a security guard at the Nova music festival when Hamas and allied Palestinian armed groups attacked southern Israel on 7 October 2023. Some 1,200 people were killed, many of them civilians, while 251 people were taken captive. Ben Gvir added that Braslavski was "the right person in the right place [...] to hang and execute them one by one." "They don't deserve to live," Ben Gvir told Braslavski, referring to Palestinian prisoners. The exchange came as Ben Gvir, whose ministry oversees Israel’s Prison Service, has pushed for harsher conditions for Palestinian detainees, with inmates reporting torture and sexual assaults. Earlier this month, an Israeli court blocked a plan by Ben Gvir to place crocodiles in moats encircling prisons where Palestinian prisoners are being held. In May, the Israeli parliament approved a bill sponsored by Ben Gvir's party to establish public trials and impose the death penalty on Palestinian detainees accused of taking part in the 7 October attacks. As of June, at least 104 Palestinian inmates have died in Israeli custody since 2023, with rights groups estimating that more than 9,000 Palestinians are held in Israel's detention facilities. 'They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people' Ben Gvir said during the interview that Palestinian prisoners were suffering and that he was pleased by their conditions. “They are suffering, it's hard for them, it's bad for them, and I'm glad it's bad for them,” he said. Pregnant and imprisoned: Palestinian women face harsh conditions in Israeli jails Read More » The interview also turned to Gaza, where Ben Gvir called for an intensification of Israeli attacks, saying Israel should kill dozens of Palestinians every night and eventually expel them. "I think we should carry out targeted assassinations in Gaza, taking down 30 to 40 every night," Ben Gvir said, adding "not just those who pose an immediate threat." "There are people there who are not worthy of life. They shouldn’t live. They’re not even people," Ben Gvir continued. Amid reports of US pressure on Israel to limit assassinations and attacks on the devastated Palestinian enclave, Ben Gvir said he firmly disagreed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the issue of limiting Israeli attacks. Apart from calling to kill Palestinians, Ben Gvir reiterated his long-standing demand to expel the Palestinian population from the Gaza Strip. "I see all of Gaza as ours," he said, adding that he wanted to see the establishment of "settlements not just in Gush Katif but throughout Gaza." 'Kill them one by one' The comments come amid continued scrutiny of Ben Gvir’s influence within Netanyahu’s government and his policies towards Palestinians in Israeli prisons, Gaza and the occupied West Bank. The Otzma Yehudit leader, whose party is currently polling around 8 to 10 Knesset seats, added that Israel should encourage "as much emigration as possible, sending them to their countries." Itamar Ben Gvir: How the man keeping Netanyahu in office rose to power Read More » "For the terrorists," Ben Gvir made himself clear, "no emigration, nothing, just to kill them one by one." In May, Middle East Eye reported that the International Criminal Court examined the issuance of an arrest warrant for Ben Gvir for committing crimes against the Palestinian people. Ben Gvir, along with Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, has also been the target of an international sanctions campaign over his policies and statements advocating the extermination and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Once a fringe politician, Ben Gvir has become one of the most influential figures in Israeli politics in recent years, with the far-right minister exerting growing influence over Netanyahu. His extreme opinions have also become more popular in recent years. A poll published last week by the Jewish People Policy Institute, an Israeli think tank, found that 22 percent of Israel's Jewish citizens are in favour of expelling the Palestinian population from the occupied West Bank, with 38 percent of them supporting the annexation of the territory. The poll also found that most Israelis, much like Ben Gvir, are sceptical about the implementation of US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan in Gaza. Gaza's Ministry of Health reported last week that 1,258 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the fragile ceasefire was signed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025. As per the ministry, 4,295 others were wounded, including hundreds of women and children. Palestinian officials in Gaza have documented thousands of Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement since it was signed. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: US considering nuclear weapons against Iran as war falters, claims Marjorie Taylor Greene
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 12:04 BST | Last update: 2 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Former US Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene has claimed that President Donald Trump's administration is discussing using nuclear weapons against Iran , as Washington struggles to sustain its months-long war. “They are discussing using nuclear weapons on Iran in strategy meetings,” Greene wrote on social media late on Sunday. “I'm not speculating, I know. And it's pure evil," she added. Greene, once one of President Donald Trump’s closest congressional allies, urged Americans to resist any attempt to escalate the war. “People need to speak out and boldly stop this insanity.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Greene's relationship with Trump collapsed after she pressed for the release of files connected to Jeffrey Epstein, the late convicted pedophile and financier whose social circle included Trump and other powerful figures. Greene accused Washington of launching the war on the back of warnings repeatedly promoted by Israel about Iran’s nuclear programme. “Trump and his admin were told by our own intelligence that Iran was nowhere near creating a nuclear weapon, then Israel said the same line it’s repeated for decades, ‘Iran is only weeks away,’” said Greene. “And now our government is the one actually discussing lowering the nuclear threshold in order to use nuclear weapons against Iran even though Trump claims he’s won the war like 40 times and says the U.S. controls the SoH,” she added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and Oman work on temporary Hormuz shipping route as Trump threatens to claim the strait Read More » The US and Israel launched their war on Iran on 28 February. Months of attacks have killed thousands of Iranian civilians, disrupted global energy supplies and failed to break Tehran’s grip over the vital waterway. Greene warned that further escalation could unleash a global “nuclear holocaust”, economic depression and casualties on a scale unseen in generations. “America is not untouchable," Greene warned. Her intervention comes as the US military struggles with depleted weapons stocks. Reuters news agency reported that American forces had used “ virtually all ” of their long-range precision missiles during the war, while heavy expenditure of Patriot and THAAD interceptors has weakened US readiness elsewhere. NBC News reported this month that the Pentagon was drafting a strategy that would give shorter-range tactical nuclear weapons a greater role in regional conflicts. “Our view is that we need credible nuclear options,” a senior US defence official told NBC. The US remains the only country to have used nuclear weapons in war, destroying Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved.
