headline: Israel’s starvation of Gaza leaves children stunted
author: Nada Nabil
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 07:32 BST | Last update: 10 hours 49 min ago
article_body: In a small room in Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood, six-year-old Amira Rashid lies on a mattress, too weak to move. Her hands are bruised and blue from the intravenous drips she has been receiving. Under normal circumstances, the Palestinian girl would be preparing to start her first year of school later this month. Instead, months of starvation by Israel during the genocide in Gaza have left her severely malnourished and stunted, with lasting effects on her physical and cognitive development. “I was hoping to enrol Amira in school, buy her a uniform, a backpack and stationery like the other children,” her mother, Aya Rashid, told Middle East Eye. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “But her health prevents her from leaving the house or interacting with her peers.” Amira was among tens of thousands of children who suffered malnutrition during Israel’s siege on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Her family was also among hundreds of thousands who remained in northern Gaza throughout the war. In August 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) declared famine in Gaza City, where the Rashid family lived. “We suffered immensely from hunger and severe food shortages,” Aya said. “We ran out of flour, and there was none in the markets. With no food aid available, I could only manage to bake barley bread.” Stunted growth But Amira’s condition had begun deteriorating months earlier. In January 2025, after Amira complained of chest pain, Aya took her to Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital. Doctors were shocked by her height and weight, which were far below what would be expected for her age. “When a doctor saw her, he was taken aback,” Aya recalled. “He said she needed comprehensive testing immediately; she was in a terrible condition.” Tests confirmed that Amira was suffering from severe acute malnutrition, which had caused severe stunting. Despite watching her daughter grow increasingly frail, Aya was unable to get her the treatment she needed during the war. Even after Amira was admitted to al-Rantisi, her condition failed to improve. Her weight stagnated, and she stopped growing. “It’s crushing. I’ve spent so much time in hospitals and with doctors, but they say the malnutrition she endured has severely and permanently damaged her body.” Today, Amira weighs just 12.5kg and stands one metre tall. Although she is six, doctors say her bone age is that of a two-year-old. 'I have lost all hope of her recovering inside Gaza after exhausting every available treatment' - Aya Rashid, Palestinian mother After the ceasefire was signed in October 2025, Aya hoped her daughter’s condition would finally improve. But little has changed. “I thought her condition would improve once the truce began and food came in. I never imagined it had reached the point of a clinical illness.” Doctors have told Aya that Amira’s body is no longer responding to treatment, despite having no underlying allergies or problems absorbing nutrients. “I have lost all hope of her recovering inside Gaza after exhausting every available treatment. Even the doctors are now saying her condition requires travelling abroad.” Aya is mourning not only her daughter’s physical decline but also what she describes as a regression in her cognitive development. Amira now mainly interacts with toddlers aged two or three. “Amira doesn’t know how to read or write, and everyone she interacts with in her surroundings are young children.” “Do you know what my wish is now?” Aya asked. “To find a pair of trousers that actually fits my little girl’s waist, to stop seeing her ribcage protruding, and to watch her join her peers in a classroom.” Starved in the womb In its August 2025 report, the IPC projected that at least 132,000 children under five would suffer from acute malnutrition through June 2026. It also estimated that nearly 55,500 malnourished pregnant and breastfeeding women would require urgent nutritional support. The crisis has left lasting effects not only on children like Amira, but also on babies who were still in the womb when their mothers were starving. Among them is 10-month-old Amna Abu al-Hasani, whose mother suffered malnutrition while pregnant with her. Amna was born prematurely by emergency caesarean section in her eighth month, weighing just 1.2kg. Two months later, doctors diagnosed her with an enlarged heart caused by weakened heart muscle, as well as severe stunting. “My daughter’s malnutrition began in the womb,” Amna's father, Youssef Abu al-Hasani, told MEE. ‘The war caused this’: Miscarriages soar in Gaza amid Israeli bombing and siege Read More » At 10 months old, Amna weighs barely 5.5kg and was recently diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition. “My daughter now suffers from major complications in her heart, kidneys and lungs,” Abu al-Hasani, 29, said. “The doctors told us all these issues stem fundamentally from her being born malnourished and underweight.” Despite using sporadic cash assistance to buy fruit and nutritional supplements, Abu al-Hasani says he is powerless to stop his daughter’s health from deteriorating. “The reality is that Gaza’s medical facilities cannot treat my daughter, neither for her malnutrition nor her other health conditions. Even though she has an urgent medical referral to travel abroad, her turn still hasn’t come.” Abu al-Hasani fears for his daughter’s future. Doctors cannot confirm whether she has underlying conditions without specialised tests that are unavailable in Gaza. “All I hope for is that my little girl is given a chance at life, that she gets her right to treatment abroad, and returns to our arms in good health.” Humanitarian crisis Despite the severely limited capacity of Gaza’s remaining hospitals, medical points and clinics, families of malnourished children have nowhere else to turn for care. Israel’s blockade has devastated the territory’s healthcare system while imposing strict restrictions on medical travel abroad. Dr Mohammed Abu Rai, head of the nutrition clinic at al-Rantisi Hospital, told MEE that the facility receives dozens of malnourished children every day, forcing staff to open additional wards to cope with the influx. 'The entry of food and meat into the Strip is not enough to treat malnutrition among children' - Mohammed Abu Rai, Palestinian doctor Although a new report by the IPC this month recorded a decline in acute malnutrition following the ceasefire, it warned that more than 74,000 children would still require treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027. An estimated 24,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women were also expected to suffer from acute malnutrition over the same period. Despite the ceasefire, Israel has failed to meet its obligations to increase the flow of aid into Gaza, perpetuating the humanitarian crisis it created. “The entry of food and meat into the Strip is not enough to treat malnutrition among children or even resolve the food crisis for the population post-ceasefire,” Abu Rai said. “Vegetables and fruits entering Gaza are sold at exorbitant prices that most people simply cannot afford.” Abu Rai also pointed to the poor quality of meat available in Gaza. With poultry and livestock farms destroyed, the territory is now almost entirely reliant on frozen meat. “Frozen meat has half the nutritional value of fresh meat, and Gaza’s severe power outages and poor storage reduce its benefits even further,” he said. Meanwhile, funding shortfalls are forcing aid agencies to cut food rations in Gaza, risking a further deterioration in food security, according to the World Food Programme (WFP). Abu Rai said aid supplies can also sit for weeks under the scorching sun at border crossings, further degrading essential food and nutritional products. The world must stop Israel's unprecedented assault on Palestinian children Read More » “Even staples like rice and lentils lose their nutritional value, while children’s supplements arrive in quantities far too small for even a single family,” he said. As more children suffer from malnutrition, the number experiencing stunted growth is also rising. “Malnutrition leads to severe growth disorders like stunting due to a lack of vital nutrients,” Abu Rai said, adding that roughly 18 percent of his patients are currently affected. While Abu Rai moves between hospital beds, monitoring his young patients, the Rashid and Abu al-Hasani families anxiously check their phones, waiting for a message or call confirming a date for their children to travel abroad for treatment. “We miraculously survived certain death multiple times during the war,” Aya Rashid said. “What I fear now is losing my little girl to malnutrition, not to bombs." headline: 'Political stunt': Cair slams Texas governor for threatening airports that install ablution stations for Muslims
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 21:07 BST | Last update: 2 days 4 hours ago
article_body: The largest Muslim civil rights organisation in the US slammed the governor of Texas on Monday for his threats to withhold funding to airports in the state that build spaces to accommodate practising Muslims. "Of all the silly controversies that @GregAbbott_TX has manufactured about Muslims over the past year, the airport washing station outrage might be the most ridiculous. And hypocritical," the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) wrote on X on Monday. The Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW) International Airport on Friday cancelled a project to install an ablution station that can be used by Muslims before they go through the international terminal's airport security. This followed a threat by hardline Republican Governor Greg Abbott to withhold state grants to airports taking part in any similar projects. Airports in the US are typically state-run in the pre-security section that is open to the public, and federally run in the post-security section, which is exclusively for ticket-holding travellers. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "My office is actively reviewing all grants to any local governmental entities involved in these schemes for possible revocation of past grant money and cancellation of any future funds that have been dedicated by my Office," the governor said in a letter to the airport authority. "Upon accepting any grant award from the State, recipients are required to certify compliance with all state and federal laws—including prohibitions on impermissible government discrimination—whether based on race, sex, religion, or otherwise." Abbott has tried to halt most projects in the state that accommodate Muslims, and called the project "illegal" in a separate letter addressed to the US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, as well as US attorney general Todd Blanche on Friday. "These facilities appear designed to single out one subset of the population for special treatment based on religion. I am unaware of either airport installing standalone facilities to meet the particular needs of the many other religious groups represented across Texas," Abbott wrote. He demanded that the Trump administration review all existing accommodations for Muslims at both the Dallas and Houston airports. 'Favor one religion over the other' "Keep in mind that Governor Abbott is currently trying to force K-12 students in Texas public schools to read (his preferred version of) the Bible and require teachers to post the Ten Commandments (that some prominent politicians routinely ignore) in every classroom," Cair wrote on X. "Unlike those unconstitutional attempts to favor one religion and impose it on schoolchildren, the washing station at DFW Airport would be a universally accessible and perfectly legal amenity. Washing stations already exist at various airports and anyone can use them," the group explained. Cair has been a frequent target for Abbott, who reportedly relies on an anti-Muslim think tank to present him with proposals to dismantle it. Abbott designated Cair as a terrorist organisation last year. Cair has taken the matter to court. "Instead of wasting taxpayer resources on this latest anti-Muslim political stunt, Governor Abbott should focus on the state’s real problems under his leadership, from harmful data centers to school shootings to economic inequality to the erosion of religious freedom," Cair said on Monday. Most large airports in the US have quiet interfaith spaces used by travellers wishing to carry out formal prayer sessions or just meditate. But the Dallas area, in particular, has one of the largest Muslim-American populations in the country. Prayer and public life There is already at least one ablution station beyond the security gates in the international terminal at DFW, so the notion is not new, but the announcement of an impending second project caused outrage among right-wing media and conservative groups last week. US administration launches federal probe into Muslim housing development in Texas Read More » Ablution stations feature low-level faucets next to a stool, so that feet can be washed before the five daily obligatory prayers for practising Muslims. Yasir Qadhi, a world-renowned imam based in the Dallas area, urged Abbott to reconsider in a Facebook post on Saturday. "Muslims are not asking airports to endorse Islam. They are asking for the same principle that has long guided our nation: people of different faiths should be able to practice their sincerely held beliefs while participating fully in public life," he said. "As Texans, we all benefit when our public institutions are welcoming to everyone. Protecting the religious liberty of one community strengthens the religious liberty of every community." The same day, President Donald Trump shared a news story about the cancellation of the project on his Truth Social platform, but did not add comment. Laura Loomer, a notoriously anti-Muslim podcaster, attached a screenshot of the president's post and wrote, "We really need Trump to unleash on the Muslims again like he did during his first term. We are so close. I pray everyday for him to go ballistic on them." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Israel suffers record emigration wave, with almost 270,000 leaving since 2023
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 14:09 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: Close to 270,000 Israeli citizens have left the country since 2023, marking the highest emigration levels in Israel's history, according to a new study by researchers at Tel Aviv University. The study, reported by Haaretz, found that roughly 90,000 Israelis left the country for three months or more in each year between 2023 and 2025. That annual average is well above the roughly 60,000 who emigrated each year between 2010 and 2019. Drawing on data from Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics and other government agencies, the study found that more than 86,000 Israelis left the country for over three months in 2023, followed by more than 90,000 in both 2024 and 2025. Itai Ater, one of the study's authors, told Haaretz that the research broke from previous emigration reports by counting anyone who spent at least three months abroad, rather than only those gone for a full year, arguing this gave a more accurate picture of the true scale of departures. Ater said the figures only include long-term Israeli residents who had lived in the country for at least three years before leaving, excluding recent immigrants from Ukraine and Russia who departed within three years of arrival. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "In 2025, we again see deeply troubling numbers of Israelis who left the country for a significant period, adding to the emigration wave of 2023 and 2024," Ater said. "These figures do not yet, in themselves, pose a threat to Israel's resilience," he added. "But looking ahead, and unless there is a change, there is growing concern that emigration from Israel will increase to a level that endangers the country's security and economy." Tel Aviv University said earlier research had already identified "a significant and concerning increase" in the departure of doctors, PhD holders, engineers, academics and high earners. While similar trends have been recorded elsewhere in the world, the university said the exodus of highly educated Israelis poses a particular risk given the country's lack of natural resources and reliance on skilled labour. 'Domino effect' The study warned that rising emigration could trigger a "domino effect", making the trend harder to reverse the further it progresses. "In such a situation, every additional emigrant increases the incentive for others to leave," the university said. "Once emigration numbers cross a certain threshold, reversing the trend will be extremely difficult, perhaps impossible." The findings have drawn sharp criticism from Israeli lawmakers. Gilad Kariv, chair of the Knesset's Committee for Immigration, Absorption and Diaspora Affairs and a member of the left-wing Democrats party, wrote on X that "Israel is facing a tsunami of emigration, and the government is doing nothing about the issue". "This is a strategic threat to Israel's future, and it is closely linked to the government's conduct and to the regime coup," Kariv said, referring to the judicial overhaul launched by the government in early 2023, which triggered mass protests across the country. Meirav Cohen, a Knesset member from the centre-right Together party, also criticised the government. "They declared they would carry out voluntary emigration from Gaza," Cohen said on X , referring to the government's plan to expel Palestinians from the strip. "In the end, the October 7 government encouraged voluntary emigration from the State of Israel." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. subheadline: Tel Aviv University study finds emigration running well above the last decade's average, with lawmakers blaming the war on Gaza and the 'regime coup' for driving Israelis abroad

headline: China steps up 'propaganda blitz' in Turkey amid investment fallout
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 16:12 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: The Chinese government has substantially stepped up its public relations activities in Turkey following the damage to its image caused by the collapse of manufacturer BYD’s planned investment in the country. The Chinese electric vehicle company in June said they had paused work on a plant in Turkey while prioritising production in Europe. BYD’s apparent change of course was a major embarrassment for the Turkish government. To attract the company, Ankara granted generous tax breaks on BYD vehicle sales in Turkey even before construction of the plant had begun. Thanks to those incentives, combined with a new commercial strategy, BYD’s sales in Turkey surged to more than 45,000 vehicles in 2025. Experts estimate that the company may already have earned between $500m and $1bn in additional profits from the Turkish market as a result of those tax advantages. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “ The collapse of the BYD deal put China’s image in Turkey in a precarious position,” one Turkish government consultant told Middle East Eye. “They are now engaged in a propaganda blitz to turn the tide.” The consultant said Ankara had grown tired of Chinese negotiating tactics, which he described as creating the impression that an agreement had been reached, only for Beijing to reopen negotiations later with an expanding list of demands. The public relations campaign has been apparent to those who closely follow China’s activities in Turkey. The Chinese embassy in Ankara has been placing unsigned propaganda articles in pro-government media outlets, highlighting the importance of high-level engagement between the Chinese Communist Party and Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP). The embassy has also promoted the launch of Volume Five of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China across government-aligned media . Propaganda blitz Nurettin Akcay, an academic specialising in Chinese affairs, said the BYD crisis had undoubtedly contributed to negative sentiment towards China in Turkey. “Although there has recently been a significant quantitative increase in China’s public diplomacy activities in Turkey, such efforts have actually been under way for a long time,” he told MEE. “Even before the BYD issue erupted, the Chinese were inviting journalists and other individuals regarded as opinion leaders in Turkey to visit China.” Turkey and China have had an uneasy relationship over the past decade, largely because of the Uyghur issue. Until 2020, Ankara sought to minimise Turkish media coverage of the suffering of Uyghurs in the hope of securing Chinese investment. 'China is seeking to minimise domestic criticism within Turkey by pursuing a broad engagement strategy' Nurettin Akcay, academic and Chinese affairs specialist At Beijing’s request, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited the Uyghur-majority Xinjiang Autonomous Region in June 2024 in an attempt to remove one of the main obstacles to bilateral relations. However, promised investments in electric vehicle plants by BYD and Chinese automobile manufacturer Chery have yet to materialise, despite lengthy negotiations since the visit. Akcay’s social media posts tracking Chinese lobbying efforts in Turkey have also placed him under scrutiny in China, where he completed his PhD at Shanghai University. In a separate post on X, Akcay said Shanghai University had emailed him to say it had received numerous complaints about his critical reporting on China. “For this reason, they asked me to stop referring to the fact that I completed my PhD at Shanghai University,” he said. “Additionally, as far as I understand, the doors to China are closing on me for good. I don’t know if they will ever let me back into China.” Akcay said China was focusing on what he calls “elite engagement”, which includes inviting prominent figures to the country as part of a form of showcase diplomacy that presents a carefully curated image of China. Last month, the Turkey-China Friendship Foundation, a Chinese state-funded entity, organised an eight-day press junket for Turkish journalists working for opposition media outlets. They were taken to the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, home to a large Uyghur population. None of the journalists, who were affiliated with T24 , Halk TV , Cumhuriyet , Haberturk TV and several independent outlets, reported on allegations of mistreatment of Uyghurs. Instead, they focused on “terrorist” attacks carried out by radicals in the region and on China’s integration efforts. The Turkish reports used similar language, with some repeating the same concepts almost verbatim. They highlighted the region’s importance to China’s industrial revival and the Belt and Road Initiative , while presenting tourism as an increasingly important part of Xinjiang’s development plans. No accountability Human Rights Watch said in its 2026 report that Chinese authorities had tightened ideological controls over the previous year while continuing the harsh, forced assimilation of Tibetans and Uyghurs . “There has been no accountability for crimes against humanity in Xinjiang, where several hundred thousand Uyghurs remain unjustly imprisoned,” the report said. Since 2017, China has placed hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs in “re-education camps”, demolished mosques and Islamic cemeteries, and banned religious education. “Everything is planned, and China gets precisely what it wants because visitors are shown only what they are intended to see,” Akcay said. “Consequently, journalists who visit China encounter a positive picture without fully understanding the broader context.” China’s recent attempts to influence Turkish public opinion have also included outreach to opposition parties, such as the Islamist-conservative New Welfare Party and the Turkish nationalist Victory Party. Turkey quietly lobbied for Uyghur rights during high-level visit to China Read More » A delegation from the New Welfare Party visited China in June, while Chinese Ambassador Jiang Xuebin met the party’s chairman, Fatih Erbakan, last month. Akcay said China had begun cultivating good relations with virtually all of Turkey’s opposition parties. “I believe the Uyghur issue is once again a major factor behind China’s interest in Turkish opposition parties of all sizes,” he said. He added that right-wing opposition parties in Turkey could speak relatively freely about the Uyghur issue because it appealed to their voter bases. “China is seeking to minimise domestic criticism within Turkey - or at least prevent such criticism from developing into radical campaigns - by pursuing a broad engagement strategy,” he said. “Is China successful? In my view, at least partially, yes. It may not completely transform public perceptions, but it is pursuing an effective strategy to prevent the emergence of a radical counter-campaign.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia in landmark trial
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 09:50 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: A Damascus court sentenced Syria 's former president Bashar al-Assad , his brother Maher and former security official Atef Najib to death on Tuesday on charges of murder, torture and incitement to murder. The court convicted Bashar of premeditated murder of multiple people, including children, as well as torture, arbitrary detention and crimes against humanity. Najib was tried in person, while Bashar and Maher were tried in absentia. Former security official Najib, a cousin of Assad, was arrested in January last year and was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15", and "torture leading to death". The ruling against Assad, who fled with his family to Moscow as armed opposition forces closed in on Damascus in December 2024, is the first issued under the transitional authorities. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The interim government began prosecuting figures from the former government this year, both in person and in absentia. Assad, born in 1965, became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez al-Assad. He maintained the family's rule and the dominance of the Alawite sect in the predominantly Sunni Muslim country, while keeping Syria aligned with Iran and hostile towards Israel and the United States . War in Syria In March 2011, government forces led by Assad violently suppressed protests that emerged during the Arab Spring, prompting an armed uprising. While Russia and Iran backed Assad, the US, Turkey and other countries supported different factions at various stages. Who is Bashar al-Assad and how did he rule Syria? Read More » Hundreds of thousands of people were killed in the subsequent years as the conflict devastated civilian infrastructure and displaced millions. The 14-year civil war left Syria facing a profound political, economic and humanitarian crisis. Human rights abuses were reported throughout the conflict, with the Assad government accused of widespread arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and attacks on civilians. A UN investigative mechanism said evidence showed a systematic pattern of torture, sexual violence and enforced disappearances across more than 100 government detention facilities. Rights concerns have continued during Syria’s political transition. UN experts have reported allegations of summary executions, forced displacement and other abuses against civilians. US withdrawal In April, the last remaining US troops in Syria left their base in Hasakah, ending a 10-year presence in the country, after which the Syrian military entered the last base previously under American control, known as Qasrak, which included an airstrip. The Syrian foreign ministry said it welcomed “the completed handover of military sites where United States forces were previously present in Syria to the Syrian government”. Syria reclaims control of key coastal sites in deal with Russia Read More » Earlier this year, the US helped facilitate an agreement between the longtime US partner Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and Damascus, under which the Syrian government agreed to take the lead in combating militant groups such as the Islamic State group. The SDF also agreed to hand over control of large swathes of territory, including Raqqa and Deir Ezzor, to Damascus. On Monday, Syria also reached a memorandum of understanding with Russia to scale back Moscow's military presence on Syria's Mediterranean coast, ending 18 months of negotiations over the future of the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval facility. US forces also withdrew from two major American bases in Syria: southern al-Tanf and al-Shaddadi in the northeast. American troops had been in Syria since 2015. Washington, which backs President Ahmed al-Sharaa's new government, previously had around 1,000 US troops in Syria. Syria after Assad After Sharaa’s militant group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, seized Damascus on 8 December 2024, ousting Assad, Sharaa became Syria's interim president. Shortly after celebrating his victory, Sharaa began embracing world leaders and appeared in western media outlets, where he spoke of Syria's "diversity as a strength" and of "unifying the country". He also promised to pursue former government personnel and loyalists implicated in war crimes, trimmed his beard and replaced his turban and thobe with a suit and tie. 'Character arc': Syrian leader watching dance performance to Missy Elliott song goes viral Read More » In April, during a visit to London, Sharaa said Damascus would stay out of the Israeli-US war on Iran unless his country comes under attack. While Syria's transitional administration has initiated economic reforms, including public-sector employee reductions, tax system reforms, and the reopening of border crossings, some have questioned the sustainability of Sharaa's transformation and pointed out that he has, to date, not publicly apologised for past actions. Meanwhile, tensions between the new government and the Alawite community have been high. Last year, armed attacks on security forces by suspected Assad loyalists in the coastal Alawite heartland of Latakia spiralled into brutal sectarian bloodshed. At least 1,500 Alawites were killed in the subsequent violence, with a Reuters investigation tracing much of the violence back to security officials in Damascus. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Exclusive: ICC issued two secret arrest warrants for Taliban members for gender persecution
author: Sondos Asem
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 16:52 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued two secret arrest warrants last year for senior members of the Taliban for the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and political grounds, Middle East Eye can reveal. According to sealed documents and sources briefed on the matter, the warrants were issued confidentially by a panel of three judges in September 2025. This was two months after the same panel publicly issued arrest warrants for the Taliban's supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Afghanistan’s chief justice, for the same crime. The secret warrants include new evidence and new alleged victims not covered by the two public applications. The ICC is charging the four Taliban members for alleged crimes committed by the group as the de facto government authority in Afghanistan from at least 15 August 2021 until at least 20 January 2025. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters MEE is not disclosing the identity of the two members in the secret warrants to protect the confidentiality of proceedings. The Taliban warrants set a historic precedent under international law. They mark the first time the ICC or any other international tribunal has recognised LGBTQ+ victims. The charge of gender persecution is also very rare under international law, and there has never been a conviction on it. The charge has been prosecuted just once by the ICC, in the Al Hassan case , but never led to a conviction. Threat of sanctions The Taliban warrants were filed in January 2025 shortly after the inauguration of US President Donald Trump. The four applications were prepared under the leadership of former prosecutor Karim Khan and Nazhat Shameem Khan, the ICC's deputy prosecutor, who oversees the Afghanistan investigation. The team has been guided by Lisa Davis, a special adviser who authored the office’s policy on gender persecution. It's unclear whether the two additional warrants were filed on the same day as those of Akhunzada and Haqqani. In his public announcement on 23 January, then-Prosecutor Khan said that more applications would be filed "soon." Sources familiar with the matter told MEE that the two secret applications were "almost ready" to be submitted that day. MEE understands that court officials decided not to publicise the two additional applications because they knew the US was opposed to them and they forsaw US sanctions being issued against the ICC as a result. A month after the applications for Akhunzada and Haqqani were made public, the US did indeed impose sanctions on ICC officials, beginning with Karim Khan. What next for the ICC and the Palestine investigation after Karim Khan's removal? Read More » Staff members were wary of potential sanctions targeting them and affecting their ability to visit family in the US, sources familiar with the matter explained. Some were even reluctant to have their names on the applications. Since April, judges have ordered the prosecutor’s office not to publicise any further requests for arrest warrants. Contacted by MEE multiple times regarding the status of arrest warrant applications, the office of the prosecutor refused to comment, citing the court’s amended regulations imposing secrecy on new filings. Since February 2025, the US has imposed retaliatory financial and visa sanctions on court officials in connection with the Afghanistan and Palestine investigations, citing efforts to prosecute nationals or allies of the US. ​​The first target was Karim Khan , the former prosecutor who was controversially removed by member states last month after an 18-month long misconduct probe. Also targeted were eight judges, three of whom - Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Luz Ibanez - were members of the 2020 Appeals Chamber that authorised the Afghanistan investigation. The sanctions came despite the decision by then-prosecutor Khan in 2021 to deprioritise the strand of the Afghanistan probe concerning US military and CIA personnel, as well as former Afghan government forces, in order to focus the investigation on the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (IS-K). MEE understands that even though the office of the prosecutor is not investigating US nationals, successive US governments, including Joe Biden's, have opposed the ICC’s prosecution of the Taliban for pragmatic reasons. The main reason is the Taliban being the de facto government, which necessitates diplomatic contacts with its members. The US is also worried about the potential of more extreme groups like the Islamic State replacing the Taliban in the event of a collapse of its government. Judges seek to split investigation The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group. That request was initially rejected by a pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed. Bensouda was sanctioned by the US government a few months later over alleged attempts to subject Americans to the court's jurisdiction. Exclusive: ICC judges order Taliban case split from Afghanistan probe that covers US troops Read More » The probe was suspended later that year after a deferral request from the then Afghan government, and only resumed in late 2022, a decision upheld on appeal in April 2023. In November 2024, six states (Chile, Costa Rica, Spain, France, Luxembourg and Mexico) jointly referred allegations of crimes against women and girls committed since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, asking prosecutors to fold them into the existing Afghanistan investigation. Weeks later, in January 2025, Khan applied for arrest warrants, arguing that the gender persecution allegations already fell within the scope of the 2020 authorisation. MEE revealed last week that ICC judges have asked the office of the prosecutor to open a standalone investigation into allegations of gender persecution by the Taliban, separating it from the original Afghanistan war crimes probe that covered US nationals. The move, if prosecutors proceed, is likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies. Khan’s two deputies, both under US sanctions, are in charge of the office until the election of a new prosecutor. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israel allows Jewish ritual at Al-Aqsa Mosque in unprecedented violation of status quo
author: Lubna Masarwa
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 15:35 BST | Last update: 2 days 8 hours ago
article_body: Israeli authorities have formally allowed Jewish prayer for the first time inside Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem, in an unprecedented violation of the site’s decades-old status quo. Israeli police allowed settlers raiding the site on Sunday to bring in siddurim, or Jewish prayer books, and perform group prayers, according to a Palestinian source from the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf. While such practices have occurred in the past, they have largely been carried out without official approval. The decision to officially permit them marks a significant shift. The source, who requested anonymity, said the move represented the latest breach of the site’s status quo. “There is an important distinction between coming to visit the site and coming to pray there,” the source said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “When I come to your place as a visitor, you impose your rules on me. But today, they come with their own rules. When the police officially allow that, it means, in one way or another, that you are allowing them to establish their own rules in the space,” he added. “This is an official breach of the status quo.” The status quo is a decades-old, internationally recognised arrangement governing access to and management of Al-Aqsa Mosque. Under the arrangement, the entire 144-dunam (14.4 hectares) complex is recognised as an exclusively Islamic holy site. Responsibility for access, prayer arrangements, maintenance and excavations falls to the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, the religious trust that administers the mosque. 'Jewish prayer at Al-Aqsa Mosque is becoming an organised practice' - Palestinian source But since occupying East Jerusalem in 1967, Israel has steadily eroded the status quo, with the formal permission for Jewish prayer representing the latest step. For years, Israeli forces have turned a blind eye to Israelis praying at Al-Aqsa during daily raids on the site. The source said the latest development transformed what were previously silent, individual acts of prayer into organised group worship, with religious texts now permitted inside the complex. “Jewish prayer at Al-Aqsa Mosque is becoming an organised practice, rather than merely an isolated individual act.” Wider restrictions The source said the latest move was part of a wider campaign of restrictions on Palestinian access to and administration of Al-Aqsa, which has accelerated since October 2023. “The pace of developments at Al-Aqsa Mosque since 7 October is staggering,” he said. “Things are changing at an incredible speed, almost daily. We have essentially lost control.” According to Haaretz, the drive to permit Jewish worshippers to bring prayer sheets into Al-Aqsa Mosque began in January. Police have also allowed prayers, dancing and singing in the mosque’s courtyard. The daily newspaper added that police said their enforcement policies at Al-Aqsa were “in accordance with directives from the political leadership”. Last month, ministers and lawmakers led a mass raid on Al-Aqsa by ultranationalist Israelis, with more than 3,500 participants taking part. Why Israel is closer than ever to building the Third Temple Read More » Among them was Itamar Ben Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, who oversees the police. Ben Gvir, a settler, has long called for what he describes as the imposition of “Israeli sovereignty” over Al-Aqsa Mosque. During July’s raid, he said: “Look at what is happening here – Jews praying, feeling like they are the owners here.” Mustafa Abu Sway, a member of the Islamic Waqf Council in Jerusalem, said the violations were part of a government plan rather than isolated acts. “This desecration, including the introduction of prayer books inside the mosque, forms part of the systematic dismantling of what remains of the historic status quo at the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque, with Itamar Ben Gvir determining what happens on the ground, with the approval of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu,” Abu Sway told MEE. He added that, alongside the expanding Jewish presence at the site, the government continued to impose heavy restrictions on Palestinian access and the work of the Waqf, which administers the complex. “Muslim worshippers are prevented from entering in a manner that appears arbitrary on the surface but in fact reflects a systematic policy,” he added. headline: Israel pitched advanced drones to UAE, leaked emails reveal: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 20:01 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: The UAE secretly pushed for the sale of Israeli drones by Elbit Systems following an attack on Abu Dhabi by Yemen’s Houthis in 2022, according to leaked emails reported by Haaretz and Drop Site News. Emails dating from 2021 through early 2023 reveal that Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest defence contractor, had already begun discussing the sale of Hermes 900 drones, SkyEye wide-area surveillance sensors, ground control equipment, training, and logistical support. The sale was described as “urgent” after the Houthis in Yemen launched a missile and drone attack on Abu Dhabi on 17 January 2022. The emails from Elbit Systems’ executives were obtained by Handala, an online hacking group, with supposed links to the Iranian government. They were verified by both Haaretz and Drop Site News. The initial drone sale was valued at $154m, with additional upgrades bringing it up to $225m. The leaked correspondence didn’t reveal whether the drones were delivered. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters SkyEye sensors comprise electro-optical cameras that allow a drone to record a vast area in real time at high resolution. The footage can be rewound through multiple viewpoints to trace objects back to their place of origin. UAE and Israel established fund for joint defence acquisition, sources say Read More » The Hermes 900 is an advanced Israeli reconnaissance and surveillance drone that has a payload of up to 990 pounds. According to reports, it can carry up to eight surface-to-air missiles. The emails revealed that in March 2022 the head of research and development at the Israeli defence ministry's arms development directorate was travelling to the UAE with a proposal to sell Hermes 900 drones with "an operational solution for maintaining surveillance beyond the country's borders – detecting missile and drone launches into the country”. At the time, the UAE had just suffered a missile and drone attack that targeted oil tanker trucks and the Abu Dhabi airport. The UAE normalised relations with Israel approximately two years before, under the Abraham Accords. That agreement, brokered by Trump's first administration, was framed as an effort to bolster defence ties between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco. The emails also contain two references to the SkyStriker loitering munition and another drone, the Hermes 650. The emails provide a rare window into the close defence ties between the UAE and Israel, along with the specific Israeli armaments and technical systems that analysts have long said entice Gulf states. The UAE is one of the closest Arab and Muslim states to Israel, and joined it and the US in launching hundreds of strikes on Iran. Middle East Eye revealed in May that Israel and the UAE have established a joint defence fund to acquire new weapons systems amid the war on Iran. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: UAE-funded mercenary targeted British activist in London, report says
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 21:02 BST | Last update: 3 hours 49 mins ago
article_body: A mercenary allegedly hired and paid millions of dollars by the United Arab Emirates carried out a covert surveillance operation against a British activist and academic in London, according to an investigation by ITV News. Abraham Golan, a dual Hungarian-Israeli citizen who ran the private security company Spear Operations Group, travelled to Britain in December 2016 to target Anas al-Tikriti, the chief executive of the London-based Cordoba Foundation think tank, ITV News reported on Wednesday. Emirati financial records seen by ITV showed that Golan, who lived in the US , was being paid by the UAE while carrying out the operation. He was receiving a six-figure annual retainer, as well as substantial bonuses, including a $1m payment weeks before his trip to London for an operation in Yemen . ITV's investigation, based on witness testimony, emails, WhatsApp messages and financial records, found that Golan worked with a former US special forces operative to locate and monitor Tikriti. According to the UK broadcaster, Golan told a British strategist assisting him that he was working for the UAE and that Abu Dhabi considered Tikriti and the Cordoba Foundation to be aligned with groups it regarded as terrorist organisations. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Golan contacted the British strategist, identified by ITV as "Victor", in November 2016, asking whether he had any "channels" to Tikriti and the Cordoba Foundation. According to the report, Golan later travelled to London, where he offered Victor £50,000 ($68,000) to help locate Tikriti, increasing the offer to £100,000 ($136,000). Golan shared photographs of Tikriti's home and car, maps and satellite images, and details of his movements between home and work. At one meeting, Golan allegedly discussed the possibility of physically eliminating Tikriti. His associate, a former US Navy Seal, reportedly made a gesture across his throat when asked what could happen to the activist. "I became increasingly worried about what this operation entailed," Victor told ITV. Britain must reject the UAE's Brotherhood bogeyman Read More » In a follow-up message, Golan appeared to suggest that the operation was part of a much wider campaign. "War is coming to Europe and we are at the beginning of a huge program," he wrote to Victor, without elaborating on what he meant. Golan subsequently left the UK for Washington but told Victor that the operation would continue, writing that his "team" remained in London. Victor eventually withdrew from the operation after concluding it could involve an assassination. The extent to which the surveillance continued is unclear. Tikriti, who has helped negotiate the release of more than 20 hostages across Africa and the Middle East, was later visited twice at his London home by police officers who warned him that his life could be at risk. The officers did not tell him the source or nature of the threat. "I feel physically sick," Tikriti told ITV News after being shown the messages and photographs gathered by Golan. "At the time, my children were three and one and a half years old," he said. UAE's Muslim Brotherhood campaign The alleged operation came amid a long-running dispute between the UAE and the UK over the Muslim Brotherhood. For years, the UAE has accused the Muslim Brotherhood of threatening its political system and has sought to suppress the movement and its influence across the region since the Arab Spring. Founded in Cairo in 1928, the Muslim Brotherhood is one of the world's largest and best-known political Islam groups. It has long maintained that it is a peaceful organisation that wishes to participate in politics democratically, but it is considered a major threat by several autocratic governments in the region. In 2014, Abu Dhabi designated the Cordoba Foundation, the Muslim Association of Britain, and Islamic Relief as terrorist organisations alongside groups including the Islamic State group (IS) and al-Qaeda. What is driving Britain's Muslim Brotherhood panic? Read More » However, a year later, in 2015, a UK government review found no evidence that the Muslim Brotherhood was involved in terrorist activity in Britain. The Cordoba Foundation has consistently denied having a formal association with the Muslim Brotherhood. Tikriti has acknowledged studying the group's ideology but rejected suggestions that he poses a threat. "I'm a Brit. I grew up in Britain," he told ITV News. "In my life, I have never done anything wrong whatsoever." According to ITV News, Golan's alleged operation in London also followed his work for the UAE in Yemen. In 2015, his company was hired to assemble a team of western military veterans to target people Abu Dhabi considered linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. One of the targets was Yemeni MP Anssaf Ali Mayo, whose office was targeted with explosives. Mayo has since said he suffers "psychological and emotional trauma" from the assassination attempt, and now lives in exile in Saudi Arabia. His wife and two children remain in Yemen. Golan later acknowledged the existence of a "targeted assassination" programme in Yemen, telling BuzzFeed News that it had been "sanctioned" by the UAE. A former member of his team, US Special Forces veteran Dale Comstock, told ITV News: "For all intents and purposes, we were Emirati soldiers." According to ITV News, the London operation took place as Britain and the UAE were publicly deepening their political and economic relationship. Two weeks after Golan first contacted Victor, then Prince Charles travelled to Abu Dhabi to strengthen bilateral ties. British officials were aware of disagreements with the UAE over the Muslim Brotherhood, but said they had no knowledge that a covert operation involving mercenaries was being planned on the UK's shores. A Home Office spokesperson told ITV: "It is our longstanding policy not to comment on security and intelligence matters." MEE contacted the UAE's embassies in Britain and the US for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Iran and Oman work on temporary Hormuz shipping route as Trump threatens to claim the strait
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 16 August 2026 16:43 BST | Last update: 3 days 8 hours ago
article_body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran and Muscat were working to establish a temporary maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz, while stressing that the talks were separate from any decision on reopening the strategic waterway. “The routes that existed previously are no longer functional, so a new route needs to be defined,” Araghchi said. “For now, we are designing a temporary route, which can then, at a later stage, be turned into a final route.” Araghchi said negotiations with Oman were continuing over maritime routes for ships passing through the strait. “We may reach an outcome soon, but I want to emphasise that these negotiations and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz are two separate issues,” he said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “Once this route has been determined, whether the strait will be reopened or not will depend on the fulfilment of other conditions to which the United States must adhere.” The development comes after US President Donald Trump said he would designate the Strait of Hormuz a territory “pretty soon”. “After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said during a speech at a police academy in New York on Friday. Iran formalises Strait of Hormuz control as US struggles to sustain war it launched with Israel Read More » “We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.” Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, responded by saying: “The Strait of Hormuz cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech.” “The Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian; this strait will only be closed and opened under Iran’s command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and cease your fanciful delusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” Gharibabadi said in a post on X. Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also appeared to respond to Trump’s remarks, quoting Fyodor Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov in a post on X. “The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others,” Baghaei wrote. On Sunday, Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, also warned that Washington would regret any attempt to take control of the strait, according to Iranian state media. The exchange comes amid continuing hostilities and stalled efforts to reach a broader settlement over the waterway. Reuters reported that oil tanker traffic through Hormuz remained severely disrupted, with only two vessels recorded passing through the strait that day and no visible crude oil shipments. ​Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz on 28 February following joint military strikes by the US and Israel and has since restricted navigation in the strategic waterway, which carries about 25 percent of global seaborne oil trade. headline: Israeli strike on Gaza port kills at least seven, including a child
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 19:22 BST | Last update: 1 day 5 hours ago
article_body: An Israeli drone attack on a cafe in the port area west of Gaza City on Tuesday killed at least seven Palestinians , including a child, and left one body so mutilated that health workers could not identify the victim, according to Gaza health officials. Most of the injured, including those in critical condition, were transferred to al-Shifa Hospital, which reported that it had received six bodies and 13 wounded, one of whom succumbed to their injuries later in the evening. The hospital said one victim appeared to have taken a direct missile hit, with the body shredded beyond recognition. Al Jazeera Arabic said the intensity of the strike pushed a number of the injured and dead into the sea, meaning the real number of casualties may be higher. Recovery efforts are currently underway. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Mohammed Alghoul, an eyewitness to the event, told AFP that “Israeli warplanes fired two missiles at the ‘Sweet and Bitter’ cafe on the fishermen’s port west of Gaza City”. In a post on Telegram, the Israeli military said that they carried out a “precise aerial strike” against “several Hamas commanders” in the Shati area, west of Gaza City. The army said that the group was planning an attack against Israeli forces operating in the strip and so were “attacked from the air to remove the threat to the forces”, adding that “steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians”. Israeli general says Gaza should remain ‘destroyed for generations’ Read More » They did not comment on the child who was killed, or provide evidence to substantiate their allegations against those targeted. Hamas has said in a statement that the strike, which they described as a "massacre", demonstrates Israel's “disregard” for US President Donald Trump’s calls to maintain the “ceasefire” deal, calling on mediators to pressure Israel “to commit to the ceasefire deal” and the peace roadmap already agreed upon. The attack comes only one day after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approved the next stage of the US -led “Board of Peace” plan for the enclave, calling discussions with the delegation led by US special envoy and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, “deep and constructive”. The agreement includes demands that Hamas fully disarm in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel originally rejected Trump’s 15-point plan after Hamas agreed to disarm and hand over its control of the Gaza Strip to a technocratic body. As of Monday, the death toll in Gaza was reported to be at least 73,399, with 174,310 injured, since the start of Israel’s genocide in October 2023, according to medical sources, including 1,265 killed since the “ceasefire” agreement signed between Israel and Hamas in October 2025. headline: Iran denies talks with US as Trump halts strikes at the last minute
author: Alex MacDonald
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 12:45 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: Iran has denied any talks are ongoing with the US despite a claim from Donald Trump, who called off strikes on the country on Saturday. Trump had announced that negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on new strikes against the Islamic Republic in order to pursue a deal. "Obviously, they don't want to be attacked," Trump told reporters on Sunday on board Air Force One. "Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon." However, Iran's foreign ministry has said there were currently no negotiations with the US but that talks were taking place with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said discussions with Oman were "constructive" and aimed at reaching an agreement on a new route. "We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a press briefing. "We hope that both regional and extra-regional actors will appreciate this responsible move by Iran and adopt a constructive approach." He added that as long as a US naval blockade on Iranian ports continues "the situation in the Strait of Hormuz will remain unchanged". Oil prices fall Despite the conflicting statements, oil prices fell sharply on Monday following Trump's statement. At around 09.15 GMT the price of a barrel of North Sea Brent crude for October delivery – trading as the benchmark contract for the first time – was down 4.59 percent at $83.89. On Sunday, Saudi Arabia 's state media said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken to Trump over the phone on developments in the region. The crown prince reportedly stressed "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce, which paves the way for diplomatic solutions". Why are Kurdish groups in Iraq being attacked amid the US-Iran flare-up? Read More » He also said diplomatic solutions should "yield positive results for preserving the security and stability of the region and prevent it from being drawn into a wider conflict". The conversation came after Saudi Arabia expressed concern over Trump's plans to strike Iran. The conflict between the US- Israel and Iran, which began in February, has left thousands of people dead and caused massive economic damage particularly in the Gulf states, which have faced repeated attacks from Iran. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has been particularly disruptive to the region's economy, and the long-term reopening of the waterway has been a primary goal. A spokesperson for Iran’s parliamentary National Security Committee, Hassan Qashqavi, said on Monday that Tehran was close to reaching an agreement with Oman over the strait. He also confirmed that the country's mediators were seeking to revive the Memorandum of Understanding with Washington. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Gaza families bury 112 people recovered nearly three years after Israeli strikes
author: Mohammed al-Hajjar
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 13:19 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: Palestinians on Tuesday buried 112 members of a single clan killed in Israeli air strikes in November 2023, after their remains were recovered from beneath the rubble last month. Relatives of the Abu Shari'a and al-Hasayna family gathered in Gaza City to bid a final farewell to their loved ones, whose bodies lay in rows draped in Palestinian flags. For many, it was a moment of both relief and renewed grief after nearly 1,000 days of waiting to recover the bodies of their relatives. "There is a feeling of both pain and joy," Amer Abu Shari'a, who lost relatives in the attack, told Middle East Eye. "Joy because we will bury and honour these martyrs after three years. But the sorrow has returned, as if the massacre happened today." New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The strike on the Sabra neighbourhood was one of the deadliest single-strike casualty events of the two-year genocide. Israeli warplanes flattened an entire residential block where hundreds of members of the Abu Shari'a and al-Hasayna clan had been living and sheltering. 'We worked for 17 days to recover the bodies in extremely difficult conditions' - Mahmoud Basal, Civil Defence spokesperson More than 300 people were killed, including 44 children, 37 women and more than 10 people with disabilities. Most remained buried beneath the collapsed buildings. Efforts to recover bodies from the rubble were halted in the early months of the war because search-and-rescue teams lacked the heavy equipment needed for the operation, which had been destroyed or blocked from entering Gaza by Israel. Civil Defence crews resumed searching the site on 14 July using limited and inadequate equipment. Officials said the force of the explosions had scattered human remains, making the recovery operation even more difficult. Scores of people attended the mass burial to pay their respects to the victims and their families (Mohammed al-Hajjar/MEE) By 1 August, crews had recovered the remains of 112 people, with more victims still believed to be buried beneath the debris. "We worked for 17 days to recover the bodies in extremely difficult conditions. In the end, we managed to recover the remains of 112 people," Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in the Gaza Strip, told MEE. "Thousands of people are still buried beneath the rubble, while their families continue to grieve and plead for the means to recover them." Reopened wounds Among those killed were prominent members of the family, including Fathi Abu Shari'a, the clan's mukhtar, or elder representative. After his home was struck, scores of people sought refuge in the house of Mofeed al-Hasayneh, who served as the Palestinian Authority's minister of public works and housing between 2014 and 2019 and held American citizenship. According to Mahmoud al-Hasayneh, who survived the attack, around 200 members of the Hasayneh family had taken shelter there, believing the house would be spared. 'Every time a body was recovered, relatives abroad would call and cry' - Mahmoud al-Hasayneh, survivor It too was bombed, killing the former minister and those sheltering with him. "Unfortunately, the Israelis respected neither children nor women, nor immunity, nor any house, nor any sanctity," al-Hasayneh said. "They struck everyone here," he added, noting that many of those killed held Romanian, British and American citizenship. Al-Hasayneh was not at the house when it was hit. His son, brother and their families were among those caught in the strike. "My son came out injured, praise be to God. But I lost my brother and his wife and children, my sister and all of her children, my other sister and her children, and many other aunts and uncles." Families said the burials brought some relief after years of waiting, but also reopened the wounds of the original attack (Mohammed al-Hajjar/MEE) He said the wait to recover the bodies and bury them had been long and painful, particularly for relatives living abroad. "This wound reopened last month, and we have been here for about 20 days," he said. "Every time a body was recovered, relatives abroad would call and cry. We opened a new wound. "We pray that God will envelop them in His mercy and honour them. This is the greatest honour for the deceased: that they are helped in being buried." Omar Nofal, head of Gaza's government committee for missing persons, said around 6,000 people have been officially registered as missing in the Gaza Strip since the war began. However, he said the true figure is likely closer to 15,000, with many still believed to be buried beneath collapsed buildings across the territory. Israeli forces have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians since October 2023 and wounded more than 170,000 others, according to the Palestinian health ministry. There are thousands more people believed to be buried under the rubble. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Thirteen years after Rabaa massacre, families urge Egypt to free political prisoners
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 15 August 2026 11:55 BST | Last update: 4 days 13 hours ago
article_body: The Families of Egyptian Detainees Association (Feda) on Friday called on the Egyptian government to release political prisoners on the 13th anniversary of the Rabaa massacre . Feda, which represents the families of political detainees held in Egypt, urged "Egyptian authorities to release those imprisoned in connection with the Rabaa events, as part of efforts to turn the page on this painful chapter in Egypt’s history". "Those who took part in a peaceful sit-in to express their views were transformed from victims into defendants and accused persons," the group said. "Large numbers were subsequently referred to trial, including 51 defendants in what became known as the 'Rabaa Operations Room' case and 739 defendants in the case concerning the dispersal of the Rabaa sit-in." On 14 August 2013, six weeks after then-Defence Minister Abdel Fattah el-Sisi seized power from Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, Egyptian forces stormed Cairo's Rabaa and al-Nahda squares and massacred at least 900 pro-democracy protesters in one of the largest killings of demonstrators in a single day in the country's modern history. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The group added: "13 years after the tragedy that shook Egypt, we call for justice to be restored and for those still imprisoned in connection with the two Rabaa cases to be released as part of a sustained process leading to the release of all political detainees." Rights groups estimate that more than 60,000 prisoners of conscience are held in Egyptian jails, including more than 1,000 women. The prisoners include students, youths and activists from across the Egyptian political spectrum. According to the Arabic Network for Human Rights Information , the total number of prisoners in Egypt in March 2021 was 120,000, with an estimated 65,000 political prisoners, at least 26,000 of whom were being held in pre-trial detention. Many, including former President Mohamed Morsi and several opposition figures, have died as a result of medical neglect and other inhumane prison conditions, according to documentation by multiple rights groups. Feda said: "We remain hopeful that this anniversary can mark a different beginning on the path towards comprehensive national reconciliation and transitional justice, as stipulated in Article 241 of the Egyptian Constitution." "The article requires the House of Representatives to enact a transitional justice law that ensures truth-seeking, accountability, reconciliation and compensation for victims." Rights groups have long documented violations faced by Egyptian detainees, including inadequate medical care, poor nutrition and ventilation, denial of family visits, overcrowded cells, denial of access to books and newspapers and denial of exercise. In September 2021, Cairo launched a national human rights strategy that included provisions concerning prisoners’ rights. The framework included goals for humane treatment, protection from torture and abuse, judicial oversight of prisons, and inspections of conditions by the National Council for Human Rights. Feda aims to liaise with institutions and authorities inside and outside Egypt in the hope of helping secure the release of political detainees. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye.
