headline: 'We will rise again': A new generation of Tunisians prepare for Ennahda's return
author: Faisal Edroos
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 08:35 UTC | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: They've watched their leaders jailed, their offices closed and their movement repeatedly attacked. But five years after President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers and dismantled Tunisia 's democratic institutions, supporters of Ennahda insist the country's largest Islamist movement is preparing to rise from the ashes. Rather than seeing the past five years as the movement's final chapter, many of the group's younger members describe the crackdown as another episode in a history marked by imprisonment, exile and political persecution. They say it has forced Ennahda to confront its mistakes, renew its leadership and prepare for a future beyond Saied's rule. "The idea that Ennahda has been defeated and that Tunisians no longer want Islamic parties is simply not true," said Ahmed, a 23-year-old resident of Ettadhamen, a working-class suburb of Tunis with a long history of support for Islamist movements. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "More and more young people want a movement that is rooted in Islam, a movement that speaks to our identity and will stand up for Muslims being oppressed across the world." "We are witnessing a resurgence and we will rise again." 'We haven't left the political scene and are still here' - Mohamed, small business owner Ahmed's optimism stands in stark contrast to the movement's current predicament. Since Saied suspended parliament on 25 July 2021, Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi and dozens of senior opposition figures have been imprisoned, while much of the movement's leadership has been prosecuted or pushed into exile. Once the dominant force in Tunisia's democratic transition, Ennahda is today weaker than at any point since the rule of former strongman Zine El Abidine Ben Ali. Inside the movement, however, few believe its story has ended. 'Muslim democracy' Founded in the early 1980s, Ennahda emerged as Tunisia's principal Islamist opposition movement under Ben Ali, with thousands of its members imprisoned, tortured or forced into exile. When the Arab Spring toppled his decades-long rule, the movement returned to public life and won Tunisia's first democratic elections, presenting itself as a model of what its leaders called "Muslim democracy". Unlike many Islamist movements elsewhere in the region, Ennahda argued that Islam and democracy were complementary rather than contradictory. Over time it moved away from the idea of an Islamist party towards what Ghannouchi described as a party of "Muslim democrats", committed to pluralism, constitutional rule and peaceful transfers of power. At its landmark 2016 congress, the movement formally separated its political and religious activities, arguing that mosques should not become arenas for party politics. The night Tunisia changed: How the Arab Spring's only democracy was destroyed Read More » Rather than advocating the imposition of Islamic law, Ennahda said religion should provide society with moral guidance while democratic institutions, competitive elections and an independent judiciary remained the basis of government. Its manifesto committed the movement to civil liberties, equal citizenship and political pluralism, positions that distinguished it from many other Islamist parties across the region. That evolution won cautious support from Western governments eager to see Tunisia succeed where much of the Arab Spring had faltered. Following Ennahda's election victory in 2011, the US State Department said it looked forward to working with Tunisia's newly elected leaders as they built "a democratic future". Britain's Foreign Office likewise welcomed the country's free and fair elections and pledged its support for Tunisia's democratic transition. For Ennahda's leaders, Tunisia offered an opportunity to demonstrate that political Islam and democratic governance could coexist. That vision, however, was soon tested by the realities of governing. Although Ennahda governed alongside successive secular coalition partners and never held power alone, Tunisia's economy stagnated, unemployment remained high and governments struggled to deliver the economic improvements many Tunisians had expected after the revolution. Increasingly, the movement became the public face of the frustrations that accompanied the democratic transition, allowing Saied to cast himself as the outsider who would sweep away the old political class. His power grab in July 2021 transformed Tunisia's political landscape almost overnight. Democracy abandoned Ennahda's supporters argue the movement's greatest mistake was not ideological, but strategic. They say that years spent trying to build consensus with secular rivals and reassure critics ultimately failed to protect the democratic system the party had worked to establish after the 2011 revolution. In the 2019 presidential run-off, Ennahda also refused to back media magnate Nabil Karoui, instead throwing its support behind Saied after its own candidate was eliminated. At the time, many within the party viewed Saied as the safer choice, seeing Karoui, a polarising businessman often dubbed Tunisia's "Berlusconi", as too closely associated with the old political establishment. Ahmed Gaaloul, a senior Ennahda official, believes the movement underestimated both the determination of its opponents, both local and regional, and the willingness of Tunisia's international partners to accept the dismantling of its democratic institutions. "We believed that no one would dare overthrow a democratic system that Tunisians had sacrificed so much to build," he said. "We misread the moment." He said that while regional powers hostile to the Arab Spring sought to undermine Tunisia's democratic transition, Europe and the US also failed to defend it. "The fragmentation and weakness was mainly in Europe," he said. "They did not defend our democracy." Instead, Gaaloul said, Western governments increasingly accepted the argument that Tunisia's democratic experiment had failed, while overlooking what he described as an authoritarian rollback. 'We spent years trying to appease everyone at the expense of our own party' - Hatim, Ennahda member "The whole democracy that survived for 10 years after the revolution was being let down," he said. For many younger members, that experience has prompted a broader reassessment of the movement's own approach to power. The arrests of much of Ennahda's senior leadership have accelerated an internal debate over whether the consensual politics that defined Tunisia's democratic transition ultimately left the movement vulnerable. "Many of us respect what Ennahda achieved after the revolution, but we also think it compromised too much," said Hatim, a 28-year-old engineer and member of the group. "We spent years trying to appease everyone at the expense of our own party. Now, the younger generation, including myself, want leaders who are confident enough to pursue their programme instead of always making concessions. "We don't want endless consensus if it means abandoning our Islamic values." That view is increasingly common among younger activists, many of whom believe Ennahda spent too much energy trying to prove to its opponents that political Islam could coexist with democracy, only to see those same democratic institutions dismantled. Former Ennahda MP Maher Madhioub says the movement has spent the past five years reflecting on those failures. "Ennahda was not born in a government or one of the state's institutions, but out of the huge sacrifices of its members over more than four decades," he said. "It was born as a civil, public and universal movement. It won some elections and lost others, but it has always stood with the Tunisian people's aspirations for liberty, dignity and justice. Governing was always a means to an end, not an end in itself.” A different movement If Tunisia eventually returns to democratic politics, Madhioub believes Ennahda will emerge a different movement. "There is no doubt that it has learned a lot from what happened," he said. "It will be more confident in itself, its choices and its competent members, and it will take all its responsibilities." Whether that opportunity comes soon remains uncertain. Saied continues to enjoy the backing of neighbouring Algeria , whose President Abdelmadjid Tebboune recently described Tunisia's security as inseparable from Algiers' own and pledged to defend it against "any threat". His remarks, made days after the fifth anniversary of Saied's power grab, underscored Algiers' continued support for the Tunisian president despite mounting criticism of his authoritarian rule. In the cradle of Tunisia's revolution, anger gave way to apathy. Then Gaza happened Read More » Inside Ennahda, however, there is little expectation of an imminent return to power. Members say their priority is preserving the movement's organisational networks, supporting imprisoned colleagues and preparing for the day Tunisia's political space eventually reopens. "We haven't left the political scene and are still here," said Mohamed, a 31-year-old small business owner. "But in the future we expect the movement to speak more forcefully about what is happening beyond our borders. "Whether it's Palestine, Sudan or other crises affecting Muslims, Ennahda should have a stronger voice and stand up for people facing oppression," he said. "We want a leadership that will challenge others that are harming Muslims. We will not accept silence for the sake of diplomacy," he added. Despite years of repression, Radwan Masmoudi, president of the Center for the Study of Islam and Democracy, believes the movement remains too deeply rooted in Tunisian society to disappear. "Ennahda specifically, and moderate Islamist parties in general, are here to stay," he said. "Any real democracy in Tunisia or in the Arab world cannot exclude such an important and critical part of society. I do think there will be a place for Ennahda in a new democratic Tunisia, just like there will be a place for all other Islamic and secular political movements." For supporters, the movement's future will ultimately depend not on whether it returns to government, but whether Tunisia returns to democracy. "People thought we had disappeared before," Madhioub said. "If Ennahda wins the first democratic elections held after the end of this terrible coup, it will be because it learned from what happened." headline: Netanyahu brands Britain an ‘Islamic republic’ as it prepares Israel sanctions
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 16:21 BST | Last update: 5 days 9 hours ago
article_body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has branded Britain an "Islamic republic", attacking a country whose governments have armed, protected and assisted Israel throughout its genocide in Gaza and wider regional wars. During an interview broadcast by Army Radio, Netanyahu complained that the favourable British coverage Israel received during the 1967 Arab-Israeli war had disappeared. The 1967 war began with Israel’s surprise attack on Egypt and ended with Israeli forces seizing the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula and Syria’s Golan Heights. “Try to find that now in Britain, which you could call the Islamic republic of Britain,” Netanyahu said. When the host responded, “Isn’t all of Europe like that?”, Netanyahu replied: “Yes, but you know, someone said the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic republic of Britain.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Netanyahu's Islamophobic remarks came as London is poised to announce a raft of new policies in September, multiple sources told Middle East Eye, including a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements. Sources said the Foreign Office is looking at imposing new sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in the Israeli settler movement in the occupied West Bank. UK support for Israel But Netanyahu’s rhetoric clashes with Britain’s record as one of Israel’s most dependable European supporters. Under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the Labour government proscribed the Palestine Action group as a terrorist organisation in July 2025. The group had targeted factories and facilities connected to companies supplying weapons to Israel. The ban made membership and expressions of support punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Police have since arrested more than 3,000 people and charged more than 1,200 under terrorism legislation. Exclusive: UK to announce raft of new policies on Israel including settlement goods ban Read More » London also conducted surveillance flights over Gaza during the genocide and shared intelligence with Israel. The Ministry of Defence trained Israeli military personnel on British courses, only pausing future participation late in 2025. Britain’s arms policy exposes the same contradiction. Labour suspended 29 export licences to Israel in September 2024 after identifying a “clear risk” that equipment could facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. Then-Foreign Secretary David Lammy stressed that the decision was “not an arms embargo”. By February 2026 , Israel appeared on 395 non-suspended export licences. Of those, 203 covered military goods, while non-F-35 military licences carried a maximum value of £130m. British support also extended to the war on Iran, with Starmer authorising US forces to use British bases for strikes in March 2026. His successor, Andy Burnham, continued that access in July, helping Washington sustain a war Netanyahu had pushed the United States to fight. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Israel’s ‘pilot zones’: Withdrawal on paper, continued occupation of south Lebanon
author: Giovanna Vial
publication_date: Published date: 15 August 2026 16:31 BST | Last update: 4 days 7 hours ago
article_body: At the entrance to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, a village in southern Lebanon , a Lebanese Army checkpoint marks the edge of what is now officially known as a "pilot zone". It is one of three villages - along with Froun and Srifa - designated as such under the framework agreement between Israel , the United States and Lebanon, signed in June 2026. On paper, the pilot zones, whose implementation began on 20 July, are meant to work as a formula: a gradual Israeli withdrawal, paired with a handover of sovereignty to the Lebanese Army, and the end of Hezbollah's armed presence in these locations. But Daniel Meier, professor of political science and director of the Master in Middle Eastern Studies at Sciences Po Grenoble, says Israel has sought to use the mechanism for a different purpose. "Israel sees these pilot zones as another tool to undermine any possibilities for Hezbollah to continue in the south of Lebanon, and not for withdrawing its army," he said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "The main goal for them is to use the pilot zones to continue their occupation and slow down to the maximum their withdrawal from south of Lebanon.’" Standing at the Lebanese Army checkpoint in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh (West Zawtar), the contradiction at the heart of the agreement is visible in real time: just a few hundred metres away, in Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh (East Zawtar) Israeli forces remain in place, carrying out near-daily demolitions and bombardments. Data gathered by Public Works Studio, a Beirut-based research and mapping collective tracking Israeli attacks on Lebanon, documented Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh among the villages targeted by house demolitions, ground incursions, controlled explosions, arson and "tajrif" - the levelling of land with heavy machinery - between late June and late July 2026. During Middle East Eye's time on the ground, five explosions coming from Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh were heard, with smoke rising over the horizon. Coordinating access with the Lebanese Army, MEE was escorted into the centre of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Lebanese armoured vehicles were present along the dirt road leading into the village. Entire structures were reduced to rubble, evidence of repeated Israeli air strikes on the village, while bullet holes scarring the remaining walls pointed to ground assaults by Israeli tanks. (Giovanna Vial/MEE) The aftermath of Israeli attacks in the southern Lebanese village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh Yet, contrary to what the scope of the pilot zones might suggest, there were no traces of a sustained Israeli ground presence, nor any signs that soldiers had occupied or lived in the village. The hallmarks of Israeli occupation documented elsewhere in Lebanon - Hebrew graffiti sprayed across walls, human waste left behind, and residents’ belongings ransacked and strewn about, as seen in villages such as Yaroun and Ayta al-Shaab in 2024 - were nowhere to be found in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Nor could the idea of the village's "return" to Lebanese sovereign control be verified on the ground, despite the presence of the Lebanese military. The main access to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, let alone anything resembling a return to normal life for its residents, remains blocked by the continued Israeli presence in the surrounding area. "There is no restoration of Lebanese authority while Israeli occupation remains,’" said Meier. "This is just another trap, another trick in misusing language, misusing words. The ‘pilot zones’ were designed to give some sort of credit to the idea of Lebanese sovereignty restoration while Israel tries to escape its responsibilities and continue its oppressive occupation strategy without any clear endgame." Uninhabitable Abbas Heri, 40, had just returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, his hometown, which he fled in February 2026. "As long as they [the Israelis] don't leave Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh, there will be no life here in the village," he said, explaining that the main road connecting the village to Nabatieh, the largest city in southern Lebanon, remains inaccessible because of the Israeli presence in Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh. 'The main goal for the Israelis is to use the pilot zones to continue their occupation and slow down to the maximum their withdrawal from south of Lebanon' – Daniel Meier, professor of political science "My house is here, but it is unhabitable. Everything is destroyed. And there's no security either. Last night, for example, I slept at some friends' place here in the village, but there were explosions all night long," he said. "In other words, they [the Israelis] are doing something that stops life from continuing, so people can't go back to living here." The framework agreement between Israel, the United States and Lebanon fails to specify when - or whether - Israel will vacate the broader "buffer zone" it has carved out along the border, an area Israeli officials say they intend to hold for as long as Hezbollah remains armed. Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, as well as Froun and Srifa, sit near the outer edge of the "Yellow Line" - the new, self–declared boundary Israel has drawn to mark its zone of military control inside Lebanese territory, and the same line that gives the buffer zone its shape. Heri spoke with MEE in the central part of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, near a tent where people had gathered around a small makeshift stall selling coffee, water and cigarettes. "It is because of these injustices that the resistance emerges and endures," Abbas said when questioned about Hezbollah's presence in the village. "Resistance movements emerge because of injustice. Would you accept someone occupying your home without defending yourself? I mean, under what law would that be acceptable?" For Lebanese like Abbas Heri, the concept of the pilot zone - much like the framework agreement that produced it - feels abstract, even irrelevant, next to the reality on the ground. "The West talks about human rights… What human rights? I have a three-year-old daughter who can already tell the difference between the sound of a plane and the sound of an explosion," he said. "If this was happening in Europe, the state would show up, the police would show up, everyone would show up. They'd film it, they'd do something to look after people's psychological state. Who is going to compensate us for what the Israelis are doing to us, and how?" No sign of occupation In Froun, the second "pilot zone" visited by MEE, residents echoed much of what Heri had said. The village used to be just a 10km drive from Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, but the road that once connected the two has been destroyed in Israeli strikes, forcing a detour that now takes more than an hour to complete. "I cannot understand how our government is negotiating with the Israelis," said Assem Jaffar, an elderly man sitting amid the rubble of what used to be the facade of his house. "I just hope they don't keep negotiating with the Israelis until they leave, until they get out of our territory." Jaffar lost his daughter, son-in-law and granddaughter to Israeli bombardments. "It's not possible to live in Froun today. The ceasefire they claim exists doesn't exist in practice. The resistance isn't attacking Israel, but they keep attacking us." Assem Jaffar lost his daughter, son-in-law and granddaughter to Israeli bombardments (Giovanna Vial/MEE) In Froun, MEE saw the same pattern of destruction found in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Civilian infrastructure has been devastated: the handful of houses still standing stick out against a landscape otherwise flattened by Israeli bombardments. Yet there is no sign that the village was ever effectively occupied by the Israeli army - no evidence of the kind of ground presence that would need to be handed over to the Lebanese Army, as its "pilot zone" status implies. "These villages, so-called pilot zones, have not been occupied by the Israeli army," Meier said, adding that the Lebanese government has been under intense US pressure to embrace President Donald Trump’s vision of a "new Middle East". "The price, however, is high: accepting to negotiate with Israel and agreeing with pilot zones which actually just reinforce the erosion of Lebanon's sovereignty." 'We, the children of the south' Abou Ali, a Froun resident who had recently returned to begin rebuilding his home, said the Israeli army never entered his village or Srifa. "The Lebanese army wasn't here before either. They only came recently to set up a few checkpoints." It's not possible to live in Froun today. The ceasefire they claim exists doesn't exist in practice. The resistance isn't attacking Israel, but they keep attacking us' – Assem Jaffar, Froun resident His account was consistent with what MEE observed on the ground. There was no Lebanese military presence in Froun itself, only in the surrounding area. At the village’s entrance, MEE found that the checkpoint was manned by Hezbollah rather than the Lebanese Army. "The agreement they made was a huge mistake," Abou Ali said, referring to the June 2026 framework agreement. "This government has brought us to where we are today, and we cannot accept this agreement, because it doesn't benefit us in any way. "We, the children of southern Lebanon, do not accept any kind of negotiation with the Israeli government." MEE’s visits to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh and Froun, along with interviews with residents and observations on the ground, point to a clear gap between the framework agreement’s premise and the reality in these villages. Israeli forces destroyed large parts of both, but there was little evidence of the sustained ground presence that the "pilot zones" designation implies. The agreement creates the appearance of a gradual Israeli withdrawal and a handover of control to the Lebanese Army. In Froun's case, however, there was no sustained Lebanese Army presence to speak of at all. Meanwhile, the "withdrawals" from these pilot zones have coincided with continued Israeli military activity elsewhere in southern Lebanon, including in the village of Hadatha. Territory framed as relinquished in one location exists alongside expanding operations in another, leaving the overall footprint of Israel's presence in southern Lebanon - which makes up about one-fifth of Lebanese territory - largely unchanged. headline: Trump labels Strait of Hormuz ‘US territory’ as Iran says Israel is biggest obstacle to negotiations
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 14:23 BST | Last update: 1 day 9 hours ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump has claimed the Strait of Hormuz as American territory as his frustration mounts over a war with Iran that has resisted his demands and dragged global shipping into crisis. Trump posted a map of the strategic waterway on Truth Social on Tuesday bearing the caption “New US Territory”. The provocation revived his threat last week to declare the strait American territory following an Iranian “surrender” that never came. Instead, Tehran has tied the reopening of the passage to Washington fulfilling an interim agreement, including ending its naval blockade, lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets. Iranian parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Tuesday the waterway would remain closed until Washington honoured its commitments. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “Let me state clearly: Until the commitments made by the United States in the memorandum of understanding, including the lifting of the blockade, the release of frozen assets, the lifting of oil sanctions, the end of threats and military operations on all fronts, and other conditions to which America agreed in the memorandum, are implemented, the strait will not be opened,” Ghalibaf said. Israel 'remains the biggest obstacle' Traffic through the strait remained in single digits on Monday as negotiations stalled. Preliminary Kpler data recorded six commodity vessels, evenly divided between inbound and outbound traffic, against a 10-day average of about 11. Only three vessels crossed on Saturday and two on Sunday. No supertankers or liquefied natural gas carriers passed through, although Kpler said ships operating without transponders may not appear in the figures. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a departing vessel had been hit on Tuesday. Centcom chief visits US carrier enforcing Iran blockade amid reports of severe strain on crew Read More » “The Company Security Officer has reported that the vessel was struck by an unknown projectile while conducting an outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz,” it said. “The impact caused damage to the engine room and resulted in a crew casualty,” it added, adding that the remaining crew were being assisted by the Omani coastguard. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused Israel of working to derail negotiations and prolong the conflict. “The Zionist regime was and remains the biggest opponent and obstacle to the implementation of the memorandum of understanding. They made every effort to prevent such an agreement from being reached, every effort to make this agreement fail, and every effort to prevent it from being implemented,” he said in comments carried by IRNA news agency. Araghchi said Trump’s demand for Iran’s “unconditional surrender” had collapsed and that Tehran forced Washington to negotiate on Iranian terms. According to the report, Araghchi said those who “sought an unconditional surrender, within a short time of the war’s commencement, were begging for negotiations. “It was us who said we would not accept a ceasefire and continued the war until we reached a point where they accepted a ceasefire and negotiations on Iran’s terms,” he said. Stalled negotiations Qatar said mediators would resume efforts to end the US-Israeli war and restart talks after Iran and Oman reached a bilateral agreement governing transit through the strait. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy said Trump had failed to establish any route towards nuclear concessions from Tehran. “It’s crystal clear that there is no current path to get Iran to give up its nuclear program,” Murphy wrote on X. “They are toying with Trump and his diplomatic ingenus,” he said. “They know they can get complete sanctions relief and all their frozen money without a single nuclear concession.” The disruption has spread through the global economy. China’s refined fuel exports rose 6.7 percent in July after Beijing eased wartime controls introduced to shield its domestic market from supply shortages. Inside Iran, annual inflation reached 66 percent, while food and drink prices surged 128.1 percent year on year. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli soldiers number Palestinian detainees on their foreheads
author: Fayha Shalash
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 13:21 BST | Last update: 16 hours 26 min ago
article_body: Israeli soldiers marked Palestinian detainees with numbers on their foreheads and arms while interrogating them in the occupied West Bank on Monday. During a military raid on Qabatiya, near Jenin, Israeli forces rounded up dozens of Palestinian residents, several of whom were marked with numbers on their foreheads and arms. Mahmoud Nazzal said that Israeli soldiers stormed his family’s home after dawn prayers, breaking down the doors of the three-storey building before gathering his parents and his brother’s family inside. The soldiers handcuffed his father and took him outside, while Nazzal was forced to sit on the floor of the stairwell with his hands bound. The family initially thought the soldiers would conduct a brief interrogation and leave. Instead, dozens of men were brought into the house and questioned. Nazzal said the number of detainees exceeded 70. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “I was sitting in the corner and couldn’t see everything that happened, but I witnessed pushing and hitting as the detainees were taken away and interrogated. They were also numbered on their hands, foreheads and stomachs,” he told Middle East Eye. The detention lasted from about 5 am until 2 pm. Nazzal said soldiers initially refused to give the women and children water or milk. His diabetic mother suffered a drop in blood sugar and needed insulin before soldiers allowed assistance to reach her. “I was left lying on the ground, unable to move, for 10 hours while handcuffed. I was also prevented from using the bathroom. I saw someone being beaten as he left the house after his interrogation,” he said. One elderly detainee with a heart condition also became seriously unwell and needed an ambulance to take him to hospital after his release, Nazzal said. 'Horror movie' Nazzal described their experience as “a horror movie” and said they needed specialised help to overcome the psychological trauma. His father, Mufid Nazzal, 67, said he was the first person arrested during the raid. He said soldiers marked his hand and forehead with a number, as they did with other detainees, and kept him handcuffed throughout his detention. “The soldiers would gather the detainees in the rooms, with about 10 people held in each room, before taking some back for interrogation or releasing others. Three floors of the house were used to detain the prisoners, while the second and third floors were designated for interrogations,” he said. Mufid said detainees were pushed and subjected to violence as they were moved between floors. He could not always see what was happening but said he heard and witnessed some of the pushing on the stairs. “They released me after 10 hours, and I was in a bad state because I was handcuffed the whole time. I felt severe pain after my release,” Mufid said. One of those brought in to the house was Ahmad al-Hathnawi, who was marked with the number 44 on his forehead. “This is the first time they’ve put these numbers on me,” Hathnawi, who has been arrested four times previously, told local media. بينهم نساء وأسرى محررين.. جيش الاحتلال ينكل بالمحتجزين خلال حملة اعتقالات واسعة في بلدة قباطية جنوب جنين. pic.twitter.com/AbL0iSxxuw — شبكة قدس الإخبارية (@qudsn) August 17, 2026 He said soldiers ask him general questions during the interrogation and said they didn't want people causing problems when settlers came to the city. “They are basically trying to send a message that if settlers come into the area, there will be no problems, and that the settlers are going to remain here for a long time.” Hathnawi said the interrogations were intended to terrorise families and deter them from resisting the expansion of settlements around Jenin. The Israeli army confirmed that soldiers had marked the detainees with numbers, saying that “lessons have been learned”, according to Israeli media. The army made similar comments in April after Palestinian women from Jenin were marked with numbers on their arms. In 2024, Israeli soldiers also marked a group of Palestinian detainees from Hebron with numbers on their foreheads. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: UAE billionaire questions normalisation with Israel after Ben Gvir calls for nightly killings of Palestinians
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 14:01 BST | Last update: 2 days 11 hours ago
article_body: A prominent Emirati businessman who championed normalisation with Israel has questioned whether regional peace can be achieved while Israeli ministers openly demand the mass killing of Palestinians. Khalaf Ahmad al-Habtoor, one of the UAE’s most prominent billionaires and a former member of the Federal National Council, accused Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir of a “dangerous moral decline”. Ben Gvir called on Sunday for Israeli forces to kill “30 or 40” men, women or children in Gaza every night. He said Palestinians were “not worthy of life” and “not even people”. In a post on X on Monday, Al Habtoor said “an Israeli government minister steps out before the world, openly and without shame, calling for the killing of 30 or 40 people in Gaza every night, and speaking of people as if they are ‘not deserving of life’!” “What mind can accept this rhetoric?” he asked. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Habtoor is not a government official, but the Dubai-based billionaire is close to the UAE’s ruling circles. The government tightly controls public expression, particularly among prominent Emiratis, making his intervention notable. “If an official in the Israeli government can speak this way openly, without shame or fear of accountability, how can we, at the same time, be asked to speak of peace, negotiations, and coexistence?” Al Habtoor wrote. Habtoor did not call on the UAE to suspend relations, impose sanctions or use its considerable economic leverage against Israel. Nor did he say how Arab and Muslim countries should respond to Ben Gvir’s call for nightly killings of Palestinians. Trading partner Nearly three years of genocide in Gaza have not stopped the UAE from maintaining full diplomatic, commercial and security ties with Israel. The UAE remains Israel’s largest Arab trading partner. Bilateral trade reached $3.2bn in 2025, even as Israel continued killing Palestinians in Gaza after signing a ceasefire with Hamas last October. Former UAE presidential aide's post mocking Pakistan exposes unease over Mecca pact Read More » Habtoor’s intervention carries particular weight because he strongly defended the Abraham Accords in 2020. He argued that Arab recognition would moderate Israel and encourage concessions to the Palestinians. “The more Israel is connected with its Arab neighbors on multiple levels, the more it will be open to making compromises,” he wrote at the time. Since then Israel committed genocide in Gaza, deepened its apartheid system in the occupied West Bank and expanded illegal settlements at record speed. It attacked and occupied parts of Lebanon and Syria , bombed Qatar , Yemen and Iraq , and pushed the US into a war with Iran that plunged the region into chaos and inflicted global economic damage. “The people of Gaza are human beings. Their children are human beings. Their women and men are human beings. And they have the same right to life and dignity as we all do,” he added in his post. This is not Habtoor’s first public intervention. In March, shortly after the Israeli-US war on Iran began, he accused President Donald Trump of dragging Washington’s Gulf partners into “danger” and betraying Americans by putting war at the “top of your priorities”. headline: UK appeals court upholds anti-Zionist beliefs as protected under equality law
author: Areeb Ullah
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 16:55 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: A UK Appeals Tribunal has upheld a landmark ruling that anti-Zionist beliefs remain protected under equality laws, rejecting the University of Bristol’s challenge to findings that it unlawfully discriminated against a professor by dismissing him over comments expressing those beliefs. In a judgement handed down on Tuesday, the Employment Appeals Tribunal (EAT) upheld an employment tribunal’s findings that Professor David Miller’s dismissal over his anti-Zionist beliefs amounted to unlawful direct discrimination because of his protected philosophical beliefs. The appeal tribunal held that the lower tribunal "had not erred in any of its conclusions on liability", including its finding that Miller's beliefs about Zionism qualified for protection under the Equality Act 2010. "It is coherent to describe as “racist” an ideology [Zionism] that promotes the establishment of a state [in this case, Israel ] for only one race of people [Jewish] in a territory that formerly contained a large number of people of a different race [Palestinians]," said the judgement. "Such an ideology, which supports the migration of members of the first group into the territory with the support of an imperial power to dislodge an indigenous population, could also coherently be described as colonial and imperialistic.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters An earlier tribunal, in 2024, had ruled that Professor David Miller’s dismissal over his anti-Zionist beliefs amounted to unlawful direct discrimination by the university, which challenged that decision. The EAT rejected Bristol's challenge and held that the lower tribunal "had not erred in any of its conclusions on liability", including its finding that Miller's "philosophical beliefs" about Zionism were "protected" under law. Miller, a professor of political sociology who joined the University of Bristol in 2018, was dismissed for gross misconduct in October 2021 following public comments he made earlier that year about Zionism, Israel and Jewish student organisations. His research focused on lobbying groups, including organisations linked to states such as Israel and South Africa. In its 2024 ruling, the employment tribunal had found that Miller had been dismissed because of comments expressing his anti-Zionist beliefs, which it held were protected philosophical beliefs under the Equality Act 2010. 'Decisive' victory It concluded that both his dismissal and the rejection of his internal appeal constituted unlawful direct discrimination. The former academic described the judgement as a "decisive" victory for the anti-Zionist movement and said the "pressure campaign" against him had "spectacularly backfired" Oxford Union declares Israel an 'apartheid state responsible for genocide' Read More » "The University of Bristol’s attempt to overturn my 2024 Employment Tribunal victory has been comprehensively dismissed. We won on every single count," Miller wrote on X. "This is a public humiliation for the genocidal Zionist regime, whose assets in Britain bullied the University into sacking me and then dragged them into this futile appeal." The appeal tribunal agreed with the court's conclusion that Miller's beliefs - that political Zionism is inherently racist, imperialistic and colonial and should therefore be opposed - qualified for legal protection. The tribunal also agreed that Miller's February 2021 statements were manifestations of those beliefs and had materially influenced the university's decision to dismiss him While accepting that the university was pursuing legitimate aims, including protecting students and its reputation, the tribunal had concluded dismissal was a disproportionate response because Miller's comments were lawful, were not found to be antisemitic, did not incite violence and did not threaten anyone's safety. It found a lesser disciplinary sanction would have been sufficient. The EAT upheld that reasoning. The appeal tribunal also upheld the original tribunal's finding that Miller had contributed to his own dismissal through comments directed at Jewish students and student societies. It agreed that any unfair dismissal compensation should therefore be reduced by 50 percent. However, it found the tribunal had not sufficiently explained its conclusion that there was a 30 percent chance Miller would have been fairly dismissed in 2023 over later social media posts, meaning that aspect of the remedy must be reconsidered. headline: Spanish commentators accuse Israel and US of involvement in Ceuta crisis
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 1 August 2026 14:03 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 4 days ago
article_body: A Spanish minister has suggested Israel was stirring problems over 60,000 migrants crossing from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta. Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, posted on X on Friday: "Spain, which never misses an opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy. "Maybe before it continues lecturing us, it's time it explained to the world why it still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa," he added. Sharing Danon's post, Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente remarked : "Well, it all seems to be becoming quite clear." This comes as numerous Spanish politicians and commentators have alleged that Israel and the United States have sought to cause trouble for Spain in retaliation for the Spanish government's opposition to the US-Israeli war on Iran and Israel's war on Gaza. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Gabriel Rufian, the parliamentary spokesperson for the Republican Left of Catalonia, a left-wing party, argued that the crisis served American and Israeli interests. Spanish journalist Jose Vizner, meanwhile, shared a 2019 social media post by Yair Netanyahu, the son of Israel's prime minister, discussing alleged Israeli support for separatism in Ceuta. Prominent Spanish actor Javier Bardem shared a video accusing Israel of being behind the crossings. Former Portuguese minister and commentator Bruno Macaes said that "whether or not the US and Israel were involved before the fact, they were deeply involved and intensely active after the fact, especially trying to use it against the current Spanish government". Ceuta, a Spanish territory on Morocco's Mediterranean coast, and Melilla, another Spanish autonomous city on the country’s northern coast, share the only land borders between the European Union and Africa. Some 60,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco this week, including around 8,000 children, according to the Spanish government. Footage posted online showed people swimming into the enclave around the border barrier, with some wearing swimsuits and using flotation rings to make the dangerous journey. Diplomatic spats over migrant crossings France said it was increasing checks along its border with Spain, while Italy threatened to suspend Spain from the EU's internal open-border scheme. But on Saturday, Spain said most migrants, around 48,000, had already returned to Morocco, ushered by Spanish soldiers. Videos online showed migrants hiding in tunnels and walking around on the streets of Ceuta. At least 67 people are believed to have died while attempting to reach the enclave. It is unclear what prompted the wave of attempted crossings, but there have previously been similar incidents. In May 2021, 8,000 Moroccans entered the enclave amid a diplomatic dispute between Spain and Morocco over Western Sahara. At the time, Spain accused Morocco of using migrants as leverage, and a Moroccan minister said Morocco was justified in relaxing its border control as a response to the diplomatic dispute. Thousands make dramatic sea crossing into Ceuta from Morocco Read More » Some commentators have accused Morocco of facilitating this week's crossings, pointing to the Moroccan government's anger at Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's recent visit to Algeria , Spain's biggest gas supplier. Lorenzo Gabrielli, a senior researcher at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona who researches migration in Ceuta, told the New York Times: "It is impossible for nearly 50,000 people to cross the border between Morocco and Spain in a single day without Morocco having a hand in it." Ceuta President Juan Jesus Vivas condemned the migration as a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity". Morocco's ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, said : "We have always prioritised legal, orderly and safe migration for all." She insisted the crossings had been against the wishes of the Moroccan government. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the situation a "catastrophe" and added that "if we're not in office our country will be invaded at levels that will make Spain look small time". headline: Israeli press review: Israel’s genocide in Gaza costs over $140bn
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 10:59 BST | Last update: 1 day 14 hours ago
article_body: Cost of Israel’s genocide in Gaza The cost of the Israeli genocide in Gaza has reached some 420bn shekels ($140bn), and is likely to hit half a trillion shekels soon, according to an investigation by TheMarker published on Sunday. “The price of one day of weakness is terrible, and therefore we must not reach that point again,” a former army chief told the Israeli outlet, referring to the military’s failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack in October 2023. “If we had received enough security, there would probably be no need to double the defence budget over the coming decade,” an economic expert told TheMarker, referring to the latest increase in the Defence Ministry’s budget. In 2026, the ministry’s budget exceeded 175bn shekels for the third consecutive year, more than double the 84bn shekel budget in 2022. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters While it is too early to determine whether the additional funds have delivered greater security for Israel, officials told TheMarker that “similar or better results could have been achieved in a shorter war”. According to the report, the Israeli military adopted a costly and wasteful approach to its wars, firing bombs and shells at unprecedented levels in the early stages of the conflict and mobilising some 220,000 reservists. “In the first weeks, too much fire was used,” a former army officer said, referring to the beginning of Israel’s war on Gaza, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. The officer added that Israel quickly ran short of tank shells and bombs. Mamdani 'enemy of Israel' in Likud campaign Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party launched a billboard campaign on Sunday depicting foreign leaders deemed enemies of Israel. Netanyahu shared a picture of the huge billboard in Tel Aviv on X, which features Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem. Zohran Mamdani, the recently elected mayor of New York City, was also featured on the Likud billboard. "They want Netanyahu to lose. Don't let them win," the billboard read. אל תתנו להם לנצח pic.twitter.com/JgvJXAPtia — Benjamin Netanyahu - בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) August 16, 2026 On Monday, Netanyahu uploaded a video featuring Erdogan and Mamdani. It showed the Turkish president comparing Netanyahu with Adolf Hitler and Mamdani describing the Israeli prime minister as a war criminal. “They want Netanyahu to lose,” Netanyahu wrote in the caption, repeating the billboard’s message. Raid on Unrwa facility in Jerusalem The Jerusalem municipality has taken over an Unrwa school and clinic in the Shuafat refugee camp in Jerusalem, Haaretz reported on Monday. According to Roland Friedrich, Unrwa’s director for the occupied West Bank, municipality officials replaced the locks and carried out repairs at the agency’s largest complex in the refugee camp, in violation of international law. 'These are properties belonging to the UN and enjoy immunity under international law' - Roland Friedrich, Unrwa’s director for West Bank Both the school and clinic were closed by the Israeli government over the past year, with the municipality promising to replace the services provided by the UN agency to camp residents. However, Haaretz reported that the municipality has yet to establish a new school for the camp’s children. "These are properties belonging to the UN and enjoy immunity under international law, which explicitly prohibits entry into them without authorisation," Friedrich told Haaretz. "Over the years, Unrwa has invested enormous sums in establishing and developing these buildings," the UN official added, stating he is worried about the latest violation of international law by the Jerusalem municipality. The municipality rejected Friedrich's claim, arguing Unrwa invaded private land and failed to pay for it, adding it intends to build a school for the camp's residents. Early Islamic-era shopping centre uncovered in car park An extraordinary Islamic-era archaeological discovery has been uncovered during excavations beneath the car park of a football stadium in Ramat Gan, a city near Tel Aviv, Haaretz reported on Sunday. Researchers from the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA), the government body responsible for archaeological excavations, said they had uncovered a 2,500-square-metre industrial and commercial complex dating to the late seventh or early eighth century. According to the report, the researchers found streets, kilns, shops and warehouses dating to the period of Muslim rule in historic Palestine. Researchers working at the site believe its construction was planned by a central authority with significant resources, which were directed towards developing the complex. "The main phase at the site was planned in detail and in advance by engineers. It was built with the knowledge of the regional authorities, and perhaps even at their initiative and with their funding," an IAA researcher told Haaretz. The site is believed to have served as a major economic centre for travellers along the road from Jerusalem to Ramla, the district capital at the time. According to the report, researchers do not know the site’s name, who lived there or how it was connected to other communities in the area. They believe it was abandoned in the ninth century, repopulated as a residential site in the 10th century and finally abandoned in the following century. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: ‘Like a battlefield’: How Yemen’s Mocha went from a town of fishermen to a city of fighters
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 12:55 BST | Last update: 2 days 12 hours ago
article_body: In Yemen ’s coastal city of Mocha, the dominant dialect is no longer that of the native fishermen who grew up relying on the sea. Instead, it is the dialect of fighters who fled Houthi-controlled areas. Once a small fishing town, Mocha has transformed into a bustling hub where almost all essential services are available, largely because fighters have settled here with their families. Mocha is a centuries‑old trading city located on the country's southwestern coast along the Red Sea, in the Taiz governorate. Historically, the Port of Mocha was world-famous for exporting Yemeni coffee . However, due to the civil war that erupted in 2014 between the Houthis and the internationally recognised government, the port was closed in 2015. It reopened in 2021 after being rehabilitated by the leadership of the Republican Guard, a faction of Yemen’s former elite military units led by Tareq Saleh and backed by the UAE . Saleh initially fought alongside the Houthis. However, after his uncle, former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, was killed by the group in December 2017, he fled Sanaa and began establishing his own forces in Mocha. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Since then, Mocha has served as the headquarters of the Republican Guard. Drawn by the higher salaries paid in Saudi Riyals, many Yemenis fleeing Houthi-controlled areas have joined the Republican Guard in Mocha. Located approximately 60km from the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Mocha holds a highly strategic position on the Red Sea. As a result, the Houthis have targeted the city repeatedly in the last fortnight. Over the past week, more than 25 Houthi attacks have struck the Port of Mocha. While the Houthis claimed to target military reinforcements and positions, government officials confirmed that 16 civilians were killed and 22 others were injured in Friday's strikes alone. Families should be safe Ibrahim Salem, who is in his 40s, originally comes from Dhamar governorate, around 300km north of Mocha. He joined the Republican Guards in Mocha just seven months ago after managing to flee Houthi-controlled areas, where he had previously served as a Houthi fighter. “The Houthis don’t differentiate between military targets and civilians, so it is better not to keep our families in Mocha. That's why I opted to rent a home for my family in this safe village,” Salem told Middle East Eye as he stood with his three children outside a grocery store in a village located in Taiz’s al-Maafer district, around 100km east of Mocha. ‘The Houthis don’t differentiate between military targets and civilians, so it is better not to keep our families in Mocha’ - Ibrahim Salem, Republic Guards fighter Salem praised the village residents for their warm reception, noting that many other fighters have similarly moved their families to rural areas in the Taiz and Lahj governorates, further east. “It is always better to keep our families far from the frontlines and targeted areas. I initially brought them to Mocha because it was quiet, and there was no fierce fighting in Mocha or surrounding regions,” he added. Yemen has experienced a truce-like status since the UN-mediated ceasefire in April 2022. However, earlier this month, the Houthis resumed attacks against Yemeni forces and critical infrastructure across the Hadhramaut, Marib, Taiz, Al-Dhalea and Hodeidah governorates. Salem acknowledged that Mocha has become a well-known destination for fighters escaping Houthi-controlled areas. “When I walk through Mocha, I sometimes feel like I'm still in Dhamar because I run into so many familiar faces. It makes me forget how far I am from home - though families still need to stay safe, which means staying out of Mocha.” This marks the second time Salem’s family has been displaced: first from Dhamar to Mocha, and now from Mocha to a rural locality. Although life in the village lacks the modern services found in Mocha, Salem said that because his family originally comes from a rural background, they easily adapt to village life. Houthi missile and drone attacks kill dozens of Yemeni government troops Read More » Ramez, 38, another fighter with the Republican Guards who joined two years ago, told MEE he rented a home for his family in a village away from Mocha from day one. He noted that Mocha's reputation as a gathering hub for fighters made him feel the Houthis could target it at any moment. “Villages or cities far from Mocha are safe for families, but we prefer villages because the rent is cheaper than in the cities,” he said. “Nowadays, most of those who have their families in Mocha are scrambling to find homes in villages all at once, as they didn't anticipate the situation becoming so dangerous earlier on.” When visiting some villages in the Taiz governorate, MEE could see many families of fighters now reside there, playing a major role in driving up local house rents. Ramez, who has over 15 years of military experience, said that housing fighters' families should be treated as a key security consideration before anyone even joins a military camp. He noted that bringing families close to active zones is a serious mistake. “Not only in Mocha, but anywhere there is a war, soldiers' families shouldn't stay in the same city or area as military camps; they should remain far away in safe areas,” he added. “I think the majority don't keep their families in Mocha; it's only a few.” ‘We miss the life we used to have’ The situation in Mocha is increasingly difficult, and local fishermen are no longer allowed to sail due to the ongoing escalation. As a result, many of them believe that choosing Mocha as the headquarters of the Republican Guards has stripped them of their livelihood. “Since the beginning of this war in 2015, we have been going from one crisis to another, and fishermen are always the most vulnerable victims,” Akram, a fisherman in his 40s who asked to use only his first name, told MEE. ‘The truth is that these fighters have ruined our town, and they are the main reason we lost our jobs’ - Akram, fisherman “The Houthis know that Mocha is full of fighters, and that is why they are targeting us every day,” he added. “The truth is that these fighters have ruined our town, and they are the main reason we lost our jobs.” Speaking with visible frustration, Akram said all residents in Mocha are suffering today. “Before the war, most residents here worked as fishermen and enjoyed a peaceful life. Since those fighters arrived in the city promising us a better life, we haven't seen anything improve; instead, we just miss the life we used to have.” Akram noted that some fishermen have abandoned their trade to join the Republican Guards because the fighters receive their salaries in Saudi Riyals - an income up to four times what a fisherman typically earns. Yemenis turn to 'Ruqyah' faith healers as medical healthcare remains in crisis Read More » “I only believe in peace and civilian jobs. What we need is peace, but there are some who only care about money and don't think about the future of our area or the next generation,” he added. “The sea used to be our primary source of income, but today it feels more like a battlefield.” Akram hopes this escalation will end soon so that locals can resume their regular lives at sea: sailing freely to catch the best fish, sell to local markets and export to neighbouring countries. Another Mocha resident, Zaher, 46, who asked not to use his real name, works as a driver for an international humanitarian organisation. While he is glad to see Mocha growing every day, attracting aid groups and new investments, he believes the city's safety must come first. “Anyone would be happy to see new opportunities coming to their city, but our biggest challenge today is that we don’t feel safe,” he told MEE. “All we need is security, and I hope the Houthis avoid targeting civilian infrastructure because we just want to live.” As Houthi attacks on Mocha have continued unabated, operations at the seaport have ground to a halt, leaving more than 1,500 port workers without a livelihood. headline: Israel’s Ben Gvir boasts of planned execution facility for Palestinian prisoners
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 15:12 BST | Last update: 10 hours 36 mins ago
article_body: Israel ’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir boasted on Tuesday about the construction of a facility intended for the execution of Palestinian prisoners. “In this place, the terrorists will be executed,” Ben Gvir said in a video posted on Instagram, where he has around 150,000 followers. In the video, Ben Gvir points towards what appears to be an active construction site and says the complex will include “viewing chambers where crime victims will be able to come and watch” Palestinians being hanged. "We are fulfilling what we promised," the minister added. Ben Gvir also celebrated what he described as a victory over his opponents, saying those who “ridiculed” and “giggled” at his plan to execute Palestinians could now see that “this place is starting to be built”. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Earlier this year, Israel’s parliament approved a bill regulating the execution of Palestinian prisoners convicted of involvement in deadly attacks. According to the law, which was sponsored by Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party, the Israel Prison Service (IPS) will be the agency in charge of the executions. Critics have described it as another discriminatory law, arguing that it can be applied only to Palestinians and not to Israeli Jewish citizens. Former Israeli soldier held captive in Gaza asks Ben Gvir to let him execute Palestinian prisoners Read More » Before the Knesset passed the law in March, the IPS had already begun preparing sites and personnel to carry out the executions, according to Israeli media reports . Three IPS volunteers are reportedly expected to carry out the executions, which would be conducted by hanging within 90 days of sentencing. Last week, Ben Gvir promised Rom Braslavski, a former Israeli soldier who Hamas held in Gaza, that he would do everything possible to allow him to execute Palestinians, after Braslavski said he wanted to kill them with his “own hands”. Ben Gvir told Braslavski that Palestinian prisoners held under his supervision “don’t deserve to live”. During the same interview, the minister also called for the killing of Palestinians in Gaza and their expulsion from the territory. Ben Gvir’s comments sparked international condemnation, with German Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil calling on the European Union to sanction the minister. “These are statements that we, as the German government, cannot accept in any way,” Klingbeil, co-leader of Germany’s Social Democratic Party, told German media on Tuesday, describing Ben Gvir’s language as “dehumanising”. ‘Another official killing mechanism’ Human rights groups have long accused Israel of pursuing a de facto policy of executing Palestinians. In March, before the death penalty law was passed, Yuli Novak, executive director of Israeli human rights group B’Tselem, said Israel “already kills Palestinians systematically and faces no demands for accountability”. B’Tselem has said that under Ben Gvir’s leadership, IPS detention facilities have become “a network of torture camps where inmates are subjected to continuous abuse and violence”. The group added that the death penalty law “adds another official killing mechanism to the existing practices”. As of June, at least 104 Palestinian prisoners have died in Israeli custody since 2023. headline: Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 20:26 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: The Trump administration seems to be struggling to figure out how to get out of its self-made Iran quagmire. According to a CNN report on Monday, the US military is now crowdsourcing ideas among military experts for what to do next in order to push Iran into a deal that is to President Donald Trump's liking. "We are looking for new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran," an email from an officer in US Central Command's (Centcom) intelligence branch read last week, according to the CNN report. A Centcom spokesperson said the move is not unusual, and that it "has a long history of thinking and working in innovative ways". But the email suggests the Pentagon did not plan for the conflict to drag out this long. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The on-again, off-again US-Israeli war on Iran, which began on 28 February, led to Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has sent energy prices skyrocketing and directly impacted Trump voters. On Sunday, Saudi Arabia's state media said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken to Trump over the phone, and reportedly stressed "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce, which paves the way for diplomatic solutions". Talks Iran has denied that any talks are ongoing with the US despite a claim by Trump, who called off strikes on the country on Saturday. Iran denies talks with US as Trump halts strikes at the last minute Read More » Trump announced that negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on new strikes against the Islamic Republic in order to pursue a deal. "Obviously, they don't want to be attacked," Trump told reporters on Sunday on board Air Force One. "Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon." However, Iran's foreign ministry has said there were currently no negotiations with the US but that talks were taking place with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. The foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said discussions with Oman were "constructive" and aimed at reaching an agreement on a new route. "We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a press briefing. "We hope that both regional and extra-regional actors will appreciate this responsible move by Iran and adopt a constructive approach." He added that as long as a US naval blockade on Iranian ports continues, "the situation in the Strait of Hormuz will remain unchanged". Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: ICC states decision on Karim Khan ‘inherently political’, says leading criminal law expert
author: Sondos Asem
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 10:52 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: International law professor William Schabas has expressed his concern over the independence of the next prosecutor of the International Criminal Court following the controversial removal of Karim Khan by member states after an 18-month long misconduct probe. The Assembly of States Parties (ASP), the ICC’s governing body, voted on 24 July to dismiss Khan after deciding that "the elected official... committed serious misconduct and a serious breach of duty" by engaging in "prohibited conduct against a subordinate staff member". The opinion was contrary to the conclusion reached by the judicial process established by the bureau - the executive body of the ASP - to make a legal determination on a United Nations fact-finding investigation that outlined the evidence from the complainant, Khan and more than 30 witnesses. In March, the panel of three judges appointed by the bureau concluded unanimously that the facts presented in the UN probe did not establish any wrongdoing under the relevant legal framework. The July removal vote was based on the recommendation of the 21-member ASP bureau a month earlier that effectively disregarded the judges' panel opinion, finding instead that Khan committed “serious misconduct” by engaging in a sexual relationship with a subordinate. Khan has denied any wrongdoing. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The bureau has also amended the voting rules to lower the threshold for Khan’s removal, from a two-stage vote - in which members would vote separately on whether Khan had committed misconduct and whether he should be removed from his job - to a single vote. 'Great harm has been done to the court in general and to the independence of the prosecutor' - William Schabas, Middlesex University The bureau’s decision and its handling of the investigation have been widely scrutinised by rights groups and legal experts, particularly over concerns that the process had been “politicised” and inconsistent with due process. “The ASP is a political body. Delegates vote on issues in accordance with instructions from their governments,” Schabas said. “A determination by the ASP that ‘serious misconduct and serious breach of duty’ has taken place is an inherently political one,” he added. “The ASP adopted a decision that refers to various sources of evidence that it says were considered. It is not a proper judgment. It is not a judicial decision. It does not indicate what was believed and what was disbelieved by members of the ASP. The Karim Khan saga: a timeline Read More » Schabas also noted that the ASP’s decision “does not identify the specific act or acts that constitute ‘serious misconduct and serious breach of duty’”. He added that while some states may have voted against Khan due to their genuine belief that he committed misconduct, in particular following the CNN interview with the complainant, others inevitably voted based on political considerations. “Undoubtedly, the anger of some States Parties at Khan’s decision to pursue prosecution of Israeli leaders contributed to the decision,” he said, adding that “others may have voted to remove him because they were promised something by Israel or by the United States.” Khan was the first prosecutor in the ICC’s history to seek warrants against sitting leaders of non-African states, including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing, Taliban leaders in Afghanistan, and Rodrigo Duterte of the Philippines. His decision in May 2024 to seek arrest warrants for Israel’s Netanyahu and then-defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza was the first such move against nationals of a western-allied state. It has since prompted sanctions by the US, including against Khan, his two deputies and eight of the ICC’s judges. Prosecutor's independence In the weeks prior to Khan’s removal, US officials have vowed to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick” over its prosecution of Israeli leaders, while President Donald Trump has declared that the US campaign against the ICC is aimed at shielding Netanyahu. The court is currently examining appeals by Israel that seek to invalidate the warrants. “Great harm has been done to the court in general and to the independence of the prosecutor,” said Schabas, when asked about the implications of Khan’s removal on the court’s future. “The next prosecutor will live with the concern that decisions to investigate certain situations and to seek arrest warrants against certain individuals will provoke the ire of some States Parties who may then use the disciplinary proceedings in order to threaten or intimidate the prosecutor.” Former UN oversight chief says ICC prosecutor Karim Khan is ‘victim of massive stitch-up’ Read More » Schabas, who is a leading expert of international criminal law and an authority on the ICC, said the Khan probe was “improvised” and that it did not follow the procedure stipulated in the Rome Statute and rules of procedure and evidence. “The legal framework of the rules, and the approach taken by the Bureau of the ASP, do not offer sufficient protection to the independence of the prosecutor,” he told Middle East Eye. “Due process is important not only in order to protect the rights of the prosecutor but also to protect the independence of the position.” He called for revising the ICC’s rules to ensure that any future decision to remove an elected official is judicial in nature. “In order to ensure prosecutorial independence, it is very important that the prosecutor be confident that she or he can only be removed if a properly constituted tribunal, composed of independent and impartial judges, has made such a determination,” he said. “If such a judgment were to rule in favour of the prosecutor, the ASP would then be without authority to decide on removal."
