headline: How loyalty between Iran and Kuwait gave way to mistrust
author: Amara Sophia Elahi
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 12:57 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: When Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, accused Kuwait of being “part of the fire of the wicked” on social media last week, it was apparent that the previously amicable relationship between the two countries had now soured. “Iran has always adhered to good neighbourliness, but the smoke of ingratitude and the absence of foresight will blind the eyes of the ungrateful,” Baghaei warned . His comments were a reference to the support Iran lent Kuwait during the Gulf War (1990-91), and were made as American military bases in Kuwait came under fire by Iranian missiles. Since the start of this year’s aggression, American bases across the Gulf have been targeted by Iran, which has long preferred asymmetrical warfare to direct confrontation, and have been significantly damaged as a result. Kuwait has denied that the USA has launched strikes from air bases on its territory, and its defence ministry spokesperson described Iran’s actions as “criminal aggression". New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Before recent tensions, relations between the two states had been tested over the decades. They took a downward turn when Kuwait aligned itself with Iraq after President Saddam Hussein invaded Iran in 1980, but became more cordial in the aftermath of the Gulf War. Iran and Kuwait had long maintained diplomatic, commercial and cultural ties, but Saddam’s war on Iran (1980-88) changed that. Kuwait provided financial and logistical support for the Iraqi president’s war efforts against Iran, offering billions of dollars in loans, and allowing its port to be used to transport Iraqi weapons and supplies. "They had concerns about Revolutionary Iran," Dr Alam Saleh, a lecturer at the Australian National University, told Middle East Eye. After the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran, Kuwaiti leaders feared that Iran’s new government might gain dominance over the Persian Gulf region. They also worried that Iran might incite Kuwait's sizeable Shia population to revolt against the Al-Sabah monarchy. During the 1980s war, Iran was blamed for attacking Kuwaiti oil ships and targeting the US and French embassies, Kuwait International Airport, and the hijacking of Kuwait Airways flights. “Direct Iranian state responsibility for these attacks has never been conclusively proven,” Saleh observed. Forever wars In August 1990, just two years after the end of the Iran-Iraq War, Saddam invaded Kuwait, allegedly because the Gulf state was overproducing oil by using American technology to drill in Rumaila, southern Iraq. This had led to a global slump in oil prices and damaged Iraq’s fragile economy, which was already in debt from war with Iran. Israeli attacks reawaken Gulf war trauma as Iranians attempt to flee Tehran Read More » Days before the invasion, Saddam held a meeting with the US Ambassador to Iraq, April Glaspie, who seemingly implied that America would not intervene in Arab regional conflicts. Saddam viewed this as a green light to invade Kuwait, a territory he had previously claimed belonged to Iraq. America did end up becoming involved, however, and led a coalition of 42 countries to fight by air and on the ground against Saddam’s forces. The war created a humanitarian crisis, with over a million people in Kuwait fleeing to neighbouring countries. Iran welcomed thousands of refugees, including foreign nationals who had been working in Kuwait, people who were stateless, and Iraqi nationals. Mobile camps in the southwestern province of Khuzestan, on the border with Iraq and Kuwait, were set up providing food, shelter and safe passage, and the Iranian government granted political asylum and organised flights for people stranded by the conflict. UK MPs who visited the camps commended Iran’s efforts to help refugees from Kuwait, according to records from the time. During a parliamentary debate in 1991, Michael Jopling, then a Conservative MP, observed: “My impression of the camps was that things were going reasonably well. “The Iranians seemed to be dealing adequately with the massive crisis which confronted them.” Burning oil wells Before Iraqi troops were forced to retreat in Kuwait by American-led coalition forces, Saddam commanded them to sabotage key infrastructure, including electrical grids, water systems, civilian buildings, and its oil industry. Not only did they blow up refineries, storage tanks and pumping stations, but they also dumped millions of barrels of oil into the Persian Gulf, causing an unprecedented environmental disaster and the largest marine oil spill in history. Blair urged Kuwait to buy UK arms in 'recognition' of Gulf war support, memos show Read More » Furthermore, Iraqi forces deliberately ignited over 600 oil wells in Kuwait, resulting in crude oil leaking out and producing toxic plumes of smoke and black rain that travelled as far as Iran. "The smoke from the oil wells spread into southwestern Iran, causing air pollution, health concerns, and environmental damage,” Saleh explained. As a result, Iran assisted with international efforts to extinguish the burning oil wells by sending a team of 47 oil industry experts and engineers to Kuwait, in what was the largest oil firefighting operation in history. "They had gained extensive experience repairing oil facilities and extinguishing fires during the Iran-Iraq war after repeated Iraqi attacks on Iran’s energy infrastructure,” Saleh said. The Iranian team was assigned to Burgan in the southeast of Kuwait, where the country’s largest and most heavily damaged oil field was located. After shipping their own machinery and equipment to Kuwait, they successfully managed to cap 28 oil wells, whilst working in dangerous conditions including being surrounded by unexploded Iraqi landmines. The operation was considered a diplomatic gesture of goodwill by Tehran towards its Gulf neighbour, as both countries now shared a common enemy in Iraq, and it helped to improve relations between them over the subsequent decade. "Throughout the 1990s Iran and Kuwait expanded diplomatic dialogue, trade and security cooperation while managing their differences pragmatically,” Saleh explained. US expansion In the aftermath of the Gulf War, the US began establishing military bases in the region, and over the decades expanded its presence there. There are 19 US bases across the Middle East today. Kuwait hosts five of them, the largest number of any Middle Eastern country, where 13,500 American troops are stationed. Iran hits US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan after 10 nights of US attacks Read More » Some analysts have suggested that America was deliberately luring Iraq to invade Kuwait so that it had a legitimate reason to permanently deploy American troops into the Persian Gulf and control regional oil production. Iran has always viewed US presence in the Middle East as a threat to its sovereignty and a symbol of imperialism. "Iran opposes all long-term US military bases in the Persian Gulf, arguing that they undermine regional security, but generally separates this issue from its bilateral relations with Kuwait” according to Saleh. Kuwait claims it does not use its territory, airspace or waters for offensive operations, contrary to media reports. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Kuwait, along with Bahrain, secretly dispatched military jets to attack drone and missile storage depots in Iran earlier this month. "Kuwait has served as an important US logistics and command hub,” Saleh said. “Public evidence suggests its facilities have supported regional military operations.” Furthermore, President Trump has publicly thanked Kuwait and other Gulf states for backing his war on Iran, which has been viewed as complicity by Iranian analysts such as Hassan Ahmadian, Professor of West Asian Studies at the University of Tehran. New defence pact This week, Kuwait ratified a five-year defence pact with Pakistan , the country chosen to act as a mediator in Iran-US negotiations, which has led to some Iranian observers raising concerns that this may complicate Islamabad's position as a negotiating partner. Kuwait and Pakistan had already signed a defence partnership in 2023, but recent talks have focused on military training as well as sharing personnel, intelligence and technology. Some analysts have observed that while the pact itself is unremarkable, the timing is not, and that it points to a change in how Kuwait is thinking about regional security, in light of the current war. “Iran will monitor the agreement but is unlikely to oppose it unless it is used against Iranian interests,” Saleh observed. “Since Pakistan has also acted as a mediator, Tehran is expected to maintain constructive relations with both countries while closely watching developments in the Persian Gulf.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Fear grows among Egyptians in UAE over residency cancellations, report says
author: Alex MacDonald
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 14:41 BST | Last update: 1 day 10 hours ago
article_body: Egyptians in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) face fears over their long-term residency in the country after a number of nationals had their permits cancelled earlier this month. Several Egyptians living and working in the UAE have reported that their residency permits were unexpectedly revoked, leaving them unable to return to their jobs. Posts shared online also suggest that a new Police Clearance Certificate requirement for Egyptian work permits may be complicating plans to change jobs or travel to Egypt, even though no official change in UAE residency rules for Egyptian nationals has been announced. The New Arab reported that Mahmud Adel, a 33-year-old schoolteacher, travelled to Egypt in July for his annual holiday and was preparing to return to Sharjah three weeks later when his employer informed him by email that his residency had been cancelled. "This was shocking, because the administration didn't mention any reasons for the residency cancellation," Adel told the publication. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The report also quoted 36-year-old interior decorator Abdel Rahman Ahmed, who said he discovered his residency had been cancelled when he arrived at Cairo Airport to return to Abu Dhabi after spending time in Egypt. "At first, I couldn't believe it, but I tried to contact the company in Abu Dhabi," Ahmed said. Ahmed said company officials did not answer his calls, bringing an abrupt end to his eight-year career in the UAE. Why Egypt held back from joining Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan's defence pact Read More » Other Egyptian workers have reported similar experiences on social media, with fear spreading among employees, forcing many to reconsider travelling home. “I’m scared that if I travel anywhere, I’ll be one of the unlucky people,” a user wrote on the social media platform Reddit. Some expatriates and business owners have also decided against travelling to Egypt for fear that they could lose their residency status before returning to the UAE. According to the Egyptian diplomatic mission in Abu Dhabi, some 1.3 million Egyptians were working and living in the UAE by the end of 2024. Egypt received $43.1bn in remittances from its expatriate community in the first 11 months of the fiscal year 2025-26. The two countries have been close allies for years, and the Gulf state has been a major investor in the North African nation. However, there have been splits over regional issues, including in Sudan, where they supported opposing sides of the conflict in the country. Middle East Eye contacted the Emirati embassy in London for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Trump 'cancels' Iran strikes as Israeli attacks on Gaza continue
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 2 August 2026 11:45 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 3 days ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump has said he would hold off on a fresh attack on Iran as long as a deal could be reached quickly on Iran's nuclear programme and reopening the Strait of Hormuz completely. The announcement came after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had informed his Turkish , Pakistani and Saudi counterparts that the Islamic Republic would act "decisively" in the event of any further US "aggression". Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that its Aerospace Force targeted the US F-35 repair hangar and ramp at Al-Azraq Base in Jordan with multiple ballistic missiles on Saturday, as the US reportedly geared up for major strikes targeting Iran's energy infrastructure. But on Saturday night, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that Iran and "other Middle Eastern Countries" asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to "the Immediate, Complete and Total" reopening of the Strait and "an end to Iran's nuclear threat". "Based on this request," Trump continued, "I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL". New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters He added that Israel "joins me in this commitment". Citing US officials, Axios said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had called Trump on Saturday and urged him to de-escalate tensions and refrain from launching the strikes. According to Saudi state media on Sunday, the crown prince stressed "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce, which paves the way for diplomatic solutions". He also said diplomatic solutions should "yield positive results for preserving the security and stability of the region and prevent it from being drawn into a wider conflict". Israeli attacks on Gaza Meanwhile, Israeli attacks on Gaza have continued. The Israeli military said it killed two Hamas commanders with air strikes on Friday and Saturday in Gaza. The two were reportedly Salem Jamal Abd al-Rahman Abu Labad, an alleged cell commander in Hamas's Nukhba special forces, and Muhammad Abd al-Nasser Muhammad Khatib, an alleged commander in Hamas's Maghazi Battalion. Then on Sunday, Israeli strikes killed nine Palestinians in Gaza, including three children, Al Jazeera Arabic reported. Israel's genocide in Gaza has killed 73,356 people since October 2023, according to the Palestinian health ministry in Gaza. The 'Board of Peace' announced a Palestinian body will take Hamas weapons. That's not what Trump said Read More » On Sunday morning, a Hamas delegation met officials from Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Cairo, with the two groups stressing the need to force Israel to end its military offensive and fully withdraw from Gaza. The groups called for "developing joint action and unified national positions, and exerting all efforts to protect the Palestinian people and restore their legitimate rights". This comes after Trump on Friday said that the "Board of Peace" would collect Hamas's weapons as the group begins to disarm, even though the board itself had announced that a Palestinian technocratic body would assume that role. Hamas insisted any agreement for "complete disarmament" of Palestinian factions in Gaza depends on Washington and Israel honouring commitments made under the 10 October ceasefire deal. Ghazi Hamad, a Hamas representative, told Reuters on Friday that the group would retain its weapons until Israel halted its attacks, allowed more aid and goods into Gaza, and withdrew its forces. headline: Israel kills nine in Gaza police station bombing
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 13:50 BST | Last update: 10 hours 27 min ago
article_body: Israeli air strikes killed at least nine Palestinians at a police station in Gaza City on Wednesday, in the latest escalation as mediators push to advance the fragile ceasefire. Gaza’s Police Department said Israeli fighter jets dropped several bombs on the Gaza Governorate Municipalities Police Headquarters. Paramedics said at least nine people were killed and 15 others wounded. Local media reported that several senior police officers were among those killed, including Colonel Faten al-Sahhar, the head of the Women's Police Department. The police officials described the attack as a “brutal massacre”. Gaza’s Ministry of Interior said Israel was seeking to spread chaos in the territory by targeting the police force. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A separate Israeli air strike in central Gaza on Wednesday killed another Palestinian. The latest killings came a day after an Israeli air strike hit a cafe in Gaza City, killing at least seven people, including a child. Tuesday’s strike was the deadliest single attack in Gaza in weeks. Hamas condemned the attack as a “war crime”, saying its timing confirmed Israel’s intention to undermine mediators’ efforts to advance the Gaza ceasefire. The Israeli military said it targeted “Hamas operatives” who were planning attacks on Israeli troops, but provided no evidence to support the claim. The military routinely uses similar allegations to justify attacks in Gaza. Kushner's green light The escalation comes after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met US special envoy Jared Kushner earlier this week to discuss efforts to advance the fragile ceasefire in Gaza. After the meeting, Kushner gave Israel the green light to “finish the job” against Hamas if it refused to disarm. Before travelling to Israel, Kushner, whose family has longstanding ties to Netanyahu, visited Egypt, where he met Hamas leaders as part of efforts to advance the talks. Hamas said last month that it had agreed to a US-led plan to gradually disarm and implement the ceasefire agreement signed in October, in exchange for a complete halt to Israeli strikes and the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza. There is no ceasefire in Gaza Read More » Israel rejected the proposal. Hazem Qasem, a Hamas spokesperson in Gaza, said the US-led so-called “Peace Council” bore responsibility for the latest escalation, accusing it of failing to “fulfil its responsibilities by pressuring the occupation and compelling it to abide by what was agreed”. “The Peace Council now faces a real test of its ability and seriousness in managing mediation and negotiations,” Qasem said. He also accused “officials” from the US-led body of making “contradictory statements” that “give the occupation cover to escalate its aggression”. In an interview with Fox News after meeting Netanyahu, Kushner said the US would not allow reconstruction in Gaza until Hamas gives up its weapons. “We’re also not going to restrict Israel’s right to defend itself if there are any imminent threats,” Kushner said. The October ceasefire was intended to end Israel’s two-year genocide on Gaza, during which Israeli forces killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and destroyed around 90 percent of homes across the territory. Israel has repeatedly violated the ceasefire, with near-daily air strikes and a continuing siege on Gaza. Since the ceasefire was signed, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians, including at least 300 children. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: UAE issues rare denial of 'imperial ambitions' in Africa
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 19:21 BST | Last update: 2 days 5 hours ago
article_body: The UAE has pushed back against a Financial Times (FT) article charting the Gulf state’s growing military and economic footprint in Africa. In a rare rebuttal published by the FT on Monday, the UAE’s director of strategic communications, Afra al-Hameli, said Abu Dhabi was “disappointed” that the newspaper portrayed it as pursuing an “imperial ambition” in Africa. “To describe partnerships negotiated with sovereign African governments as evidence of ‘imperial ambition’ is deeply patronising,” Hameli wrote. “It relies on a stereotypical and outdated narrative portraying African states as passive recipients of foreign influence incapable of identifying priorities that serve their national interests”. The article came in response to a series of FT articles that have examined the UAE’s expanding footprint in Africa, often corroborating Middle East Eye’s coverage of Abu Dhabi’s activities. An FT article published earlier this month exposed how the UAE has built up a network spanning ports, logistics, agriculture, mining, finance, and security interests in Africa. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A follow-up investigation by the FT revealed that a UAE-based security company with links to the government recruited and deployed Colombian mercenaries to fight alongside Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan’s civil war. Though the UAE continues to deny it, there is now widespread evidence supporting the claim that the UAE supports Sudan’s paramilitary RSF, which has been accused by the United Nations and the US of committing genocide during the war in Sudan. UN experts , human rights groups and reporting from MEE have documented arms transfers to the RSF facilitated by networks based in Libya, Chad and the breakaway region of Somaliland. The FT investigation published on 4 August opened with the RSF's pilferage of 1.5 tonnes of gold bullion, worth roughly $100m, from the state-owned Khartoum gold refinery at the onset of Sudan’s war. The report said the UAE supplied military and civilian cargo planes to remove the gold, which transited through Chad and South Sudan. The investigation also documented the network of Emirati airstrips, naval bases, and military facilities instrumental to mercenary deployment and the illicit gold trade in Sudan, alongside evidence gathered by UN experts, flight-tracking specialists and human rights organisations concerning arms-trafficking networks sustaining the counterrevolutionary war. 'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance Read More » On the commercial side, the UAE has expanded throughout Africa with groups like DP World and Abu Dhabi Ports, securing port concessions and logistics infrastructure across the continent. DP World now operates or is developing ports, inland terminals and free zones in 13 African countries, while its distribution networks extend into more than 25 African states. Emirati entities have committed billions to mining copper in Zambia, gold in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia and Mali, iron ore in Mauritania, and tin in eastern Congo. The FT said the UAE has become the most “consequential foreign power to stamp its mark on the continent in the past decade”. Cameron Hudson, a former US intelligence official and expert on Africa, said the UAE’s rebuttal contained “a flaw [in] logic”. “Two things can be true simultaneously: UAE can make mutually beneficial, strategic economic investments AND harbor imperial ambitions that leverage those investments for political and strategic gain. In fact, they are both true,” he wrote on X. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia
author: Miriyam Ilavenil
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 09:49 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: On 15 July, Anwar Ibrahim, the prime minister of Malaysia, said authorities would deport any Israeli nationals found in the Southeast Asian country, while strongly expressing that Malaysia would "not compromise" on its immigration policies. "If we find any Israeli, we will deport them immediately because we do not recognise Israel," the prime minister said, according to local media reports. His comments came as officials investigated allegations that Israelis were involved in a private residential and technology community in the southern state of Johor. Johor Chief Minister Dato Onn Hafiz Ghazi stated that at the state level, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) and relevant agencies would re-examine the Network School's business regulations. He also called on the federal bodies of the Home Affairs, Immigration Department, Police and Customs Department to investigate the allegations of Israelis in the Network School. Malaysia's federal Home Affairs Ministry later that day ordered a probe. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters After two rounds of investigations, the Immigration Department said there were no violations among the 379 foreign nationals it investigated at the Network School, adding that 19 individuals' movements could not be traced. The Immigration Department's Director-General Dato Zakaria Shaaban said that these individuals could have entered or left the country illegally. He added that authorities are on the lookout for the untraced individuals. Then, on 17 July, Ghazi issued several notices to the Network School after authorities found that one of the premises linked to the school was operating without a valid business licence. On 23 July, the United States summoned Malaysia's ambassador to the US, Tan Sri Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob, to explain the nation's position on Israel. The Malaysian government stated that it would not change its immigration stance towards Israel. Founder of the Network School, Balaji Srinivasan, announced on X that he wanted an audience with the prime minister to restore his confidence in Malaysia as an investable jurisdiction. Balaji Srinivasan: Venture capitalist and Zionist ally Balaji Srinivasan, a former Silicon Valley venture capitalist and Stanford professor, publicised the Network State in 2022. Marketing it vaguely as a startup society focused on peace, Srinivasan proposed building a "startup country" from the internet up. The Network State describes the idea on its website as "crowdfunding territory" and "eventually gaining diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states". Malaysia vows to deport Israelis found in digital nomads community Read More » The website calls this new state a composition of an "ethnic diaspora" in which emigrants are connected with "the motherland" and come together in person to build dwellings and structures. "In a sense, you can think of each physical outpost of this digital community as a cloud embassy," it says, adding that "recruits can visit either the virtual or physical parts of a network state, beta test it, and decide to leave or stay". Along with Srinivasan, the Network State is financed by tech entrepreneurs Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Joe Lonsdale, Patri Friedman, as well as crypto firms like Coinbase and Praxis . Peter Thiel's Palantir has invested in Israeli military and surveillance startups accused of providing technological support to Israeli intelligence in the Palestinian genocide. Praxis, a company funded by Marc Andreessen, Sam Altman and Peter Thiel, has proposed building a tech-owned city on Greenland after US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to take the territory by force. Trump has also shared the intent to build a Trump luxury resort in Gaza. Critics argue that the Network State model resembles historical settler projects because it envisions digitally organised communities purchasing or controlling physical land. Some scholars have also pointed to Srinivasan's frequent references to Israel as an example of successful nation-building, arguing that his writings draw inspiration from Israel's state-building experience. In 2024, centring the pitch around proximity to Singapore, Srinivasan formed the Network School in Malaysia's Forest City, in the southern state of Johor. Making of Forest City: Fisherfolk and reclaimed land The project's location in Malaysia's Forest City in Johor has added another layer of complexity. In a recent video podcast , Srinivasan alludes to the Network School being born out of "nothing into something". The "nothing" on which the multibillion-dollar development is built is termed "reclaimed" land in Johor and has faced criticism for its environmental impact on coastal ecosystems and local fishing communities. Forest City is a joint venture between China's Country Garden Group and Malaysian private company Iskandar Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd (EDBS), whose shareholders include Johor's Sultan Ibrahim and interests linked to Johor's ruling political party, United Malays National Organisation. Palestinian engineer 'killed by Mossad' in Malaysia, says family Read More » Between July 2024 and June 2025, Malaysia attracted about $759m in data centre investments, with Johor emerging as a key hub alongside the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. An extensive investigation by Mongabay revealed how a Chinese builder began construction in the Forest City without an environmental impact assessment, devastating local seagrass and sparking strong community criticism. The project also saw massive sand dumping , which destroyed marine habitats and hundreds of hectares of traditional fishing grounds. Rights groups have previously raised concerns that most of Forest City's workforce comprised low-wage labourers from South Asia, especially Bangladesh. The project has drawn controversy again, after allegations circulated online that Israeli nationals were participating in the Network School. The dispute exposed contradictions between Malaysia's pro-Palestine foreign policy and its efforts to attract international technology investment, even as government officials have maintained that enforcement actions were based on regulatory compliance rather than political considerations. Neocolonial Malaysia: US imperial base, pro-Zionist hub The developments surrounding the Network School have fuelled a wider debate over Malaysia's balancing of its support for the Palestinian cause and economic relationship with the United States and western capitals. The country is shaped by a constitutional monarchy, where political and economic power is concentrated among the federal government, state authorities and royal institutions. Israel condemns Malaysia's decision to bar its athletes from competing Read More » The Federation of Malaysia was violently formed in 1963 and has since come down heavily on the people's movement in Malaya (West Malaysia) and Borneo (East Malaysia). Some scholars and Bornean political movements in the Sabah region have described the federation as a colonial project aimed at resource extraction, allowing projects like the Network State to be built without much public resistance. In 2024, Malaysia allowed a subsidiary of BlackRock to join a consortium to take ownership of Malaysia Airports (MAHB), Khazanah Nasional and the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), under the jurisdiction of the finance ministry led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. Civil society organisations in the country called on Ibrahim to make "the right and conscionable decision" by excluding the "Zionist entity conducting a settler-colonial and racist genocide in Gaza". Local media reported that the administration "launched an aggressive media campaign to discredit critics of the plan". In April, several international defence companies with business relationships with the Israeli military participated in the Defence Services Asia (DSA) and National Security (Natsec) Asia 2026 exhibition in Kuala Lumpur. Companies included Lockheed Martin, a US defence contractor that supplies aircraft and other military equipment to Israel, MBDA, a European missile manufacturer whose products have been exported to Israel, and Colt's Manufacturing, a US firearms producer whose weapons are used by the Israeli military. Malaysia police free Palestinian kidnapped by Mossad agents: Report Read More » Civil society members pointed to investment links between Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby and Caterpillar, whose bulldozers have been used by the Israeli military in demolitions in the occupied Palestinian territories. They also cited the operations of Australian rare earths producer Lynas in Malaysia, arguing that rare earth minerals are used in global defence supply chains, including those serving Israel. Malaysian ports have also been used to facilitate shipments linked to Israel's military supply chain during the ongoing genocide in Gaza, transporting $885 million in weapons to Israel between 2023 and 2025, Al Jazeera investigations have found. In 2025, Ibrahim welcomed Trump during the ASEAN Summit despite protests against his visit. Police maintained tight security, while rights groups accused Malaysian authorities of detaining and intimidating pro-Palestine protesters during peaceful demonstrations. While officials have maintained that the country cannot sever ties with every international company that has business links to Israel, the Network School controversy has exposed Malaysia's projection of a pro-Palestine foreign policy alongside its ambition to attract foreign technology investment. Johor remains a key destination for data centres and AI investments as part of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli settlers paralyse Palestinian nurse in West Bank shooting
author: Fayha Shalash
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 13:08 BST | Last update: 2 days 11 hours ago
article_body: Israeli settlers shot and partially paralysed a Palestinian nurse in a town near Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Saturday. Muhammad Mutoor, 26, suffered gunshot wounds that severed his spinal cord during a settler attack on Sa'ir, a town northeast of Hebron. Another Palestinian man was also shot in the shoulder with live ammunition. Khalil Mutoor, Muhammad's uncle, told Middle East Eye that Muhammad went to the area after hearing about the attack. As a nurse, he wanted to help the injured. But when he arrived, a settler shot him in the back. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters He said settlers had spread through the area, terrorising residents and firing live ammunition at them. "They aimed to kill, and they didn't care about anything,” Khalil said. “They were firing live ammunition randomly and had climbed onto the hill adjacent to the houses, aiming their weapons at the residents. One of their bullets struck Muhammad in the back. They intended to kill him.” 'They intended to kill him' - Khalil Mutoor, wounded nurse's uncle Ambulances were unable to reach Muhammad because settlers had blocked access to the area after establishing a new outpost in the al-Adisa neighbourhood in the town, to force Palestinian residents out. Residents instead drove him to the nearby town of Bani Na'im before he was transferred to hospital. "Like any Palestinian patient or injured person, Muhammad faced difficulty reaching the hospital. When he arrived, it was discovered that the bullet had severed his spinal cord," Khalil added. “He knew immediately after being shot that he was paralysed, given his work as a nurse.” Muhammad is preparing to transfer to Al-Makassed Hospital in Jerusalem for further consultations, despite doctors giving little hope that he will regain function in his lower limbs because of the severity of the injury. Muhammad recently built a house in the area and had planned to marry and settle there. He worked at Dura Governmental Hospital. Now, his uncle says, those plans have been shattered and his future is uncertain. "Now he only hopes for treatment and to adapt to his new reality. He knows perfectly well that his injury is serious and will affect him for the rest of his life," Khalil said. Eight settlement outposts The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in army-protected settler violence against Palestinians in villages and towns across the occupied West Bank, with Hebron one of the main targets. Around 1,800 Palestinians live in al-Adisa, where the attack took place. The area sits on the frontline of settlement expansion, east of Route 60, a settler bypass road that has taken over large swathes of land belonging to Sa'ir, Hebron and neighbouring towns. To the west lie the settlements of Kiryat Arba and Kharsina. For years, Palestinians in the area have faced attempts to restrict construction and development, alongside attacks on agricultural land and olive trees. The pressure has gone beyond preventing Palestinian expansion to the gradual seizure of land. In 2012, settlers, protected by the Israeli army, planted trees on parts of the lands of al-Adisa and al-Buq'a. The area affected was estimated at around 500 dunams (50 hectares) at the time and later became the site of attacks on trees and property. Yousef Tarwa, an activist from Sa'ir, said that settlers have established eight outposts on the town's lands since May 2025, spreading in all directions, seizing thousands of dunams and making life increasingly difficult for residents. Israeli settler who stripped Palestinian naked and zip-tied his genitals released from house arrest Read More » He said al-Adisa is repeatedly targeted by settlers seeking to terrorise residents and drive them from the area, despite some homes dating back to 1940. "A month ago, they entered the area and carried out extensive bulldozing operations on Palestinian lands under the protection of the Israeli army. They burned an entire hill, erected caravans, assaulted the residents and then began blocking the roads," Tarwa told MEE. With settlers blocking the main road, residents have been forced to use rough, unpaved tracks to reach their homes, turning journeys that once took minutes into hours of hardship. "On the day Mutoor was wounded, the Israeli army was present alongside the settlers and did nothing to stop them,” Tarwa explained. “It has become clear to us that the settler, the soldier and the Israeli policeman are all the same.” Just hours after the attack in al-Adisa, Palestinian media reported another settler attack nearby in Hebron's al-Ja'bari neighbourhood. Ten Palestinians were wounded, including two who were shot with live ammunition. The Israeli army arrested one of the wounded men. Rising toll The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it had documented more than 1,330 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across 250 Palestinian communities since the beginning of 2026, as of 20 July. The incidents amounted to more than six attacks a day. At least 18 people have been killed and 880 more wounded during settler attacks in 2026. The figures mark a sharp rise from the previous year. In 2025, Ocha documented around 830 Palestinians wounded by settlers across the entire year. More than 2,300 Palestinians had also been displaced in 2026 as a result of settler attacks and related access restrictions, according to Ocha. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem across roughly 300 settlements and outposts. The settlements are regarded as illegal under international law, according to the International Court of Justice. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: US-Saudi strikes test Iraq's balancing act between Riyadh and Tehran
author: Zahra Ladha
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 13:43 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: The unprecedented joint US - Saudi strikes on Iran -linked militias in Iraq last week have done more than raise the prospect of retaliation. They have exposed the fragile foundations of Baghdad's effort to balance closer ties with Riyadh and Washington while containing powerful armed groups aligned with Tehran, potentially forcing Iraq to make difficult choices that it has long sought to avoid. On 29 July, US and Saudi forces launched joint strikes on bases belonging to Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 members of the paramilitary and four advisers from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, according to Iraqi and Iranian media. The strikes, which marked the first time Riyadh has publicly joined strikes alongside the US, were in retaliation for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities launched from Iraqi territory. However, neither Riyadh nor Iraq's Iran-linked militias currently appear to want a sustained military confrontation. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry described the joint attacks as an act of "self-defence" while signalling that the kingdom would carry out further strikes if attacks on its soil resumed. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters These strikes also come at a sensitive moment for Iraq as it moves to bring weapons held by non-state armed groups under state control and deepen political and economic ties with the US and Saudi Arabia, placing renewed pressure on Baghdad to balance internal security with regional relations. Saudi deterrence Riyadh’s statement suggests it is seeking to avoid opening a new front with Iran-linked militias in Iraq while continuing to face Houthi threats from Yemen targeting its oil facilities and maritime trade. The strikes therefore appear aimed primarily at restoring deterrence against Tehran and its Iraqi allies, rather than opening a new front. Iraq's new PM wants business deals with Trump, but militias cloud visit Read More » “The strikes were targeted at specific militia sites linked directly to drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities, to deter these groups,” Dr Hesham Alghannam, a Carnegie Middle East scholar based in Riyadh, told Middle East Eye. “But killing Iranian military advisers alongside militia fighters was not accidental. This was a message to Tehran that Saudi Arabia holds Iran responsible for what its personnel direct from Iraqi soil, regardless of which formation pulls the trigger.” Similarly, while the Islamic Resistance in Iraq (IRI), an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias that includes the PMF, has vowed retaliation for the strikes, its rhetoric towards Riyadh has been more measured than its stance towards Washington. In a statement released on its Telegram channel on 29 July, the IRI said its “response to the American enemy is inevitable” while adding that it may target Saudi Arabia “if circumstances require”. Sending a message The IRI has given Baghdad until 7 August to respond to the US-Saudi strikes, but the deadline and threats of further escalation may also be aimed at influencing the government’s domestic policy. Some IRI-linked groups, including Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba and Saraya Awliya al-Dam, have called on Baghdad to sever ties with Saudi Arabia, suggesting that the pressure is also intended at shaping Iraq’s broader political response rather than signal an imminent escalation. 'Killing Iranian military advisers alongside militia fighters was not accidental. This was a message to Tehran that Saudi Arabia holds Iran responsible' - Hesham Alghannam, Carnegie Middle East scholar “These factions typically don’t set deadlines for retaliation or attacks, rather they launch surprise attacks,” Mustafa Alsaray, director of research at Al-Bayan Centre for Research and Planning, told MEE. “When they set such deadlines, they intend to send a message and achieve something, perhaps politically or in terms of security,” he added. Still, the groups may also be holding off until they can coordinate their response with Tehran. “Another possibility is that the groups are waiting for developments in the Iran-US conflict before coordinating their response with the wider Axis of Resistance,” Alsaray said. The Iran-US war has shown signs of de-escalation in recent days, with US President Donald Trump saying that direct negotiations with Tehran are under way. He also warned that the latest round is Iran's “last chance” to secure a deal. However, a renewed confrontation could prompt these groups to launch further attacks on Saudi Arabia, and potentially Jordan or other Gulf states. Complicating reform efforts The recent developments are likely to test whether Baghdad can advance its long-stalled security reforms and preserve growing economic and political ties with Riyadh. The US-Saudi attacks come as Baghdad seeks to further integrate the PMF, which is formally part of Iraq’s security apparatus but includes factions that retain significant autonomy. The government is also pursuing its disarmament plan, setting a 30 September deadline for armed groups to comply. However, the recent strikes on PMF bases, and Baghdad’s perceived inability or unwillingness to prevent them, have hardened some factions’ refusal to disarm. Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, secretary general of Kataeb Hezbollah, said that the US-Saudi attacks on Iraq have “reinforced the group’s commitment to retaining and developing its weapons”. Exclusive: Syria, Iraq and US plan to unveil Mediterranean pipeline deal to bypass Strait of Hormuz Read More » Likely in a bid to maintain public support, the IRI has also explicitly linked the strikes to Baghdad's disarmament push, challenging the government, which has "called for the Resistance's disarmament" to prove it can defend Iraq. As resistance to disarmament grows, the economic costs of Iraq’s stalled security reforms are becoming increasingly apparent. During an official visit to Washington in mid-July, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi signed 48 partnerships and agreements with US firms. However, US officials have indicated that deeper economic ties will depend on Baghdad’s ability to constrain or disarm militias involved in recent attacks on US military and diplomatic facilities. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq claimed responsibility for dozens of such attacks during the US-Israel war on Iran. Saudi Arabia could adopt a similar approach to investment in Iraq. Prime Minister Zaidi has said Baghdad is seeking an “economic partnership with Saudi Arabia”, but a failure to constrain these groups could undermine prospects for Saudi investment. “September 30 is the real test. If the disarmament process fails - on the same day US forces are set to withdraw from Iraq - Riyadh and even Abu Dhabi will quietly conclude that Baghdad cannot deliver, and their willingness to invest in Iraq will be reconsidered accordingly,” Alghannam said. headline: After three years apart, a Gaza father returns to his wife - and six death certificates
author: Nada Nabil
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 12:58 BST | Last update: 12 hours 6 min ago
article_body: Ahmed al-Siqali had been dreading his return to the Gaza Strip for almost three years. The father of seven left the Palestinian enclave to work in Israel a week before the genocide began in October 2023. With the crossing closed, he remained trapped in the occupied West Bank, unable to return to his family for more than two years. In December 2023, an Israeli strike hit the home where his family was sheltering in Gaza City’s al-Sahaba neighbourhood, killing six of his children. Since then, the prospect of returning had been a source of anguish. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Last month, Israeli forces raided a compound in Qalqilya in the West Bank where he was staying with other Gaza labourers. He was detained for two weeks before being finally sent back to Gaza. “Returning to Gaza and embracing my family had been my dream, especially during my time in prison and after everything I was subjected to,” al-Siqali told Middle East Eye. “The torture and humiliation were so unbearable that every moment, I wished for death,” he said. “But I wanted to run away from that moment. I was terrified of seeing my wife and my daughter without my six children.” A final goodbye Before 7 October, Palestinians regularly travelled to Israel and the occupied West Bank for work under permits issued by the Israeli authorities, taking jobs in construction, agriculture and services. “I never imagined that the moment I said goodbye to my children before leaving to work in another part of our homeland would be the last moment I would ever spend with them,” al-Siqali recalled. 'We were scared to die': The West Bank workers hiding in bins to reach Israel Read More » “I never imagined the journey meant to build their future would separate our fates, leaving me unable to protect them or even say goodbye.” As the war began, he struggled to contact his family as communications repeatedly went down across Gaza. On the rare occasions he reached them, his children pleaded with him to come back. “We want you beside us. We don’t want work or money. We just want you to be with us,” they would say. On 8 December 2023, after numerous failed attempts, al-Siqali managed to contact his family using an eSIM. “In those few minutes, they were terrified, and my words couldn’t protect them from their reality,” he said. “I had a terrible feeling. I asked my wife to write their names on their hands in case something happened to them. Then the call was cut off.” Dream house Minutes later, one of al-Siqali’s relatives called. “He said the house where my family had been sheltering had been bombed. My wife and children had been caught in the strike.” Al-Siqali could not believe the news. “There are no words that can describe what I felt at that moment. It was something no human being should have to endure.” 'What did my children do to have their dreams taken away and be killed like this?' - Ahmed al-Siqali, Palestinian father Six of his seven children had been killed. Rosan was the only child to survive. “What kept me going was learning my wounded wife and daughter Rosan were pulled alive from the rubble.” Separated from his family, al-Siqali spent his days looking at photographs and videos of his children. “I thought of them constantly, endlessly rewatching photos and videos of our family trip to al-Nour resort just days before I left,” he said. “They were so happy. They told me how grateful they were to me.” He had bought a house near the sea in al-Sudaniya, north of Gaza City, hoping to fulfil his children’s dream of living close to the beach. The house was later destroyed. “I worked to fulfil their dreams. I still remember their joy walking through the house, picking rooms and wall colours.” Mohammed and Muhannad had dreamed of a large room. The twins, Kinan and Rayan, and Basant dreamed of going on outings with their father. Eileen was only two months old when the attack happened. Her father had seen her just once. Al-Siqali spent the years of war waiting to return to his wife and Rosan, but the closure of the crossings made that impossible, until last month. ‘Incomplete reunion’ On 21 July, while speaking to his wife on WhatsApp, al-Siqali heard unusual movement outside and the sound of dogs. He warned her to take care of herself and Rosan, believing the army was about to arrest him. Israeli forces raided the building and arrested all the workers inside, including al-Siqali. Two weeks later, he was released from Ofer prison and transferred back to Gaza alongside 23 other workers. Handcuffed and blindfolded during the four-hour journey to Kerem Shalom, they were handed over to the Red Cross and taken to Nasser Hospital. “As I walked towards the crossing, my legs could barely carry me. I felt as though I was about to lose consciousness,” al-Siqali said. “All I could think about was my incomplete reunion, the reunion I had waited so long for. It had finally come, but my family was no longer whole. 'Instead of my children being there to welcome me, I was welcomed by their six death certificates' - Ahmed al-Siqali “What did my children do to have their dreams taken away and be killed like this?” Since the beginning of the war, Israel has killed more than 21,000 children in Gaza and the West Bank, according to the United Nations. Thousands more are missing and presumed dead. “Instead of my children being there to welcome me, I was welcomed by their six death certificates,” al-Siqali said. At Nasser Hospital, al-Siqali’s wife, Hayat, 36, was waiting for him. “I received the news of his release at 2pm, after two weeks without knowing anything about him,” Hayat told MEE. “My heart pounded, and I wanted to fly to him, yet I didn’t know how to face him without our six children.” When the Red Cross bus arrived, relatives and friends ran towards al-Siqali and embraced him. Hayat remained frozen. “I couldn’t run. I couldn’t even walk. I felt completely unable to move.” When al-Siqali approached her, their reunion after nearly three years apart was silent and filled with tears. Then Hayat told him: “Forgive me. I couldn’t protect what you entrusted to me.” Hayat had endured the family’s loss while recovering from her wounds and being repeatedly displaced. “After the strike that killed our children, I was in terrible psychological pain because of losing them. I was also physically injured,” she said. A new reality The family now lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. For al-Siqali, adjusting to life there has been another ordeal. “It is extremely difficult for him to adjust to life in a tent, especially during the summer, when the heat burns our bodies,” Hayat said. Gaza genocide: How Israel made horror a ritual of daily life Read More » More than 90 percent of Gaza’s buildings have been damaged or destroyed, forcing nearly 1.9 million people into displacement, including 800,000 living in makeshift tents, according to the United Nations. The tents offer little protection from the elements and leave people exposed to insects, rodents and disease. “When we returned from the hospital to our tent, I cannot describe the expression on my husband’s face,” Hayat said. “He was shocked by the scale of the destruction and the broken roads. Now, inside the tent, he is facing another shock: the primitive conditions in which we are living.” For Hayat, her husband must now find a way to rebuild a life that has been shattered. “Beyond losing our children, he now has to support us, yet as a construction worker, he faces a completely collapsed sector in Gaza.” Back in the tent, al-Siqali spends much of his time lying on a thin mattress, scrolling through photographs of his children saved on his phone. Their six death certificates lie beside him. He looks at them, holds them close and repeats: “This is all I have left of them.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: 'They almost killed my child': Women in Syria's Roj camp describe night of gunfire and fear
author: Reem Aouir
publication_date: Published date: 2 August 2026 16:01 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: Kurdish-led armed forces opened fire inside Syria's Roj camp on Friday evening, with bullets tearing through tents housing children, after several days of protests by women demanding better treatment inside the facility, according to multiple accounts shared with Middle East Eye. No one was reported killed or wounded. But women inside the camp, which holds thousands of foreign women and children, relatives of suspected Islamic State (IS) group fighters, described a night of chaos and terror that has left them and their children severely traumatised. MEE reviewed videos, images and voice recordings obtained from sources inside Roj camp, which appear to show the aftermath of the confrontation, including the sound of gunfire and scenes of panic among women and children. Friday's violence followed several days of what women in the camp described as peaceful protests demanding an end to alleged abuses and repatriation to their home countries. The incident comes amid growing concern from rights groups over conditions inside Roj and renewed calls for international intervention. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters MEE reported in June that violations inside Roj had increased "significantly in both frequency and severity" since January, according to a report by the Swedish-based organisation Repatriate the Children (RTC), which drew on testimony from more than 40 women held in the camp between January and May. According to several women who spoke to MEE, the confrontation began around 6pm when Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) personnel entered the camp in armoured vehicles and established a “human shield” on the main road. Detainees said women began gathering to understand why the forces had entered, before being ordered back to their tents. Hoda Muthana, a woman detained in the camp, said the situation escalated after women challenged the soldiers' presence. "The Kurds provoked the women for their own propaganda. The women then reacted, and the Kurds began to shoot in the air, but one soldier shot through the tent," she told MEE. War on Iran: Who are the Kurds and what does Trump want from them? Read More » Muthana said bullets tore through a neighbouring tent belonging to an Indonesian family before passing dangerously close to where her son was sheltering. "My child had been lying there for about half an hour already before the shots went through," she said. "The tent is all material. We don't know where to hide. Our nightmare came true. We are always in a routine of shielding ourselves inside the tent." "If the shot had been one or two feet lower, it would have hit my child," she added. "I couldn't move from fear. We were only a few feet apart. They almost killed my child." Muthana’s testimony also shed light on what she described as calculated propaganda tactics employed by the SDF. She claimed that soldiers used their mobile phones to record the women’s reactions during the confrontation, aiming to create a narrative that would portray the detainees as “inhumane and radical” to international observers. "The administration in Roj camp is propaganda con artists," she said. "They are always thinking of ways to make us look inhumane and radical so the public and governments don't sympathise with us." Muthana said the stand-off lasted roughly four hours. She added that several women nearest the guards were beaten during the confrontation. According to Dalal*, a Bosnian woman detained in Roj camp whose name has been changed for safety reasons, the protests were triggered by a violent beating of a Russian detainee who refused to hand over her money and mobile phone during a night raid earlier that week. "The protests were a few days ago... and they started because the Kurds beat up a woman from Russia because she didn't want to give them her personal money and phone," she told MEE. Syrian government and SDF agree ceasefire and integration deal Read More » She said the assault reverberated across the camp. "That night they hit her so hard that it echoed through the camp." According to Dalal, the incident marked a turning point after months of alleged night-time raids, beatings and confiscation of personal belongings, prompting women to resist security personnel entering the camp openly. "That night the women gathered their courage for the first time, and everyone came out to see what was happening," she said. "Since then we haven't let them enter the camp." Dalal said the women believed the confrontation on Friday was a direct consequence of that resistance. Dalal travelled to Syria in 2015 on the urging of her husband, who was later killed. She said she remained trapped in IS-held territory because she had no safe way to leave until she eventually escaped in 2017, but was then subsequently detained by Kurdish forces before being transferred to Roj camp, where she has remained ever since with her two children. "I want deportation," she said. "I do not want to stay in Syria." Another woman inside the camp, who spoke to MEE on condition of anonymity, citing security concerns, said many of those who confronted the guards on Friday were unwell, unarmed and had gathered only to protect their children. "Those mums in the camp, the majority are sick - no medical attention for years - or [have] had injuries from before, overweight and unarmed," she said. "All they do is just gather to protect a child and to speak with the soldiers." She said her two young children believed they were about to be shot after gunfire erupted inside the camp, saying they had already experienced bullets passing through a neighbouring tent during an earlier incident. "My daughter, who is just seven, ran and hid under a plastic chair," she said. "The kids were screaming. Even I found myself screaming. It's a moment you can't control, especially when your whole family is already living with PTSD." She also expressed that years of detention had left many families physically and psychologically exhausted, arguing that the latest violence underscored the urgency of finding a lasting solution for those still held in the camp. "We are humans, and those innocent children have rights too," she said. "For a decade we've been seeing our children live in extreme danger. Please react before it's too late." Images shared with MEE from sources inside Roj camp (Provided) Several women who spoke to MEE believed the latest escalation was linked to broader political developments in Syria, arguing that tensions inside the camp had intensified as the country's new authorities gradually assumed a greater role in the northeast. "I can tell the PKK [Kurdish Workers Party] and YPJ [Women's Protection Units] are extremely angry with the coalition and the new government, and they take it out on unarmed, sick women and children," one woman said. Muthana elaborated on her belief that Friday's confrontation had been deliberately staged to portray the detainees as violent and extremist. "They want to provoke us to create reactions, and these reactions are then shown to countries or the Syrian government to keep us under their control," she said. “The Kurds use a blanket judgement on us all and treat us inhumanely because they believe we came here to commit genocide against their people. I was 20 when I came to Syria and had never even heard of the Kurdish race before. Many younger women have said the same,” she said. “Our captivity is personal for them, and in their ideology, which in my opinion is similar to ISIS, they are allowed to do anything they want to us. They've told us numerous times that if the world wasn't watching, they would've raped and killed all of us,” she added. 'We knew it was coming': Belfast violence leaves Syrian supermarket in ruins Read More » Most of the women now hoped the Syrian government would eventually assume responsibility for the camp. "We want the Syrian government to take control of this camp," Muthana said. "All we want is to go home and be with our families." Friday's shooting is not the first time women in Roj have reported guards firing weapons during a confrontation. Human Rights Watch reported in February that a Trinidadian woman described a similar episode on 31 January, when security forces arrived at her tent "shooting in the air" before ordering women out into freezing temperatures. Roj camp, near the Iraqi border in Hasakah province, is administered by the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (DAANES) and guarded by the Kurdish-led SDF. It holds around 2,300 people, mostly foreign women and children, as of MEE's most recent reporting, and became the country's last major detention camp for relatives of suspected IS fighters after the collapse of the larger al-Hol camp in January. MEE has contacted the SDF for comment, but received no reply by the time of publication. As Damascus seeks to expand its authority in eastern Syria, women such as Muthana say they are increasingly placing their hopes in the government, which she described as the only possible escape from a camp that has become unbearable. "If the devil offered us a safe haven away from the Kurds, we would take it," she said. "All we want is to go home and be with our families." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Why are Kurdish groups in Iraq being attacked amid the US-Iran flare-up?
author: Alex MacDonald
publication_date: Published date: 1 August 2026 10:52 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 4 days ago
article_body: As the US has continued its war against Iran , the Islamic Republic has responded by launching retaliatory strikes across the Gulf, mainly targeting American assets. At the same time, Iranian forces or those aligned with them are widely believed to have been carrying out attacks on Iranian Kurdish groups based in northern Iraq . Keywan Faramarzi, international relations officer for the Komala party, told Middle East Eye that attacks in recent weeks on bases and "centres of activity" belonging to his party in Iraqi Kurdistan had killed 10 fighters. Though no one has claimed responsibility for the strikes, Faramarzi blamed Iran. "These attacks are part of the Islamic Republic's ongoing policy of targeting Iranian Kurdish opposition parties based outside Iran's borders," he said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Other Iranian Kurdish groups have reported similar attacks in Iraq, as well as within Iran's borders. The attacks raise questions about how great a threat the Iraq-based groups pose to the Islamic Republic. Iran's strikes come in the wake of reports in Israeli media that Turkey had pressured the US into abandoning an operation to send Iranian Kurdish fighters across the border to try to overthrow the government. Though the possibility of a Kurdish incursion had been mooted several times since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, this latest suggestion seems to have had higher ambitions and the Iranian government, at least, seems to have taken it seriously. 'We make use of every available method of resistance' - Hana Yazdanpanah, PAK In an interview released on 19 July, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Israel and the US had plotted to break up the country using the Kurdish groups. "I said that if any threat comes our way from Iraqi Kurdistan, we will definitely respond," he said . As with all previous claims, however, Kurdish groups in Iraq have denied any involvement in fighting in Iran, or that Trump had proposed any ground operation to them. "We have no information about such a plan, and there is no credible evidence to confirm these claims," said Faramarzi. "Such reports appear to be media speculation and do not reflect the realities on the ground." A representative of the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK) echoed the sentiment to Middle East Eye. "We likewise have no such intention," said Hana Yazdanpanah. She said that PAK had been involved in defending people in Iranian Kurdistan from the security services during the anti-government protests in January, but that any claims that they were involved in an operation to oust the government were nonsense. "Neither the Kurdistan Region nor we as PAK - and I can say the same about the other Kurdish parties - have participated in any such operation, nor have we received any weapons or military equipment." Despite this, the continuing attacks suggest Iran still views the groups as a threat. MEE contacted the Iranian foreign ministry for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. 'Neutrality' According to research cited by Minority Rights Group International , Kurds make up around 10 percent of Iran's population, living mainly in the provinces of Kurdistan, Kermanshah, West Azerbaijan and Ilam. Several Iranian Kurdish opposition movements, which Tehran generally considers to be terrorist groups, have operated for decades from bases in northern Iraq. These include Komala, PAK, the Kurdistan Democratic Party-Iran (PKDI), Khabat, and the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) - an organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). 'The Islamic Republic is attempting to weaken this political and organisational capacity and simultaneously send a threatening message to all opposition forces' - Keywan Faramarzi, Komala The groups have a range of political ideologies, though most are united on the need for self-defence of Kurdish communities in Iran and the eventual liberation of Iranian Kurdistan. On 22 February, these parties announced a new coalition with the stated aim of working together towards "the overthrow of the Islamic Republic of Iran". In April, US President Donald Trump claimed that he had sent "a lot" of guns to anti-government protesters in Iran and that the Kurds "took" them, something they denied . "We have established an alliance to strengthen and intensify the struggle in East Kurdistan and throughout Iran against the Islamic Republic," said Yazdanpanah. "In that struggle, we make use of every available method of resistance." Nevertheless, she said the coalition had "declared and maintained its neutrality" in the US-Iran conflict. Overthrowing the government? PAK said in 2019 that it had around 1,000 members, while the PDKI, Komala and Khabat are believed to have similar numbers. PJAK officials have boasted of as many as 3,000 active fighters - but even combined, the numbers pale in comparison to the hundreds of thousands of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) personnel and hundreds of thousands more in its Basij volunteer units. It is generally accepted, therefore , that the Kurdish coalition does not have the power to overthrow Iran's government - and there has been deepening frustration among the Kurdish parties at the repeated reports of their military involvement in the ongoing conflict. Israeli media says Turkey was ready to intervene over Kurdish incursion into Iran Read More » "The parties reacted to the war with great caution. We should take that seriously and indicative of their own thinking about their capabilities and the quality of the opportunity that the moment presented," said Winthrop Rodgers, an associate fellow at Chatham House. "This probably disappointed the expectations of some foolhardy US and Israel planners, who did not seem to appreciate the dynamics on the ground." And yet Iran has continued to attack Iranian Kurdish targets in northern Iraq - indicating that they still see them as a thorn in their side, if not an existential threat. Faramarzi said Komala's main role was in "organising, supporting and strengthening civil and protest movements across Iran" and that was the government's concern. "Through these attacks, the Islamic Republic is attempting to weaken this political and organisational capacity and simultaneously send a threatening message to all opposition forces," he said. headline: Trump warns US will 'bomb shit out of' Oman if it strays from Washington's line on Iran
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 15:04 BST | Last update: 2 days 10 hours ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of Washington’s efforts to reach a deal with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, according to Fox News. Fox reporter Trey Yingst said he asked Trump about parallel talks between Iran and Oman over control of the Strait of Hormuz. According to Yingst, Trump responded: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” The threat comes as Iran and Oman say they have reached an understanding on a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz and are working to finalise details for a joint statement. Iran and Oman continued talks on Monday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said, adding that there had been security complications caused by US and Israeli military actions. “Drawing up the maritime transit route plan with Oman has been time-consuming due to security complexities,” Baghaei said, adding that “the issue is inherently complex”. Speaking on the proposed mechanism, Baghaei said it would aim to protect the sovereign rights and interests of both Iran and Oman while ensuring the safe passage of commercial vessels. “This is the first time that a mechanism is being developed to simultaneously safeguard the sovereign rights of the two littoral states and ensure the safe passage of commercial vessels,” he said, adding that intensive talks to finalise a joint statement were continuing. Iran, Oman to jointly charge fees along Strait of Hormuz: Report Read More » Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passes, slowed over the weekend. A total of five commodity vessels transited the strait on Saturday, with none recorded for Sunday, in comparison to 31 vessels transiting last weekend, according to ship tracking data from Kpler. Trump on Monday said that Iran should raise a “white flag of surrender”, adding: “They're good poker players, but they're dying.” He also said that Washington had a backchannel with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). “We have a backchannel with the IRGC. We are speaking directly with the IRGC officials in Iran,” Trump said. On Gaza, he added: " Israelis should not be striking in Gaza. Hamas agreed to lay down their weapons." Trump also confirmed that the US maintained a separate channel of communication with Hamas. “We have a different channel with Hamas, and ultimately they are giving up their guns,” he said. Washington is attempting to continue pursuing Trump’s peace plan in Gaza, which seeks to disarm Hamas in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from the enclave, despite Israel saying it rejected the proposal. headline: Saudi Arabia tightens rules on financial transfers to UAE
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 14:50 BST | Last update: 1 day 10 hours ago
article_body: Saudi Arabia has tightened its oversight of financial transfers to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the latest sign of growing tensions between the two countries. The extra layers of regulatory oversight are normally reserved for countries considered high-risk for illicit money flows, according to Reuters. Three people with direct knowledge of the matter told the news agency that the measures, which have not been announced publicly, put the UAE among more than a half dozen countries in the region deemed high risk in Saudi Arabia for financial crime. A number of businesspeople told Reuters that they had experienced difficulties making transactions, and that their companies had transfers in various currencies delayed or returned by Saudi banks with no official explanation. The Saudi central bank told Reuters there were "no ​direct restrictions on specific countries," while a UAE official said its ​economy ministry had not received any reports from private-sector companies "regarding difficulties or unusual delays in completing bank transfers between the two nations". New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Saudi Arabia and the UAE have had divergent interests and disagreements for years, but recently, they have been most pronounced in the oil sector, the war in Yemen and the US-Israeli war on Iran. Last month, reports suggested Saudi Arabia had delayed or blocked money transfers to accounts in the UAE, raising fears that the rift between the Gulf neighbours was hitting trade. Several sources told The Financial Times that payments from Saudi banks to UAE-based accounts belonging to companies and individuals in Dubai had been returned or held up since May, often without explanation. One western executive at a Dubai-based healthcare company told the FT that Saudi banks had blocked and returned several payments from a long-standing Saudi client since mid-May. Saudi Arabia’s central bank denied imposing any “direct restrictions on specific countries” in comments to the FT. Conflict and attrition In December, a Saudi air strike on a shipment of UAE military equipment to the Southern Transitional Council, the separatist Yemeni organisation Abu Dhabi is aligned with, was a major recent salvo in rising tensions. Saudi Arabia deletes 'the Muslims will never give up Jerusalem' from its textbooks Read More » Since then, several widely followed Saudi and Emirati social media accounts, pundits, and news organisations have had heated debates and feuds with each other. In March, the UAE banned Saudi TV Al-Arabiya’s X accounts. This rift only deepened during the war on Iran, which has imperilled the Gulf. The UAE took a more hawkish approach to the war, reportedly carrying out dozens of air strikes on Iran, revealing a far deeper and earlier role in the conflict than previously acknowledged. Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, hedged its position, condemning Iran’s strikes on Gulf countries and agreeing to open King Fahd Air Base in Taif to the Americans while simultaneously pushing for negotiations with Iran through Islamabad. Then in May, the UAE exited Opec, the intergovernmental oil producers’ cartel led by Riyadh, after almost 60 years as a member. The UAE massively boosted its oil production after its withdrawal. In July, Middle East Eye characterised the two neighbours as “embroiled in an economic war of attrition” , as business executives were reportedly making contingency plans in case of a growing feud between Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
