headline: Drone strike on North Darfur court kills at least 35, rights group says
author: Victoria Amani Mwaniki Kishoiyian
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 21:59 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: On Sunday, a drone strike, purportedly carried out by the Sudanese army, targeted Sudan's Customary Court in al-Zawiya Ghara, killing at least 35 people and injuring others. All the victims were inside the court building and its immediate surroundings when the attack occurred, according to the Emergency Lawyers Group , which monitors violence against civilians in Sudan. Al-Zawiya Ghara is one of many villages in North Darfur state controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The drone fired at least four missiles at the court building while local leaders conducted a meeting. Among the dead are two RSF field commanders, four tribal elders, and traditional leaders hailing from the Mahameed branch of the Rizeigat, according to the Sudan Tribune. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Sunday's attack comes amid heightened Sudanese army drone operations across Darfur, closing in on RSF positions to weaken the paramilitary group after successive defeats in North Kordofan. The largely RSF-dominated Sudan Founding Coalition, known as Tasis, blamed the Sudanese army for the strike. In the Sudan Tribune, a Tasis spokesperson, Ahmed Tugod Lisan, urged an independent investigation to hold those responsible to account. The Emergency Lawyers Group has demanded an investigation into the drone strike and denounced the targeting of the court, deeming attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure a “grave violation of international humanitarian law”. It further stated that drones are increasingly used to target civilian areas and gatherings, exacerbating the risks faced by the population. The RSF also stands accused of committing war crimes, including carrying out drone strikes on civilians over the past three years of the war. The paramilitary group’s siege on el-Fasher, one of Darfur’s largest cities, in October of 2025, bore the “hallmarks of genocide” per a United Nations fact-finding mission. RSF commanders sentenced In early July, the anti-terrorism and crimes against the state court in Port Sudan sentenced RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, and 15 other defendants to death in absentia. UK hosting 'discreet' Sudan event featuring UAE-aligned RSF representatives Read More » According to the Sudan Tribune, they were convicted of their roles in the killing of West Darfur Governor Khamis Abdullah Abakar, crimes against humanity, war crimes, prohibited warfare, and genocide in el-Geneina. Presided over by special judge Mohamed al-Amin, the ruling constitutes the first judicial conviction of the paramilitary group’s leadership since the outbreak of Sudan’s war on 15 April 2023. The trial centred heavily on the 2023 assassination of Governor Abakar, a day after he denounced an RSF shelling on the el-Jamarik neighbourhood. Human Rights Watch concluded in 2024 that actions in the capital of West Darfur, el-Geneina, constituted ethnic cleansing and possibly genocide against the Masalit people and other non-Arab communities. Although video footage circulated online of Abakar’s body being mutilated by known RSF soldiers, the paramilitary group repeatedly blamed the Sudanese Armed Forces and denied responsibility. Middle East Eye reported in June 2023 that around 1,500 people were killed in el-Geneina in the first two months of the war, forcing tens of thousands of Masalit residents to flee el-Geneina and West Darfur on foot to seek refuge across the border in eastern Chad. Among the trial’s defendants were two brothers of Hemedti: RSF deputy leader Abdel Rahim Hamdan Dagalo and Algoney Hamdan Daglo Musa, also known as al-Qoni. The court also handed down convictions to Abdel Rahman Juma Barkallah, the RSF commander in West Darfur, and al-Tijani al-Tahir Karshoum, the state’s former deputy governor. The court held Hemedti legally responsible for directing the genocide of the Masalit and siege of el-Geneina, citing the systematic destruction and looting of property, as well as deliberate attacks on civilians, residential areas, schools, and places of worship. Dagalo was convicted of co-organising the siege of el-Geneina, the civilian displacement, and the genocide of the Masalit. Qoni was found liable for facilitating the siege, while Barkallah was liable for leading frontline RSF soldiers during systematic assaults on Masalit neighbourhoods. The court ordered the confiscation of all RSF assets and instructed the state to request Interpol red notices to secure the arrest and extradition of those convicted. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Israelis are second least wanted migrants in UK after Russians, poll finds
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 12:10 BST | Last update: 1 day 13 hours ago
article_body: Almost half of Britons want the UK to allow fewer Israelis or none at all to move to the country, a new study has revealed. Israelis have become the second most unwanted group in Britain after Russians . The YouGov poll released last week showed that Pakistanis , Indians , Turks , Egyptians and Nigerians rank above Israelis in popularity among the British public, although all these groups are relatively unpopular. Only one in 20 Britons want the UK to allow more Israelis into the country, with 23 percent saying the country should allow fewer and 24 saying none at all should be let in. Only 24 percent of Britons think the current number of Israelis in the country is fine, while 23 percent said they don't know. In comparison, 34 percent of Britons said no Russian migrants should be allowed into Britain, and 15 percent said no Indians should be admitted. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Migrants from Ireland are the most popular among the British public, with 23 percent saying more should be allowed in. Canadians, Australians, Swedes and Germans are also relatively popular, although the study identified a general increase in anti-immigration sentiment compared with an equivalent poll conducted in 2016. UK-Israel relations plummet The poll comes as the British government gears up to announce a raft of new policies on Israel in September, including a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, as Middle East Eye reported last week. Relations between the two historic allies are at an all-time low. Last week Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu branded Britain an "Islamic republic" in an interview. Netanyahu complained that the favourable British coverage Israel received during the 1967 Arab-Israeli war had disappeared. “Try to find that now in Britain, which you could call the Islamic republic of Britain,” Netanyahu said. When the host responded, “Isn’t all of Europe like that?”, Netanyahu replied: “Yes, but you know, someone said the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic republic of Britain.” Exclusive: UK to announce raft of new policies on Israel including settlement goods ban Read More » Britain is a monarchy, not a republic, and the first "Islamic republic" with nuclear weapons was in fact the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. Downing Street hit back at Netanyahu's comments this week, with a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham denouncing them as "completely unacceptable". British public opinion has been steadily hardening towards Israel. A YouGov study in June last year found that 55 percent of the public opposed Israel’s actions in Gaza , with only 15 percent in support. Of those 55 percent, an overwhelming 82 percent believed Israel was committing genocide . The poll also found that nearly two thirds of Britons (65 percent) wanted the UK to implement the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant for Netanyahu if he were to visit the UK. The British Foreign Office is currently looking at imposing new sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in the settler movement in the occupied West Bank, according to sources with knowledge of the matter. There have also been discussions within the government on potential sanctions on more Israeli ministers, after far-right ministers Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were sanctioned last year. headline: Iran war pushes Middle Eastern airlines towards $4.3bn loss in 2026
author: Gaspard Rouffin
publication_date: Published date: 16 August 2026 13:21 BST | Last update: 3 days 11 hours ago
article_body: As the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026, Iran struck back near US military installations in the Gulf, including in Qatar and the UAE . Several international airports were hit by Iranian strikes, including Dubai, the world's busiest for international passengers, as well as Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Bahrain . The UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait closed their airspaces due to safety concerns, gradually reopening them a week later as hostilities lessened. The war has had long-lasting consequences for regional aviation: falling passenger and cargo demand, fewer private jet flights, and global repercussions from high jet fuel prices. The International Air Transport Association's (IATA) June outlook estimated that airlines operating from the Middle East will see a $7.2bn net profit in 2025 become a $4.3bn net loss in 2026. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Most major regional carriers have resumed operations, including Emirates, Etihad and Qatar Airways, but not at full capacity. Emirates CEO Tim Clark told the Financial Times in June his planes were flying at three-quarters capacity. Conversely, most European and Asian airlines' flights in the region remain suspended. Air France expects to resume in late August and Lufthansa in September, while British Airways, Cathay Pacific and Singapore Airlines are all targeting late October. Air Canada is not planning to resume before mid-January 2027, and many others have not announced a restart date at all. Satellite imagery shows smoke plumes billowing in the vicinity Kuwait International Airport on 25 March 2026 (European Space Agency/AFP) Regional airspaces have reopened, but are still facing intermittent closures and disruptions. The EU Aviation Safety Agency’s most recent bulletin advises operators to “avoid the airspace of Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and part of the Gulf of Oman until 31 August 2026”. The result is limited choice for travellers. For a one-week round trip between the UAE and London in September, the only options are Emirates to Dubai, Etihad to Abu Dhabi, or Air Arabia to Sharjah, while to fly between Doha and Tokyo on those same dates, only Qatar Airways is available. Business under threat Gulf airlines organise their activity around a hub-and-spoke model concentrating traffic at a central base and operating flights worldwide from there. Passengers connect onward from the main hub , offering connections that are otherwise unavailable or sometimes cheaper fares than direct flights. This model has long relied on the Gulf’s strategic position between Europe and Asia, forming what analysts describe as a “bridge” between the two continents. But the war has put this model at risk. '[Gulf airlines are] connecting carriers whose economics depend on moving large volumes of passengers' -Naveed Kapadia, aviation lecturer Naveed Kapadia, an aviation lecturer at Buckinghamshire New University, told Middle East Eye that while competition for airlines such as Qatar Airways and Emirates is “greatly reduced”, allowing them to “capture market share and maintain stronger fares”, they remain “connecting carriers whose economics depend on moving large volumes of passengers efficiently through Dubai and Doha”. Kapadia said IATA’s June data showed Middle Eastern passenger demand fell 13.9 percent year-on-year, while direct traffic between Europe and Asia rose 11 percent, already revealing a strain on the Gulf carrier’s model. This leads to cost increases across the board. “Where flights must use longer or less efficient routings, airlines face higher fuel burn, longer crew duty periods and reduced aircraft utilisation,” Kapadia said. The extra fuel many now carry in case of disruption also directly limits “passenger or cargo payload that can be carried”. The hub-and-spoke model leaves airlines susceptible to disruption, as aircraft and crews can be stranded far away, causing cascading delays and cancellations across the entire schedule. Emirates innovates Emirates has been innovating to win back the customers it had before the war, as many are hesitant to book flights connecting through Dubai in case hostilities resume. One measure is an unprecedented travel insurance policy, offering comprehensive coverage even in case of conflict-related cancellation. Until now, most travel insurance voided cover in the event of war-related disruption, leaving passengers to absorb the costs themselves. The policy aims to prevent passengers from being stranded, with Emirates offering to fly them home on other airlines if needed. CEO Tim Clark told the Financial Times the aim was to guarantee “we would get you back irrespective [of whether it's] on Emirates or not”. Dubai has also been trying to reboost tourism more broadly, offering complimentary packages for visitors invited by Emirati nationals and free hotel stays for long connecting flights. An Emirates Airbus A380 aircraft prepares for landing as a smoke plume rises from an ongoing fire near Dubai International Airport in Dubai on 16 March 2026 Cargo demand lags Cargo carriers have also been impacted by regional disruptions. Kapadia said Middle East cargo demand grew roughly a third slower than the rest of the industry’s, at 5.6 percent year on year, behind the global rate of 8.5 percent. Citing IATA figures, Kapadia said traffic between Europe and the Middle East remained 41.1 percent below the previous year, while Asia-Middle East traffic was down 4.1 percent. He added that while “disruption to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is creating demand for faster alternatives, particularly for urgent, high-value and time-sensitive shipments”, this was not a "straightforward windfall" for Gulf-based cargo airlines. Middle Eastern carriers such as Qatar Airways Cargo and Emirates SkyCargo account for around 13 percent of global air cargo traffic. “The more important question,” he said, “is whether they can convert short-term urgency into sustained and profitable cargo flows.” Private jets staying Similar disruptions have also been observed in the private jet sector. Nick Koscinski, an aviation analyst at WINGX, told Middle East Eye that as of 10 August, overall private jet traffic originating in Gulf countries was down 46.5 percent since the war began. 'The vast majority of flights stayed within the Middle East region' -Nick Koscinski, aviation analyst “The vast majority of flights stayed within the Middle East region,” he said, though volumes there are “still down considerably”. Europe remains the second most common destination from Gulf origins, but Gulf-to-Europe flights are down 41.0 percent. Koscinski said Qatar Executive, one of the top Gulf-based private jet operators, had been more resilient than UAE or Saudi Arabia-based competitors. Total flights are down 6.7 percent since the war began, against 28.7 percent for a comparable UAE-based operator and 39.0 percent for a Saudi one. Koscinski said operators “likely have some ability to pass increased operating costs, like fuel spikes, through to the consumer via surcharges”, but lags in repricing and “softer demand overall” mean they will still take a financial hit. Fuel costs squeeze margins Jet fuel prices fell 20 percent in June as Gulf oil flows temporarily improved, Kapadia said, but remained “45.8% higher than a year earlier”. IATA forecasts the 2026 jet fuel price average will run 70 percent above 2025 levels. Kapadia expects “Gulf airfares to remain elevated and volatile rather than rise uniformly” because “airlines will try to recover higher fuel and disruption costs through fares to some extent, but they cannot pass on every additional cost without weakening demand, particularly among price-sensitive leisure travellers.” Low-cost carriers around the world have been particularly vulnerable to the jump in fuel cost: US-based Spirit Airlines ceased operations on 2 May 2026, while Air Baltic and Wizz Air face growing bankruptcy risk and are forced to restructure operations. A McKinsey report found that around 70 percent of jet fuel surcharges are passed directly to consumers, with airline margins recovering only briefly when fuel prices fall. It said the economic pressure will force airlines to retire older aircraft, cut less-booked routes, and further trim overhead costs. Not every carrier is equally impacted. Israel’s national airline, El Al, has recently reported record profits, more than double the previous year. Many passengers have criticised the “outrageous” fares, as the continued flight suspension by international carriers leaves the airline in a near-monopoly. Harsha Jaison, an aviation consultant at ICF, told Middle East Eye the conflict has set a precedent that will probably outlast it. “Airport investment deals, geopolitical risk is increasingly being reflected in downside scenarios, valuation assumptions and risk premiums,” she said. headline: Morocco's Gaza deployment is reshaping its ties with Israel
author: Caroline Dupuy
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 12:01 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: In July, Morocco became the first Arab and African nation to deploy its military to the International Stabilisation Force (ISF) in Palestine under Donald Trump’s "peace plan" for Gaza, bolstered by his equally dubious Board of Peace (BoP). Morocco signed an agreement in Rabat on 15 July to formalise its participation in the ISF. The signing ceremony took place in the presence of Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita; Nickolay Mladenov, director general of the BoP; senior defence officials and ISF commander Jasper Jeffers. Morocco’s participation follows instructions from King Mohammed VI, Supreme Commander and Chief of General Staff of the Royal Armed Forces and chairman of the Al-Quds Committee. The ISF was originally planned to deploy 500 Moroccan military officials to a refugee camp in the southern city of Rafah. The figure has now been reduced to just 200 Moroccan soldiers, Al Jazeera reported. The force is expected to work in collaboration with the Israeli military. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Since Morocco signed the agreement, Hamas has announced its conditional disarmament proposal in keeping with Trump’s Gaza plan. However, Israel has disregarded its side of the agreement and shows no sign of withdrawing from Palestine and the territories in which it continues to occupy illegally. Instead of giving a withdrawal timeframe, Israeli far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich proposed to extend its illegal settlements into the Gaza Strip. According to an official statement by Morocco’s National Defence Administration, Morocco's contribution “demonstrates its commitment to peace, international cooperation, and regional stability”. The move also aligns with Morocco’s role as a founding member of the BoP, the statement says. Explaining the benefits for Rabat, international relations professor Said Saddiki, at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University in Fez, noted that joining the force “provides Morocco with an opportunity to regain a more visible diplomatic role in the Palestinian issue, complementing its longstanding role through the Al-Quds Committee and the Bayt Mal Al-Quds Agency”. Humanitarian narrative While other sources such as the Council on Foreign Relations also indicate the aim is for the ISF to serve as the primary security force in Gaza, replacing the Israeli military, Morocco has leaned heavily on the narrative that it will help establish a field hospital in Gaza under the ISF mission. The field hospital is “nothing more than a narrative,” according to Saadia*, a key member of Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) in Morocco and an organiser for the most recent Global Sumud flotilla. Fuelling the ‘machinery of genocide’: Morocco’s backdoor support for Israel’s war on Gaza Read More » Considering Morocco’s role, Saadia told Middle East Eye, “It is possible that Morocco is helping Palestine, but it is helping the Zionist entity more,” such as the kingdom’s role in shipping arms to Israel, she added. According to Professor Saddiki, the field hospital “should primarily be viewed as a humanitarian initiative rather than a military one”. While he noted Morocco’s good relations with both Palestinian and Israeli leadership, he emphasised that “the current regional environment leaves little room for any Arab state to play an effective mediation role. Morocco is therefore more likely to contribute through humanitarian assistance and diplomacy than through active mediation.” However, Morocco’s Ministry of Defence has not shared details of the role that Morocco will be playing under the ISF in Palestine. “I don't know what Morocco’s role will be [in the ISF] other than perhaps disarming the resistance [Hamas] and even supervising a new colonisation of the Gaza Strip by the American-Zionist entity,” Saadia said. Professor Saddiki suggests Morocco’s “participation does not represent a strategic alignment against any party, nor does it come at the expense of the Palestinian cause.” The professor highlighted that “domestically, Morocco has sought to balance its foreign policy with public support for Palestine”. Saddiki also recalled that pro-Palestinian and anti-normalisation movements in Morocco have remained highly active since October 2023. 'Complicity in genocide’ Despite the Moroccan state’s overt support for Israel, many Moroccan citizens have warned that any normalisation deals with Israel amounts to "complicity in genocide" of the Palestinian people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Younes*, a central figure in Morocco’s pro-Palestine protest movement and the last two Global Sumud flotillas, told MEE: “Joining the ISF is full complicity in genocide.” Morocco accused of using Israeli weapons to kill civilians in Western Sahara Read More » The activist added, “Entering Gaza on a Zionist tank to ‘impose’ peace from one side and oblige Palestinians to surrender and be demilitarised is a great sin which will not be tolerated.” The peace plan and board have been widely condemned for breaching international law, from grassroots activism to country level. Younes added, “There is no peace plan, based on the history of deals with the Zionist entity [...] they believe they can do whatever they want.” A Moroccan activist from Rabat, who preferred to use the name Shams, described Morocco’s involvement as “very disheartening and disappointing”. Despite her disappointment, Shams said she is “not surprised” by Morocco’s involvement. That’s not to say the public is for the continued normalisation with Israel, she added: “I cannot speak for all Gen Z Moroccans, but I would say that most are opposed to the Moroccan military support joining the ISF.” The 2025 Arab Index by the Arab Center Washington DC, published earlier this year, found that 89 percent of Moroccan’s oppose recognising Israel, with just six percent supporting normalisation with Israel. Israel recognises Morocco’s sovereignty over disputed Western Sahara Read More » A Moroccan journalist, who preferred to stay anonymous, told MEE that “the Moroccan state narrative frames normalisation as leverage, cooperation and support for a two-state solution in exchange for US backing”. However, the journalist noted that “Moroccan public trust is breaking down,” due to the gap between the official framing and what is visible on the ground, with Israel's continued settlement expansion on occupied land, “moving further away from any two-state outcome". For Shams, further military intervention with the help of Moroccan forces will not bring peace to Palestinians. “I don’t think military intervention is going to facilitate peace when the oppressor has been destroying and bombing and blockading and [committing] genocide for decades on end,” she said. “The US and Israel will only continue to destabilise, murder, kill and wreak havoc in Gaza, and destroy the lives of millions of Palestinians,” she added. Screaming into the void Morocco is the only North African and Arab nation deploying military forces to the ISF, joining Kosovo, Albania, Kazakhstan, Indonesia, and more recently Uganda . Meanwhile, neighbouring Egypt has limited its involvement to training and logistical support. This unique positioning has sparked deep outrage among local activists. Younes expressed his frustration at how rapidly normalisation has spread across the country. Israeli flag flies in Morocco during military drill, sparking indignation Read More » “Zionists in Morocco successfully penetrated every single sector within a short period,” he explained. “What we gather as voluntary efforts and popular mobilisation to face this cancer during the past years isn't enough.” Acknowledging the heavy weight of his assessment, he continued, “I think the more we struggle against accepting cooperation with Israel, the more Moroccan authorities normalise with these terrorists. We must change approaches and look for alternatives.” Despite intensifying pressure from Moroccan state authorities, the pro-Palestinian movement maintains its defiance. Saadia argued that governments participating in the ISF are labouring under a dangerous illusion. She warned that these nations wrongly think that “this American-Zionist axis will bring them some kind of security or protection”. Pointing to the broader geopolitical escalation across the region, she reflected on the current US-Israeli war on Iran: “From this war we can understand that the Americans don't protect anyone other than the Zionist entity.” * Names have been changed Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Columbia University student workers’ union withdraws Israel divestment demand
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 31 July 2026 22:27 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 5 days ago
article_body: The Columbia University student workers' union withdrew its demand that the university divest financially from Israel at a bargaining meeting this week. The union constitutes over 3,000 undergraduate and graduate student workers. At a general body meeting on Monday, the union’s members voted on the decision. SWC-UAW pulled a contract article entitled “Obligations Under International Law,” which pressed the university to divest from companies and state actors in violation of international law, as defined by the United Nations and the International Criminal Court. It also demanded that the university publicise its finances twice a fiscal year, including all direct and indirect investments and holdings, and permit the union to submit a “list of entities from which the University shall divest”, detailing how the entities violated international law. The union argued for the article on the basis that its members, as workers who produce value for the university, hold a stake in how its money is invested. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters This withdrawal signifies a major shift in the union’s politics and orientation, as it has devoted itself to Columbia’s pro-Palestinian student movement since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Over 73,000 people have been killed since Israel began its assault on the enclave after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel in October 2023. Columbia University, Cuny most 'hostile' campuses for Muslims: Cair Read More » Financial divestment from Israel has been the central goalpost for the Columbia pro-Palestinian student movement, which established the “Gaza Solidarity Encampment” and occupied Hamilton Hall in April of 2024. In the aftermath of those actions, SWC-UAW passed a June 2024 resolution championing the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement. The union further campaigned for Columbia to suspend its dual degree programme with Tel Aviv University and halt plans to open a new facility in Tel Aviv. Following two New York Police Department sweeps of the encampment and Hamilton Hall, the union attempted to permanently prohibit NYPD officers from its Morningside Heights campus through another June “Cops off Campus” resolution. The union has engaged in negotiations with Columbia for a successor contract since March of 2025, initially expecting the expiration of its first contract that June. However, a general stalemate has persisted due to contention over what constitutes a "workplace issue". The union has since proposed 34 contract articles, from matters of compensation to demands for job assurance in the face of AI. The university did not respond to them, and asserted that the proposals lay outside the 2018 framework, which confines bargaining about academic or operational matters. The National Labor Relations Act legally obligates both the union and the university to bargain over mandatory subjects such as wages or working conditions. Columbia will open its global centre in Tel Aviv this summer. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Labour Friends of Israel defends major West Bank settlement blocs
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 16:27 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: The Labour Friends of Israel (LFI) lobby group has published a report apparently justifying some illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestine and urging the British government not to ban goods produced by them. This comes as Andy Burnham's Labour government is believed to be considering imposing a ban on imports from Israeli settlements, which according to British policy are all in occupied Palestinian territory. LFI is a group within the Labour Party which is believed to count more than 70 MPs as affiliates, although it no longer keeps a public list. The group published a policy briefing report late last week titled "Settlements and Solutions: A Guide to the Issues". The report, reviewed by Middle East Eye, argues against a ban on Israeli settlement goods. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters All Israeli settlements in the West Bank, including the major blocs, are illegal under international law. The International Court of Justice also ruled in a 2024 advisory opinion that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory is itself illegal and places obligations on countries to take measures to end the occupation. But LFI's report says: "While Israel asserts that settlements are legal under international law, much of the international community disputes this position." It criticises settlement outposts not recognised by the Israeli government which are "established without legal authorisation", and advocates for adopting a different approach to major blocs from other settlements, tolerating the former but opposing the latter. The report calls on Britain to urge "the next Israeli government to remove illegal settlement outposts; halt settlement expansion outside the major blocs; issue more building permits for Palestinians in Area C; and expand Palestinian autonomous areas". This suggests the government should not object to the major settlement blocs. The report argues that "a boycott of all trade with settlements is practically and politically impossible". It says a full boycott would "impact all Israeli businesses operating in the settlement blocs, as well as East Jerusalem and the Old City". The report adds that a boycott could inadvertently affect "Israelis living within the state’s borders. A settlement boycott would thus become a de facto boycott of all of Israel. "This will rightly be perceived within the UK Jewish community as a further example of the government singling out and targeting Israel for punitive action and harsh rhetoric." Burnham mulling ban on settlement goods Prime Minister Burnham recently said he is considering "further measures to deter unacceptable violence" in the occupied West Bank, and Whitehall sources have said that his government is considering announcing a ban on settlement goods after parliament returns from recess. Wes Streeting, now Burnham's defence secretary, last year said in leaked text messages to the now-disgraced former ambassador to the US, Peter Mandelson, that he had been a supporter of LFI for "over 20 years". But he endorsed sanctions on Israel and accused the country of "committing war crimes before our eyes". The same failed policies have broken six prime ministers. Can Burnham break the mould? Read More » Jonathan Reynolds, the business and trade secretary, was previously a vice-chair of LFI. In opposition, Labour called for a ban on the import of settlement goods, with the then shadow foreign secretary, Lisa Nandy, saying in June 2020 that the move would require "courage that so far ministers have not been willing to show". France and Sweden recently put forward a proposal calling on the European Union to enforce strict import controls on settlement goods. The Netherlands also banned trade in such goods last month. Polling of Labour members earlier this year showed that a staggering 87 percent support a ban on trade with Israeli settlements, with only 6 percent opposing it. The LFI report criticises the "current Netanyahu government, which took office in January 2023, [for having] accelerated expansion of settlements beyond the 'settlement blocs', while also failing to uphold the law and crack down on the noxious activities of extremist settlers". It adds that there "is a long-standing consensus - previously accepted by Israeli and Palestinian negotiating teams alike, as well as influential segments of the international community - that the key settlement blocs will remain under Israeli control through land swaps". headline: US has lost roughly 25 percent of its Reaper drones in Iran war: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 21:16 BST | Last update: 5 days 3 hours ago
article_body: The US-Israeli war on Iran has depleted or destroyed more than $1.3bn worth of the US's MQ-9 Reaper drones, roughly translating to 25 percent of the country's pre-war fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles, according to a report by The Washington Post published on Friday. The report underscores how Iran's air defences have continued to be operational despite claims by President Donald Trump and his aides that they have been obliterated. The Washington Post story reveals a slightly higher number of MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed compared to a Bloomberg report published in May, which put the figure at 20 percent of the pre-war inventory. The MQ-9 Reaper drone is valued between $30m and $50m, depending on its sensor, radar, and ordnance configuration. The unmanned aerial vehicle serves as a high-altitude platform for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeted precision strikes, as documented by the US Air Force . It is capable of carrying Hellfire missiles or Joint Direct Attack Munition guided bombs. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The drone flies slowly, at low altitude, making the MQ-9 Reaper a simple target for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its regional allies in Yemen and Iraq. The aircraft is frequently used near the Strait of Hormuz, where the US and Iran are battling for control. Trump says he has enforced a “wall of steel” naval blockade on the waterway. US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles during Iran war: Report Read More » The MQ-9 Reaper is one of a burgeoning list of American weapons and munitions that have experienced stock depletion during the war on Iran. The Pentagon is phasing out the General Atomics-produced Reaper and foresees a replacement fleet of cheaper armed surveillance drones capable of swarming their targets. The US has depleted its stockpile of sophisticated standoff munitions. The US has fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and more than 1,000 Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense missiles. The Trump administration has denied reports that US weapons stockpiles are facing shortages as a result of the war. The Trump administration has requested from Congress more than $ 67bn in supplementary funding to address operational costs incurred by the Department of War during Operation Epic Fury and to replenish weapons supplies. On 6 August, Trump confronted Secretary of War Pete Hegseth at a Cabinet meeting over Washington's critical shortage of munitions, saying that it is one of the reasons behind his administration’s decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. headline: 'They want to make us leave': Israel destroys West Bank wells serving Palestinian herders
author: Mojahid Nawahda Teebah Assi
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 12:10 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: As first light reaches the scattered tents and animal pens of Ras al-Ahmar in the northern Jordan Valley, the silence is broken only by the cries of thirsty livestock waiting for water that no longer comes. Days after Israeli forces destroyed three of the Palestinian community's main water wells, residents are scrambling to secure enough water for their families, crops and animals in one of the occupied West Bank's driest regions. For 60-year-old Ali Bani Odeh, the destruction of the wells was more than merely the loss of infrastructure. A father of four and grandfather of 14, he has spent decades farming and raising livestock to support his family in Ras al-Ahmar. Now, like dozens of other families, he is uncertain how long they can continue living on the land without a reliable water supply. "Water is everything for us," Ali told Middle East Eye. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Without water, we cannot live. We need it for our families, our sheep and our crops. Since the wells were destroyed, we have been forced to bring water from town at a much higher cost, and even then, we're not always allowed to pass." Families must now haul water from distant towns at far greater expense, while military checkpoints and movement restrictions frequently delay or prevent tankers from reaching the village. 'The wells were the lifeline of this community' – Abdullah Bisharat, head of the village council According to Ras al-Ahmar village council head Abdullah Bisharat, the three destroyed wells supplied more than 47 Palestinian families, serving over 600 people and irrigating around 7,500 dunams of farmland. The wells also sustained thousands of sheep and goats, the main source of income for many families. "The wells were the lifeline of this community," Bisharat said. "Their destruction has affected every aspect of daily life, from drinking water and agriculture to livestock, leaving dozens of families struggling to meet their most basic needs." Settler attacks Residents say the destruction marked the worst escalation in a months-long water crisis caused by Israeli settler attacks. They say settlers repeatedly cut the pipelines supplying the community, forcing families to rely on costly water tankers. This time, however, the wells themselves were destroyed, eliminating the community's main source of water. Ali's son, Obeida Bani Odeh, fears the loss of the wells threatens not only his family's livelihood but also their future in Ras al-Ahmar. How Israeli settler terrorism threatens the basics of Palestinian survival Read More » "We cannot survive here without water," Obeida said. "For months, the pipelines supplying our community were repeatedly cut, and we had to bring water from nearby towns, often at three times the usual cost. "Now the wells have been destroyed, and there is no reliable source of water left for our families or our livestock." He said the challenges extend beyond water shortages. Settler attacks and movement restrictions have made it increasingly difficult to bring in water, animal feed and other essential supplies. "The settlers attack everyone, from the young to the old," Obeida said. "They want to make people afraid and force them to leave. But we have been living on this land for generations." The three destroyed wells supplied more than 47 Palestinian families, around 600 people (Mojahid Nawahda/MEE) Around 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem across roughly 300 settlements and outposts. The settlements are regarded as illegal under international law, according to the International Court of Justice . Settler attacks on Palestinian herding communities have increased sharply in recent years. Between January 2023 and April 2026, at least 5,910 Palestinians were internally displaced due to settler violence in the West Bank, according to UN data. ‘A silent war’ Aref Daraghmeh, a human rights activist, says the destruction of water infrastructure in Ras al-Ahmar reflects a broader struggle over control of natural resources in the Jordan Valley. "Water has become a silent war against Palestinians in the Jordan Valley," Daraghmeh told MEE. "The occupation has taken control of many Palestinian water sources, while the water available to Palestinian communities is insufficient for agriculture and sustaining life on the land." ‘Policy to displace us’: How settler attacks are drying up the West Bank Read More » Daraghmeh said restrictions on water access have contributed to the decline of Palestinian agriculture, making it increasingly difficult for farmers and herders to sustain their livelihoods. As water becomes harder to access, he argues, communities face growing pressure to leave their land while settlement agriculture continues to expand across the Jordan Valley. He added that movement restrictions have compounded those challenges. "The Jordan Valley is effectively under closure," Daraghmeh said. "Military checkpoints control movement, roads are restricted, and residents often have to wait for hours before they can enter or leave their communities." For farmers and herders, those restrictions make it harder to reach grazing land and transport livestock, produce and agricultural supplies, adding to the pressures already created by limited access to water. But for Ali Bani Odeh, leaving Ras al-Ahmar is not an option. Displaced from his home as a child, he says he will not leave again. "I have left before, but I will not leave this place," Ali said. "If we leave, they will take over the land. We are staying because this is where our lives and our history are." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: German court rules comparing Israel to Nazi Germany constitutes 'protected speech'
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 3 August 2026 14:55 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 2 days ago
article_body: A German court has acquitted a woman convicted of comparing Israel’s actions in Gaza with those of Nazi Germany, ruling that her posts constituted protected political expression. The Zweibrucken Higher Regional Court overturned a €2,400 ($2,700) fine last week after it was imposed by a lower court over two Instagram posts published during the height of Israel’s genocide in Gaza . One post contained a table comparing Israel’s conduct with the methods of the Nazi regime. It appeared beneath a divided image of the Israeli and Nazi flags, with part of a swastika visible. Another depicted Israeli soldiers firing into an enclosed area as blood flowed beneath its walls. A swastika appeared inside a Star of David. The woman accompanied the posts with the hashtags #FREEPALESTINE and #GAZAUNDERATTACK. The court ruled that the images expressed condemnation of Israel’s actions rather than support for Nazi ideology. It said freedom of expression protected the use of banned symbols when the context clearly conveyed criticism, parody or rejection of Nazism. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Judges found that the appeal "FREEPALESTINE" made the woman’s position clear and that neo-Nazi supporters would not interpret the post as promoting their ideology. Germany moves to criminalise denial of Israel’s existence while refusing to recognise Palestine Read More » The court also rejected the suggestion that comparing Israel’s conduct with Nazi Germany automatically trivialised the Holocaust or incited hatred. Sharp criticism of a state, it said, did not by itself cross that threshold. It reached the same conclusion over the image combining a swastika with the Star of David. The scene of soldiers shooting defenceless people made its condemnatory purpose clear, while the hashtag "GAZAUNDERATTACK" established that it referred to Israel’s assault on Gaza. The ruling does not prohibit criticism of such comparisons. It establishes, however, that Germany cannot automatically criminalise them when they form part of an unmistakable condemnation of Israeli violence. The court acquitted the woman of all charges. headline: UAE-backed Chinese company acquires stake in Ethiopian gold mine near Sudan war zone
author: Zecharias Zelalem Oscar Rickett
publication_date: Published date: 19 August 2026 10:45 BST | Last update: 14 hours 17 min ago
article_body: Last week, after protracted negotiations and various plot twists, Canadian mining company Allied Gold sold a minority stake in its assets to China ’s Zijin Gold International. “With the completion of the strategic investment, Zijin Gold holds approximately 9.2 percent of the issued and outstanding common shares of the company,” Allied Gold announced in a statement. This is the latest, most significant development in a saga that involves investment from the United Arab Emirates , nearby Ethiopian army bases supporting Sudan ’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and a large stretch of Ethiopian land on the Sudanese border that could now be mined extensively for gold. The agreement, which is worth just under $300m, grants Zijin, a private company with at least three Chinese state-owned corporations among its leading shareholders, partial ownership of a portfolio that includes mining sites in Mali, Cote d’Ivoire and the Kurmuk concession in western Ethiopia. The Kurmuk site is in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, which hosts at least one army base used by the paramilitary RSF, which is supplied by the UAE, currently also the main buyer of Ethiopian gold. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The site is about 20km from the Sudanese locality of the same name, where on Monday last week mass graves believed to contain the bodies of people killed by the RSF were discovered on the same day the deal was announced. The region, which has a recent history of civilian displacement and conflict, is known for informal, semi-illegal and semi-mechanised mining operations, including in the area marked out for exploration by Allied Gold. Publicly, the Canadian company is bullish about the Ethiopian site, saying it expects to start operations in August and to produce between 240,000 and 270,000 gold ounces in 2027, a figure that would amount to a value of around $1bn. UAE and Chinese investment in Ethiopia The deal ends a year-long saga that has involved two failed acquisition attempts, first by an Emirati company last year, then by Zijin itself. Zijin had initially agreed this year to acquire Allied Gold in its entirety for around $4bn until the deal collapsed because it didn’t obtain Chinese regulatory approval . With the full buyout scrapped, the parties proceeded with the partial investment instead. The completed agreement will bring a joint Chinese-Emirati footprint to Ethiopia’s mining sector, as the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), the UAE’s sovereign wealth fund, has been a major shareholder of Zijin Mining, the parent company of Zijin Gold International, since 2022. Exclusive: The Ethiopian army base covertly supporting Sudan’s RSF Read More » There was also a significant financial interest from the UAE in Allied Gold. In February 2025, the Canadian company announced that it had inked a half-billion-dollar deal giving a 50 percent stake in its mining assets to Ambrosia , a little-known Emirati company headed by prominent Emirati businessman Ahmed Amer al-Amry, who runs the Abu Dhabi-based Al Amry Group. Months later, Allied Gold announced that the Ambrosia deal had fallen apart, citing unmet conditions and a surge in the valuation of gold. In January, Zijin and Allied Gold jointly announced their intention to arrange the buyout of the Canadian company but that deal was eventually scuppered. Months after that announcement, first-quarter reports revealed that the ADIA had poured some $680m into Zijin Mining, listing the UAE’s sovereign wealth fund among Zijin’s top ten shareholders . There could be subsequent deals, as Allied Gold CEO Peter Marrone has indicated a willingness to sell more of his company to more than one buyer if an offer meets his evaluation. For now, Allied Gold’s immediate plans for the company is to use the proceeds of the transaction to expand operations at all three of the company’s mining sites, including “operational optimizations, the completion and ramp-up of Kurmuk”. Middle East Eye asked Allied Gold if it was in a position to ensure that its new partners would not try to exploit the Kurmuk mine's gold to support militant groups in Sudan but received no response on the record. Ethiopia's mines minister has welcomed "expanding investments in gold, critical minerals, petroleum and fertiliser production". Zijin Gold did not respond to Middle East Eye's questions. Both the UAE and Ethiopia deny involvement in the Sudan war. Proximity to Sudan war With the proximity of the Kurmuk mine to both a major Ethiopian-RSF logistics hub in the Ethiopian city of Asosa and to the war front in Sudan’s Blue Nile State, the new mining acquisition involving investors affiliated with RSF-allied governments could prove a strategic coup for the RSF. Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region is a security-sensitive region. The regional capital of Asosa is, as MEE revealed earlier this year , home to a major logistics hub used by the UAE and Ethiopia to train and arm fighters from the RSF, which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces since April 2023. The site is also about 100km away from Ethiopia’s Grand Renaissance Dam on the Nile river. It’s unclear what impact mining activity involving investors affiliated with the governments of the UAE and China could have on war-torn Sudan, where three long years of conflict have displaced millions and created what UN officials have described as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Sudan's war economy: How hunger, gold and smuggling routes fuel an escalating crisis Read More » Both countries stand accused of fuelling the bloodshed and facilitating the transfer of weapons to the RSF, which has carried out a catalogue of gruesome atrocities, including sexual violence and civilian massacres that UN investigators say amount to a genocide. The UAE in particular has used illicit gold mining to bolster its support for the RSF, which has its own gold trading company, al-Junaid. The group has accumulated considerable wealth by smuggling gold from areas of Sudan under its control into Dubai. Human rights researchers and diplomatic sources have long identified the UAE as a major hub of Sudanese conflict gold. “For gold, in most of these processes – whether it is RSF or SAF territory - the final destination of the gold is still the UAE, especially the gold market in Dubai. It goes through many brokers and mediators,” one Sudanese gold trader, who also runs a small mine, told MEE. “The production of gold in Sudan is dominated – up to 85 or 90 percent – by artisanal miners,” Suliman Baldo, a Sudanese expert on the gold trade, told MEE. “Therefore the gold is bought by traders and the export and smuggling of gold is mostly done by private individuals,” he said. “These individuals are wholesale traders who are able to buy the gold from the artisanal miners and smuggle it to the United Arab Emirates.” China officially maintains a policy of neutrality in Sudan’s civil war, but has done nothing to stop the UAE from transferring sophisticated Chinese armaments, including howitzers, heavy machine guns and armed drones, to the RSF. This is despite the UN’s continuous renewals of Sudan-wide arms embargoes, and demands by the Sudanese government that Beijing take action to curb the flow of its weapons into Sudan. Canadian mining companies also have a controversial history of chasing mining interests amid conflict in East Africa, including during Ethiopia’s deadly Tigray war, which killed hundreds of thousands from 2020-2022. headline: Saudi Arabia deletes 'the Muslims will never give up Jerusalem' from its textbooks
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 12:00 BST | Last update: 1 day 12 hours ago
article_body: An Israel -based organisation has praised Saudi Arabia for removing the phrase “the Muslims will never give up Jerusalem” from its school textbooks, as it seeks to reshape how the kingdom teaches Islam, Palestine and Israel . Israeli research group Impact-se published its review of the Saudi curriculum at the end of July. “The statement implied that Muslim control over or presence in Jerusalem was under threat,” the report said, adding that the reference “could be interpreted as framing Jerusalem as a site of ongoing struggle between Muslims and other groups, particularly Israel.” The criticism comes as Israeli politicians regularly call for the destruction of Al-Aqsa Mosque, Islam’s third-holiest site, and the construction of a Jewish temple in its place. On Monday, Israeli authorities formally allowed Israeli settlers to conduct Jewish prayers inside Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem for the first time, an act of provocation that further violated and dismantled the site’s decades-old status quo. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters With government support, Israeli settlers also continue building settlements on Palestinian land to alter Jerusalem’s demographic character. The report also said that "all instances of antisemitism" as defined by Impact-se had been removed from the curriculum. Passages from the Quran removed The report celebrated as a “positive development” the removal of passages from the Quran and Hadith, the recorded sayings and teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. Saudi textbooks notably dropped a well-known hadith about Muhammad visiting a sick Jewish boy who later accepted Islam. “The removal of this example in the 2025 edition marks an improvement in the acceptance of religious minorities, as students are no longer taught that unbelief in Islam leads to damnation,” Impact-se said. 'While the change of terminology reduces hostility toward Israel, the use of the term 'the Israeli Occupation' [...] continues to reflect a position of non-recognition of Israel' - Impact-se report The organisation also welcomed the truncating of Quranic verses addressing disbelief and sin. It however criticised Saudi schools for continuing to teach Muslim pupils that Islam represents humanity’s natural religion, despite similar teachings appearing across major faiths. The report also turned its attention to maps and terminology. Impact-se said several maps had previously “omitted Israel” and labelled the entire territory Palestine. In the 2024-25 textbooks, Saudi authorities removed the Palestine label. “[W]hile Israel is still not identified on these maps, the revision removes the explicit designation of the entire territory as Palestine.” A Grade 11 history textbook also replaced “the Zionist Enemy” with the “Israeli Occupation”. Impact-se still deemed the change insufficient. “While the change of terminology reduces hostility toward Israel, the use of the term 'the Israeli Occupation,' especially as it appears to refer to Israel as a whole rather than specific territories, continues to reflect a position of non-recognition of Israel,” it said. The complaint is issued in the context of the Israeli government’s declared rejection of Palestinian statehood. “There will not be a Palestinian state. It's very simple: it will not be established,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in November. 'Cunning and devious' Impact-se also objected to Saudi textbooks describing Zionists as “cunning and devious”. One textbook recounts how Chaim Weizmann, a Zionist leader who later became Israel’s first president, tried to bribe Saudi founder King Abdulaziz to “abandon the issue of Palestine” and not be “a major obstacle to the Zionist movement’s ambitions”. The textbook describes Ibn Saud’s response, who regarded Weizmann’s “criminal audacity” as despicable. Impact-se said the account “presents Zionists in a conspiratorial way, encouraging a negative view of the movement as a whole”. However, the historical record supports the central facts. Why the Mecca Agreement has given the UAE-Israel alliance the jitters Read More » A US State Department memorandum dated 6 February 1940 records Weizmann saying that “the only thing the Jews had to offer was money”. Weizmann said he was prepared to raise three to four million pounds Sterling in exchange for Ibn Saud’s support for a plan under which Palestinians would be “voluntarily transferred” to Transjordan and Iraq . That language echoes the “voluntary migration” promoted by Israeli ministers seeking to ethnically cleanse Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Founded by figures closely connected to the Israeli state and Zionist institutions, Impact-se campaigns to change textbooks across the Middle East and promotes an Israeli version of regional history. It demands that Palestinian and Arab textbooks recognise Israel explicitly. Neither the organisation nor its founders appears to have offered equivalent recognition of the State of Palestine. Washington has reinforced this campaign through diplomatic pressure, including work led by the Israeli-born US special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism, Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun. Following the report, Impact-se wrote on X: “We appreciate Saudi Arabia’s continued efforts to improve school curricula, including work to address concerning themes in textbooks. “The portrayal of Israel and Zionism continues the gradual moderation documented in previous IMPACT-se reports,” the report said. headline: US sanctions International Criminal Court president, trial lawyer in bid to dismantle body
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 18 August 2026 21:25 BST | Last update: 1 day 3 hours ago
article_body: The US announced on Tuesday that it is sanctioning the Japanese president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Tomoko Akane, as well as the body's Senegalese senior trial lawyer, Abdoulaye Seye. The move is just the latest step in implementing US President Donald Trump's stated mission of dismantling the ICC for investigating Israeli and, potentially, US officials for war crimes. Neither country is a signatory to the Rome Statute, which established the court in 2002. There are, however, 125 countries that are ICC member states, several of which have been roiled by extrajudicial US and Israeli military action. "The Trump Administration has been clear: the ICC is a corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Akane and Seye, he added, "have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction... This sets a dangerous precedent for all nations". Just days after he assumed power in late January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to sanction the ICC over its investigations into top Israeli officials. British barrister Karim Khan, who was the ICC's chief prosecutor, was the top sanctioned individual at the time. He has since been removed through a vote by member states, albeit due to sexual misconduct allegations. Khan has denied them. Three out of eight ICC judges were also sanctioned, alongside two of Khan's deputies, the United Nations special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories, and three Palestinian human rights organisations. The judges have since sued the Trump administration. The Trump executive order followed a White House visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023. Netanyahu and his then defence minister, Yoav Gallant, were issued arrest warrants in November 2024, alongside three Hamas leaders, who have since been killed by Israel. All non-US individuals and their family members who assist in ICC investigations into US citizens or allies fall under the sanctions order. Their assets are frozen, they cannot use the international banking system, and they cannot enter the US. "The Trump Administration stands ready to take additional measures, if necessary, to systematically dismantle the ICC until it is incapable of threatening American sovereignty," Rubio said. 'Brick by brick' Last week, four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration for its sanctions on the ICC. In a statement, the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute called the sanctions "blatantly illegal". They said they are being forced "to curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of... First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act", given that anyone who appears to associate with ICC cases or officials could now face legal repercussions. And in July, advocates for Palestinian rights in the US also filed a lawsuit in a New York City federal court, seeking an injunction to stop the Trump administration's enforcement of sanctions against groups or individuals liaising with the ICC. US Treasury lifts sanctions against UN rapporteur on Palestine Francesca Albanese Read More » Democracy for the Arab World Now, founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, as well as the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, said they felt compelled to immediately go to court after Rubio wrote in an opinion piece that the US was willing to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick". Earlier this year, former ICC chief prosecutor Fatou Bensouda said the previous head of Israel's Mossad intelligence agency pressured her in a series of meetings to drop her investigation into alleged war crimes in occupied Palestine. Bensouda, who served in her role from 2012 to 2021, said unidentified men came to her home in The Hague after she opened a preliminary examination into the situation in Palestine in 2015. "They came directly to my house," Bensouda told Al Jazeera in an interview published on Sunday. "I got the message that they’re sending." She said the men handed her an envelope containing $500 and indicated it was from someone she had helped. Bensouda said she later concluded the gesture was intended to show that those behind it knew where she lived. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Iran says US went from demanding surrender to seeking talks as oil price rises
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 14:02 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran has proved itself “a tough and invincible power” by resisting the US and Israel , as collapsing shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz pushes oil prices higher. “I have heard this many times from foreign ministers and officials from other countries: ‘You Iranians created a miracle; you surprised the whole world,’” Araghchi told a televised news conference covered by the semi-official Tasnim news agency on Tuesday. “No one thought that Iran could resist America like this,” he said, noting that Washington entered the war with Israeli, western and other international support. “The US president wrote two words [on social media] at the beginning of the war: ‘Unconditional surrender’,” Araghchi said. “That was what they wanted from us and, 20 days later, the same enemy was begging for negotiations.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Araghchi's bullish comments were tempered by Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who warned on Tuesday that the Middle East could not remain trapped between "neither war nor peace". “The goal is to transition to sustainable stability governed by clear and shared rules,” Gargash wrote on X . The veteran Emirati official said the next phase of an agreement between Iran and the US could not rest on “shaky foundations or arrangements detached from international law”. Gargash called for a regional settlement based on “peaceful coexistence, respect for sovereignty, and the logic of peace”, as US-Iranian talks remain stalled and both sides warn that fighting could resume. The war on Iran also continues to choke the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important trade routes. ​Only six vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters, down from a 10-day average of about 11. Before the war, between 130 and 140 ships used the waterway each day. A sculpture overlooking the Strait of Hormuz is seen along the seafront in the port city of Bandar Abbas, in southern Iran on 10 August 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP) Iranian business leader Majid Reza Hariri warned that Tehran could not simply adapt to the US maritime blockade. “Whether through negotiations, requests, threats, or even using force and starting a war again, this maritime blockade must end,” he told Khabar Online. 'Whether through negotiations, requests, threats, or even using force and starting a war again, this maritime blockade must end' - Majid Reza Hariri, Iranian business leader Hariri said replacing sea routes with overland transport could add $18bn annually to Iran’s import bill. Shipping a container from China costs about $3,000 by sea but $12,000 by land, he said. “The worst thing that could happen today is to think we can bypass the maritime blockade and try to run the country despite it,” Hariri said. “We must not allow our economy - or the enemy - to get used to the maritime blockade.” Brent crude rose to almost $90 a barrel on Tuesday, while US crude broke past $84. US Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of launching an illegal war without an exit strategy. “Donald Trump got us into an illegal war, is losing his illegal war, and has no way out of his illegal war,” Schumer wrote on X. “His lack of strategy, discipline, and any ability to seriously negotiate is endangering our troops and raising prices for everyday Americans,” he said. Israel intensifies attacks on Lebanon Israel has meanwhile sharply escalated attacks on southern Lebanon despite a US-mediated ceasefire framework agreed on 26 June. The resurrection of Hezbollah Read More » Lebanon’s National News Agency reported a “concentrated artillery bombardment” on the Ali al-Taher hills near Nabatieh. Israeli earthmovers also demolished homes in Zawtar el-Charqiyeh and Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh on Monday as tanks advanced. Unifil, the UN's force in Lebanon, recorded 455 Israeli projectiles and 97 breaches of Lebanese airspace between Friday and Sunday, the heaviest bombardment in months. It described Saturday’s 229 projectiles as “the highest single-day total since 21 June”. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei “strongly condemned the brutal attacks”, which killed and wounded civilians and destroyed homes and infrastructure. The escalation followed the seventh round of Lebanese-Israeli talks in Rome, exposing the gulf between US-sponsored diplomacy and Israel’s continuing military attacks. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: UAE's Adnoc announces $8bn gas expansion, as it mulls Hormuz bypass
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 19:48 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: The UAE’s state-owned energy giant, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), said on Monday it will invest $8bn to expand its gas business, doubling down on increasing capacity after the Gulf state pulled out of the Saudi Arabian- led energy alliance, Opec. Adnoc said it plans to build a new domestic natural gas processing unit at the country’s largest natural gas processing facility, Habshan, in addition to a new gas export facility at Ruwais. Separately, Adnoc Gas’s CFO, Peter van Driel, told Bloomberg on Monday that the company was also weighing plans to build a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility outside the Strait of Hormuz. That facility would be in addition to the facility at Ruwais that Adnoc Gas is building to more than double its export capacity to about 15 million tonnes a year. The move comes at a time when the Gulf’s LNG powerhouse, Qatar , has declared a force majeure on LNG shipments through the autumn as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran . Qatar relies on vessels to ship gas in liquefied form. Iran and the US are locked in negotiations over the status of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical corridor through which roughly 25 percent of the world’s energy passes. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Qatar resumed some LNG shipments after the US and Iran extended a ceasefire in June, but Qatari vessels have been attacked while transiting Oman’s territorial waters in recent months. The UAE’s vessels have also been struck by Iran, but the Gulf state has taken a more risk-prone approach to sending vessels through the Strait of Hormuz with their ship tracking signals turned off. Reuters reported in June that the UAE paid Iran billions of dollars in return for a halt to attacks on the country, in an about-face for the Gulf state that launched dozens of attacks on Iran alongside the US and Israel during the war. The UAE has also benefited from an oil pipeline that terminates at Fujairah, outside the Strait of Hormuz. Exclusive: Syria, Iraq and US plan to unveil Mediterranean pipeline deal to bypass Strait of Hormuz Read More » That pipeline has helped the UAE continue exporting oil even as other Gulf states, such as Kuwait and Bahrain , are effectively locked out of the market. The UAE boosted oil production to an all-time high in June, pumping 4.1 million barrels per day (bpd) of oil, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in a report released in July. Like the UAE, Saudi Arabia has the East-West Pipeline, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz via the Red Sea. Experts told Middle East Eye that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz. “When we speak to our customers in the region, they say they never want to deal with this again,” Artem Abramov, the deputy head of analysis at Rystad Energy, previously told MEE. “These bypass projects will move forward.” The UAE is building a second pipeline to the port of Fujairah to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, doubling its export capacity by 2027. Meanwhile, Iraq - the second-largest producer in the oil cartel Opec - signed a deal with Syria in July to rehabilitate a pipeline from its northern oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast. MEE was the first to reveal the project and its US backing The UAE’s surging production also reflects analysts' assessments that Abu Dhabi long felt constrained by Saudi-led Opec. The UAE has invested heavily in boosting its production capacity but complained for years that Saudi Arabia, in a bid to support prices, had stopped it from producing more. The UAE left Opec in May 2026. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. Middle East Eye ISSN 2634-2456

headline: Israeli settler who stripped Palestinian naked and zip-tied his genitals released from house arrest
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 13:45 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: An Israeli settler who took part in a brutal attack in which a Palestinian man was stripped naked, had his genitals bound with a zip-tie and was paraded in front of his family has been released from house arrest. The Israeli army said in a statement on Monday that Tal Yinon Dardik, who reportedly took part in the 13 March attack on the Palestinian community of Khirbet Humsa in the occupied West Bank, was being freed from house arrest but would have to report to a police station twice a day. The army said that the decision came after the Jerusalem District Court ruled that the location of his house arrest was untenable. According to reports, Dardik had been staying at his mother-in-law's house in the central West Bank settlement of Adei Ad, but the court found that the order was not workable as she did not want him in the house. Dardik, who became the focus of a campaign by settler activists and right-wing politicians, had denied taking part in the attack when settlers stormed the community before dawn, restrained several Palestinian residents, including women, children and the elderly, and beat them. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters One of those attacked, 29-year-old Qusai Abu al-Kebash, said the settlers stripped him, tied his arms and legs, fastened a zip-tie around his genitals and paraded him around the village. An American activist, who was present at the time of the assault, said that she was "swarmed" upon by "six masked Israeli settlers armed with heavy wooden sticks," as she slept in a tent. "They immediately beat the three of us to the ground, smashing our faces with their fists and clubs," the activist told Haaretz earlier this year. "They zip-tied our hands and feet, and were yelling things like, 'We are going to kill you!'" The activist said that the during the course of the attack, the settlers "pulled down the Palestinian man's pants, poured water all over him and brutally beat him into the dirt". "All he could do was curl into a fetal position and scream when they beat him with their clubs," she added. Clothes ripped Several other residents told Haaretz that the assault lasted about an hour and involved dozens of masked settlers. A woman who was there said she was beaten and dragged outside before her head covering was torn off and some of her clothes ripped. 'They want to make us leave': Israel destroys West Bank wells serving Palestinian herders Read More » "They pulled the girls out and beat them, even the little ones. They mocked us and celebrated our humiliation," she told Haaretz. Meanwhile, a 74-year-old resident said three attackers repeatedly hit him on his head, hands and stomach while another destroyed security cameras, a router and lights. Following the attack, Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz repeatedly criticised the restrictions imposed on Dardik and ordered officials not to renew his detention. Katz also visited Dardik in prison last month, when the settler was reportedly on hunger strike. Katz later threatened to replace Major General Avi Bluth, the head of the military’s Central Command, after Bluth appealed against a ruling that would have allowed Dardik to serve his house arrest at his preferred location. Katz subsequently backed away from the threat following an outcry. More than 700,000 Israelis live in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, according to the International Court of Justice . According to UN data, settler attacks on Palestinian herding communities have increased sharply in recent years with at least 5,910 Palestinians internally displaced due to settler violence between January 2023 and April 2026.
