headline: Why Egypt held back from joining Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan's defence pact
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 16:25 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: When Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan travelled to Mecca on Friday to sign a security pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia , Turkish officials chose to keep the trip secret. The visit did not appear on Erdogan's official schedule. Instead, the three countries decided abruptly on Tuesday that the signing ceremony would take place on Friday. People familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye that senior Turkish officials feared that publicising Erdogan's schedule would give unwanted powers an opportunity to disrupt the agreement. Their concerns were understandable. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Ankara had spent two years trying to persuade all of the parties involved to sign the security pact. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The agreement, despite leaving specific military commitments vague, includes a collective-defence provision resembling Nato's Article 5, under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. For several months, officials from Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia have held regular foreign minister-level consultations under a grouping known as "The Regional Four", moves that have triggered outrage in Israel. In February, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett accused Turkey of "trying to flip Saudi Arabia against us and establish a hostile Sunni axis with nuclear Pakistan." What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East Read More » Several Turkish sources in Ankara told MEE that, in recent months, both Egypt and Saudi Arabia had shown palpable hesitation in establishing a closer regional security architecture with Turkey. Expressing frustration with the matter, a Turkish official told MEE earlier this year: "We are trying to keep the Egyptians and the Saudis on this platform, while the Israelis are constantly trying to bully them." Although Turkish officials initially envisioned a trilateral treaty, the sources said that Egypt emerged as a natural candidate for inclusion in the mechanism. Possessing a powerful military, Egypt increasingly found itself aligned with Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia on issues ranging from the negotiations to end the war on Gaza to developments in Africa. An Ankara-based source familiar with the discussions told MEE that Turkey had made considerable efforts to include Egypt in the treaty and had formally proposed its participation. However, once it became clear that Cairo was not prepared to join, the other countries decided to proceed without it. Fidan downplays Egypt's decision In an interview on Saturday, Fidan sought to downplay Egypt's decision not to join the treaty at this stage. "I believe that, in the next stage, Egypt will also be part of the alliance," he said. "We are already acting as if we are members of the alliance; that is the nature of our relations with all these countries. There are a few technical issues. Once they are resolved, there is no reason why Egypt should not be there." A second Ankara-based source said Egypt's decision was primarily driven by its sensitive relationship with Israel. As a US ally, a neighbour of Israel and an Arab country with full diplomatic relations with Tel Aviv, Egypt must carefully manage its complex engagement with the Israeli government. Israel has the power to dominate, but not to lead the region Read More » The source said Cairo would have to withstand pressure from Israel if it were to join the treaty. Egyptian publication Madamasr reported on Sunday, citing sources, that Cairo indeed declined to join. Regional officials who spoke to MEE did agree, however, that Cairo also had its own reasons for declining to join for now. Amid rising tensions between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Egypt is struggling to choose a side. Staying out of the alliance gives Cairo some breathing room. Egypt has a defence treaty with Abu Dhabi and deployed Rafale fighter jets in response to Iranian strikes against the UAE in May. According to the second source, this predicament has also led Saudi Arabia to view Egypt as somewhat unreliable. The source added that Egypt does not want to choose sides between emerging blocs comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on one side, and Israel, the UAE and India on the other. Cairo lacks a broader strategic vision beyond the region and remains interested in deepening its commercial ties with New Delhi, while also relying on financial assistance from Abu Dhabi. Turkish officials nevertheless hope that as the alliance takes shape and establishes itself as a credible deterrent against potential regional aggression, Cairo will be more receptive to joining. headline: Dubai ruler confronted in London over UAE involvement in Sudan war
author: Oscar Rickett
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 16:00 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: The ruler of Dubai and prime minister of the UAE has been confronted on the streets of central London over his country's involvement in the Sudan war . A video posted on Sunday shows a Sudanese man shouting at Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Maktoum and his entourage as they walk from Selfridges department store down through the affluent Mayfair area of central London. “Emiratis and UAE, they’re killing Sudanese people,” the man shouts from across the road at the ruler of Dubai and the group he is with. “UAE is killing people in my country. Stop killing my people.” One man, who appears to be Emirati and part of Maktoum’s entourage, then appears to racially abuse the Sudanese man, shouting: “Fuck you, fuck you and fuck your people… Motherfucker, Black bitch.” “You said Black?” the Sudanese man asks him. “Shut the fuck up,” replies the Emirati, who then crosses the road to confront the Sudanese man. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “Stop killing Sudanese,” the man says. “Emirati and UAE they’re killing Sudanese people. They are killing people in my country… Mohammed bin Zayed, they are killing people in my country,” he says, referring to the president of the United Arab Emirates. The ruler of Dubai and prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, Mohammed bin Rashid Al-Maktoum, has been confronted in central London over the UAE’s alleged involvement in Sudan’s ongoing war. A video posted on Sunday shows a Sudanese man confronting Mohammed bin Rashid and… pic.twitter.com/GPtQPXcaYj — Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) August 11, 2026 Last Thursday, Emirati media reported that Mohammed bin Zayed (MBZ) had met with al-Maktoum at the Jumeirah Carlton Tower Hotel in London. The get-together was described as a “fraternal meeting that reflected the enduring bonds of unity, mutual respect and shared values that define the UAE's leadership”. In a statement, a Met Police spokesperson told MEE: “We are aware of a video circulating online appearing to show an individual shouting a racial slur. Officers will review the footage to assess whether any offences have been committed. “Should anyone wish to come forward to report information in relation to the video, they should call 101.” UAE involvement in Sudan war Though the United Arab Emirates continues to deny it, there is now widespread evidence supporting the claim that the UAE supports Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces , which have been accused by the UN and US of committing genocide during the war in Sudan. United Nations experts , human rights groups and reporting from Middle East Eye has documented arms transfers to the RSF facilitated by networks based in Libya, Chad and the breakaway region of Somaliland. Earlier this year, MEE revealed the use of an Ethiopian army base supporting the RSF in Sudan. How the UAE continued supporting Sudan's RSF through Haftar and Libya Read More » Western nations including the UK have been accused of failing to publicly oppose Emirati involvement in the Sudan war, which began in April 2023 and has led to the widest humanitarian catastrophe in the world, because of economic capture by the UAE. Figures close to the Emirati leadership and analysts sympathetic to the UAE have recently seemed to tacitly acknowledge the support provided over many years to the RSF and its leader, Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, who owns property in Dubai through a network of shell companies. Earlier this year, Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, an Emirati academic and former adviser to MBZ, criticised the “singling out” of the UAE over its support for the RSF, noting that the Sudanese paramilitary also “has support from Uganda, from Ethiopia, from Chad”. Referring to Egyptian and Turkish support for the RSF’s enemy, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), Hussain Abdul-Hussain, an analyst who describes himself as an “advocate of immediate, unconditional, Arab-Israeli peace”, posted on social media: “So Turkish and Egyptian intervention in Sudan is ok but Emirati intervention is not? What am I missing here?” When the RSF captured el-Fasher, the capital of Sudan’s North Darfur, the paramilitary executed, raped and extorted thousands of civilians as part of a campaign the UN said bore “all the hallmarks of genocide”. UAE rulers in London Maktoum, the ruler of Dubai confronted on London’s streets, has previously been found by a British court to have kept his daughters Latifa and Shamsa captive, and to have conducted a campaign of harassment against his now former wife, Jordan’s Princess Haya. In 2020, a judge in London ruled that Maktoum had organised the kidnapping of Latifa, who attempted to flee Dubai in 2018, and her older sister Shamsa, who in 2000 temporarily escaped her family in the UK. headline: Turkey suspects Israel fabricated Trump Air Force One assassination plot to derail US-Iran deal
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 15:05 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Turkish officials suspect that an Israeli intelligence report that said Iran planned to assassinate US President Donald Trump during the Ankara Nato summit last month was a ruse to undermine negotiations with Tehran, Middle East Eye has learnt. It was around 2pm on 8 July when journalists heard that Turkish security forces were unusually deploying additional units to Ankara Airport, where Trump’s Air Force One was parked. Ankara was under lockdown for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (Nato) summit on 7-8 July. Roads were blocked, pavements were closed, public servants had been granted a week of administrative leave, and the city was largely deserted. The Turkish government had even transformed an airbase of the Turkish Air Force, Etimesgut Air Base, officially known as Ankara Airport, for the event, allowing heads of state to reach the summit venue within 10 minutes. Against the backdrop of these extensive security precautions, US officials told their Turkish counterparts that they had received an intelligence report from Israel suggesting Iran could target Trump. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters People familiar with the matter told MEE that the report warned an Iranian covert operations unit could target Trump’s brand-new Air Force One near Ankara Airport. “Supposedly, the Iranians could target the aircraft from within a one-kilometre radius using shoulder-fired missiles known as Manpads,” one person familiar with the matter told MEE. Unlike Esenboga Airport, the international airport serving the Turkish capital, Ankara Airport is surrounded by civilian buildings, some of which are as close as 500 metres to the runway. Their proximity prompted Turkish officials to take additional precautions. The people familiar with the issue added that the US Secret Service wanted to take further protective measures. Officials first moved Trump’s departure from Ankara Airport to Esenboga Airport, where civilian buildings are farther from the perimeter. They then brought back the old Air Force One because it had air defence systems that the new aircraft lacked. The threat of an Iranian attempt on Trump’s life appeared credible to many US officials, as Iran had reportedly tried to orchestrate such an attack twice before. In July 2024, Pakistani national Asif Merchant was arrested over an alleged plot to kill US politicians, potentially including Trump. Then, in November 2024, the justice department announced charges against Afghan national Farhad Shakeri, alleging that Iran’s government had instructed him to devise a plan to assassinate Trump. Iran has denied targeting Trump or other American officials. The Secret Service took the latest report so seriously that, according to The Washington Post, Trump was secretly moved after boarding the old Air Force One. He was reportedly bundled into a catering vehicle and taken to an accompanying US government aircraft, a C-32. My favorite part: This Turkish catering truck nonchalantly moving from Air Force One to the other plane pic.twitter.com/KYVm4FsG4W — John Hudson (@John_Hudson) August 11, 2026 A Turkish official confirmed to MEE that US officials had sought additional landing permits for the C-32 as part of the plan and pushed for last-minute changes, leaving Ankara with the impression that something was amiss. Yet the Israeli intelligence report arrived at a sensitive moment. Trump was negotiating a deal with Iran to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. During his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Trump repeatedly said that the war with Iran had ended and expressed hope about the negotiations, a source who attended the meeting told MEE. That position sharply contradicted the agenda of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was pushing for a resumption of hostilities, including heavier strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure and a new assassination campaign targeting Iranian leaders. 'No way this report was true' Turkish officials now say they believe the Israeli intelligence report was probably a ruse by Netanyahu’s government to portray itself as protecting Trump, derail negotiations with Iran and undermine Trump’s apparently close relationship with Erdogan. During his meeting with the Turkish head of state the day before the alleged assassination plot, Trump also signalled that he was prepared to lift sanctions imposed on Turkey over its 2019 purchase of the Russian -made S-400 missile system and to sell F-35 fighter jets to Ankara. Netanyahu also strongly opposes F-35 sales to Ankara, arguing that it would change the balance of power in the region, eroding Israel's " Qualitative Military Edge ". “Of course, we took the report very seriously and tried to assist our American counterparts as much as possible,” one person familiar with the matter told MEE. “Yet it was very clear to us that there was no way this report was true.” Although Iranian cells have previously kidnapped or assassinated Iranian dissidents in Turkey, Tehran has never dared to carry out a sophisticated operation there involving anything beyond a simple firearm. 'I guess they need heroes for an attack that never happened and, most likely, was never planned' - Ankara insider Such an attack would require extensive knowledge of the country, as well as safe houses, covert routes into and out of Ankara, and the transportation of Manpads through numerous roadblocks and security checkpoints ahead of the summit. An attempt of this kind could also put Turkey on a collision course with Iran, which has managed to maintain relatively stable relations with Ankara since the beginning of the war. Iranian officials have publicly thanked Turkey several times for not supporting what they described as a Mossad-CIA plot to trigger an insurrection in western Iran with the involvement of armed Iranian Kurdish groups. An Ankara insider told MEE it was ironic that details of the Secret Service operation to protect Trump had been leaked just a month after the summit. “I guess they need heroes for an attack that never happened and, most likely, was never planned,” the insider said. MEE has reached out to the White House and Israeli foreign ministry for comment. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli ministers incite against 'Arabic-speaking' medical staff at Haifa hospital
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 16:13 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: A body representing Palestinian citizens of Israel has condemned what it called an “obsessive campaign of incitement” by Israeli ministers against Arab medical staff in recent days. The High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel was referring to comments by Defence Minister Israel Katz and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, who called for an investigation into allegations that Arab medical workers mistreated wounded Israeli soldiers. The claims were made by relatives of a soldier wounded in Lebanon and treated at Rambam Health Care Campus in Haifa. Yehoshua Shani, chairman of a forum that opposes the Gaza ceasefire and supports continuing the war, claimed his nephew was mistreated by Arab staff at the hospital. In a post on X on Sunday, Shani said the nurses on duty were all “Arabic speakers” who ignored the patient’s request for water and turned him over in his bed “like a sardine”, hitting his head against the bed. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters David Chesterman, the soldier’s brother, made similar claims on Instagram. He said the family had been denied entry to his brother’s room, which is standard procedure in intensive care units. “I broke down the door to make sure he was okay. He wasn’t. He begged for water and no one was around,” Chesterman claimed. 'This is a Jewish state': Arabic banned at work for Palestinian citizens of Israel Read More » “He whispered to me that they had brutally turned him over in bed ‘like a sardine,’ his head was slammed against the bed and no one cared.” The unproven allegations were subsequently amplified by Katz and Ben Gvir. “I view with great seriousness the testimonies that have been published regarding the behaviour toward wounded IDF (Israeli army) soldiers in the hospital,” Katz said. “I have instructed the IDF (Israeli army) to immediately and thoroughly examine all the allegations that have been raised with the hospital and the relevant parties,” he added. Ben Gvir said: “If the disturbing testimonies coming from Rambam hospital are true, this is a grave scandal that should trouble every citizen in Israel.” He said the allegations “demand an immediate, thorough, and un-whitewashed investigation, including an examination of whether in some cases this constitutes harassment on a nationalist basis”. 'Disappointing' hospital response Rambam said after reviewing the incident that it “rejects the claims that the patient was treated inappropriately”. Some Palestinian doctors, however, criticised the hospital’s response, saying it failed to address the allegations targeting Arab medical staff, according to Haaretz . “At the end of the day, this is an attack on all Arab medical staff,” one medical professional said. The hospital’s director, Dr Michal Makel, later sent an internal message of support to staff. Coerced into silence: The reality of being a Palestinian doctor in an Israeli hospital Read More » “Any attempt to make generalisations or create divisions among staff members based on language, background or identity is unacceptable and does not reflect the spirit of Rambam,” Makel wrote, according to Haaretz. One Palestinian medical professional said the hospital’s response was insufficient. “If there isn't clear, unequivocal and public backing even from the hospital itself, it is insulting and disappointing,” the professional said. The High Follow-Up Committee, an umbrella organisation representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, condemned the ministers for using the allegations to “incite” against Arab doctors. “Fascists launch campaigns spreading lies and baseless accusations for no reason other than that those targeted are Arabs,” it said. “There have been many allegations and accusations, but no one has produced any evidence that any member of the Arab medical teams discriminated between patients.” It added that such racist campaigns of incitement against Arab medical staff in hospitals and medical institutions have been ongoing for a long time in Israel. “There are those who are displeased by the high proportion of Arabs working in the health sector: male and female doctors, nurses, pharmacists and others working in the field.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Less than four percent of US safety funding went to Muslim institutions: Report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 22:15 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Over the past decade in the US, since Donald Trump first ascended to the White House in 2017, less than four percent of US government grant funding to keep religious institutions safe has gone to Muslim nonprofits, a new report by the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) has found . The funds are awarded annually through the Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP), which is operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). An institution can typically receive a maximum of some $200,000 for each site it operates, and the money must be put toward physical safeguards: security cameras, bulletproof glass, guardrails around properties, and the training of security guards, among other tools. Nearly 60 percent of the pot has gone to Jewish groups, followed by Christian groups at a little over 25 percent, the figures in the report showed. "Of the $850m awarded through this program over nine years, Muslim organisations only got 3.8 percent of the funding... it's a really, really small amount going to a community that is under threat, and a growing threat," Dr Sarah Mohamed, a co-author of the report and a senior researcher with MPAC's Center for Security, Technology, and Policy, told Middle East Eye on Monday. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A year ago, the conservative think tank, Middle East Forum, published a report claiming that DHS was using US tax dollars to fund "terror-linked and extremist groups" between 2013 and 2023. That report listed 49 Muslim-American organisations, and said the NSGP "remains the greatest source of DHS funding to extremist groups". "Even members of Congress have not been able to verify that," Sameer Hossain, MPAC's managing director in Washington, DC, and the other author of the report, told MEE. "What we do know for sure is that the terms and conditions that DHS has put out for this year and the previous year under the current administration make it even more difficult for American Muslims and other community organisations to apply for these very critical grants," he added. That's because the administration has been cracking down on initiatives that go against its policy platform: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI); assistance to undocumented immigrants; and boycotts of Israel. "If you as a grantee were found to be engaging in those prohibited activities, you expose yourself to more legal risk," Hossain said. So was the limited funding for Muslim groups inevitable, given the current political climate? That's not certain, Mohamed said. "We don't have any public information about how many institutions applied. So the denominator isn't available for us to be able to say [that]," she told MEE. MPAC has engaged with Jewish-American groups on the issue, Hossain noted, and they tend to be better resourced and practised at the cumbersome and bureaucratic process of applying for the grant, he said. Jewish nonprofits were among the first to request a programme like NSGP, following the establishment of DHS, in the wake of the 9/11 attacks. Anti-Muslim sentiment on the rise Anti-Muslim sentiment in the US has skyrocketed since the Trump administration assumed power in January 2025. The president's agenda, largely pre-orchestrated by the far-right Heritage Foundation in its Project 2025 document, puts Muslim-American communities and Muslim countries in the crosshairs. Republican lawmakers have openly derided Muslims and called for legal action or violence against them - most notoriously Florida Congressman Randy Fine, Tennessee Congressman Andy Ogles, and Alabama Senator Tommy Tuberville. Trump himself recently shared an image of a group of Minnesota Muslim kindergarteners in hijabs to his Truth Social platform, where he has often called for Somali Americans in the state to be investigated and deported, including hijab-wearing Congresswoman Ilhan Omar. In the lead-up to the election of the very first Muslim mayor of New York City last year, The Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH) revealed in a 20-page document that Islamophobic and xenophobic discourse surrounding Zohran Mamdani on X had a reach of some 1.5 billion between his Democratic primary win in June and the end of October. Anti-Muslim lawmaker Andy Ogles loses Republican primary Read More » The organisation called on the platform to implement election-specific safeguards, enforce community guidelines against attacks on race and religion, and enhance corrective counterarguments in its algorithm. CSOH also reported a sharp increase in anti-Muslim content on X since Israel and the US launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February. The Washington, DC-based social media monitor said it tracked posts that explicitly dehumanised, excluded, and incited violence against Muslims from 1 January to 5 March, during which Trump was consistently threatening to start the war. On the day the war began, the volume of such posts surged from just under 2,000 per day to more than 6,000, the report said . In April, MPAC revealed that attacks on Muslim-American individuals and institutions were at a 15-month high under the Trump administration. The group documented an eleven-fold increase in targeted incidents in the first three months of this year alone. At least nine of the attacks occurred in March, ranging from vandalism and bomb threats at mosques to sexual assaults against Muslim women, according to a policy paper entitled "The Pitfalls of Operation Epic Fury: How the Undeclared War Against Iran Hurts Americans’ Interests Abroad and at Home." In May, after a shooting that killed three people outside a California mosque that housed a school with children inside, Muslim-American groups blamed what they said was the mainstreaming of anti-Muslim hate speech by lawmakers and other right-wing influential figures. "We are deeply disturbed, but not at all surprised," the Council on American-Islamic Relations said in a statement at the time. "Hate against American Muslims is completely out of control." Now, with Michigan Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed potentially on his way to becoming the first-ever Muslim US senator in the country's history, his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, has released an attack ad on Sayed featuring images of Osama bin Laden. headline: Inside the growing rift between Iran’s dealmakers and ultraconservatives
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 15:42 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Iran ’s political landscape appears to have entered a new phase as two competing camps emerge: those advocating a deal with the United States and those determined to block any agreement. Principlists have intensified their pressure on reformist President Masoud Pezeshkian and conservative Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, both of whom are seeking to reach an agreement with Washington and bring an end to almost six months of hostilities. Principlists fear that any deal could marginalise them politically and weaken their influence over Iran’s future direction. It was in this climate that a leaked video of Mohammad-Bagher Kharrazi, the brother-in-law of Masoud Khamenei, the younger brother of Iran’s supreme leader, emerged as part of what critics describe as a broader hard-line campaign. In the video, Kharrazi claimed that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had “formally and publicly announced” that if Pezeshkian attempts to resign one more time, his resignation would be accepted. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Kharrazi said that Pezeshkian, who he said had threatened resignation “27 or 28 times”, “no longer dares” to raise the issue. He added that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had been completely sidelined from negotiations with the United States after an order from Khamenei. In response, the public relations office of the supreme leader denied, without directly naming Kharrazi, the reported remarks attributed to him regarding the president’s resignation. Soon afterward, however, another audio file surfaced in which Ali Saeedi, a conservative senior figure close to the Khamenei's office, claimed that the supreme leader had expressed support for the negotiations and criticised hard-line opposition to diplomacy. According to Saeedi, Khamenei told one of his brothers: “I have never opposed negotiations, and I still do not. I was the one who authorised the negotiations, and I am not satisfied with the hard-line positions adopted by some people.” Saeedi also claimed that Khamenei supports Ghalibaf, saying: “He is like [the late Quds Force commander] Haj Qassem Soleimani.” Behind the curtain of the power struggle A senior reformist source told Middle East Eye that principlists had not initially wanted Khamenei to succeed his father, instead favouring their own candidates for Iran’s top leadership post. According to the source, their preferred options included the late president Ebrahim Raisi, who was killed in a helicopter crash, and hard-line cleric Mohammad Mahdi Mirbaqeri, who advocates a civilisational confrontation with the West and views many forms of modernity and western-origin technology negatively. The source added that, in recent years, principlists had repeatedly targeted members of Khamenei’s inner circle, including Mahdi Khamoushi, who has been tipped as a possible future chief of staff to the supreme leader, accusing them of corruption in an effort to undermine their credibility. 'They want to turn Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf into political outcasts and ultimately push the supreme leader into turning against them' - Reformist political analyst “Mojtaba may also hold some hard-line views,” the source said, “but he was not the figure leading ultraconservatives over the past decade.” “Instead, he was involved in a succession struggle in which influential hard-line figures, including Raisi’s camp, acted against him. However, [US President Donald] Trump’s war changed the political dynamics and created a more favourable environment for Mojtaba.” A conservative source told MEE that principlists are now attempting to mobilise conservative and hard-line supporters against Ghalibaf, portraying themselves in the eyes of Khamenei and religious class as the only reliable protectors of the leader. The source said that, as part of this strategy, principlists have repeatedly attempted to weaken Ghalibaf by accusing him of bypassing the supreme leader. However, Khamenei continues to trust and support Ghalibaf, the source said, adding that if the supreme leader had lost confidence in him, he would have removed him from his role overseeing negotiations with the US. Political outcasts A political analyst at a reformist newspaper told MEE that principlists are determined to preserve their grip on power, and that their most effective strategy is to remove Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian from the political equation. War on Iran: What is Tehran's 'shadow fleet' really and how does it work? Read More » “They want to turn these two figures into political outcasts and ultimately push the supreme leader into turning against them,” he said. The analyst said ultraconservatives are also likely to continue obstructing negotiations, because they believe any agreement with the US would significantly weaken their influence by empowering more moderate political forces. "But the ultraconservatives lack sufficient influence within Iran’s key centres of power to achieve this on their own," the analyst said. "As a result, they have increasingly relied on their grassroots base to fill that gap. “It is in this context that they have staged a series of angry sit-ins and protests targeting the negotiators, seeking to raise the political cost for both Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over Golan Heights
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 12:11 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Colombia's far-right president Abelardo de la Espriella recognised Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights on Monday. “The Government of Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over this territory, as well as that State’s right to protect itself against external threats,” read an online statement. It added that, “Colombia recognises that maintaining Israel’s control and sovereignty over the Golan Heights is an essential component of its national defence.” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar thanked his “good friend” de la Espriella for the “historic” recognition on Sunday. The Golan Heights is a Syrian territory occupied by Israel since Syria's defeat in the 1967 war against Israel. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Only one other country, the US, recognised Israel's claim of sovereignty over the territory. The Syrian foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it "categorically rejects and condemns" Colombia's recognition of Israeli sovereignty over Golan Heights and said that the area "is an inseparable part of [Syrian] territory". Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said that Colombia's position “contradicts international law and relevant international legitimacy resolutions”. The Saudi foreign ministry said the Gulf kingdom's firm position is that the Golan “is occupied Syrian Arab land”, and that any measures aimed at changing its status “do not create a right or confer legitimacy”. President de la Espriella, who was inaugurated last week, has vouched to reverse the policies of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro. Petro was an ardent supporter of the Palestinian cause and loudly condemned Israel's genocide of Palestinians in Gaza , which began in October 2023. Colombia summit: What's next for The Hague Group? Read More » Under Petro, Colombia was a co-chair and co-founder of the Hague Group, a collection of countries working to hold Israel to account for its treatment of Palestinians under international law. Bogota withdrew its ambassador from Israel after the genocide began and also halted coal exports to the state. De la Espriella's election to the presidency has been welcomed in Israel, which is enjoying a wave of elections of pro-Israel candidates across Latin America. Bolivia resumed cordial relations with Israel after the election of conservative candidate President Rodrigo Paz in 2025. In Chile, Jose Antonio Kast, another supporter of Israel, took power in March 2026. Israel's most vocal ally, is Argentina's President Javier Milei, who has said, "'If Israel falls, all of the West is next." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement'
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 17:06 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: Iran has played down the mutual security agreement signed between the leaders of Saudi Arabia , Pakistan and Turkey in the Muslim holy city of Mecca on Friday. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Monday that Tehran saw no reason to be concerned that a new security pact is directed against Iran. Baghaei said the pact showed a "change in perception" towards the US, as well as a shift in the regional approach to security. He added that the agreement represented a shift towards greater reliance on the states' own capabilities rather than outside powers. "Any plan that is based on the geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy and its allies," Baghaei said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Many analysts have suggested that the alliance between Ankara, Riyadh and Islamabad is targeted at Tehran. The three states have largely Sunni populations, but while Saudi Arabia has had frosty relations with Iran, Turkey and Pakistan have remained relatively cordial with Tehran. Islamabad has been a key conduit for negotiations between the US and Iran as they engage in a prolonged conflict over the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded in response to the US and Israeli war on the country, which was initially aimed at toppling its government. Why Egypt held back from joining Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan's defence pact Read More » Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, has been the subject of Iranian retaliatory action primarily aimed at US military assets within its borders. As the conflict has dragged on, hostilities have reignited between Saudi Arabia and its neighbours to the south, the Houthi-led administration in Sanaa, which controls most of northern Yemen. The Houthis have responded to Saudi air strikes and attacks by its allies in the internationally recognised Yemeni government with attacks on Riyadh's energy facilities. Most recently, a Saudi Aramco refinery suffered widespread fires after a drone struck its facilities in the province of Jizan early on Sunday . Turkish and Saudi relations have been on the mend in recent years due to a rapprochement that followed soured relations over the murder of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, as well as the backing of rival factions in conflicts in Libya. Pakistan has been a long-time military backer of the government in Riyadh, albeit one that tries to maintain amiable relations with other Muslim-majority states, including Iran. headline: Iran warns enemies to 'anticipate strategic surprises' as it shifts from a defensive stance
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 17 August 2026 12:20 BST | Last update: 2 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Iran has warned its adversaries to "anticipate strategic surprises" as a senior military official said the country was set to shift from a defensive stance to an offensive one. Yadollah Javani, the head of the political bureau of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told state media on Monday morning that "The enemy should know that it cannot catch us off-guard.” “Instead, it is the enemy that must anticipate strategic surprises,” he added. "Whatever is necessary to defend this land, ensure security, and neutralise enemy threats will be executed at the appropriate time." Javani's comments came as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passes, slowed over the weekend. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A total of five commodity vessels transited the strait on Saturday, with none recorded for Sunday, in comparison to 31 vessels transiting last weekend, according to ship tracking data from Kpler. Iran and Oman on Monday continued talks to establish a secure maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said, blaming security complications caused by US and Israeli military actions. “Drawing up the maritime transit route plan with Oman has been time-consuming due to security complexities,” Baghaei said, adding that “the issue is inherently complex”. Speaking on the proposed mechanism, Baghaei said it would aim to protect the sovereign rights and interests of both Iran and Oman while ensuring the safe passage of commercial vessels. “This is the first time that a mechanism is being developed to simultaneously safeguard the sovereign rights of the two littoral states and ensure the safe passage of commercial vessels,” he said, adding that intensive talks to finalise a joint statement were continuing. Baghaei also said that a 60-day period linked to the 17 June memorandum between Tehran and Washington was no longer relevant, accusing the US of violating the agreement weeks after it was signed. “There is no provision in the memorandum of understanding referring to a ‘60-day deadline’, and the Islamic Republic of Iran never formulates its policies under pressure, ultimatums or time limits,” he said. Baghaei said the memorandum envisaged a 60-day period for talks on “the lifting of sanctions” and “the nuclear issue”, which could have been extended if no agreement was reached. However, he said “gross and widespread” US violations meant talks never began. “As a result, the issue of a 60-day deadline became entirely moot,” Baghaei added. Iranian drone targets Iraqi Kurdistan Also on Monday, two Iranian drones targeted the Iraqi Kurdistan prime minister's office and the home of the autonomous region's intelligence chief overnight, authorities said. "Following an investigation by the Kurdistan Counter-Terrorism Unit, my personal office and the home of the head of the Security and Intelligence Agency were targeted by Iranian drone attacks earlier today," Kurdistan Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said in a post on X. Iran and Oman work on temporary Hormuz shipping route as Trump threatens to claim the strait Read More » "This is a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the security and stability of the Kurdistan region." The regional counterterrorism directorate said there were no casualties in the attack. Since the start of the war on Iran in late February, the Kurdistan region, which hosts US troops and international oil firms as well as rebels exiled from Iran, has been targeted with more than 1,000 attacks by Tehran and pro-Iran armed groups inside Iraq. Meanwhile, Iran's foreign ministry has blamed pollution in Gulf waters on decades of US wars in the region, after several oil spills were reported. “This environmental damage stems from the US military presence and the wars it has waged in the region over the past five decades,” foreign ministry spokesperson Baghaei said on Monday. “The damage caused to the environment of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman is not solely linked to this war.” He called for the US to be held accountable, estimating the damage at "trillions of dollars". Last week, Iran demanded compensation after an oil slick in the Strait of Hormuz reached the island of Qeshm, affecting beaches and an environmentally sensitive mangrove forest. At the time, Baghaei cited preliminary evidence identifying “a foreign bulk carrier” as the source of the spill, which Iranian officials later said had been “completely cleaned up”. Missing pilots 'prisoners in Qatar' Elsewhere, Baghaei said on Monday that Iran will consider three missing pilots to be prisoners in Qatar , despite Doha's denials, until it clarifies their fate. Tehran has said the Iranians went missing while carrying out an operation against the US’ Al Udeid air base in Qatar on 2 March. On Saturday, Iranian authorities alleged for the first time that the pilots had been captured in Qatar, after previously saying one pilot had been killed and three others were missing. "It is imperative to obtain clarification on their situation," Baghaei said. "Until the pilots' situation is clarified, we consider them prisoners and will spare no effort to shed light on their fate." Qatar denies holding the pilots and said an invitation had been sent to Iran "to be briefed on the details of the search and rescue operations in April, but the Iranian side has yet to respond". Last month, Iran's military said it had retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during the attack on Al Udeid, the largest US military base in the Middle East. The base hosts forward elements of US Central Command, as well as US air and special operations forces. In early March, Qatar's defence ministry said it had shot down two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers but it was not immediately clear whether they were the same aircraft referred to by Iran. headline: Trump asks Iran for war reparations in new tit-for-tat demand
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 21:59 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek compensation from Iran for the deaths of US soldiers as part of any peace negotiations in a tit-for-tat demand after Tehran requested war reparations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. “I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five-month Military Conflict (started because, THEY WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON), even though it was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran," he added. Trump said he wanted reparations not only from damages arising from the current war, but also attacks Iran is widely believed to have facilitated through allied militias on US soldiers going back more than two decades after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq. Trump referenced the deaths and injuries of US soldiers from roadside bombs that Iranian General Qassem Soleimani is believed to have orchestrated. Iran began arming Shia militias with roadside bombs in the mid-2000s during the US occupation of Iraq. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The campaign was part of Iran and the US’s battle for influence in Iraq. Trump ordered the assassination of Soleimani inside Iraq in 2020, citing his role in supporting militias aligned with Tehran. Trump’s post also cited the October 2000 bombing of the USS Cole warship, but US intelligence agencies have blamed al-Qaeda for the attack, not Tehran. Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement' Read More » Trump also requested that Iran pay its own citizens compensation for the death of protesters at the start of the year. Trump partially justified the February 2026 US and Israeli war on Iran by citing its crackdown on protesters. Trump said 50,000 people were killed, while an Iranian official put the number at at least 5,000 people. It’s unclear how serious Trump is about conditioning a ceasefire on compensation for the death of US service members, let alone Iranian nationals. But his comments came after Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Iran needed war reparations in order to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump’s rebuttal fits a pattern of him matching Iranian demands with his own. The US president contradicted his own secretary of state, Marco Rubio, in July when he said that the US could charge a toll of 20 percent in the Strait of Hormuz in return for being its “guardian”. Rubio has insisted that any toll in the waterway is “completely illegal”. Trump’s latest post underscores how a ceasefire extension between the two sides announced in June has effectively broken down, as Washington and Tehran look for an advantage on the battlefield. However, The Wall Street Journal reported over the weekend that Trump had effectively given up on his main stated objective when he started the war - ensuring a nuclear agreement with Tehran that prevents it from pursuing a path to a nuclear weapon. The report said Trump would end the war in order to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israel holding bodies of 1,700 Palestinians as bargaining chips, says report
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 13:07 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Israel is holding the dead bodies of about 1,700 Palestinians as potential bargaining chips despite there being no Israeli hostages currently held by Palestinian armed groups, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz has reported. According to the report, Shin Bet chief David Zini has urged Israel to retain the remains for possible use in future hostage negotiations, a position supported by the Israeli military. Haaretz reported that most of the remains belong to Palestinian combatants involved in the Hamas-led 7 October attack in 2023 but also include Palestinian civilians and 13 Israeli citizens. Legal sources cited by Haaretz argue that Israel lacks the authority to hold the remains of Palestinian non-combatants, as the decision is not backed by Security Cabinet policy. In July, the Israeli daily reported that the authorities admitted in response to a High Court of Justice petition to holding the body of a Palestinian detainee, a photographer and father of four, who was arrested in December 2023 and died a day later while being held in a detention centre at the Erez Crossing. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The body has reportedly not undergone an autopsy. His family discovered what happened to him in July 2025, after filing a petition through the rights group Gisha. Even after notifying the family, the government did not disclose information relating to the date, location or circumstances of his death, as well as the legal basis for retaining his body. It claimed that he had been a “military Hamas operative”, which the family refutes. In July, Gisha reported that Israel "continues to hold the bodies of more than 100 Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza who died in its custody", at least 68 of them Gaza residents. The state told the court it was conducting a review into the decision to continue holding the body and those of other Palestinians, but that it had been paused as a result of the war with Iran. Palestinian ‘doctor of the poor’ says he faces abuse, medical neglect in Israeli prison Read More » Israel has long maintained a policy of seizing the bodies of Palestinians killed by its forces. Several human rights groups have repeatedly condemned the policy, calling for them to be returned to their families. International humanitarian law requires treating the dead with dignity. The International Committee of the Red Cross says the rules are intended, among other things, to prevent people from becoming missing and to ensure families can learn of the fate of their relatives. The Fourth Geneva Convention also requires the bodies of deceased internees to be honourably buried and their graves maintained and marked so they can be identified. It states that the dead must be treated with dignity, "honourably buried" and "if possible according to the rites of the religion to which they belonged". Under Israeli law, the retention of Palestinian bodies is permitted and has been implemented across the occupied Palestinian territory. Reuters reported in November 2025 that Palestinian armed groups had returned all Israeli captives' remains as part of an exchange involving Palestinian remains. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Social media platform X says it is challenging block of jailed Istanbul mayor's account
author: Alex MacDonald
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 15:31 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: An announcement by X that it is challenging a request to ban imprisoned Mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoglu's presidential candidacy account in Turkey has been met with scepticism by digital campaigners. The account, created to support Imamoglu's candidacy for the next presidential election, was first blocked in Turkey late last month following a government request. In a post on X on Wednesday, the company said Turkish laws "force" them to comply with the order last week, at risk of Turkey's Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) "throttling" the site's access in the country. “Although Turkey’s laws force us to comply with the order, we are challenging the order in court and, in the spirit of full transparency, are sharing the court order,” it said, posting a copy. Imamoglu's main X account, which had nearly 10 million followers, was blocked in Turkey in May 2025 under a similar order from the government, which X also said it had challenged in the courts. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Meta and YouTube have also complied with requests from the Turkish government to block accounts and content associated with Imamoglu. Yaman Akdeniz, founder of Turkish freedom of expression organisation IFOD, said he was sceptical of the willingness of the site, owned by self-proclaimed "free speech absolutist" Elon Musk, to actually challenge the Turkish authorities. Elon Musk reiterates claim that UK is on verge of 'reckoning' due to Muslim immigration Read More » "It is true to say that every now and again they appeal against decisions and lodge a few applications with the Constitutional Court - however, this is very selective and X chooses not to provide further details about the judicial challenges," he told Middle East Eye. According to the most recent X transparency report, the company received 11,107 removal requests from Turkey between July and December 2024 and took action in 86 percent of cases. A Washington Post review of past disclosure data found the social media site acted on 71 percent of legal requests it received to remove content in the first half of 2024, up 20 percent from its previous reported figure in 2021. The report said X had taken action in 68 percent of the cases requested by Turkey, which amounted to 9,364 requests in the first half of 2024. "I must say Meta and the others are no different as they have all become the long arm of the Turkish law enforcement mechanism," said Akdeniz. Saudi dissident blocks Turkey is not the only country to which X has responded to takedown requests for accounts belonging to government critics and dissidents. The Guardian revealed on Tuesday that X had blocked the accounts of a number of prominent critics of the kingdom, including human rights campaigner Yahya Assiri and activist Abdullah Alaoudh, son of imprisoned cleric Salman al-Ouda. It came on the heels of similar bans on Snapchat, Meta and Instagram over claims from the Saudi authorities that their accounts violated local laws. 'A triumphant failure': How Israel's use of social media influencers to win back support backfired Read More » However, at the time X had claimed it would not be following suit, and said that in a statement that it "strongly believes in defending and respecting the voice of our users". Saudi Arabia has previously invested billions of dollars into xAI, the company (now known as SpaceXAI) that runs both X and the controversial Grok chatbot. Abdullah Aljuraywi, a monitoring and campaigns officer at rights group ALQST who was among those whose accounts have been blocked, told MEE that he did not believe the assertions by Musk or other tech companies that they valued freedom of speech above all else. "I do not believe these companies are willing to meaningfully defend freedom of expression when doing so conflicts with their commercial or strategic interests in wealthy authoritarian states such as Saudi Arabia," he said. He pointed out that there had been recurring reports suggesting that the Saudi government had had the technical capability to block major social media platforms if it considered doing so necessary. "However, it appears to have found it more effective to pressure platforms into restricting the accounts of Saudi dissidents living abroad - particularly those who advocate for the rights and demands of people inside the country and maintain contact with audiences in Saudi Arabia," he said. MEE contacted X for comment, but had received no response at time of publication. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Palestinian-Israeli movement calls for multinational force in occupied West Bank
author: Fayha Shalash Mohammed Turkman
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 15:26 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: A joint Palestinian - Israeli movement launched a campaign on Tuesday calling for a multinational protection force to be deployed in the occupied West Bank amid escalating Israeli settler attacks. A Land for All – Two States, One Homeland said growing settler violence, coupled with the Israeli government's failure to protect Palestinians, had made international intervention an urgent necessity. The appeal was announced at a press conference in the village of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah, where residents described months of settler attacks, restricted access to farmland and mounting fears of displacement. The movement said an international protection force would not replace a political solution or the establishment of a Palestinian state. Instead, it would provide an immediate mechanism to protect civilians and help preserve the prospect of a future political settlement. Launched under the slogan "Multinational Force in the West Bank — Now", the campaign argues that international condemnation of settler violence is no longer enough. It calls for a force mandated to protect civilians and document violations on the ground. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Rula Hardal, the Palestinian co-director of the group, said they sent a statement last week to international actors and diplomatic missions in Palestine and Israel, urging them to support the deployment of an international protection force for Palestinians in the West Bank following the escalation in settler violence. 'We see a government that is entirely backing the settler militia' - Yael Berda, board co-chair of A Land for All – Two States, One Homeland Hardal said Kafr Malik had been chosen for the press conference because it lies in the centre of the West Bank and has also been affected by settler violence, while remaining more accessible and relatively safer than many other Palestinian communities for both Palestinian and Israeli Jewish members of the movement. "We are a Palestinian-Israeli political movement that advocates for a confederative two-state solution on the agreed international borders of 1967," Hardal told Middle East Eye. "But we cannot continue speaking about the old classic two-state solution because the reality on the ground has changed over the last 30 years," she added. The movement aims "to update and improve" the model by addressing issues including settlements, the right of return for Palestinian refugees, Jerusalem and security. "This is something that we are working on in our political platform," she added. ‘Mass atrocities’ Meron Rapoport, an Israeli co-founding president of the movement, said the situation in the occupied West Bank had deteriorated sharply over the past year. He accused the Israeli government and military of pursuing "a clear plan of ethnic cleansing" in the occupied territory. "We hear about plans to go after the refugee camps. It is very clear. The time to wait, ask and beg Israel to protect the lives of Palestinians is over," he said during the press conference. 'The settlers are in control': How the West Bank is being ethnically cleansed Read More » Other Israeli members of the movement echoed the call, saying they no longer believed the Israeli authorities were willing or able to protect Palestinians living under occupation. Professor Yael Berda, co-chair of the movement's joint board, said Kafr Malik in particular is "a village that is undergoing a consistent threat of violence from settler militias". She said the movement had organised the press conference in the town to show solidarity, call for an international protection force and remind the international community of its responsibility to protect civilians in the face of mass atrocities. "Those mass atrocities include ethnic cleansing, and what we see is imminent ethnic cleansing happening. International pressure in the abstract is no longer enough. "We see a government that is entirely backing the settler militia. We see a military that either can't or doesn't want to stop the settlers. Confronting the ‘settler-colonial aggression’ For residents of Kafr Malik, the discussion was less about political proposals than the reality they say they face every day. Villagers described repeated settler attacks, blocked roads and growing restrictions on access to their farmland. Abdel Fattah Hamayel, a resident of Kafr Malik, welcomed the solidarity visit. 'They want to make us leave': Israel destroys West Bank wells serving Palestinian herders Read More » "We appreciate this step, and we hope it will be built upon to help the Palestinian people confront this settler-colonial aggression," he said. Hamayel said a single meeting could not fully convey the suffering experienced not only by residents of Kafr Malik but by Palestinian rural communities more broadly. "In my opinion, this issue is no longer hidden from anyone. This government, through several fascist figures, declares this openly and clearly. The situation isn't easy for us because we face two main challenges," he said. The first, he said, was the absence of an official Palestinian strategy or institutions with the capacity to confront the violence and support Palestinian farmers. The second was that the attacks were taking place with the backing of Israel's far-right government, which he said had emboldened settlers who had "broken free from all moral standards". headline: Israel pursuing ‘undeclared annexation’ of West Bank, Peace Now says
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 12:03 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: A leading Israeli advocacy group has accused the government of pursuing the undeclared annexation of the occupied West Bank through coordinated measures that undermine the Oslo Accords. Peace Now, which monitors Israeli violations in the West Bank, said the measures include broadening the powers of the Israeli Civil Administration, expanding settlements and weakening the Palestinian Authority. “Netanyahu’s government is playing with fire, disregarding its international commitments and endangering Israel’s security - all in order to take control of more territory and land in the West Bank,” the movement said in the report, obtained and reported by Ynet on Tuesday. One of the measures was introduced in February , when the security cabinet authorised the Civil Administration to enforce regulations and oversee environmental protection, water and archaeology in Areas A and B of the West Bank. The Civil Administration is a body under Israel’s defence ministry that implements civilian policies in the occupied West Bank. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The government said the move was aimed at preventing environmental hazards and damage to heritage sites. Peace Now said the environmental and archaeological measures use definitions broad enough to enable Israeli civilian authorities to intervene in Palestinian construction across much of the West Bank. Under the 1995 Oslo Accords, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C as a temporary administrative arrangement that remains in place. Area A is under full Palestinian Authority control for civil administration and internal security and includes major Palestinian cities. Area B is under Palestinian civil administration, while security responsibilities are shared with Israel. It includes smaller towns and rural villages. Area C, which accounts for about 60 percent of the West Bank, is under full Israeli civil and security control. Most Israeli settlements and military bases are located there, built on Palestinian land. Despite the accords, Israeli forces have operated inside Areas A and B for years. However, civilian interventions have largely been restricted to Area C until now. Explained: The Israeli measures imposing de facto annexation in the West Bank Read More » In June, the Civil Administration also moved to strip the Palestinian municipality of Hebron of broad planning and construction powers relating to settlements and several holy sites in the heart of the city. The Peace Now report also cited Israeli military orders issued in July to requisition Palestinian land inside Area A for a road connecting two settlements. The movement said it was the first time since the Oslo Accords were signed that military land-requisition orders had been used inside Area A for an explicitly civilian settlement purpose, rather than for military purposes. The group said it had also documented at least 23 settlement outposts established in Areas B over the past two and a half years. Even when the military occasionally removes the outposts, Peace Now said, they are rebuilt and expanded, including with permanent structures. The outposts have been accompanied by the construction of roads, the takeover of water sources and the displacement of Palestinian residents. Settlers have also taken over abandoned Palestinian homes in Areas B and C after residents were forced to leave following repeated settler attacks. “The government’s actions in Areas A and B are not isolated incidents but part of an organised policy whose ultimate goal is to collapse the Palestinian Authority and create chaos that would allow it to expand settlements into cities and villages deep inside the West Bank,” the report said. ‘Only the beginning’ The measures in the West Bank come as the government carries out an organised and “consistent” campaign to weaken the Palestinian Authority economically, politically, territorially and in terms of security, Peace Now said. One of the main tools used to pressure the Palestinian Authority is the withholding of tax revenues collected by Israel on its behalf under the 1994 Paris Protocol. The revenues amount to about 11 billion shekels (around $3.66bn) a year and have historically accounted for more than 60 percent of the Palestinian Authority’s budget, according to Ynet. 'I am proud of the settlement revolution I have led to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian terrorist state' - Bezalel Smotrich, Israeli minister Peace Now said only about half of the funds owed to the Palestinian Authority were transferred under the current government between 2022 and 2025. Since June 2025, not a single shekel has been transferred, according to the report. Peace Now stressed that the government has not formally announced the cancellation of the Oslo Accords, nor has it introduced legislation to annex the West Bank or dismantle the Palestinian Authority. However, the group argues that the measures combined amount in practice to a process of undeclared annexation. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said the report was a “certificate of achievement for the Israeli government”. “What they call ‘the erosion of Oslo’ we call correcting an injustice resulting from 30 years of neglect,” he said, according to Ynet. “What they call ‘de facto annexation’ we call establishing Israel’s security belt. “I am proud of the settlement revolution I have led to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian terrorist state in the heart of the country. This is only the beginning.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. Middle East Eye ISSN 2634-2456
subheadline: Group says expanded Israeli civilian powers, settlement growth and pressure on Palestinian Authority are eroding Oslo framework

headline: Tommy Robinson defends Muslim student subject to social media hate campaign
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 12:35 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: Anti-Islam activist Tommy Robinson , real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, has defended and apologised to a Muslim student at Oxford University after she faced a barrage of abuse and anger from prominent right-wing personalities in Britain and the US , over a video clip from an Oxford Union debate which was taken out of context. The debate at the prestigious debating society, held on 17 June, was on the motion "This House believes the West is right to be suspicious of Islam". Robinson was debating on the motion's proposition team, which lost the debate. A clip circulating online after the debate was published on YouTube late last week showed Aisha Khan-Aziz, a student speaker delivering the first speech for the opposition, introducing the speakers on the side opposite to her by making a joke about each of them, as is union tradition. She introduced "Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known to his hooligans as Tommy Robinson". Robinson could be seen chuckling in response. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Khan-Aziz added in a light-hearted manner: "Stephen, there is a crowd outside rioting against you tonight, and without the protection and generosity of a Muslim Palestinian president and a largely South Asian executive committee, you would be quite literally cooked." The comments seemed to be aimed at stressing the commitment of Muslim students at the union to free speech, and there was laughter and applause from the crowd. The large left-wing protest outside had barred many people, including Khan-Aziz's own family members, from entering the debate. At the start of his own speech, Robinson congratulated Khan-Aziz on her speech and praised the union president, Arwa Elrayess, for her "defence of free speech". But over the past four days Khan-Aziz has received a litany of abuse on X, with prominent commentators accusing her of threatening Robinson with violence. Robinson initially shared some of these posts, but then published a video on Tuesday saying the student's words were being taken out of context. Inside the Oxford Union debate where Tommy Robinson lost to a Palestinian student from Gaza Read More » He later published a longer video on Tuesday evening saying he had watched "something be spun globally against a young girl who didn't intend that meaning... it was not meant as a threat and she couldn't have been nicer". Robinson explained: "There wasn't a mob of Islamists outside the university. It wasn't a Muslim mob, it was a far-left, woke, white, liberal pathetic, middle-class mob. "It wasn't Muslims. So when people listen to a Muslim woman talking about that and saying I'd get cooked, I can see how it can be taken as that. But it wasn't that." Robinson added that Khan-Aziz's "family got attacked outside... her family would have been proud to see her standing there debating the way she debated, and they didn't get to see her". He said "I spent most of the night talking to that girl. She was lovely. You couldn't meet a nicer girl." Robinson also said: "I should have said this four days ago when it first come out. And I feel bad because I point scored because she was on the side of Islam. And I allowed what I know not to be true to continue momentum, which was a misrepresentation of what that girl meant." He called this a "wanker move" and apologised to Khan-Aziz. Storm of abuse That same day Kevin Sorbo, an actor with 2.6 million followers on X, shared the short clip of Khan-Aziz's comments and captioned it: "You’re lucky we have paid security otherwise the Muslims outside would murder you for saying Islam is violent." John Cleese, one of Britain's most famous comedians and actors, shared the clip on Sunday and remarked : "If this isn't a threat of violence, what is?" His post received 748,000 views. American right-wing YouTuber Ben Shapiro, who has almost 9 million followers on X, remarked : "'You're lucky we Muslims in here are nice, because if we weren't, our co-religionists outside would burn you to death' isn't an amazing argument". "You're lucky we Muslims in here are nice, because if we weren't, our co-religionists outside would burn you to death" isn't an amazing argument https://t.co/i1B0QOMMCr — Ben Shapiro (@benshapiro) August 2, 2026 Laurence Fox, one of Robinson's fellow debaters, said : "The confidence, dominance and arrogance to casually drop in a threat like this was menacing." Steven Barrett, a barrister and writer who has been published in The Spectator, claimed the clip showed a "clear threat of violence" and wrote on X: "I expect the University, her College and the Oxfordshire police to act." Peter Savodnik, a prominent journalist who has written for Vanity Fair and the New York Times, posted : "The students applauding should be expelled because they clearly know nothing about liberal education, and the adults who admitted them should be fired." Meanwhile Peter Hague, a British scientist and writer, wrote on social media: "There is a gleeful menace to this, isn’t there? She loves violence, and loves the power it brings." And Rod Dreher, an American conservative writer with more than 130,000 followers on X, posted : "She's essentially saying that life and safety of English dissidents depends on the goodwill of UK Muslims. At Oxford University. Think about that." Larry Alex Taunton, who has been published by the New York Times, used abusive language about Khan-Aziz and said she "should be in jail". Mike Cernovitch, a US media personality with more than a million followers, shared the clip and said : "In a war, we know how this would go. We don't need to guess. It would be 100 to 1 kill ratios. The primitives rely on state power to commit their crimes and are helpless without it. Yet they gloat and continue to threaten. Deport them all." 'I apologise' Robinson said in his video on Tuesday: "I can only imagine for the last four days, when I know she didn't mean that, and I should have said that four days ago, I know she didn't mean that. She knows she didn't mean that. But yet the whole world's taken it that she meant that." Robinson added: "I've been in that position, where your words are taken out of context and weaponised. And I guess I allowed it to be weaponised. "So I apologise Aisha, if you're watching this. I apologise, because I know you didn't mean that. And I should have spoken up from the first minute, but I was too interested in point scoring on the side of us against Islam, which is a wanker move because I know you didn't mean it." I WAS NOT THREATENED - I APOLOGISE Please take a moment to watch this, and SHARE it. I have to be honest with all of you as well as myself. Aisha Khan said something very silly, however, it's been taken out of context and mischaracterised. pic.twitter.com/HrnxHaErah — Tommy Robinson 🇬🇧 (@TRobinsonNewEra) August 4, 2026 Robinson also said he had spoken to "white English students" at Oxford who "are friends with Aisha" and "couldn't speak highly enough" of her, calling her a "wonderful soul". During the debate, Khan-Aziz had argued "I agree that western values are worth defending... western critical thinking means I can read a scholar's commentary on a Quranic verse and decide that it might be right or wrong. 'I can hold my faith up to scrutiny without it shattering' - Aisha Khan-Aziz, Oxford student and debater "It means I can hold my faith up to scrutiny without it shattering, because a thing that cannot survive a question probably deserves to be questioned." Elrayess, who was the union president, argued during the debate: "Free speech and debate is not something I do despite being a Muslim, it is something I do because of it. I'm not betraying my religion, I'm practising it." She said: "Vote against [the motion] to protect what is best in your own tradition, the right of every person in this country to be seen as a human being." The motion was ultimately defeated by 41 to 57. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters.
