headline: What's driving the rising unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir?
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 20:54 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: For decades, global attention on Kashmir has focused overwhelmingly on the Indian-administered side of the Line of Control (LoC), the heavily militarised de facto border that divides the disputed Himalayan region between India and Pakistan. International headlines have largely revolved around repression, insurgency , military deployments , and diplomatic confrontation. Far less attention has been paid to the political currents unfolding across the LoC in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, officially known as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). Long portrayed by Islamabad as a model of self-governance in contrast to Indian-administered Kashmir, the territory is now witnessing some of the most significant popular unrest in recent decades. What started as frustration over soaring electricity bills and flour prices has rapidly transformed into a systemic challenge to Islamabad’s authority in the region. Rather than rehashing the old geopolitical tug-of-war with India, this new wave of unrest reflects deep-seated frustration with local governance. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Protesters are demanding genuine political participation, arguing that while Kashmir’s international fate hangs in limbo, their basic political and economic rights cannot remain frozen. In a region long treated as a geopolitical pawn, domestic disillusionment is now taking centre stage. From economic grievances to political awakening The protests have been led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a loose coalition of traders, lawyers, students, civil society activists, and local political figures that emerged in 2023 outside the traditional party structure. Rejecting established Pakistani political parties as ineffective or overly dependent on Islamabad, the JAAC focused directly on basic issues: high electricity bills, rising flour prices, heavy taxation, and poor public services. 'What we need to know is who will provide us with jobs and a fair life today' - Mujtaba Naqvi, JAAC supporter This message quickly united a region facing serious economic hardship. Youth unemployment in the area sits at roughly 27 percent, nearly triple Pakistan’s national average, while fewer than eight percent of women are in the formal workforce, Danish Khan, co-director of ‘The Inequality, Poverty, Power and Social Justice Initiative’ at Franklin & Marshall College, recently wrote in a piece for The Friday Times . As he noted, the region was generating a growing “reserve army of young unemployed people”. Development in the mountainous region continues to lag behind the rest of the country. Substandard roads severely restrict access to essential public services like healthcare and education, a situation that becomes especially dire during its harsh winters. Meanwhile, many communities still bear the visible scars and lingering devastation of the 2005 earthquake that killed tens of thousands of people. What began as a fight for affordable living soon sparked massive demonstrations across major towns, shutting down markets and forcing officials to negotiate. By 2024 and 2025, the government yielded to key demands: lowering electricity rates and subsidising wheat compared to the rest of the country. But many activists view these concessions as temporary quick fixes. “The price reductions addressed immediate grievances,” says political economy researcher Faisal Mir, “but they did not address the deeper structures of economic exclusion.” The campaign against inflation has now mushroomed into a broader critique of governance, linking daily hardship directly to political arrangements that concentrate power away from the region. A younger generation, weary of traditional rhetoric about competing nationalisms, is now demanding accountability, transparency, and genuine representation. Rather than debating Kashmir’s future status, they are asking who governs them today and whose interests those leaders truly serve. “No one knows when the Kashmir dispute will finally be resolved,” Mujtaba Naqvi, a JAAC supporter in the regional capital of Muzaffarabad, told Middle East Eye. “What we need to know is who will provide us with jobs and a fair life today.” Battle over refugee representation These questions have led directly to one of the most contentious features of Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s constitutional framework: the legislative seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees living outside the territory. 'Erasing historical facts': India orders massive crackdown on books in Kashmir's libraries Read More » On paper, AJK, with a population of around five million, functions under a semi-autonomous structure complete with its own president, prime minister, parliament, and supreme court. Candidates must swear allegiance to Pakistan to run for office. The core of the current disputes lies in how the assembly is structured. Out of 53 total seats, 33 are elected by residents living inside the territory. The remaining 12 are reserved for Kashmiris who migrated to Pakistan from Indian-administered Kashmir during and after the 1947 and 1965 wars. Although these voters reside across Pakistan’s four provinces rather than in AJK, they continue to elect representatives to the regional assembly. Supporters maintain that these 12 seats safeguard the political rights of displaced families and uphold Islamabad’s diplomatic argument that the entire former princely state remains disputed internationally. Stripping refugee representation, they contend, would weaken Pakistan's position in a high-stakes standoff with India - a conflict that has triggered multiple wars since British India's partition in 1947, as well as a brief four-day military confrontation last year. The region’s supreme court in early June ruled that the 12 refugee seats are constitutionally protected. However, the JAAC and other local critics view the arrangement as a backdoor for federal meddling. Federal parties frequently use these 12 constituencies to swing majorities in Muzaffarabad. This setup has fuelled acute political turbulence, leaving AJK with four different prime ministers in the current regional assembly in rapid succession. “These 12 seats continuously dictate government formation,” political activist Raja Nafees, who supports JAAC's demands, told MEE. “Voters who don't even live here end up deciding who rules us.” A crisis of legitimacy For decades, mainstream political parties in AJK, acting largely as extensions of Islamabad, dominated regional politics unchallenged. Today, that status quo has shattered. Unsettled by widespread unrest and informal boycott calls led by the JAAC over the 12 reserved refugee seats, authorities staggered the regional elections across three phases between 27 July and 10 August. The strategy backfired: voter turnout plummeted during the first two phases, leading analysts to declare the election null and void, and warning that the resulting assembly will lack a credible mandate. Political infighting has further eroded trust, with the Pakistan People’s Party, led by President Asif Ali Zardari, accusing the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of rigging the polls. At the same time, the nationalist slogan “Kashmir Banega Khudmukhtar” (Kashmir will be sovereign), promoted by groups like the Jammu Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF), has gained unprecedented public traction in the protests. This reflects an emerging political vocabulary that moves beyond the traditional choice between India and Pakistan. Negotiation, crackdown and uncertainty Since protests flared up in 2024, authorities in Islamabad and Muzaffarabad have tackled the uprising using a volatile mix of concessions and coercion. While early negotiations yielded subsidies on electricity and flour, the government adopted a harsher stance as demonstrations expanded into demands for structural political reform. When the JAAC announced a protest march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad on 9 June, Pakistani authorities accused the group of disrupting public order. On 5 June, the movement was banned under anti-terrorism laws, and key leaders, including JAAC leader Shaukat Mir, were arrested. After negotiations failed again on 26 July, the JAAC called for a renewed march. However, the group accused state forces of using lethal violence to stop protesters. Independent estimates indicate over 45 people, primarily protesters, alongside law enforcement personnel and bystanders, have been killed in clashes since 5 June. Official details remain scarce as widespread internet blackouts and strict curfews severely hinder independent verification. A Kashmiri man searches for mobile phone signal following a partial internet shutdown imposed ahead of the first phase of the regional elections in Muzaffarabad, on 23 July 2026 (Sajjad Qayyum/AFP) Government officials maintain that constitutional disputes should be handled through legal avenues rather than through street protest. In a press briefing on 31 July, military spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry stated that the region has historically received state attention, care, and resource allocation. He said that authorities had “wholeheartedly” urged the JAAC to contest elections and pursue reform through courts and parliament. “But they want to pursue this by force, but only the state has the monopoly of violence," he added. Other government ministers went further, dismissing the JAAC as an “armed mob” and levelling unfounded accusations that the group had ties to India and Taliban militants. JAAC leadership firmly denies these claims, maintaining that their campaign remains peaceful and rooted in basic democratic rights. Amid the standoff, locals are bearing the brunt of the consequences. Continuous internet network blackouts have crippled daily commerce and tourism. In Rawalakot, the movement’s stronghold, where leaders called for a mass march, heavy curfews and road blockades brought the peak summer season to a halt. Local traders face mounting financial ruin, while residents endure severe communication outages and disrupted basic services, leaving the region locked in deep uncertainty. Fallout from Article 370 in India The constitutional debate in AJK has also unfolded against the backdrop of India's August 2019 revocation of Article 370. After ‘testing ground’ in Kashmir, pellet guns used on student protesters in India's capital Read More » By ending the limited autonomy and erstwhile "special status" of Indian-administered Kashmir and placing it under direct federal control, New Delhi fundamentally transformed the political landscape across both sides of the LoC. The move sparked widespread criticism from Pakistan and ignited major local demonstrations. When protesters, organised by groups like the JKLF, attempted to march toward the LoC in solidarity, Pakistani authorities forcibly stopped them. Analysts note that key organisers of those marches now help lead the JAAC. Perceiving Islamabad’s diplomatic response as inadequate, many AJK residents began questioning Pakistan’s commitment to preserving their distinct identity. Crucially, the region’s unresolved status complicates major infrastructure investments, particularly under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. This has fuelled widespread speculation that Islamabad might eventually redefine AJK's legal status, potentially merging it with neighbouring Pakistani districts or converting it into a province. Although the government has never voiced those ambitions, this pervasive anxiety has reshaped public discourse, deepening institutional distrust and strongly reinforcing local demands for greater regional autonomy. headline: Israel's army to set up polling stations in occupied Gaza, Lebanon and Syria
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 15:40 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: The Israeli military has begun preparing to install polling stations in occupied areas of the Gaza Strip, Lebanon and Syria ahead of the general election on 27 October, Army Radio reported on Wednesday. According to the report, Israeli army chief Eyal Zamir has instructed military officials to facilitate voting for soldiers deployed beyond Israel's internationally recognised borders. The military will "deploy polling stations deep in enemy territory - within Lebanon, Syria and Gaza - to enable the right to vote for combat troops stationed beyond the borders", Army Radio said. The broadcaster described the move as "something that hasn't happened in decades", overlooking the fact that Israeli soldiers have long voted at military bases in the occupied West Bank. Last week, Israel's Central Elections Committee approved a series of regulations for the election, including measures that would allow soldiers to cast ballots from military positions in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Israeli news site Ynet reported that because soldiers are prohibited from carrying identity cards into Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, those voting at military polling stations will instead be identified using their service number and by another soldier. The number of Israelis voting outside their local polling stations has risen in recent years, with soldiers and other security personnel making up the largest group eligible to vote at special polling stations. According to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), an independent research centre, around 425,000 people cast ballots at special polling stations during the March 2021 election. The figure includes members of the security services, diplomats, hospital patients and prisoners. While voting patterns are difficult to determine, the IDI said most voters using the special polling stations are young Israelis serving in the military, with right-wing parties believed to benefit most from their votes. Protecting army ‘neutrality’ According to the Central Elections Committee, around 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in the upcoming election, including nearly 550,000 first-time voters since the previous election in late 2022. How Israel is encroaching in southern Syria Read More » While the committee publishes details of polling stations in hospitals, prisons and Israeli diplomatic missions abroad, it has not disclosed how many polling stations will be established in Gaza, Lebanon or Syria. Army Radio also reported that Zamir had instructed commanders to prevent soldiers and officers from campaigning for political parties during the election. At a meeting with senior officers, he ordered commanders to maintain the military's political neutrality. He instructed them to closely review letters sent to soldiers to ensure they contained no political messaging. "There is a need to uphold current regulations, orders and instructions on the issue," Zamir said, adding that army staff needs "to avoid innovations that could bring about the undermining of public trust in the IDF [Israeli army]". Zamir's directive came after the military faced criticism earlier this week for dismissing a reservist who had regularly posted videos expressing support for the government. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz later intervened to reinstate the soldier. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Exclusive: Trump demanded direct talks with Hezbollah but was denied
author: Adam Chamseddine Daniel Hilton
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 10:20 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 15 hours ago
article_body: Donald Trump called the Lebanese ambassador in Washington in late May and demanded a direct conversation with Hezbollah , a request that was then denied to the US president, Middle East Eye can reveal. According to two sources intimately familiar with events from the Hezbollah side and a Lebanese diplomatic source, Trump called Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad in frustration as the ceasefire in Lebanon frayed. Soon after, on 1 June, Trump claimed he had spoken to Hezbollah through unidentified intermediaries and secured a commitment from the group to halt attacks against Israel. “Through highly placed representatives, I had a very good call with Hezbollah, and they agreed that all shooting will stop,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform at the time. According to the Hezbollah sources, Trump’s request rattled Lebanese officials, who were confused about whose number they should offer the president. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “Officials then began to panic and try and find a phone number for anyone in Hezbollah. They were calling anyone they knew who was Shia, even random sheikhs, to try to find the right person to speak to,” one source said. However, a senior diplomatic source said officials made no such attempts. “Before Trump announced that he had communicated with Hezbollah, he contacted Ambassador Nada Moawad,” the diplomatic source said. “He angrily told her that he wanted to speak to someone from Hezbollah. The ambassador responded that she was unable to arrange such contact.” Middle East Eye has asked the White House for comment. Politically difficult position According to a source familiar with the conversations, Moawad then informed the Lebanese presidency of the exchange and asked how she should proceed. “The ambassador contacted the presidential palace and explained what had happened,” the source said. “She was instructed not to do anything and to disregard the request.” The resurrection of Hezbollah Read More » The source said Lebanese officials feared that facilitating direct contact would place the presidency in a politically difficult position. Since April, the Lebanese government and presidency had been attempting to be the sole representatives of Lebanon in any international negotiations. The US-Israeli war on Iran spilled over into Lebanon in March after Hezbollah responded to the killing of the Iranian supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, by firing six rockets into Israel. When Iran agreed a ceasefire with the United States in April, it demanded the devastating Israeli attacks in Lebanon end simultaneously. While the Lebanese state welcomed any ceasefire, it then sought to centre itself as the sole representative of the country and decouple the conflicts, and began direct negotiations with Israel under American auspices. “The assessment was that direct contact between Trump and Hezbollah would negatively affect the presidency’s image,” the source said. “Hezbollah itself communicates with the presidency through channels, while the American president was asking to speak to the group directly.” Earlier attempts A senior Lebanese security official told MEE that Trump’s claim came after several unsuccessful American attempts to establish a channel with Hezbollah. “There have been many repeated offers from the United States, both previously and under the current administration, to open channels of communication with Hezbollah,” the source said. “They were all rejected. The political decision within the group has been not to open direct communication with the Americans.” According to the source, the most recent approach was made through the CIA station in Beirut, which asked a senior Lebanese security figure to facilitate contact with Hezbollah. 'The political decision within the group has been not to open direct communication with the Americans' - Military official “The response was the same: the request was rejected,” the source said. “There had also been an earlier attempt, before Trump’s statement, to open a channel through a former senior security official. That attempt received the same response.” The US government designates Hezbollah as a terrorist organisation and has long maintained a formal policy of refusing direct political engagement with the group. According to a senior Lebanese official, the US embassy in Beirut had no knowledge that Trump was going to try and speak to Hezbollah directly before he called Moawad. “The US embassy in Beirut contacted an intermediary whom it believed was in communication with Hezbollah and asked him to establish whether contact had actually taken place between Trump and the group, because the embassy in Lebanon knew nothing about it,” the source said. “The answer came back that no such communication had taken place.” One version circulated after Trump’s announcement suggested that the exchange had taken place through Abdallah Safieddine, a Hezbollah representative in Tehran, during US-Iran negotiations held in Islamabad. “But, according to our information, Abdallah Safieddine did not travel to Islamabad in the first place,” a source familiar with the matter said. headline: After Michigan upset, Aipac looks to back Republican candidate against Abdul El-Sayed
author: Yasmine El-Sabawi
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 22:08 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: After spending more than $30m on a candidate who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary on Wednesday, the leading pro-Israel lobbying group in the US has now indicated it will pivot to the Republican in that race come November. The move highlights how the one-issue behemoth does not see itself as ideologically bound to one party or the other. "Our members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda," the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) said in a statement. "Our community is proud to support pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who stand for our values." The race between pro-Israel Congresswoman Haley Stevens and former Detroit public health official Abdul El-Sayed quickly became the most expensive Democratic primary race of all time. Stevens was backed by a further $30m from outside groups who bankrolled round-the-clock attack ads on Sayed. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Sayed, an Egyptian-American Muslim who has never held elected office, won the exceptionally tight race by one percentage point, in what was a stunning upset for establishment Democrats, and a boon to the progressive wave taking hold across the country. Half a million more Democratic voters showed up to the polls than in previous primary races, which typically see low turnouts, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said on Wednesday. Sayed has repeatedly said he's never met with corporate lobbyists. Last quarter, he out-fundraised Stevens in small-dollar donations, according to data analysed by the campaign finance tracker, OpenSecrets. " An average of $95 was spent for every vote against Abdul, more than 10 times as much as Abdul’s $9 per vote average," his campaign said in a statement. But outside spending by groups that don't coordinate with the candidate - which, according to US law, can be unlimited - is how Aipac and other special interest outfits have gained what seemed like a permanent foothold in US politics. Craig Holman, government affairs lobbyist for the non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, told Middle East Eye that in 95 percent of US electoral races, "whoever spends the most, wins". Thomas Massie's defeat shows Aipac's enduring grip over US Republicans Read More » "Yes, money buys elections. It's very effective, and that's why these candidates work overtime continually raising money," he said. Few groups are willing to spend as much as Aipac does - especially in a climate where emboldened criticism of Israel has proliferated both the left and the right of the political spectrum in the US. In 2022, Aipac helped Stevens secure her seat in the House of Representatives by ousting longtime Jewish lawmaker Andy Levin for his support of US policies to punish violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. "Today, Michigan launched a new chapter in our political history," Levin wrote on his Instagram account on Wednesday, accompanied by a photograph of him hugging Sayed. "Out with all the big money, dark money and corporate and special interest control of our politics. We the people hunger for authenticity." Earlier this year, Aipac helped oust Republican Thomas Massie, who voted against US foreign aid to Israel, in his Kentucky primary race by spending more than $4m against him through its United Democracy Project political action committee. That was just part of a coalition of pro-Israel groups that spent $9m against him. 'Truth and justice' The IMEU Policy Project - an outfit less than three years old that advocates for Palestinian rights - revealed that it contributed $400,000 in support of Sayed's campaign. Sayed has described Israel's nearly three-year-old assault on Gaza as a genocide, echoing language used by leading human rights organisations, genocide scholars and the United Nations. Israel, as well as most US lawmakers, reject the term. His position resonated strongly with many voters in Michigan who played a crucial role in organising against former President Joe Biden during the 2024 election, given his immovable support for Israel, even as Palestinian casualties mounted in the tens of thousands. Certain suburbs of Detroit, which house more than 200,000 registered Arab-American voters, voted overwhelmingly for Donald Trump at the time. This was despite Wayne County on the whole backing Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris with more than 62 percent of the vote. But Trump ended up winning the entire state by just over one percentage point. "People in Michigan, they're looking for leaders that are going to call out bold solutions and that are going to try and speak out against the status quo because the status quo hasn't been working," Alabas Farhat, a member of the Michigan House of Representatives who appeared in a social media video backing Sayed, told MEE. "The status quo has led to our state being 49th in unemployment. It's led to us being 47th in third grade literacy. It's led to our middle class having less wealth than they did in previous years," he added. "Trump came along, and he sold a false bag of goods, but he was at least willing to say things were wrong. Now comes Abdul El-Sayed, somebody who has made truth and justice two central pillars to his campaign." The tactic is similar to that of a recent spate of winning progressive Democratic candidates around the country, from New York to New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Colorado. But according to Sally Howell, an expert on Arab American Studies at the University of Michigan-Dearborn, Sayed's polling numbers actually went up after he pivoted away from incessant talk of Aipac funding and moved to getting "money out of politics" entirely - a tagline that became central to his campaign. "He started talking about not getting money from DTE, the energy company here in Michigan... and this issue of the AI data centres, and how they would drive up our water bills," she said. "These are issues that really matter" to Michiganders across the political spectrum, she added. America considers electing its first Muslim governor: Abdulrahman El-Sayed Read More » In his victory speech on Wednesday, Sayed said he spoke to Stevens and was assured of her endorsement as he gears up to face former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in November. Hertel, the state Democratic Party chair, insisted in his remarks that Democrats are now "united" to defeat Donald Trump-backed candidates in November. The outcome of that vote may tip the balance of the US Senate, and turn the chamber blue for the final two years of President Trump's term in office. If Sayed wins, he would become the very first Muslim elected to the upper chamber on Capitol Hill. Writing on his social media platform Truth Social on Wednesday, Trump called Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel", but added that his win is also "great news for the Republican party", suggesting that he will be easy to defeat. "I think that it's going to go a lot darker than the negative campaigning we've seen, and it's going to be very anti-Arab and a lot more Islamophobic," Howell said of the race between now and November. For his part, Sayed told supporters and the media on Wednesday that the focus on his name and identity is "the only play they got" against him. "It's like, wow, he's different," he said of Republican attacks. "That's the best you got? You can't actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can't afford your groceries." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli army launches large-scale assault in East Jerusalem refugee camp
author: Fayha Shalash
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 12:01 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: Israeli forces launched a large-scale operation in the Qalandiya refugee camp in occupied East Jerusalem on Wednesday. The Jerusalem Governorate said dozens of military vehicles stormed the camp before dawn, carrying boxes, equipment and maps. Soldiers deployed across several neighbourhoods as home raids and searches continued. Palestinian sources said troops raided the headquarters of the camp's Popular Committee and forcibly removed several residents from their homes. One family was ordered to evacuate its house completely, while dawn prayers were prevented in all of the camp's mosques. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters A Palestinian man was wounded after being struck by a military vehicle near the camp, suffering leg injuries. Soldiers also severely beat journalist Muhammad Sumrin while he was covering the raid and fired stun grenades at other journalists. The army also carried out a wave of arrests, with several Palestinians reportedly assaulted during their detention. The Palestinian Red Crescent said a 53-year-old man was injured after being beaten. Eyewitnesses said soldiers breached the wall near the camp to allow bulldozers to enter. The machinery later demolished a car wash on Almatar Street. During the operation, soldiers distributed leaflets warning residents against "harming the security and lives of Israelis". Similar messages were also sent directly to residents, urging them not to confront Israeli forces. Rights groups call for help stopping Israeli 'pogrom' against Palestinians in West Bank Read More » The Israeli military's coordinator for activities in the West Bank, known as Cogat, said in a Facebook post that the military had launched a large-scale operation in Qalandiya refugee camp targeting "terrorist elements, terrorist infrastructure, and the phenomenon of weapons possession and trafficking, which poses a threat to the security of the entire region". It was not immediately clear what “terrorist” activity the military was referring to. There are no known recent attacks against Israelis originating from the Qalandiya refugee camp. Earlier, Israeli media quoted security sources as saying the military was considering expanding attacks on several refugee camps across the occupied West Bank, including Qalandiya, following the raids in Jenin and Tulkarm. Israel says the campaign is aimed at dismantling armed infrastructure in the northern and central West Bank. Qalandiya camp is home to more than 15,000 Palestinian refugees living in a densely populated area. Its location between Jerusalem and Ramallah, close to Israeli settlements and other Israeli-controlled areas, has made it a frequent target of Israeli military raids over the years. headline: From Michigan to Missouri: Democratic primaries deliver mixed bag on Israel and Gaza
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 20:12 BST | Last update: 6 days 14 hours ago
article_body: Voters went to the polls across five US states on Tuesday for a series of closely watched Democratic and Republican primaries. The races in Michigan, Missouri, Kansas, Virginia and Washington were not all solely focused on foreign policy, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and Israel's genocide in Gaza loomed large. The primaries delivered a muddled verdict on how Democratic voters respond to politicians' positions on the issues. Michigan produced the evening’s defining result with former Wayne County health director Abdul El-Sayed defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for the open Senate seat by roughly one percentage point, 48.5 percent to 47.5 percent. El-Sayed staked out a progressive position on healthcare, but he also put immigration and US foreign policy at the centre of his campaign. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters He promised to vote to end US military aid to Israel, abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and work to end the Trump administration’s war on Iran, which he argued imperils Americans through the risk of regional war without congressional authorisation. Stevens' campaign, by contrast, championed Israel's right to self-defence and supported continued US taxpayer aid. She received firm backing from Democratic establishment figures and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as Aipac. Stevens also staked out a hawkish position on Iran. El-Sayed's stance resonated with Wayne County's large Arab American and Muslim electorate. The county includes Dearborn, Hamtramck, and the city of Detroit. Trump made inroads with Wayne County in the 2024 election, including an endorsement from Hamtramck's Yemeni-American mayor. Missouri: Democratic establishment prevails Former St Louis County prosecutor and incumbent Congressman Wesley Bell defeated former Democratic Congresswoman Cori Bush by 59.2 percent to 36.9 percent in the primary, denying Bush a re-entry to Congress after her defeat for the same seat in 2024. Bush was one of Congress’ outspoken advocates for a ceasefire in Gaza. She made the genocide in the enclave and the US war on Iran central pillars of her campaign. Bell advocated ironclad support for Israel and was backed by Aipac. Kansas: Gazing towards November The Democrats of Kansas nominated state Senator Cindy Holscher for governor, while Republicans chose state Senate President Ty Masterson, setting up one of the country's most closely watched gubernatorial contests in a state where Republicans have dominated statewide politics for decades. Unlike Michigan, foreign policy held little weight in the primary campaign. Candidates focused on rural development, agriculture, and abortion. Virginia: Senator tied to intelligence committee wins The sole candidate in Virginia’s Democratic primary was former Governor and incumbent Senator Mark Warner, who emphasised his tenure on the Senate Intelligence Committee and attention to national security. Warner is a staunch advocate for Israel and has received support from Aipac. Republicans chose former Trump campaign advisor and retired Army Major General Bert Mizusawa in a multi-candidate race. Warner criticised the absence of congressional consultation surrounding the Trump administration's war on Iran while stating that Iran's nuclear programme presents a significant security threat. Virginia has not elected a Republican to the Senate since 2002. Washington: Establishment wins again In Washington, Democratic Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez fended off a challenge from progressive Brent Hennrich. Gluesenkamp Perez was endorsed by Aipac while Hennrich campaigned as a Democrat opposed to the group. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Ceuta migrant disaster death toll rises to 141, Morocco's deadliest in recent history
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 12:49 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: At least 141 people died after Moroccan authorities opened the border gates into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, triggering what appears to be Morocco’s deadliest migration disaster in recent history. Migrant rights organisation Caminando Fronteras said hospitals in northern Morocco had received 63 bodies recovered from Moroccan waters by Tuesday. The Moroccan government has not officially confirmed this. Spanish officials told Cadena SER that authorities had found another 78 bodies in Spanish waters. The overall toll has therefore reached 141, far exceeding previous disasters along Morocco’s borders with Spain. The 2022 Melilla border crush killed at least 23 people, according to the official toll, while rights groups recorded 37 deaths. Fifteen people died at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach in 2014. Tens of thousands of people entered Ceuta, Spain’s North African territory, through the Tarajal crossing after Moroccan authorities opened the gates on Thursday. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Moroccan hospitals in Tetouan, Tangier, Fnideq and M’diq are holding the bodies. Most victims were Moroccan men aged between 20 and 30. Sub-Saharan Africans, women and children were also among the dead. Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco Read More » Spanish authorities have invoked the “multiple victims” protocol normally reserved for mass-casualty disasters such as train crashes and aviation accidents. About 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said. Spain has since returned approximately 70,000 of them to Morocco, while an estimated 1,000 unaccompanied children remain stranded in Ceuta. Anger is growing in Morocco over the authorities’ decision to open the border and the absence of accountability for the resulting deaths. The mother of Moroccan footballer Faten Ben Omar El Azizi, who played for Moghreb Atletico Tetuan and died during the crossing, demanded answers before her daughter’s burial. "The youth are lost… Who opened the door the first time? Why did they open it so that our children could be killed?" she said in a video published by Al Ayoum 24. Meanwhile, the European Union praised Spain’s “swift response”. Irish Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan said the bloc supported Spain and that migration required "a united European response". headline: 'Collective punishment': US Supreme Court greenlights $656m judgement against Palestinian officials
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 21:28 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: The US Supreme Court has refused to freeze a $656m judgement against the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) after the two groups said they were too cash-strapped to compensate Americans for attacks in Israel during the Second Intifada. The decision was announced on Monday by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a liberal justice who is tasked with taking on emergency case reviews. This comes 22 years after the lawsuit was first launched, and it means the collection of the funds can begin immediately. In 2015, the plaintiffs, who said they were victims of attacks between 2002 and 2004, won the damages. Then in 2016, the US Circuit Court of Appeals tossed out the judgment on the grounds that US courts cannot consider lawsuits against foreign groups if the violence was not aimed at American citizens. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Last year, the supreme court revived the case by voting 9-0 to uphold the Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act passed by lawmakers. By March of this year, the US Circuit Court of Appeals reinstated the judgment. "Congress passed special laws to make the Palestinian Authority submit to US jurisdiction against its will if it continued to provide families of martyred Palestinians with salaries," Raed Jarrar, advocacy director with Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), told Middle East Eye. The PA, he added, was "forced into accepting US jurisdiction [and it's] really unprecedented". The PA and PLO have said that a $656m payout would destabilise their governing abilities in the occupied West Bank, where Israel has long withheld Palestinian tax revenue from the PA. "The judgment will affect ordinary Palestinians who are already operating on a 70 percent salary because the PA is a dysfunctional and for-profit institution that is unable to even pay the full salaries of its employees," Jarrar explained. "It will be levied against doctors and engineers and government employees. It is the closest we can get to an act of collective punishment... these are ordinary Palestinians." The uprisings The PA is the governing body that has overseen areas of the occupied West Bank since 1994, as part of the Oslo Accords peace agreement between Israel and the PLO. 'They want to make us leave': Israel destroys West Bank wells serving Palestinian herders Read More » The PLO is an umbrella political coalition that is internationally recognised as the official representative of the Palestinian people in both the Palestinian territories and the diaspora. The Second Intifada, or uprising, began on 28 September 2000, when then-Israeli opposition leader, the vehemently right-wing Ariel Sharon, led a delegation to the Al-Aqsa complex, in what was seen by Palestinians as an act of provocation. When mass rallies broke out in response, the Israeli army responded with deadly violence, killing nearly 50 Palestinians in the first five days. The Second Intifada is largely remembered for Israel's killing of 12-year-old Palestinian Mohammed al-Durrah as news cameras were rolling, in what became the first instance of a live-streamed shooting of a child hiding behind his father. The father survived. Mohammed became a symbol of the Palestinian struggle against the occupation. The Second Intifada lasted some five years, with Israeli forces killing nearly 5,000 Palestinians. A thousand Israelis were killed in bombings and attacks carried out by Palestinians inside Israel. Separate rules Monday's supreme court decision brings into sharp focus the notion that foreign governments and leaders can face legal repercussions in the US, while the US repudiates and undermines the international courts that were specifically designed to bring accountability to victims of mass murder. Israel: Court blocks prison crocodile plan for Palestinians out of concern for the reptiles Read More » In July 2025, the US said it was placing sanctions on officials in the PA and PLO over their work taking Israel to those courts. According to the State Department, the unnamed officials were “not complying with their commitments and undermining the prospects for peace”. It cited “initiating and supporting actions at international organizations” and “taking actions to internationalize its conflict with Israel such as through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)”. Washington accused the figures of violating the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 (PLOCCA) and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002 (MEPCA). Since the Israeli assault on Gaza began in October 2023, killing more than 74,000 Palestinians, Israel has found itself diplomatically isolated. This has been furthered by deadly Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem. In September 2025, the Trump administration announced it would revoke and deny visas to anyone affiliated with the PLO and PA, and demanded the groups "consistently repudiate terrorism”, citing the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on southern Israel, according to a US State Department press release . headline: Saudi Aramco reports bumper profits as it bypasses Strait of Hormuz
author: Sean Mathews
publication_date: Published date: 4 August 2026 21:45 BST | Last update: 2 weeks 1 day ago
article_body: Saudi Aramco said on Tuesday its profits surged 33 percent in the second quarter of this year, as the kingdom benefited from the US-Israeli war on Iran , which drove up energy prices, while its oil pipeline allowed it to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The state-owned Saudi Arabian oil giant’s adjusted net income rose to $33.4bn from $25.2bn a year ago. The second quarter runs from early April to the end of June. The US and Iran reached a ceasefire in April that was extended in June, but fighting has continued to rage, keeping energy prices inflated. Iran is attempting to assert its control over the Strait of Hormuz and has attacked dozens of vessels trying to transit the strait via Oman’s territorial waters. The US has bombarded Iran, and in response, Tehran has targeted Gulf states, particularly Kuwait and Bahrain. The war drove Brent, the international benchmark, up above $100 per barrel in May and then again in July. Prices for refined products, like diesel, jet fuel, and gasoline, are up substantially. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar have all had to cancel or massively curb energy shipments. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters However, Saudi Arabia has been able to export around two-thirds of its pre-war oil capacity because of the East-West Pipeline , which connects the kingdom’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser noted the pipeline’s importance to the company while commenting on the results, according to a press statement. “Despite the unprecedented supply disruption through the Strait of Hormuz, we continued to demonstrate our ability to maintain business continuity by capitalising on our diverse asset base and multi-decade planning, including strategic infrastructure such as the East-West Pipeline, storage capacity, and export terminals,” he said. A model The East-West Pipeline has become a model for other Middle Eastern states looking to bypass the Strait of Hormuz in the coming years. Experts told Middle East Eye that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz. From Syria to UAE, the race to bypass Strait of Hormuz is on Read More » “When we speak to our customers in the region, they say they never want to deal with this again,” Artem Abramov, the deputy head of analysis at Rystad Energy, previously told MEE. “These bypass projects will move forward.” The UAE is building a second pipeline to the port of Fujairah to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, doubling its export capacity by 2027. Meanwhile, Iraq - the second-largest producer in the oil cartel Opec - signed a deal with Syria in July to rehabilitate a pipeline from its northern oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast. MEE was the first to reveal the project and its US backing. Aramco is not the only energy company that has benefited from the war. ExxonMobil and Chevron, the US’s energy behemoths, reported sky-high earnings in the second quarter also. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled from a year earlier while Chevron had its highest quarterly earnings on record. Trump, who is grappling with an unpopular war and frustration over high gasoline prices, has singled out the companies. “Chevron: too much money. ExxonMobil: too much money,” Trump said. “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price,” he told reporters on Monday. Brent has dropped about eight percent to $79 per barrel since Sunday, after Trump retreated from his threat to unleash the "biggest" bombing campaign since WWII on Iran. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that the US and Iran were close to a deal to stop fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: UK charity regulator to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlements
author: Areeb Ullah
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 13:57 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: The UK's charity regulator has launched an investigation into several British charities donating funds to illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine . The Charity Commission said the probe will look into how funds were used in illegal settlements, the purpose of these funds and whether they fit charitable purposes. Stephen Roake, assistant director of high-risk compliance at the Charity Commission, confirmed that the charity regulator would begin investigating eight unnamed charities. “Serious allegations have been made about UK charities operating in illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine. Our first step is to establish the facts,” Roake said in a statement. “Only then can we determine if regulatory action is required, based on our findings and the evidence we see. Our fact-finding will also help us develop regulatory guidance for charities, which will help to ensure public trust and confidence in charities.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Abtisam Mohamed, a Labour MP for Sheffield Central and member of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee, welcomed the investigation but called on the commission to go beyond investigating eight charities linked to illegal Israeli settlements. “The Government recognises Israeli settlements as illegal, so it follows that British money must not be allowed to sustain them. The Charity Commission’s decision to open 8 statutory inquiries is a welcome step, but evidence concerning at least 32 charities shows the scale of the problem," Mohamed told Middle East Eye. "Every organisation implicated must be investigated urgently, so there is consistency between Britain’s commitment to international law and the actions of British institutions. Money raised under the banner of charity must never be used to support settlement expansion, dispossession or violence against Palestinians.” Last month, Middle East Eye revealed details of a London synagogue holding an event advertising illegal Israeli settlements. Photos of brochures and leaflets from the event given exclusively to MEE showed the event advertising properties in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. The event led to a UK legal group, the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians, submitting a formal complaint to the Charity Commission. The Charity Commission’s announcement also comes after the charity regulator declared it unlawful for British charities to raise funds or send money to soldiers in the Israeli army. Since October 2023, the commission has opened more than 200 regulatory cases related to the war on Gaza . It said the investigations involved charities with different positions on the war. Israeli forces in Gaza have been accused of war crimes and genocide by organisations including Amnesty International , Human Rights Watch and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights . In 2024, the charity regulator told Middle East Eye it was assessing a complaint against AAC, a Jewish fundraising organisation accused of facilitating donations to an Israeli charity providing equipment to soldiers fighting in Gaza. The Charity Commission also said it was investigating the Boys Clubhouse , a charity based in Hendon, north London, after it held an event marking the return to the UK of a British man who had been fighting for the Israeli army in Gaza. headline: Exclusive: Cambridge University backtracks on divesting from arms companies
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 16:21 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: The University of Cambridge has backtracked on a move towards divesting from all weapons companies, Middle East Eye can reveal. A policy adopted earlier this year required the university to at least partially divest from the arms industry, but this has quietly been scrapped without students knowing. According to documents seen by MEE, on 16 April the University Council, Cambridge's central governing body, approved the introduction of a "monitoring regime" for investments in "conventional weapons". This monitoring regime was proposed by the Cambridge University Endowment Trustee Body (CUETB), which oversees the university's investments, and would track the endowment fund's "exposure to companies which primarily manufacture conventional weapons", according to the Council. If the fund's exposure to weapons companies was to exceed "a certain threshold as a proportion of its assets", discussions "would then be initiated with UCIM [University of Cambridge Investment Management Limited, which runs the endowment fund] as to how to manage a reduction in exposure of the [fund] in this category in due course." New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters This came in response to a report by a working group on investments that the university established in 2024, due to a student encampment organised by Cambridge for Palestine. Exclusive: Cambridge put £140m in fund with stakes in firms linked to Israeli abuses Read More » Documents also showed that in July 2026, the Cambridge University Endowment Trustee Body agreed to set the threshold for arms investments at zero percent under the monitoring regime. This unprecedented development would mean that any exposure at all to arms companies would automatically require discussions to be opened on "a reduction in exposure". It appeared to signal at least partial, if not full, divestment from weapons companies. However, multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told MEE that the university has quietly replaced the plan introduced in April with another that no longer requires divestment. According to the new plan, the zero percent monitoring threshold will remain in place but the "action plan" in response to exposure to conventional weapons would not need to lead to a reduction in exposure. MEE understands that this new decision, which has not been publicised, was made by the endowment trustee body but has not been put to the University Council. Some council members said they were not informed of the change. It is unclear when the decision was made and the university did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 'Maximal obfuscation' A spokesperson for Cambridge for Palestine told MEE that the group was "shocked, but not surprised, to learn that the university has once again backtracked on one of its commitments to our demands. "The notice in April issued by the University Council made clear that if arms investments were to exceed a yet-to-be-decided threshold of overall investments, then exposure to such investments would be reduced as part of a new monitoring scheme," the spokesperson said. "This mechanism was reaffirmed by Council in a statement responding to staff demands for full divestment last month. "Now that this threshold has been set at zero percent, we are hearing that the university has chosen to ignore and sideline its own statements and commitments by... removing any process of investment exposure reduction." The spokesperson added: "What’s worse is that this decision appears to have been imposed by another body, rather than the University Council, whilst the Grace [motion] on divestment that initiated the process has yet to be voted on by the Regent House, the University's democratic body of faculty and staff." King's College Cambridge to divest millions from 'occupation' and arms industry Read More » The spokesperson further said: "The University can backtrack all it likes, and obfuscate language to avoid scrutiny and accountability. But Cambridge for Palestine re-emphasises that students, staff and local activists will never stop campaigning... until the University’s money is used for education as it should be, not for funding war and occupation." This comes after MEE revealed in February that Cambridge's endowment fund had invested more than £140m ($189m) in a fund that owns shares in companies linked to Israeli human rights violations. The fund has previously refused to disclose companies in its portfolio, citing “legal reasons of confidentiality”. In the last quarter of 2025, the UCIM invested more than £140m in the iShares ESG Select Screened S&P 500 fund, which owns shares in companies including Palantir Technologies, Caterpillar and GE Aerospace. In January, dozens of Cambridge academics accused the university of "maximal obfuscation" over details about its £4.2bn ($5.74bn) endowment fund and its links to arms manufacturers. Senior staff said they were unable to properly examine these investments because the university had not been open about which companies are involved. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Abdul El-Sayed defeats Aipac-backed rival in Michigan Democratic Senate primary
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 5 August 2026 09:00 BST | Last update: 2 weeks ago
article_body: Progressive advocate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate in Michigan on Wednesday, defeating Congresswoman Haley Stevens in a race that became one of the most expensive and closely watched primaries in US history. NBC News projected El-Sayed's victory late on Tuesday after a bruising campaign in which more than $60m was spent, much of it by outside groups seeking to block his path to the Senate. As of 15:30 BST, NBC reported that El-Sayed had received 48.5 percent of the votes to Stevens' 47.5 percent, with 98.7 percent of expected votes tallied. Mallory McMorrow, a state legislator who was in the US Senate race but dropped out weeks before the elections, endorsed El-Sayed shortly after NBC made the announcement. The result is being viewed as a major setback for pro-Israel lobbying groups, particularly the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), which spent more than $30m backing Stevens in an effort to unseat one of the Democratic Party's most outspoken pro-Palestinian candidates. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters El-Sayed touted his narrow lead as results started to trickle in early on Wednesday, but said there was still a big fight to come. "I wish I could tell you that I was declaring victory right about now," he told his supporters at a watch party in Detroit. If declared the winner, the 41-year-old doctor will face former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in November in what is expected to be one of the country's most competitive Senate races. The contest could help determine control of the Senate during the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. "I know you’re listening, Mike. Mike, we are coming for you," El-Sayed added. The projected victory marks a watershed moment for progressive Democrats and Arab American voters, who rallied behind El-Sayed after months of organising around opposition to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and frustration with the Democratic Party's traditional alignment with pro-Israel advocacy groups. Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed accused Aipac and affiliated political action committees of attempting to "buy" the election with unprecedented outside spending. Stevens rejected suggestions that she was beholden to outside interests, arguing that she had a strong record of delivering for Michigan. El-Sayed also described Israel's military campaign in Gaza as a genocide, echoing language used by many human rights organisations and Palestinian advocates but rejected by Israel and successive US administrations. He also argued that billions of dollars in US military assistance to Israel should instead be invested in healthcare, affordable housing, education and infrastructure at home. His position resonated strongly with many voters in Michigan who played a crucial role in organising against former President Joe Biden during the 2024 election over his strong support for the war on Gaza. headline: 'Morocco has given me nothing': The young migrants risking everything to reach Ceuta
author: Olivia Hooper
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 12:23 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: In recent days, the Spanish enclave of Ceuta has been grappling with a mass migrant crisis. According to the latest figures 72,000 people entered the territory irregularly from Morocco last week. The Spanish government says 70,000 people have since been returned. Speculation on what caused the unprecedented migration crossing, which began on 31 July, on King Mohammed VI’s Throne Day, has been mounting, so far without any clear answers or accountability. Some say it was a kneejerk reaction from Morocco, following Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s recent visit to Algeria . Other commentators claim Israel or the US is involved due to Spain’s solid stance against the genocide in Gaza and the war on Iran . What is clear is that thousands of people, including around 8,000 children, felt they had no choice but to risk their lives in the fight for a better future. At least 141 people have died in the crossing, with the figure expected to rise. Morocco’s Association for Human Rights (AMDH) released a statement saying the “harrowing scenes” on the border “reflect the profound despair among young people, fuelled by the lack of prospects, endemic corruption, the rise of authoritarianism, the absence of social justice, and the lack of employment opportunities and decent living conditions”. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The AMDH attributed “full responsibility to the Moroccan state” for the exodus, comparing the situation to one it would expect to see in war and conflict zones. Morocco’s Ministry of the Interior said on 1 August that it blamed the migration surge on a misinterpretation of data spread on social media, and human trafficking networks that took advantage of the decision on 8 July by a Spanish Supreme Court to ban the immediate return of migrants arriving by sea. 'The Moroccan border security stood back and watched us cross' – Hamza, 19 Carla Hobbs, head of the Madrid Office and policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), disputes this statement, saying: “It would have been very hard for this to happen without Moroccan complicity.” While Hobbs agrees that the immediate trigger appears to have been a viral online campaign following the court ruling, she also pointed to the timing of the crisis. Just 10 days earlier Sanchez had travelled to Algeria , which is at odds with Morocco because of Algiers' support for the Polisario Front's bid for independence in Western Sahara. “The reduced border controls; migrants' own accounts that their authorities encouraged them to cross; and the fit with a well-established pattern of Moroccan migration coercion – all points to Moroccan complicity,” she told Middle East Eye. ‘Spanish and Moroccan police helped us cross’ Hamza, a 19-year-old from Kenitra who walked around 41 kilometres from Tetouan to Ceuta, told MEE that Moroccan guards encouraged migrants: “The Moroccan border security stood back and watched us cross; they would tell us, ‘Go on, hurry up, get into the water.’” Hamza noted that violence only occurred if migrants hesitated: “Then Moroccan police would hit migrants with a stick,” shouting, “If you don’t want to go across, go back home.” Spanish guards were also receptive: “They'd say, ‘Give me your hand, get up, climb up!’" Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco Read More » Refusing to return, Hamza explained, “Even if they try to force me, I will never go back. Morocco has not given me anything.” Despite holding diplomas, he added, “Morocco doesn’t value them. You can work for just a few dirham even in a big city; that’s why we fled.” Asmae, 23, from Casablanca, hitchhiked to Ceuta after seeing Instagram posts about the crossing. She agreed that authorities were passive: “The Moroccan police treated migrants well; they didn’t beat us as long as you don’t cause fights or problems, they talk to you calmly and diplomatically.” Asmae noted that people “leave of their own free will; the police won’t grab you or beat you”. The latest wave of migrants consists mostly of young Moroccans like Asmae and Hamza. According to Hobbs, this marks a strategic shift from historic border-crossing attempts, which were typically led by sub-Saharan migrants fighting Moroccan police. Pointing to a similar anomaly during the 2021 crisis, when thousands entered the Ceuta enclave amid a diplomatic dispute between Spain and Morocco over Western Sahara , Hobbs highlighted that recent reports from The New York Times show that "Moroccan police did not let sub-Saharans through, while letting Moroccans pass [into Ceuta]." A dream turned nightmare Another young Moroccan, Younes, made the journey like thousands of others, full of hope. Despite his bachelor’s degree and knowledge of multiple languages, he says there is nothing for him in Morocco. “I felt like in Ceuta I would finally get an opportunity in life,” he told MEE. As Younes swam across the last stretch before reaching Ceuta, he saw three teenagers die in the water. “Who knows if their parents know that they are gone,” he said. Upon arriving in Ceuta, Younes felt “unmatched happiness”. The feeling was short-lived, as he was beaten by the authorities. Young men pose for a picture while being escorted to the Ceuta-Morocco border in the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta on 1 August 2026 (AFP) He quickly noticed all the stores in Ceuta were closed and there was no water: “People are suffering; people arrived and collapsed unconscious, some people were threatened by guns.” Younes’ dream quickly turned into a nightmare: “My dream was to get in, and now I swear to god I advise every parent to not send their kids here,” he said, warning of the risk of violence. Family members are still waiting at the border, trying to find out whether their loved ones made it across or not. Najaat, a mother of six, is one of them. She told MEE that three of her children tried to reach Ceuta. Two of her girls, aged 12 and 13, took their birth certificates and wrote down their mother’s phone number before they fled. Their mother, inconsolable with worry, said: “They told me they would call me, but I haven’t heard anything. I just want to know if they got in safely, and to know if my son [aged 14] is dead or alive. Najaat expressed deep fear for her daughters and the risk of sexual violence. “I work to take care of my children; I don’t want them to emigrate like this. I deprive myself of things to give to my children,” she said. ‘They’re fleeing hell’ No Name Kitchen (NNK), an NGO that responds when migration flows shift or bottlenecks occur, is on the ground and has witnessed the authorities using what NNK coordinator Ric Fernandez describes as irregular return processes. “We've seen the army use ‘trawling’ tactics , forming human chains of people to force them toward the border with shoves, kicks, shouting and insults, threatening to beat them further if they didn't move,” Fernandez told MEE. NNK has filmed police beatings; Fernandez said it has been happening “at night and out of sight, when people refuse to board the trucks being used for group deportations”. He described the situation as “appalling”, saying that no one, including the police, the Guardia Civil or the military, “asks people how they are, what they need, or why they came to Spain... Even though we sense they're fleeing hell, the priority is to send them straight back into it.” Relatives wait for the return of people who had previously crossed into Ceuta, at Morocco's Bab Sebta border crossing, on 2 August 2026 (AFP) The NNK team is helping by mobilising resources and connecting migrants with accommodation. Fernandez said that it had to scale up its normal four-person team in Ceuta to 18 members. One of the toughest challenges has been reaching vulnerable people who are hiding in the mountains and warehouses, he added. “NNK doesn’t want to be followed by the police and be the bait that gives away their location. That's not our role,” he said. Fernandez noted that a massive legal documentation effort is under way to record all the cases of vulnerable people entitled to seek international protection. “NNK’s biggest concern is that by the time those cases are reviewed and legally upheld, those people will already be gone, returned, or will have suffered the worst possible consequences. But we won't give up,” he said. ‘The Spanish government won’t forget’ Spain and Morocco have been steadily rebuilding ties after relations broke down in 2021 , when Madrid allowed Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali to receive medical treatment, angering Rabat over the Western Sahara dispute. Recent events are expected to leave relations “smooth on the surface but worsened underneath”, Hobbs said. 'I felt like in Ceuta I would finally get an opportunity in life' – Younes The official line “is never to blame Morocco publicly”, Hobbs added, as Spain needs the kingdom in the medium-long term, for migration and security operations in general. However, she emphasised that: “This latest [migration] move will not be forgotten by the Spanish government, particularly with Spanish elections approaching and the images perfect fodder for Vox,” Spain’s far-right anti-immigration party. Describing the bilateral relationship as deeply asymmetric, Hobbs noted: “There is not much left for Madrid to concede after changing its position on the Western Sahara following the last round of coercion.” From Rabat’s perspective, Hobbs said: “I would find the EU's immediate response very encouraging – it confirmed that migration pressure costs very little, producing no unified European response. There is no reason why Morocco would not use that lever again.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Malaysia seizes container suspected of carrying goods bound for Israel
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 14:14 BST | Last update: 1 week 4 days ago
article_body: Malaysian authorities seized a container at the Port of Tanjung Pelepas in Johor, suspected of carrying merchandise intended for export to Israel, local media reported. The container was seized Friday by the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) following intelligence received by authorities, which prompted an inspection, according to the report. AKPS said preliminary checks indicated that the shipment may violate customs law, which prohibits the direct or indirect export of goods to Israel. "Based on preliminary checks, the shipment is suspected of not complying with Item No 15, Second Schedule, Customs (Prohibition on Export) Order 2023, which provides for the prohibition of direct or indirect export of goods to Israel," AKPS said in a statement cited by Berita Harian newspaper. The agency said it would investigate the nature, specifications, intended use and classification of the goods to determine whether the cargo constituted strategic goods regulated under Malaysia's Strategic Trade Act. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Any attempt to export goods directly or indirectly to Israel that is against the law and government regulations will be dealt with strictly," AKPS said. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim welcomed the seizure, saying it demonstrated Malaysia's opposition to its territory being used as a conduit for trade that could support Israel. "Congratulations to AKPS for the swift action in seizing a container suspected of carrying strategic trade cargo intended for export to Israel at the Port of Tanjung Pelepas," Anwar said in a statement shared on X. "This action demonstrates Malaysia's firm stance to ensure that our country will never serve as a conduit for trade that could support or contribute to the Israeli regime's atrocities against the Palestinian people," he said. Anwar said the action was also consistent with Malaysia's commitments under The Hague Group and with restrictions imposed by the government in December 2023. 'Practical effect' In a statement, The Hague Group said that the seizure gives practical effect to obligations that all states carry under international law. "The Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice of July 2024, affirmed by United Nations General Assembly Resolution ES-10/24, determined that states are under an obligation not to render aid or assistance in maintaining the unlawful situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory," the statement said. Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla, Executive Secretary of The Hague Group, said: "The defence of humanity is won at ports, courts, and factories, not from the podium. Law that goes unenforced is no law at all. By halting this cargo, Malaysia has upheld the obligations that bind every UN member state under international law. We invite all states to join The Hague Group and do the same." How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia Read More » Malaysia is a founding member of The Hague Group, a coalition of countries that pledged to prevent the transfer of arms, ammunition, military fuel, related military equipment and dual-use items to Israel where there is a clear risk they could be used to violate international law. The group's founding declaration also calls on member states to prevent vessels from docking at their ports if they are being used to transport such material to Israel. The seizure follows Malaysia's decision in December 2023 to prohibit Israeli-owned shipping company Zim from docking at Malaysian ports and to bar Israeli-flagged vessels from entering the country. At the time, Anwar also announced that vessels travelling to Israel would not be permitted to load cargo at Malaysian ports. The government described the measures as part of its response to Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its stated support for Palestinian rights. The latest seizure indicates that Malaysian authorities are also applying restrictions to cargo suspected of being destined for Israel, rather than limiting enforcement to Israeli-owned or Israeli-flagged vessels.
