headline: Israeli media eye Rebeca Grynspan's Jewish identity as she emerges as UN chief frontrunner
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 13:34 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: Israeli media have highlighted the Jewish background and family ties of Rebeca Grynspan to the country as she emerges as the early frontrunner to become the next United Nations secretary-general. If selected, the Costa Rican economist and diplomat would become the first woman, first Central American and first Jewish person to lead the organisation. Grynspan secured 10 "encourage" votes, four "no opinion" votes and one "discourage" vote in the Security Council's first secret straw poll held on 30 July. The five permanent and 10 elected members assessed seven candidates, without publicly revealing how individual countries voted. Although further rounds could reshuffle the contest, receiving only one objection places Grynspan in a strong opening position. The Security Council is expected to settle on a candidate by October. Any of its five permanent members can effectively end her campaign with a veto. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Antonio Guterres, the current secretary-general, will complete his second term on 31 December. Under the UN's informal regional rotation, his successor is widely expected to come from Latin America. Israeli family ties Grynspan, who leads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), was born into a Jewish family in Costa Rica in 1955. Her parents were European Jewish refugees who fled persecution in the lead-up to the Second World War, while members of her extended family were killed in the Nazi Holocaust. UN secretary-general race: What it takes to be the world’s top diplomat Read More » Israeli coverage has focused heavily on that history and her relatives in Israel. Her sister, Frida Greenspan, moved to Israel at 17 and lives in Mevaseret Zion, near Jerusalem. Her children served in the Israeli military, including as officers. "We are Zionists by birth," her sister told Ynet . The Israeli newspaper described Rebeca Grynspan as "one of the distinctly pro-Israel candidates" and reported that she has relatives living in the occupied West Bank. Ynet added that "she herself is proud of her Jewish heritage, and has maintained close ties with officials in Jerusalem over the years". Those family connections do not, however, establish how Grynspan would handle Israel and Palestine as secretary-general. She has rarely placed Israel at the centre of her public political identity, leaving her approach to longstanding UN positions on Palestine largely untested. Ynet acknowledged that her perceived closeness to Israel could also become a liability in a contest requiring support from governments with sharply differing positions on Israel's occupation and war on Gaza. Record at the UN Under Grynspan, UNCTAD has continued producing some of the UN system's strongest assessments of the damage Israel has inflicted on the Palestinian economy. Its reports have examined the costs of occupation, Israeli restrictions across the occupied West Bank and the destruction of Gaza's economy, linking the collapse of Palestinian economic life to Israeli policies and military operations. US vetoes Palestine from becoming full member of the United Nations Read More » In January, Israel's foreign ministry cut ties with several UN agencies and international organisations over their reporting on Israel's genocidal war on Gaza. Israel included UNCTAD on the list and accused the bodies of publishing "dozens of virulent anti-Israel reports". Yet Israeli officials have not publicly targeted Grynspan in the way they have repeatedly attacked Guterres and other senior UN figures. Israel Hayom, a newspaper widely regarded as supportive of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, paid closer attention to her public position on Gaza. Grynspan has called for "humanitarian agencies to have unrestricted access to Gaza" and said aid must not become politicised or weaponised. The newspaper concluded that, "despite the candidate's identity", she continued to represent the UN system's traditional position. An Israel Hayom opinion piece went further, arguing that "Grynspan's candidacy is quietly being sold to select member states, especially the US and Israel, wrapped in a carefully crafted personal narrative: daughter of Holocaust survivors, familiar with Hebrew, with close family living in Israel". Ynet suggested that Israel could influence the contest indirectly because "what Israel thinks of a particular candidate seeps into the place where decisions are really made - with the US, Britain and France". It also reported that "several of the candidates have already sent envoys and courtship messages to Israeli Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon". Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Saudi Aramco refinery erupts in flames in Jizan as Houthis claim drone attack
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 9 August 2026 12:47 BST | Last update: 1 week 3 days ago
article_body: A fire broke out early on Sunday at a facility belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in the coastal city of Jizan. Authorities said the blaze was later extinguished and no casualties were reported. Saudi Arabia ’s energy ministry said the fire occurred at an Aramco refinery facility in Jizan and that emergency authorities had completed the necessary procedures to deal with the incident. “The competent authorities are completing the necessary procedures to deal with the incident,” the ministry said in a statement on X. The ministry did not say what caused the fire. The military spokesperson for Yemen’s Houthi movement, Yahya Saree, said the facility had been targeted by a drone. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The group “succeeded in targeting the Aramco refinery in Jizan with a drone, and the strike was precise”, Saree wrote on X. He said the attack was carried out in response to Saudi Arabia’s “breach of the airspace of the provinces of Saada and Hajjah” with drones. Jizan lies on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast near the border with Yemen and has repeatedly been targeted by the Houthis in attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. The group also claimed responsibility for attacks on Aramco facilities in Jizan last month, as well as strikes on oil installations in Yanbu, a major Saudi export hub on the Red Sea. Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said last week that attacks on the company's facilities had caused some disruption to production but that he was confident operations could be restored quickly. Houthi missile and drone attacks kill dozens of Yemeni government troops Read More » He said the attacks had not had a material operational or financial impact. The Houthis also said they had targeted Saudi troops and equipment in the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha using “a large number of ballistic missiles and drones”. The latest incidents come as fighting intensifies between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, following years of relative calm after a 2022 truce. The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and control large parts of the country’s north, while the internationally recognised government controls much of the south. The group also announced a blockade targeting Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month and threatened shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The fire in Jizan was reported separately from an explosion and fires in the eastern Saudi city of Jubail. A loud explosion was heard in the Jubail region, Turkey’s state-run Anadolu Agency reported, while local media said gas facilities in Jubail Industrial City had been targeted and caught fire. Defence pact The incidents come as Saudi Arabia seeks deeper military cooperation with regional partners amid renewed security threats from Yemen. On Friday, Saudi Arabia signed a trilateral defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in Mecca, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries would be treated as an attack on all three. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday said the agreement was not directed at Iran and did not identify any country as a common threat. “There is no common threat that we have put in writing,” Fidan told Anadolu Agency. He described the agreement as “technically” similar to Nato's Article 5 collective-defence clause, while stressing that the nature of any response would depend on the circumstances. The pact is expected to include joint military training, intelligence sharing, logistics, threat assessments and defence-industry cooperation. Fidan also said Ankara wanted the arrangement to expand beyond its three founding members and suggested that Egypt could eventually join. The development comes amid heightened regional uncertainty following the US-Israeli war on Iran and renewed fighting involving armed groups across the region, particularly in Iraq and Lebanon. headline: Three Palestinians killed and dozens wounded in Israeli attacks across Gaza and West Bank
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 21:13 BST | Last update: 1 week 4 days ago
article_body: Three Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while Israeli forces and Jewish settlers wounded dozens more across the occupied West Bank on Saturday. In the West Bank city of Tubas, Israeli forces stormed the city with military vehicles and deployed soldiers through the centre. The Palestinian Red Crescent Society treated 15 people after troops fired tear gas at residents. Israeli forces also raided al Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, and fired tear gas inside a house, leaving members of a family, including children, struggling to breathe. Troops entered the nearby town of Turmus Ayya and the village of Abu Falah, while another Israeli force raided Kobar and fired tear gas in its streets. Further south, Israeli settlers opened fire during an attack on Wadi al-Rakhim in Masafer Yatta, wounding four Palestinians. Medical workers took a 57-year-old man to hospital after a bullet struck his hand. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Settlers, operating under the protection of Israeli forces, also attacked the area surrounding the Prophet Saleh Mosque in Idhna, west of Hebron. They assaulted residents, fired live ammunition and erected a tent on privately owned Palestinian land. 'Used as human bait': Leaked image shows elderly Palestinian men before execution by Israeli forces Read More » Israeli soldiers entered the mosque during the settler assault and detained seven worshippers, including its imam, Mu’taz Sa’di Tmaizi. Troops fired bullets, stun grenades and tear gas during the raid, while settlers vandalised a Palestinian vehicle. Settlers also attacked Abu Falah and fired near the village school. Separate groups entered Beit Ur al-Tahta and roamed Palestinian farmland outside Jaljalia as Israeli forces provided protection. The violence extended to Gaza, where Israeli troops shot three Palestinians in northern Khan Younis killing one. Nasser Medical Complex received the wounded. Gaza’s Health Ministry said two more Palestinians had died from wounds sustained in previous Israeli attacks. Hospitals also received six wounded people, bringing the toll since the start of the genocide in October 2023 to 73,384 killed and 174,242 wounded. headline: Turkey and Saudi Arabia's rocky relations: A brief history
author: Rayhan Uddin
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 16:00 BST | Last update: 1 week 4 days ago
article_body: In a highly symbolic move, the leaders of Saudi Arabia and Turkey were pictured performing Friday prayers together this week in the holy city of Mecca. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman were joined at the holiest site in Islam by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. For years, Ankara and Riyadh have been moving closer together and mending previously turbulent relations. That process was further solidified in recent days after Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a historic joint defence agreement . The agreement brings the three Muslim powers under a single security umbrella for the first time as part of a trilateral framework. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters While Pakistan has maintained close ties with both countries for decades, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have not always seen eye to eye. From historical rivalries over territory and religious sites to periods of cordial relations and a rupture over the killing of a journalist, Middle East Eye takes a brief look at the history of relations between the two countries. Sunni Muslim powers There has long been low-level tension between Riyadh and Ankara over their competing claims to leadership of the Sunni Muslim world, dating back to the establishment of both states in the early 20th century. The House of Saud fought the Ottoman Empire during the Ottoman-Saudi war in the 19th century, with the Saudis taking control of swathes of territory before a brutal crackdown by the Ottoman rulers. After the fall of the Ottoman dynasty following the Arab revolt in 1916, the Saudis defeated local rivals and took control of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina by 1924. Footage: Saudi Crown Prince MbS, Erdogan and Sharif together perform Friday prayers in Mecca pic.twitter.com/tsVx6yV5Nt — Ragıp Soylu (@ragipsoylu) August 7, 2026 The Ottomans had controlled Islam's two holiest sites almost continuously for more than 350 years. The nascent states of Saudi Arabia and Turkey formally established relations in the 1930s, and the two countries remained cordial for many decades. Both supported Iraq during the Iran - Iraq war, though Riyadh did so more openly, and both supported the US during the Gulf war. Tensions occasionally simmered over Islamic cultural heritage, with Turkey long criticising the demolition of Ottoman sites, including fortresses, cemeteries and railways, in Saudi Arabia. In 2002, the Turkish culture ministry condemned the Saudi demolition of the then 220-year-old al-Ajyad fortress, which overlooks the Grand Mosque in Mecca. Murat Sokmenoglu, then Turkey’s parliament speaker, called it “sinful behaviour in breach of the moral values of Islam”. Riyadh defended the decision, stating that it was exercising its sovereignty and using the site to house pilgrims in Mecca. The Clock Tower in Mecca, one of the world’s tallest buildings, was later built where the fortress once stood. Arab Spring divergence Cordial relations, punctuated by occasional minor disputes, gave way to much deeper disagreements following the Arab Spring in 2010. Although both countries supported the overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in Syria , their wider approach to revolutionary movements in the region diverged. In Egypt , Turkey supported Mohamed Morsi - the first democratically elected president - and strongly opposed the 2013 military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, a friend and ally of Riyadh. Following the coup, Turkey was welcoming of Egypt’s opposition, allowing dissenting media platforms to base themselves on Turkish soil. What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East Read More » For years, Erdogan refused to recognise Sisi’s rule and called for the release of 65,000 political prisoners. Ankara and Riyadh diverged in other arenas too. In 2017, when Saudi Arabia (alongside the United Arab Emirates , Bahrain and Egypt) imposed a blockade on Qatar , accusing it of meddling in regional countries and supporting terrorism, Turkey sided with Doha. Meanwhile, in Libya , following the fragmentation of power after the 2011 revolution, Ankara supported the internationally recognised government in Tripoli, while Riyadh initially aligned itself with eastern-based warlord Khalifa Haftar. A war of words between Riyadh and Ankara came to a head in early 2018, when Mohammed bin Salman said Turkey was part of a “triangle of evil” alongside Iran and extremist religious groups. Khashoggi killing Ties between the two hit their lowest in modern times later that year following the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi . Khashoggi, a former MEE journalist, was murdered by Saudi agents at the country's consulate in Istanbul in October 2018. Turkish prosecutors later indicted 20 Saudis over the killing, based on an analysis of the suspects’ mobile phone records, records of their entry into and exit from Turkey, their presence at the consulate, witness statements, and an examination of Khashoggi's phone, laptop and iPad. Erdogan said the killing was ordered at the "highest levels" of the Saudi government. Turkey’s state broadcaster and news agency were blocked in Saudi Arabia in 2010, and Ankara responded by blocking Saudi and Emirati news websites. Riyadh also launched an unofficial boycott of Turkish goods, causing Turkey’s exports to the Gulf kingdom to drop 92 percent year on year in 2021. The Saudi government had systematically pressured local businesses not to trade with Turkish companies and to drop their goods from their shelves. Regional rapprochement The two countries ended their years-long rift in 2022 as part of a wider period of rapprochement in the region. Mohammed bin Salman visited Ankara in June that year for the first time since Khashoggi’s killing. He met Erdogan at the presidential palace, where the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation on monetary policy, defence, energy and tourism. Bab al-Mandeb: US war on Iran gives Houthis new leverage over Saudi Arabia Read More » The meeting came after a Turkish court transferred the Khashoggi murder case to Saudi Arabia, meeting a key demand from the Gulf kingdom for mending ties. The reconciliation came amid a wider regional shift towards rapprochement led by the Saudi crown prince. That included ending the three and a half year rift with Qatar, seeking to engage with the Houthis in Yemen , as well as restoring diplomatic relations with Iran following a China -brokered agreement. At the same time, Ankara, for its part, restored fractured relations with Egypt and the UAE. At a time when Turkey was dealing with a fragile economy and a massive slump in its currency, ending its rifts with oil-rich Gulf states was seen as key to economic stabilisation. Since patching up ties, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have signed deals on technology, defence and renewable energy. In the summer of 2023, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy Turkish drones in the biggest defence contract in Turkey's history. Aligning goals More recently, Turkey and Saudi Arabia appear to be coming closer together due to a shared understanding over events in neighbouring countries. In Syria, both Riyadh and Ankara support the new government led by Ahmed al-Sharaa and are among Damascus’ closest allies. Why are Kurdish groups in Iraq being attacked amid the US-Iran flare-up? Read More » Both countries were involved in lobbying for the US to lift sanctions on Syria. In Libya, while they had at times backed rival camps, they now both appear to support the internationally recognised government. Meanwhile in war-torn Sudan , Riyadh and Ankara both support the Sudanese Armed Forces, led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. The UAE is the main backer of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Somalia is another arena where Turkey and Saudi Arabia find themselves on one side and Abu Dhabi on the other. Ankara and Riyadh stand firmly behind the central government, while the UAE has steadily supported Somaliland’s efforts to gain international recognition. Rather than Qatar or Turkey, it now seems that Saudi Arabia's growing rift is with its erstwhile Gulf ally, the UAE. That came to a head publicly for the first time in Yemen in late December. Ankara appears increasingly aligned with Riyadh amid those tensions, although it is unlikely to take sides publicly because of its strong financial ties with Abu Dhabi. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Israeli general says Gaza should remain ‘destroyed for generations’
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 9 August 2026 21:30 BST | Last update: 1 week 3 days ago
article_body: A former head of Israel’s National Security Council has called for Gaza to remain devastated for decades, openly presenting Palestinian despair and destruction as desirable outcomes after Israel’s genocide in the enclave. Retired Major General Giora Eiland told Israel’s 103FM radio station on Sunday that rebuilding Gaza would run against Israeli interests. “Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt, it is better for us that it be destroyed for generations to come,” Eiland said. “The greater the despair in Gaza and the greater the destruction, and the greater the monument to what they did on October 7, years to come, that is good" he added. Eiland, a secular Israeli nationalist aligned with opposition politician Avigdor Lieberman, opposes Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu politically. Yet his prescriptions for Gaza have frequently gone beyond Netanyahu’s publicly declared policies. Calls for Israel to occupy Gaza land Eiland described the 15-point Gaza plan backed by US President Donald Trump as “pro-Hamas”. Netanyahu formally rejected the proposal on Sunday. “In war...the losing side loses. Germany, which lost the Second World War, was forced to surrender 25 percent of its territory,” he noted. Eiland used the comparison to argue that Israel should retain the Yellow Line, which marks the territory its military occupies inside Gaza which Israel has continued to expand and may ultimately amount to 70 percent of Gaza's territory. “Along with this, there is the territorial need for the Yellow Line, which we must not give up under any circumstances. This is a war, the enemy has lost, and we need land, not for settlement, but as a security buffer between the settlements and where the IDF can be located." Eiland nevertheless criticised Netanyahu’s handling of Washington, arguing that Israel had become too dependent on his relationship with Trump. Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, says Netanyahu Read More » “I believe Israel’s entire approach towards the US in recent years has been outrageous. It relies excessively on the personal relationship between Netanyahu and Trump, which is good on some days and less so on others.” He advised Netanyahu to accept the US plan conditionally while protecting Israel’s central demands. "Where did Netanyahu go wrong in my opinion? You should never say no, you should always say yes but... or yes in the sense of I agree if certain points happen," he clarified. Eiland said Israel could temporarily suspend "assassinations" in Gaza as a tactical concession to Washington but insisted it must maintain control of the Yellow Line. Since the ceasefire took effect on 11 October, Israeli forces have killed at least 1,258 Palestinians and injured 4,139 others, the sources said. Earlier this week the United Nations Children's Fund said that at least 300 children have been killed in the Gaza Strip by Israel over the last 10 months. Israel’s genocide on Gaza has killed at least 73,386 Palestinians and wounded 174,250 since 7 October 2023. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East
author: Zia Ur Rehman
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 13:15 BST | Last update: 1 week 4 days ago
article_body: A new security pact between Pakistan , Saudi Arabia and Turkey is reshaping the Middle East's strategic map, bringing together three of the Muslim world's most influential powers under a collective defence framework. Named after the holy city where it was signed on Friday, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement stipulates that an attack against one member is an attack against all three. Echoing Nato's Article 5, the clause gives the pact immediate geopolitical significance, even as the joint statement leaves specific military commitments vague. For Pakistan, the world's only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority state, the accord marks a striking departure from its traditionally cautious stance as a regional mediator. By standing alongside Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Islamabad is positioning its armed forces as a potential security guarantor at the heart of an emerging axis spanning South Asia and the Gulf. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The pact signals a potentially significant shift. As the long-standing regional order anchored by Washington comes under increasing strain amid war and shifting alliances, Middle Eastern powers are seeking to take greater control of their own security, with Pakistan's nuclear and conventional military capabilities potentially providing a new anchor. The deal also comes as the Middle East's traditional security order faces unprecedented strain. The US and Israeli war on Iran has transformed the regional strategic landscape, with direct strikes reaching Saudi territory and commercial shipping severely disrupted across both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. "All three countries have a shared economic and security interest in preventing further escalation, which ultimately compelled them to sign the pact," a Pakistani security official monitoring the region told Middle East Eye on condition of anonymity. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have affected supplies of Saudi energy and fertilisers, sending shock waves through the global economy. Import-dependent countries such as Pakistan and Turkey have been among those particularly exposed to the disruption. 'All three countries have a shared economic and security interest in preventing further escalation, which ultimately compelled them to sign the pact' - Pakistani security official But the security calculus is even more consequential. Both Saudi Arabia and Turkey have experienced attacks linked to the broader regional conflict, while Islamabad and Ankara remain deeply concerned about cross-border instability spilling over from their lengthy frontiers with Iran. Ankara faces an additional security dilemma: the prospect that the arming of Iranian Kurdish militias by external powers could unravel its fragile, hard-won peace process with the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK. The wider conflict has also emboldened Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, who have escalated direct attacks on Saudi territory. For Gulf leaders, the failure of traditional US security guarantees to deter such strikes has raised questions about Washington’s reliability as a security partner. The result is a decisive push by regional heavyweights to construct defence arrangements that rely less on external guarantees. Former Pakistani ambassador Asif Durrani described the pact as the "first concrete building block of an emerging regional security architecture", arguing that it signals a move towards greater regional ownership of security. "If this momentum continues, it could open the door to addressing decades-old conflicts, including the enduring Palestinian issue, through a more regionally driven approach,” Durrani wrote on X. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan sign defence pact Read More » Analysts emphasise that the pact is not an isolated development, but rather the culmination of deepening trilateral cooperation. Michael Kugelman, senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, described the pact as "a logical outgrowth of deepening security ties" among the three countries in recent months. It builds upon existing foundations. Riyadh and Islamabad signed a bilateral mutual defence agreement in late 2025, which saw roughly 8,000 Pakistani troops, fighter jets and air defence systems deployed to the kingdom, while Turkey remains a major defence supplier to both nations. For Washington, the pact could be particularly welcome. With its major focus on collective regional deterrence, with an eye to Iran, "it'll be received well in Washington, which wants to see more burden-sharing from top allies", Kugelman said on X. An economic lifeline in military uniform For Pakistan, however, the pact is about more than geopolitics. It is also deeply connected to the country's economic vulnerabilities, analysts said. The pact marks a notable shift for Islamabad, which spent recent months positioning itself as a diplomatic bridge between Washington and Tehran. While Pakistan helped broker the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June to temporarily halt regional hostilities, subsequent escalations narrowed its neutral stance. For a government battling persistent inflation and fiscal distress, strategic defence policy is now increasingly inseparable from financial necessity. Historically, Pakistan has leveraged its military strength to secure economic backing, particularly from the US and Saudi Arabia. This collective defence framework institutionalises that model, allowing Islamabad to monetise its operational capabilities, ranging from joint training and troop deployments to arms exports, in exchange for vital Gulf investments, energy concessions and diplomatic support. For Riyadh, Pakistan offers access to a large, experienced military with decades of combat and counterinsurgency experience. For Islamabad, closer security cooperation with Saudi Arabia offers the prospect of investment, financial assistance and a stronger economic relationship with one of the region’s most powerful states. "In this sense, Pakistan's military strength is becoming an economic asset as well as a strategic one," the security official told MEE. Saudi money, Turkish technology, Pakistani military power The emerging partnership also brings together three distinct forms of strategic power. Sheharyar Khan, a political analyst and senior adviser at Pakistan’s Ministry of Law and Justice, described the emerging combination as one in which Saudi Arabia provides the financial power, Turkey contributes technological innovation, and Pakistan supplies core military capability. 'Together, the three countries could form a security partnership whose capabilities extend far beyond traditional troop deployment' - Sheharyar Khan, political analyst "Together, the three countries could form a security partnership whose capabilities extend far beyond traditional troop deployments," Khan told MEE. Each state brings a complementary asset. Saudi Arabia, home to Islam’s holiest sites, provides vast capital, energy market dominance and regional diplomatic weight. Turkey, which operates Nato's second-largest military, has an advanced and increasingly self-reliant defence industry, including expertise in unmanned aerial systems, electronic warfare and precision-guided munitions, reducing reliance on foreign suppliers. Pakistan contributes a massive, combat-hardened army and the Muslim world’s sole nuclear deterrent. The risk of entrapment Yet the agreement also carries significant risks for Pakistan, experts said. Iran's response to the pact has been swift and critical. "The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan does not bring them security, just as years of unilateral milking of the Americans did not bring them security," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of Iran's parliamentary National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, wrote on X, dismissing the arrangement. The response underscores Islamabad’s fundamental dilemma: deepening involvement in Gulf defence architecture risks fracturing its delicate, traditionally cautious relationship with Tehran. Analysts warn of "entrapment", the danger of Pakistan being dragged into foreign confrontations that do not serve its own national interests. Historically, Pakistan has avoided direct entanglements in Middle Eastern power struggles. Its parliament famously declined to join the Saudi-led Yemen coalition in 2015 because of domestic political and sectarian concerns. Home to a large Shia minority, some of whom see Iranian clergy as political and religious guides, Pakistan must also ensure that closer alignment with Saudi Arabia and Turkey is not perceived at home as an anti-Iranian stance that could inflame internal sectarian fault lines. 'Muslim security bloc' The agreement has sparked intense debate over whether it could evolve into a broader, multi-nation security bloc across the Muslim world. Retired senior Pakistani military official Muhammad Saeed suggested that additional Muslim countries from the region, and potentially beyond, could eventually join the framework. Bab al-Mandeb: US war on Iran gives Houthis new leverage over Saudi Arabia Read More » But he cautioned that military power alone would not determine the success of such an arrangement. "For Muslim states, the real and collective strength will not come only through military capabilities but primarily through long-term investments and collaboration in knowledge, innovation, discipline, character, and tolerant interpretation of sectarian sentiment," he wrote on X. The prospect of a more cohesive security grouping has already attracted attention in Israel. In February, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett explicitly warned against Turkey seeking a "hostile axis" with Pakistan's nuclear capabilities, "to surround Israel". Analysts, however, argue that Pakistan's nuclear status inevitably changes the strategic calculations surrounding the pact. For Saudi Arabia, closer defence ties with Islamabad could provide an additional layer of deterrence at a time when the kingdom faces threats from Iran while also navigating its relationship with Israel. The India factor The pact also has implications far beyond the Middle East. For Pakistan, closer ties with Saudi Arabia and Turkey could provide a strategic counterweight to India. While Saudi Arabia maintains extensive economic and trade ties with New Delhi, the collective defence framework further strengthens Pakistan's role as a security partner for key Gulf powers. Although India's Ministry of External Affairs responded cautiously, saying that New Delhi was "closely following developments", Indian national security analysts are monitoring the situation with growing concern. "While most are obviously seeing this from a Middle East lens, it impacts other theatres as well. Pakistan's conflict-laden relationship with India [is] at the top of that list," Kabir Taneja, executive director of the Middle East programme at the Observer Research Foundation, a New Delhi-based think tank, wrote on X. Former Foreign Secretary Kanwal Sibal, in a post on X, described the pact as "a very negative development for Indian interests", suggesting that India expand its strategic options with the United Arab Emirates, Israel, Greece, Cyprus and Afghanistan. headline: The Caspian gamble: Iran-Ukraine tensions widen the 'geography of instability'
author: Amara Sophia Elahi
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 14:49 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: Nima Moradi was a 23-year-old sailor on his maiden voyage aboard Anna, a commercial ship in the Caspian Sea, carrying iron from Russia to Iran . He was from the port city of Bandar Anzali in northern Iran and had dreamed of becoming a mariner since he was a child. The boat he was travelling on was hit by a Ukrainian long-range drone on 25 July - Moradi was killed in the attack, and another crew member was wounded. In a post on social media, Moradi's father Masoud wrote: “My son, I can’t believe the sadness your absence brings – you left me... we are in pain without wet tears.” After the incident, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the attack as “a blatant UN Charter violation done at Israel 's behest to drag Europe into its war”. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Israel has remained silent about the strike, however. Iran had vowed to respond and was reportedly planning to launch ballistic missile attacks on three sites in Ukraine. For the moment, further escalation has been avoided following an apology from Kyiv, although Iran is still seeking financial reparations for the fatal attack. Two Wars Merging According to Trita Parsi, vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, the Ukrainian attack on the Iranian vessel was not completely unexpected. “Narratives were being formed on the Ukrainian side for some time portraying Iran and Russia as being completely aligned, and viewing those two wars as a single war,” Parsi told Middle East Eye. There was also some resentment from Ukraine that the US-Israel war on Iran took away attention and resources from its conflict with Russia. “The Ukrainians knew from the outset that that war was going to come at their expense,” Parsi said. “We have examples of munitions and Patriot batteries that were sent to Ukraine which had to be taken back and given to the Israelis.” Nima Moradi, a 23-year Iranian old sailor, was killed in a Ukraine attack on a commercial ship in the Caspian Sea (supplied) For Parsi, the possibility of Iran getting pulled into a war with Ukraine could still materialise. “I don’t believe that Iran has truly called it off. I think they’re putting a pause on it because they’re dealing with other issues. They don’t want to do something now that would see them walk into a trap if they strike back at Ukraine,” he said. Parsi believes that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was taking a gamble on merging the Russia-Ukraine war with the US-Israel-Iran war. “I don’t think Ukraine is doing particularly well right now. The narrative in the media is that they’re winning but I don’t see clear signs of that,” he said. “Because of [US President Donald] Trump’s vulnerability in the Iran war, the Ukrainians have found an opportunity to say to him – ‘we can be helpful to you here if you help us in Ukraine’. “The benefit is that if you merge these two wars, it leads to the US becoming part of the Ukraine war, and that’s what Ukraine has wanted from the outset - but something that the Iranians obviously do not want.” The US has consistently refused to get dragged into direct confrontation with Russia. Former President Joe Biden rejected Ukraine’s demands for American ground troops and F-16 fighter jets, as well as their request for a no-fly zone over their country. In attacking the Iranian commercial ship however, the Ukrainians are trying to present themselves as an asset to the US in their war on Iran. “The Ukrainians are trying to offer the type of horizontal escalation that the Iranians have effectively used against the US when they’ve struck many of the Gulf Cooperation Council states,” Parsi said. “They can help the US create a new front in the Caspian Sea to the north of Iran and escalate that way, which would stretch the Iranians, while showing the utility they can play to the US.” Reframing Israel’s war on Iran Merging these two wars could not only benefit Ukraine, but also Israel, according to Parsi. “First of all it would prolong the war between the US and Iran, which is something Israel is constantly trying to do,” Parsi explained. Two mountain ranges, two deserts, two seas: Iran’s geography is its greatest weapon Read More » “It would also bring the Europeans into the war in a way they haven’t been so far, which Israel would also be happy about. “But perhaps most importantly, it would give the Israelis the opportunity to reframe the war - defeating Iran would no longer be about defending Israel, it would be about defending Ukraine, and given how much Israel has plummeted in public opinion in the United States while Ukraine still enjoys significant support, this would be a helpful way for the Israelis to lessen their own centrality in this war.” Israel has already entered the stage in the Caspian region – last June and in March of this year, they hit Iranian naval assets and military infrastructure there. “It wouldn’t be an unprecedented situation if the Caspian ended up becoming a front in this war, but there would be a difference in terms of how the war has been conducted over the last few weeks, and it certainly would be different if Ukraine were to enter it with their long-range drone capabilities,” Parsi observed. “If Ukraine were to have their own name on this war, it would carry a lot of weight in Europe. The Europeans are already very upset with Iran for being a supporter of Russia in the Ukraine conflict.” Russia and Iran: From suspicion to pragmatism Historically, Iran and Russia have not always been allies. In the 19th century, Iran lost almost a fifth of its territory due to the expansionism of the Russian Empire, which seized the South Caucasus region. Twentieth-century relations were defined by how the two countries dealt with common challenges and changes to the international order, according to Professor Lana Ravandi-Fadai, head of the Eastern Cultural Centre at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences. “For a long time in Iranian historical memory, Russia was not a partner but a great power located uncomfortably close to Iran’s borders, and one that had repeatedly interfered in the country’s internal affairs,” Ravandi-Fadai explained. 'The Ukrainians are trying to offer the type of horizontal escalation that the Iranians have effectively used against the US' - Trita Parsi, the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft During World War Two, Iran was invaded by the Soviet Union and the British , who wanted to secure a supply route for Western military aid and prevent Nazi Germany from seizing control of the region's oil fields. “Although Iran formally declared neutrality in the war, its leadership was strengthening relations with Germany, who viewed Tehran as a possible 'third force' capable of balancing British and Soviet influence,” Ravandi-Fadai said. During Mohammed Reza Pahlavi’s reign (1941-79), Iran grew more aligned with the West, particularly after the CIA-backed coup which overthrew Mohammad Mosaddegh’s government in 1953 and reinstalled Pahlavi as Shah. While initially regarding the Soviet Union as a threat, the Shah’s attitude towards them changed from the 1960s onwards. “He remained an ally of the United States, but at the same time developed economic cooperation with the Soviet Union,” Ravandi-Fadai said. “The Soviet Union participated in the construction of the Isfahan steelworks and contributed to the development of engineering, mining and energy infrastructure – in return, Iran supplied natural gas to them.” After Iran’s Islamic Revolution in 1979, relations became more hostile, with Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini condemning Russia as the “Lesser Satan” (America being “The Great Satan” and Israel “Little Satan”). “The leadership of the Islamic Republic regarded both liberal capitalism and Soviet atheistic communism as alien to the Islamic model,” Ravandi-Fadai said. Iran also opposed the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in the 1980s, but at the time was itself dealing with an invasion by Iraq , something which the Soviet Union, which had supplied arms to then Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, found unsettling. “In Moscow, concern grew that the fall of Saddam’s regime might lead to the spread of the Iranian revolutionary model into the Arab world and destabilise the regional balance,” Ravandi-Fadai said. Turning point Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani’s presidency (1989-97) marked a change in Iran-Soviet relations. “In 1989 Rafsanjani visited Moscow, where major agreements were reached in the fields of military, technical and economic cooperation. This marked an important transition from a revolutionary and ideologically driven foreign policy towards a more pragmatic approach to cooperation with the East,” Ravandi-Fadai observed. From Syria to UAE, the race to bypass Strait of Hormuz is on Read More » Proximity between the two countries continued to grow over the subsequent decades. Both states formed a military coalition to protect Bashar al-Assad's government in Syria from collapsing in 2015, and Iran has aligned itself with Russia during the Ukraine war, providing it with Shahed drone technology. Last year’s signing of the 20-year Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership by Iran and Russia formalised cooperation between the two countries, including on military and security matters. “Moscow and Tehran are trying to adapt to a new multipolar international order in which states seek to diversify their economic and political partnerships,” Ravandi-Fadai said. Russia and Iran have both faced international isolation and have been impacted by Western sanctions. In many ways, the treaty represents a pragmatic partnership between two major regional powers who have been forced to reduce their financial and political dependence on the West, according to Ravandi-Fadai. It may also have played a part in Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran, just a few months after it was signed. Warfare on waterways Both the Strait of Hormuz and the Caspian Sea have afforded Iran a considerable amount of leverage in this year’s war. 'It would bring the Europeans into the war in a way they haven’t been so far, which Israel would also be happy about' - Trita Parsi, the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft By blocking the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has been able to severely disrupt global trade, drive up energy prices and target US military assets in the region. The Caspian is also part of Iran’s resilience architecture, that is, a key element of their defensive shield against the threat from Western powers. It is the largest landlocked body of water in the world, bordered by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, all of whom have a share in it. Under the 2018 Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea , external states are prohibited from establishing a military presence there. The Caspian also contains major offshore oil and gas fields, as well as ports and pipelines that connect Central Asia to global markets. Furthermore, it is an important area for energy cooperation and trade between Iran and Russia, who have used the waterway to bypass western sanctions and military blockades. “For centuries, it has served simultaneously as a border, a trade route and an arena for strategic competition,” Ravandi-Fadai explained. “It’s a geopolitical bridge between Europe, the Middle East and Asia – whoever controls the major transport routes across the Caspian gains significant economic and political advantages. “While the conflict in Ukraine spilling into the Caspian region, even in isolated incidents, does not necessarily mean the two wars are merging into a single conflict, it should be taken as a warning: we are witnessing an expansion of the geography of instability.” Bypassing the Strait of Hormuz For Parsi, the Caspian offers a way for Iran and other countries to circumvent the unpredictability in the Strait of Hormuz. “One of the things that has happened as a result of this war is that other countries are building pipelines that would bypass Hormuz, and the Iranians too are investing further in railways and other means of trading with China and the East, through Central Asia,” he said. “I think you’re going to end up seeing an ecosystem of supply chains that will reduce the significance of the Strait of Hormuz – it will take 10 to 15 years for it to be effective but it will not just be driven by other countries, it will be driven by the Iranians themselves in order diversify their supply chain and reduce their vulnerability in the Strait, and any attempts by the United States to try to choke them off.” 'The conflict in Ukraine spilling into the Caspian region should be taken as a warning: we are witnessing an expansion of the geography of instability' - Lana Ravandi-Fadai, Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences Despite the strategic advantages and leverage the Iranians have with these two bodies of water, Parsi believes that they alone aren’t enough to sustain Iran in this war. “Yes, the Iranians have managed to inflict the strategic defeat on Israel and the United States in this war, but in the longer term, if Iran can only trade with Russia, China and a few Asian states, that’s not going to be enough for Iran to really be able to live up to its full potential or for it to be able to prepare itself for any future confrontation with the US or Israel,” he said. “In that sense, sanctions relief is essential from an Iranian standpoint not only to grow its own economy but also to restore its own defences and deterrence.” Days after the Iranian ship was attacked in the Caspian, Iran launched a drone attack on the Egyptian port city of Damietta, which according to Parsi was an attempt by Iran to showcase their asymmetrical warfare capabilities. “That was probably aimed at deterring the US from going down the path of escalation in the Caspian, and showing that the Iranians have even greater escalation potential - which probably gave planners in Washington pause, because this is a completely different escalation, far beyond bringing the Caspian back into the war,” he remarked. headline: Anti-Muslim lawmaker Andy Ogles loses Republican primary
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 17:12 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: A Tennessee lawmaker known for his frequent anti-Muslim remarks lost his primary race on Thursday, even though he had the endorsement of US President Donald Trump. The president's backing is seen as a golden ticket for Republican candidates. Two-term congressman Andy Ogles lost the Republican primary race to dairy farmer and state agriculture official Charlie Hatcher, who also expressed his fondness for Trump. Campaigning with the tagline "hire a farmer", Hatcher's website describes him as "pro-gun, pro-life, pro-Trump". He also outspent Ogles in the race with an influx of cash from outside groups backing Hatcher's platform, which was focused on reviving renewable energy production. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The upset can be attributed to the redrawing of the lines around the district that Ogles was running in - something that became possible because a recent US Supreme Court ruling undermined the Voting Rights Act . But Ogles was also very fixated on certain groups. In a now-deleted post on X, he said in June that "homosexuality has no place in America". But he went after Muslims more than anyone else. A staunch supporter of Israel and a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, Ogles has floated several hardline proposals targeting Muslims. He recently said he intends to introduce legislation banning immigration from certain Muslim-majority countries. Ogles also declared that "diversity is our weakness" and called for the deportation of naturalised Muslim Americans, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. "Zohran 'little muhammad' Mamdani is an antisemitic, socialist, communist who will destroy the great City of New York," Ogles wrote on X in June. "He needs to be DEPORTED. Which is why I am calling for him to be subject to denaturalization proceedings." Rise in anti-Muslim sentiment Earlier this year, Ogles sparked widespread condemnation after declaring on social media that Muslims have no place in American society. He wrote on X in early March that "Pluralism is a lie." Social media monitors reported a sharp increase in anti-Muslim content on X since Israel and the US launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February. The Washington, DC-based Center for the Study of Organized Hate said it tracked posts that explicitly dehumanised, excluded, and incited violence against Muslims from 1 January to 5 March, during which Trump was consistently threatening to start the war. On the day the war began, the volume of such posts surged from just under 2,000 per day to more than 6,000, the report said . The Council on American–Islamic Relations (Cair) condemned Ogles, calling him "an anti-Muslim extremist". "Ogles is a member of the so-called 'Sharia-Free America Caucus,' a group of US representatives who support extremist legislation that would, if enacted, essentially ban the practice of Islam in the United States," the statement said. "Islam is an American faith that has been present since the colonial-era when large numbers of Muslims were imported as slave labor, without any individual liberty or freedom of religion," said Cair. The comments triggered swift condemnation from Democratic lawmakers, who described the rhetoric as openly Islamophobic. Judy Chu called the remarks "abhorrent", while Lisa Blunt Rochester urged Republican leaders to publicly denounce the Tennessee congressman. Katherine Clark, the House minority whip, wrote on X: "This disgusting shit doesn’t belong in American society. And Republicans who support it don’t belong in Congress." But there were never any consequences, such as an effort to censure Ogles - a largely symbolic move - in the House of Representatives. Palestinian-American Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib was censured last year for using the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free". Andy Ogles' current term will end in January 2027. headline: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, says Netanyahu
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 9 August 2026 14:04 BST | Last update: 1 week 3 days ago
article_body: Israel has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza and will not withdraw until Hamas fully disarms, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday. The Board of Peace, spearheaded by Trump, announced last month that it had made a breakthrough in a plan to end the war. Israel and Hamas agreed to the plan last year, beginning with a ceasefire. Israel has continued to carry out near-daily strikes on Gaza since agreeing to the ceasefire last October. Trump said that Hamas had agreed to lay down its weapons. “Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, he added. Middle East Eye obtained a copy of the 15-point agreement last month . Under the deal, Hamas and other Palestinian factions would not hand Gaza’s weapons to Israel. Instead, the weapons would be placed under the control of a body called the National Committee. The document seen by MEE states that the weapons would remain in Palestinian hands. Full text: 15-point draft peace plan between Hamas and Israel in Gaza Read More » "No weapons will be transferred or surrendered to Israel or any non-Palestinian parties," the text states, and by the end of the disarmament process, "the National Committee alone shall retain, store, or control weapons in Gaza". The agreement describes weapons collection as a domestic process: "The National Committee, as the transitional authority in Gaza, shall be the sole authority for registering weapons, issuing and revoking licenses, and enforcing the law... all factions, clans, and elements of Palestinian society in Gaza shall cooperate with the National Committee in this process." Hamas has publicly said it will not implement any part of the roadmap unless Israel meets its obligations, including a full, phased withdrawal from the territory it still controls in Gaza. The document makes that condition central to every stage, stating that “the transition from one phase to the next will be contingent upon the verified completion of the previous phase’s obligations”, with an international commission responsible for verification. “This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY,” Trump wrote on Truth Social after the plan was revealed. He said Israeli forces would withdraw “as disarmament is completed”, while the UN-mandated International Stabilization Force would work alongside a new Palestinian police force. Hamas official Ghazi Hamad told Reuters at the time that the group would retain its weapons until Israel halted its attacks, allowed more aid and goods into Gaza, and withdrew its forces in accordance with the ceasefire agreement reached in October last year. headline: Iran says its people are ‘professional chess players’ in dealing with the US
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 13:31 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: Tehran has described Iranians as “professional chess players” in their dealings with the US , as it insisted that Washington must meet its demands for the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump on Sunday indicated that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount against Iran, appearing to back away from more military strikes after Tehran issued a list of demands for opening the Strait of Hormuz. Trump was quoted by Axios as saying he was "low-keying it" with Iran. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he said. "It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," Trump added. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Responding directly to Trump’s remarks, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said: "Lights out or lights on, Iranians showed they are professional chess players." Trump’s remarks came after Iran issued over the weekend a list of conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The strategic waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passes, has largely been kept closed by Iran since the US and Israel launched its war on the country in late February. Iranian official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out Tehran's demands, including an end to the "war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon , Palestine , Yemen and Iraq ". He also called for the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets and compensation for wartime damage, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported. Baghaei on Monday said that "as long as the US naval blockade continues... as long as other violations by the United States continue, the necessary conditions for saying that the Strait of Hormuz has become a safe waterway will not exist". Iran: Trump says he'd rather make deal than 'kill people' amid reports of weapons shortages Read More » Iran has said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with Oman on the strait was in its "final stages" but reiterated that Tehran would not reopen the channel unless the US met its demands. The Oman-Iran deal would set out the new shipping lanes to be used once the US fulfils those conditions and the strait is reopened, Iran's Mehr news agency quoted Araghchi as saying. Iran and the US are not engaged in direct talks, and Tehran will not start them as long as Washington breaches the interim deal signed in June, Araghchi said. He added that messages were being exchanged through intermediaries. The US military said on Monday it had rerouted 55 commercial vessels sailing towards Iran as part of its operations to enforce restrictions on Iranian ports. The US Central Command (Centcom), which coordinates US operations in the Middle East, said in a statement published on X that it had rerouted the vessels, disabled two others and inspected two additional ships to ensure compliance with the restrictions. Iran not worried by 'Mecca agreement' Also on Monday, foreign ministry spokesperson Baghaei said that Tehran saw no indication that a new security pact between Pakistan , Turkey and Saudi Arabia was meant to be directed against Iran. Baghaei said the pact showed a "change in perception" towards the US, as well as a shift in regional countries' approach to security, with greater reliance on their own capabilities rather than outside powers. "Any plan that is based on the geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy and its allies," he added. What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East Read More » Meanwhile, tensions between Israel and the US are growing amid Washington's efforts to wind down fighting in Gaza , Lebanon and Iran, according to a report from Israel’s Channel 13. Centcom chief Brad Cooper conveyed the message of Washington wanting to shift toward "closing the three fronts" during a visit to Israel over the weekend, the broadcaster indicated, citing a military source. It came after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected on Sunday Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza and said Israel would not withdraw until Hamas fully disarms. The Board of Peace, spearheaded by Trump, announced last month that it had made a breakthrough in a plan to end the war. Israel and Hamas had agreed to an initial ceasefire last October. However, the Israeli army has continued to carry out near-daily strikes on Gaza and violations of the agreement since then. Trump said that Hamas had agreed to lay down its weapons. “Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: France shuts mosque over Quran verses and Islamic texts used in Muslim worship
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 18:12 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: A French court has upheld the six-month closure of a mosque near Paris in a case that has raised fresh concerns over the state's policing of Islamic belief and worship. The Montreuil Administrative Court on Friday rejected an attempt to suspend the July order against the Chanteloup mosque in Aulnay-sous-Bois. The mosque will remain closed until January. Rafik Chekkat, a human rights lawyer representing the mosque, questioned whether imams in France remained free to recite Islam’s sacred text. “In France, can an imam still quote the Quran in the mosque where he preaches?” said Chekkat. Chekkat said the authorities based part of their case on imams “quoting...seven passages from the Quran and references to major works of the Islamic tradition, such as The Garden of the Righteous and The Forty Hadiths.” New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The major works in question form part of the body of work of the 13th-century Syrian scholar Imam al-Nawawi, who is widely regarded as one of the Muslim world’s most important thinkers. “We will file an appeal before the Council of State to defend religious freedom, freedom of expression, and the principle of secularism,” he added. The authorities also objected to sermons “evoking ‘hell’ and the ‘punishments of the grave’ reserved for ‘unbelievers’”, despite similar teachings forming part of religious preaching in churches and other places of worship. Eight out of 10 Muslims experience 'widespread' hatred in France, survey says Read More » Judges ruled that the prefect of Seine-Saint-Denis, Julien Charles, “did not commit a serious and manifestly illegal infringement of either the freedom of worship or the freedom of expression”. “We are very disappointed by the decision and very surprised by its content. We will obviously go before the Council of State,” Chekkat told AFP, adding that parts of the ruling went “totally against religious freedom”. “I understand that the administrative judge did not want to contradict the prefect of Seine-Saint-Denis, now I think that before the Council of State we will have a little more chance, it will be a little more legal and a little less political,” he said. The decision follows years of expanding state pressure on Muslim institutions. French authorities closed 22 mosques in 18 months by April 2022, often using intelligence documents whose sources remained hidden. The government has also dissolved Muslim organisations, including the Collective Against Islamophobia in France and the charity BarakaCity, deepening fears that France is using security laws to restrict Muslims’ freedom of belief. headline: 'Used as human bait': Leaked image shows elderly Palestinian men before execution by Israeli forces
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 8 August 2026 11:44 BST | Last update: 1 week 4 days ago
article_body: A newly leaked photograph shows two blindfolded elderly Palestinian men from Beit Lahia in Gaza, hours before Israeli forces killed them in November 2024, according to Palestinian journalist Younis Tirawi, who published the image. The photograph shows Israeli military personnel standing between two blindfolded men, whom Tirawi identified in a post on X as Nadi Marouf and Ali Marouf. He said the photograph was taken hours before their deaths and that the two men were "used as human bait and then executed". In an earlier post in October 2025, Tirawi had said that troops from the 92nd Battalion of the Kfir Brigade abducted the men from Beit Lahia and held them as human shields for several days. "Israeli troops from the 92nd Battalion of the Kfir Brigade abducted two elderly Palestinians from Beit Lahia and used them as human shields for days before killing them," Tirawi wrote. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The Palestine Chronicle reported in October 2025 that the men had been detained for several days before being released near al-Tawam roundabout and shot. The report said that images showed the men stripped to their underwear, with one apparently having his hands tied behind his back. It added that they had been forced to enter buildings before Israeli soldiers went inside. Ramy Abdu, chairman of the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, said at the time: "After being used as human shields, their relatives found them after three days and they had been executed." Israeli soldier says every unit 'keeps a Palestinian as human shield' Read More » The newly shared photograph adds to a series of images and testimonies that have raised allegations about the treatment of Palestinian civilians during Israeli military operations in northern Gaza. Independent reporting has previously documented incidents in which Palestinian civilians were forced to enter buildings and tunnels ahead of Israeli soldiers to check for explosives or fighters. In May 2025, the Israeli army said it was investigating several such cases and acknowledged that using Palestinians as human shields or coercing them into participating in military operations was "strictly prohibited" under its orders. A United Nations investigation into Israeli military conduct in Gaza previously concluded that forcing Palestinian civilians to enter houses ahead of soldiers amounted to the use of human shields and violated international humanitarian law. Wider abuses An Associated Press investigation published in 2025 included testimony from Palestinians who said they had been forced to enter buildings and tunnels ahead of Israeli troops. Israeli soldiers also described the practice as widespread. Al Jazeera subsequently reported on the findings, citing seven Palestinians and two Israeli military officers who described the practice. The developments also come as Palestinian prisoners continue to report harsh detention conditions. Dr Mazen Rantisi, a 71-year-old Palestinian physician known as the "doctor of the poor", was detained during a pre-dawn Israeli raid on his home in Ramallah on 21 June, according to Palestinian and rights organisations. He serves as chairman of the board of the Health Work Committees, a Palestinian organisation that provides medical services. Rantisi told a lawyer that prison authorities had withheld his regular medication during his first 10 days in Ofer Prison and continued to deny him one of his medicines. He also said that prison units repeatedly raided his cell and beat detainees. His lawyer, Saja Misherqi Baransi, said Rantisi had rapidly lost weight after being given small portions of food that he described as unfit for consumption, including mouldy bread, almost-rotten tomatoes, uncooked hummus and foul-smelling rice. Palestinian ‘doctor of the poor’ says he faces abuse, medical neglect in Israeli prison Read More » Belgian rights group Viva Salud said Rantisi and another Health Work Committees official were arrested on June 21 and expressed concern about their health and access to appropriate medical care. Meanwhile, Gaza’s broader humanitarian crisis continues to deepen. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 Palestinian deaths since the war began in October 2023, according to recent reports . The scale of the killings remains difficult to establish fully because thousands of bodies are believed to remain beneath destroyed buildings. A mass funeral in Gaza on 4 August included 112 people killed in a 2023 Israeli air strike whose remains were only recently recovered. Gaza authorities have estimated that thousands more people remain buried beneath rubble. The UN has previously recorded 193 malnutrition-related deaths in Gaza, including 96 children. In July 2025 alone, 11,877 children between six and 59 months who were screened were found to be suffering from acute malnutrition, including 2,562 with severe acute malnutrition. UN agencies have continued to warn that food insecurity and malnutrition remain critical. An analysis cited by the UN humanitarian office projected that more than 100,000 children between 6 and 59 months could suffer acute malnutrition through October 2026, including more than 31,000 severe cases. The continuing allegations over the treatment of civilians, detainees and the dead have added to international scrutiny of Israel's conduct in Gaza, where humanitarian agencies continue to report severe restrictions on access to food, medicine and other essential supplies. headline: India to Israel and back: How a fake IRGC quote on nuclear weapons reached Netanyahu’s speech
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 9 August 2026 16:20 BST | Last update: 1 week 3 days ago
article_body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated an alleged quote attributed to a senior Iranian commander about Tehran's determination to develop nuclear weapons, even though the statement had no identified primary source and was later traced to an Indian pro-Israel account on X. An investigation by Israeli news outlet Ynet and New York Times journalist Ronen Bergman found that Netanyahu used the alleged quote, attributed to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ahmad Vahidi, in an official address to warn Israelis about Iran's nuclear plans. Ynet's investigation traced the source of Netanyahu's remarks to Ritika, an Indian Hindu-nationalist and pro-Israel X account, which posted the alleged quote on 5 August. "There will be no discussion over enriched uranium or nuclear weapons. As long as the United States and Israel possess nuclear weapons, we will continue working on them for our national security. If they disarm, we will disarm," the post attributed to Vahidi said. According to Ynet, the quote began circulating rapidly after it was posted. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters About four and a half hours later, Mossad Commentary, which presents itself as an unofficial account of Israel's intelligence agency on X but has no connection to the Mossad foreign intelligence agency, repeated the claim to its more than 1 million followers. "THERE WILL BE NO FINAL DEAL. The sooner we understand that, the better," the account said, before citing the alleged remarks by Vahidi. The account added: "The regime is not preparing to abandon its nuclear ambitions. It is buying time. There will be no deal." Activists raise alarm over 'flood' of military supplies from India to Israel Read More » Israel’s Channel 14 repeated the alleged Vahidi quote, describing it as the first direct admission by an Iranian official that Tehran was developing a nuclear bomb. It did not provide a primary source for the quotation. Channel 14 News is widely regarded in Israel as a mouthpiece for Netanyahu and his far-right government. A recent report found that the Israeli government had bought millions of shekels worth of commercial airtime from the channel in recent years. Ynet reported that Yair Netanyahu, the prime minister's eldest son, subsequently reposted content from the two Israeli accounts to his near-300,000 followers on X. Yair Netanyahu is one of the most influential figures in the Prime Minister's inner circle, with numerous reports indicating that he and his mother, Sara Netanyahu, are heavily involved in the prime minister’s decision-making. Netanyahu's eldest son is known for promoting far-right politics and false information through his social media accounts, with many of Netanyahu's Likud party members seeking his approval. A record of false claims About two hours later, Netanyahu himself referred to the alleged statement during an official ceremony in Jerusalem. "Today, we heard the commander of the Revolutionary Guards, Vahidi, explicitly declare Iran’s intention to continue developing nuclear weapons - ‘continue’, as he put it," Netanyahu said, according to Ynet's investigation. Narendra Modi: India’s most pro-Israel leader Read More » The alleged quote subsequently spread to the United States. According to Ynet, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations, reposted the Channel 14 report before later deleting it. US conservative commentator Mark Levin also reposted it. Fox News later reported that Vahidi had said Iran would continue working on nuclear weapons as long as the US and Israel possessed them. The outlet subsequently clarified its report, saying the remarks "were previously taken out of context and amplified as comments made this week". The alleged quote continued to circulate in Israeli media, with journalists close to Netanyahu, including Yaakov Bardugo and Avishay Ben Haim, repeating the prime minister’s warning on Israeli television, Ynet reported. The Israeli foreign ministry's Persian-language X account also posted Netanyahu's remarks about Vahidi. About 13 hours after the original post appeared on the Indian X account, Fox News reported on the alleged statement, saying it was "intensifying concerns that Iran is using negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz to postpone concessions on its nuclear program". Two days later, the outlet clarified that Vahidi's remarks "were previously taken out of context and amplified as comments made this week". Two hours after Fox's initial report, Asian News International, a major Indian news outlet, repeated the claim, citing Israeli media reports. Israel's disinformation campaign Vahidi's alleged quote, Ynet said, served Netanyahu to bolster his claim that Iran seeks to develop a nuclear weapon amid reports suggesting that Netanyahu opposes a deal between the US and Iran. In June, Netanyahu told Channel 14 News that "as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons", adding that he saved Israel from "annihilation" twice by claiming Iran possessed atomic bombs. How Israel uses Bollywood to whitewash the occupation Read More » While Ynet could not determine whether Netanyahu or his inner circle directed the circulation of Vahidi's alleged quote, the investigation pointed "to a series of familiar markers of disinformation distribution". It said that Netanyahu had faced similar accusations in the past. In September 2024, Netanyahu’s office allegedly provided the UK-based Jewish Chronicle and Germany-based Bild newspaper with false information claiming that Hamas intended to smuggle Israeli captives through the Rafah area between the Gaza Strip and Egypt to Iran. Two Netanyahu aides are also under investigation over allegations that classified documents were leaked to influence Israeli public opinion about military operations in Rafah. Ynet's investigation said recent reports suggested Israeli influence operations had increasingly targeted audiences outside Israel, including in the US, amid growing criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and Iran from both Democratic and Republican figures. Last month, Iran's embassy in India also accused Indian media of spreading false information about Iran. "Indian media should not compromise the public trust and its professional credibility by disseminating fake and fabricated news," the embassy said , adding that it expected outlets to "avoid participating in external propaganda efforts".
