headline: Syria reclaims control of key coastal sites in deal with Russia
author: Reem Aouir
publication_date: Published date: 10 August 2026 11:19 BST | Last update: 1 week 2 days ago
article_body: Syria and Russia have reached a memorandum of understanding to scale back Moscow's military presence on Syria's Mediterranean coast, ending 18 months of negotiations over the future of the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval facility. The Syrian foreign ministry announced the deal on Sunday, describing it as the outcome of "a year and a half of negotiations and intensive discussions led by the ministry". Under the terms of the agreement, the Syrian state will take over management of civilian facilities at both sites, including Hmeimim airport and Tartus's fourth commercial pier, gradually folding them into civil administration, according to key points of the memorandum shared by the state news agency Sana. The military facilities will be converted into "joint training and qualification centres", under arrangements intended to preserve the interests of both countries. The transition is expected to be completed within three months, according to the ministry. The new arrangements represent a "reorganisation of the Russian presence" along Syria's coast, the ministry added. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations." Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and an accompanying delegation visited Latakia International Airport and Tartus port on Sunday to inspect the facilities covered by what officials described as a "historic" memorandum. The agreement is the latest sign of how Syria's relationship with Russia has changed since the toppling of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Why Syria will not join the fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon Read More » Russia had been one of Assad's most important international backers. Its military intervention in Syria in 2015 helped turn the war decisively in his government's favour, while Tartus and Hmeimim became the centre of Moscow's military presence in the country. Russia had not issued a public response to Sunday's agreement. Tartus has been Russia's central naval facility in the Mediterranean and its only overseas naval base outside the former Soviet Union. The facility has allowed Moscow to resupply naval forces and project military power across the region. Hmeimim, meanwhile, became the main hub for Russian air operations in Syria following Moscow's 2015 intervention. Together, the two facilities provided Russia with a strategic military foothold on the Mediterranean and supported its broader operations in the Middle East. The new arrangement means Moscow will no longer operate the sites in the same way as it did under Assad, but it will not be completely removed from them either. Damascus is using the deal to affirm control over all assets on Syrian territory, framing it as a message that "its national sovereignty is not up for negotiation", Al Jazeera's Damascus correspondent, Obaida Hitto, reported. Trump lavishes praise on 'fantastic' and 'highly respected' Sharaa Read More » President Ahmed al-Sharaa has travelled to Moscow twice since taking power to discuss the bases' fate directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin. These diplomatic efforts come as his government pursues sanctions relief from Washington and closer ties with Paris . The agreement also comes as Damascus seeks to reshape the wider role of Syria's Mediterranean coastline. In July 2025, Damascus signed an $800m, 30-year concession handing Tartus's main commercial port to Dubai's DP World. The company's chief executive, Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem, described Tartus as "an essential hub for trade and exports". Tartus is one of Syria's main gateways to international markets and has become a focus of foreign investment since Assad's fall. Before that, in May 2025, Damascus also renegotiated its contract with French shipping company CMA CGM to run Latakia's container terminal, agreeing a fresh 30-year concession that includes a $265m investment and a new deep-water berth. headline: Iran formalises Strait of Hormuz control as US struggles to sustain war it launched with Israel
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 13:01 BST | Last update: 5 days 12 hours ago
article_body: Iran has taken another step towards formalising its control of the Strait of Hormuz, as the US threatens unprecedented sanctions while struggling to sustain the war it launched alongside Israel . An Iranian parliamentary committee has approved the principles of a strategic plan governing security and development in the strait and the Gulf. Valiullah Bayati, a spokesperson for the parliament’s internal affairs and councils committee, said on Friday that the proposals would now advance for further consideration. “The strategic action plan to ensure the security and progress of the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf was reviewed by the Councils’ Commission and, after hearing the opinions, its general outline was approved,” said Bayati to the Tasnim news agency . The plan would prevent vessels and equipment belonging to the US, Israel and other countries Iran designates as hostile from passing through the waterway. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “This is because these countries have used the Strait of Hormuz to carry out hostile actions against our country, and have committed unjust and aggressive acts against the Iranian people,” Bayati said, Al Jazeera reported . Washington responded with another threat of economic punishment, even as its military remains unable to break Iran’s grip on one of the world’s most important energy corridors. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration would announce new measures against Tehran next week. “Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures that have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” Bessent told Newsmax. “It will be a combination of economic isolation the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports,” he added. An Iranian man walks past an anti-US billboard at Enghelab Square in central Tehran on 3 August 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP) Tehran, meanwhile, continues seeking alternatives to US-controlled financial institutions. The governor of Iran's Central Bank, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said Iran would soon join the Brics-backed New Development Bank, although the lender has not confirmed its accession. Struggling US war effort Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said its forces continue to decide which ships can use the waterway. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. Our control over movements is complete and decisive,” Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei told Tasnim news agency on Friday. “No movement in this strait escapes the eyes of the IRGC Navy fighters,” he said, adding that “the reality should be seen in the field, not in the communiques and statements of US officials”. Shipping data supports Tehran’s assertion that traffic remains severely restricted. Maritime analytics company Kpler recorded nine commodity vessels passing through Hormuz on Thursday, up from five on Wednesday but still below August’s daily average of 12. Iran attacks US failures as scepticism grows over Israeli role in Trump 'assassination plot' Read More » Five ships entered the Gulf and four sailed towards the Gulf of Oman , with most using the Iranian shipping channel. The data excludes vessels operating with their tracking equipment switched off. Oil markets reacted to Washington’s threat to maintain its naval blockade indefinitely. Brent crude climbed above $88 a barrel on Friday, while West Texas Intermediate rose beyond $82. The US is also sending the USS George Washington towards the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose crew has spent more than 260 days at sea. The deployment would leave the Pacific without a US aircraft carrier for an undetermined period, exposing the widening military cost of Washington’s Iran campaign. Families and lawmakers have raised the alarm about shortages, unsanitary conditions and deteriorating mental health aboard the Lincoln. California Representative Mike Levin and three other lawmakers demanded an explanation from the Pentagon, saying that “the plans in the works to relieve the USS Lincoln are not enough”. The US Central Command (Centcom) has rejected reports that sailors have died aboard the carrier, saying that “the Sailors and Marines of the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea”. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, or the “Secretary of War”, as he likes to be called, dismissed reports of worsening conditions as “completely misrepresented”. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer demanded Hegseth’s dismissal. “When Pete Hegseth was nominated, everyone knew he was completely incompetent. Now our brave sailors are paying the price in a horrific and unfathomable way,” he said. “Pete Hegseth must be fired immediately,” Schumer added. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Families of Egyptian political prisoners launch UK advocacy group
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 12:19 BST | Last update: 6 days 12 hours ago
article_body: A new organisation was launched in London on Thursday to represent the families of political detainees held in Egypt , according to a statement shared with Middle East Eye. The Families of Egyptian Detainees Association (Feda) said it will liaise with institutions and authorities both inside and outside Egypt, in the hope of helping secure the release of political detainees. It said it would “work with anyone who can contribute to closing this painful chapter and securing the release of political detainees from prison”. Since 2013, when Abdel Fatah el-Sisi led a military coup which deposed Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, there has been a huge increase in political detentions. Rights groups estimate that over 60,000 prisoners of conscience are held in Egyptian jails, of whom over 1,000 are women. Many of them are students, youths and activists from across the Egyptian political spectrum. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters According to the Arabic Network for Human Rights Information , the total number of prisoners in Egypt in March 2021 was 120,000, with an estimated 65,000 political prisoners, at least 26,000 of whom were being held in pre-trial detention. Many, including former President Morsi and several opposition figures, have died of medical neglect and other inhumane prison conditions, according to documentation by multiple rights groups. Feda said it would work to represent families of detainees, wherever they are in the world. “[We aim] to keep the issue of detainees at the forefront of national and international attention, advocate for Egyptian detainees in national and international forums, work tirelessly to ensure fair trials and humane conditions of detention, and pursue their release through all available means,” it said. The association will engage international institutions, religious and political leaders, the media, and human rights groups. It also said it would “organise visits to the United Nations and its various bodies concerned with detainees and victims of enforced disappearance, pursue legal action before competent courts over violations suffered by detainees, and organise public events in solidarity with them”. Egypt prison deaths a 'warning sign' as conditions deteriorate sharply Read More » Rights groups have long documented violations faced by Egyptian detainees, including inadequate medical care, poor nutrition and ventilation, denial of family visits, overcrowded cells, denial of access to books and newspapers and denial of exercise. In September 2021, Cairo launched a national human rights strategy, in which provisions were set out concerning prisoners’ rights. The framework included goals for humane treatment, protection from torture and abuse, judicial oversight of prisons, and inspections of conditions by the national council for human rights. The strategy also touched on the government seeking to reduce prison numbers through periodic releases of detainees, including conditional releases, as well as presidential pardons on national occasions and holidays, and the release of detainees suffering from illnesses. “Detainees and their families had hoped that this strategy would be implemented, but they say they have yet to see its impact inside prisons,” Feda said. “They continue to await the implementation of the strategy and the legislative amendments that followed it as a step toward closing this dark chapter.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Balochistan’s dangerous fuel trade is a lifeline. The Iran war is choking it
author: Hazaran Changeez Nazir
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 17:48 BST | Last update: 6 days 7 hours ago
article_body: About 150 kilometres west of Gwadar, the port city often described as the heart of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), lies Kuntani Hor, a small creek near the Iranian border on Balochistan’s remote and picturesque Makran coast. The creek is one of the spots along the border where "informal" trade between Iran and Pakistan takes place, with boats bringing Iranian petrol, diesel and other goods into Pakistan. The trade is, for all intents and purposes, smuggling. But it has become so foundational to the local economy that, in April of this year, Balochistan’s provincial government even set the price per litre at which fuel from this trade could be sold. The policy set a price below that of government-imported fuel and outlawed it from being sold outside the province. When the trade is active, thousands of labourers, drivers, boat crews, and depot workers from Balochistan and other parts of Pakistan depend on Kuntani for their livelihoods. Workers, boats, and vehicles gather at Kuntani Hor, one of the sides of the creek where Iranian fuel is unloaded into Pakistan’s informal network (Hazaran/Changeez Nazir/MEE) New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters It was into this economy that Siraj, a 26-year-old anthropology graduate from Panjgur, came looking for stable income that his university degree failed to provide. Siraj had twice returned to his hometown of Paroom with less than he had hoped for. The first time, arriving with a degree in anthropology from Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad. Reaching one of Pakistan’s leading universities meant travelling hundreds of kilometres from his remote hometown in Panjgur district, near the Iranian border. He believed the degree would lead to stable work. But that turned out to be false hope. Then, after his father died, he could no longer afford to wait for government vacancies that attract thousands of applicants per position. So he decided to travel south to Kuntani Hor, near Jiwani on Pakistan’s southwestern coast. The second time Siraj returned to Paroom, he carried neither the promise of a degree nor the wages on which his family had come to depend. The US-Israeli war on Iran had sharply disrupted the movement of fuel, bringing much of the work at Kuntani Hor to a standstill. 'Every day was another chance to earn, but also another chance to die' - Mohammad Asif, worker in the informal fuel trade The war began on 28 February, when Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, opening another full-scale confrontation after the 12-day Israel-Iran war of June 2025. Iran retaliated with strikes on Israel and US military installations across the region, most prominently in the Gulf states. The fighting subsequently reached Iranian ports, coastal defences and shipping routes around the Strait of Hormuz. By July, thousands of people had been killed and millions displaced , mainly in Iran and Lebanon . Along Pakistan’s not-so-distant coast, the war arrived not through an air strike but through the disappearance of this informal coastal economy. Although formal trade continued through some Pakistan-Iran crossings during the early weeks of the conflict, supplies of Iranian petrol and diesel fell. In May, fuel dealers said the border closure at Kuntani Hor had pushed the price of Iranian petrol in Gwadar up by 30 to 40 Pakistani rupees (11-14 cents) a litre. For Siraj and thousands of others, the consequences were immediate and dire. An economy built around fuel Bakshi Baloch, from the coastal town of Pasni, runs a fuel depot at Kuntani Hor. Under normal circumstances, he said, around 50 people depend directly on his operation. These include an accountant, labourers who unload the fuel, boat crews, and others who move the barrels between the shore and the depot. Bakshi estimated that more than 5,000 depots had operated around Kuntani Hor, each supporting dozens of people. The figure could not be independently verified by Middle East Eye, but the rows of depots and the variety of workers involved reveal an economy that extends far beyond a few boat owners or fuel dealers. Workers stand beside pickups loaded with fuel containers at Kuntani Hor, while rows of motorcycle transporters gather in the distance (Hazaran/Changeez Nazir/MEE) Bakshi, too, has now returned home. Almost every day, he said he gets voice notes from former workers asking the same question. "When will the depot reopen?" He has no answer. “They ask me about the work, but what can I tell them?” he told MEE. His workers came from different corners of Pakistan. Some boat crews came from neighbouring Sindh province. Among the labourers unloading petrol and diesel were men who came from much further north, like Dera Ghazi Khan in southwestern Punjab, and even as far as Kashmir. They arrived speaking different languages and unfamiliar with the culture of the Makran coast. What brought them together was the absence of viable work closer to home. Now they have scattered again, carrying the effects of a Middle Eastern war back to their families and communities across Pakistan. Mohammad Asif from Punjab was one of them. Speaking by phone after returning to Dera Ghazi Khan, Asif described the work at Kuntani Hor as both his means of survival and a daily encounter with death. The labourers handled large amounts of highly flammable fuel in extreme heat, without protective equipment, fire services or emergency medical facilities. “Every day was another chance to earn, but also another chance to die,” Asif said. Motorcycle fuel transporters cross the sandy desert stretch near Kuntani Hor, dragging their feet to steady bikes loaded heavily with flammable fuel (Supplied to MEE) On a busy day, he said he could make as much as 10,000 rupees ($36) - income difficult to find in his hometown and high enough to take the risks involved. On average, unskilled labour in Pakistan will net a worker anywhere from 1,400-1,500 rupees per day ($5). Since returning home, Asif has called former colleagues and searched for news of the conflict, trying to learn whether the fuel boats might begin moving again. A dangerous livelihood, and the only one At first sight, Kuntani Hor appears to be little more than a muddy creek surrounded by barren land. But when the trade is functioning, its shoreline is bustling with labourers, boat crews, motorcycle riders, drivers, and depot workers. “When your family’s bread depends on this work, you have to do it, no matter the risk,” said Sakhi Baksh, a labourer known locally as an "ammaal". 'People lose their lives, but we still have to earn. For us, it is better to risk death here than to die of hunger' - Noroz, worker in the informal fuel trade Sakhi and other ammaal wait at the shoreline for vessels carrying fuel from Iran. When a boat arrives, they lift barrels holding around 70 litres and carry them 20 to 30 metres through thick mud to the nearby depots. Their feet can sink almost a foot beneath the surface. With a heavy barrel balanced on their shoulder, a labourer must pull each leg free before taking another step. Sometimes a worker's feet sink deeper, tripping them and causing them to drop the load. The drum may rupture, spilling petrol or diesel over the mud and exposing everyone nearby to a fire risk. Yet Sakhi said the labourer can still be blamed for the loss and have the cost deducted from his wages. Once the barrels leave the shore, motorcycle riders known locally as "cycali" carry the fuel towards depots further inland. Workers said thousands of such riders once operated around Kuntani Hor. Their motorcycles are fitted with four to five drums, creating a load that is both unstable and highly combustible. Part of the journey passes through deep sand, where riders must use their feet to push and steady the motorcycles beneath the desert sun. Noroz, one of the cycali, said the exhaust pipe can become dangerously hot. A small leak from one of the containers can ignite the entire load. A motorcycle fuel transporter, known locally as a cycali, pulls his loaded bike, carrying two barrels of fuel, out of the muddy shoreline at Kuntani Hor (Hazaran/Changeez Nazir/MEE) He recalled several fires in which riders were injured or killed. “When I load the fuel, I don’t know whether I will make it to the end of the journey,” Noroz said. A motorcycle fuel transporter lies beside his fallen bike after getting stuck in deep sand along a desert stretch near Kuntani Hor (Photo supplied to MEE) A successful journey could earn him as much as 15,000 rupees ($54), he said. Noroz himself suffered burns in an accident but returned to work after recovering because he had no reliable alternative. “Death is normal at Kuntani,” he said. “Sometimes a boat catches fire ; sometimes it is one of us on a motorcycle. In summer, the waves become rough, and boats can sink. “People lose their lives, but we still have to earn. For us, it is better to risk death here than to die of hunger.” A war reaches the coast The danger does not end with fire, rough seas or overloaded motorcycles. 'It felt as though the war on Iran had also become a war on our economy' - Rahim Baksh, worker in the informal fuel trade Several workers, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Pakistan’s Coast Guard personnel of periodically entering restricted areas around the creek, dispersing the cycali and clearing the site by force. Kuntani Hor has also been repeatedly closed because of militant attacks and security concerns in Balochistan, where the Pakistani state has fought a decades-long separatist insurgency. Gwadar-based journalist and author Javed MB said the Iranian fuel trade had operated along the Makuran Coast for decades. Once spread across several coastal points, much of it has become concentrated at Kuntani Hor during the past decade. Previous closures generally lasted days or weeks. Workers waited, borrowed money or returned home temporarily, knowing the trade would eventually resume. The latest disruption has been different. The war in Iran has made fuel supplies less reliable, increased purchasing and transportation costs, and reduced the number of profitable journeys. Traders say business has not disappeared completely, but it is operating at only a fraction of its former scale. “All the profit that depot owners and workers expected to earn has disappeared,” said Nawab Shah, a Karachi resident who works as an accountant. “No one knows when the work will begin again.” Rahim Baksh once used his boat for fishing off Gwadar. He later moved it to Kuntani Hor because carrying fuel offered better earnings than the increasingly uncertain fishing industry. When the US and Israeli attacks began, he said, confusion spread quickly through the border economy. Communities in Balochistan depend on Iran for more than petrol and diesel. Food and other everyday goods pass through formal and informal cross-border routes. When supplies slowed, Rahim said, prices rose throughout the region. “It felt as though the war on Iran had also become a war on our economy,” he said. Only a small number of boats now continue to transport fuel, according to Rahim. Fuel has become harder and more expensive to obtain, the journeys are less predictable, and profit margins have narrowed. Beyond the shoreline, the disruption moves through every stage of the supply chain. Trucks and pickups normally transport the drums from Kuntani Hor to Gwadar, Turbat, Panjgur, Mastung, Quetta, and other parts of Balochistan. Traders say some fuel travels further inland towards Punjab. When boats stop arriving, labourers lose their wages. The cycali h ave nothing to carry. Drivers have no loads, depots stand empty and small fuel sellers lose their supplies. A 2021 study of the Jiwani-Iran border found that the local economy depended heavily on informal trade in diesel, petrol, gas, food, and other Iranian goods. Rather than existing outside the economy, the trade had effectively become one of its foundations. The contradiction is central to Kuntani Hor: the authorities treat the activity as smuggling, but it is also one of the few viable forms of employment. Sahar Baloch, a Berlin-based journalist who has reported extensively on Balochistan, said the immediate shock of the US-Israeli war on Iran was felt not merely in disrupted trade, but in the sudden loss of livelihoods across the region. “Thousands of people in Gwadar, Kech, Panjgur and Washuk depend directly or indirectly on cross-border trade,” she said. “While fuel receives the most attention, the border economy also revolves around food, household goods, construction materials, spare parts, and transport services.” When movement across the border was disrupted by the conflict, she said, daily-wage labourers, loaders, drivers, shopkeepers, and small traders all lost income at the same time. “The issue is not only that the trade stopped,” Sahar said. “It is also that the state has failed to create alternative employment opportunities in Makuran.” Workers rest on a hillside as pick-ups line the rough coastal track leading from Kuntani Hor to transport Iranian fuel to depots and other areas across Balochistan (Hazaran/Changeez Nazir/MEE) Fishing, traditionally one of the region’s principal livelihoods, is already under pressure and increasingly controlled by powerful commercial interests, she said, while agriculture is constrained by chronic water scarcity. In the absence of viable alternatives, cross-border trade has become one of the few ways thousands of families can generate an income. Sahar said the impact also extended far beyond communities immediately bordering Iran. Fuel and other goods are moved from the border into cities across Balochistan and onwards to other parts of Pakistan. When supplies were interrupted, transport costs increased, businesses faced uncertainty, and people working throughout the distribution chain temporarily lost their livelihoods. “For many families, the informal cross-border economy functions as a form of social protection in the absence of state support,” she said. “The war has made that vulnerability even more visible.” She added that repeated interruptions also carry political consequences in a province already grappling with unemployment, inflation and declining purchasing power. “Every closure increases frustration among people who already feel economically marginalised,” Sahar said. “When the government neither provides employment alternatives nor sufficient support, it deepens distrust between communities and the state.” An ocean, but no water “There is an ocean in front of me, but not a drop of water I can use,” said Gwahram, a boat operator from Pishukan. At Kuntani Hor, there is no reliable supply of drinking water, no sanitation or toilets, and little shelter from the sun. Workers spend their days and nights beneath the open sky. The sea surrounding them offers no relief. Along parts of the shoreline, it is contaminated by spilt petrol and diesel. Gwahram said workers cannot use it even to wash their hands and feet. Every container of fresh water must be transported to the site and purchased. Gwahram estimated that water and other basic necessities can consume nearly half of some workers’ earnings. Boats loaded with plastic fuel containers rest along the muddy shoreline at Kuntani Hor (Hazaran/Changeez Nazir/MEE) Even that precarious income has now diminished. Gwahram claimed that only about 100 of the thousands of depots that once operated at Kuntani Hor were still active. Most of the workers had returned to their hometowns. “Life here is lived in the name of Allah,” he said. “We work under the open sky. We rest under the open sky and we sleep under the open sky. There is nothing else.” Back in Paroom, Siraj is waiting again - not for employment suited to his anthropology degree, but for word that the boats have returned. The war did not create the economic fragility surrounding Kuntani Hor; it merely exposed it. In a region beset by poverty, underinvestment and a shortage of formal employment, an illegal and potentially fatal trade has been left to perform the function of a labour market. Thousands of people across Pakistan accept the risk because neither the state nor the formal economy offers them a dependable alternative. For these workers, war is not measured only through missile strikes, military statements or negotiations over distant waterways. It is measured through empty depots, unanswered voice notes, rising fuel prices, and wages that disappear without warning. Even if the boats return, Siraj, Asif, Sakhi, and Noroz will not be returning to safety. They will return to mud, leaking petrol, overloaded motorcycles, contaminated water and nights spent beneath the open sky. At Kuntani Hor, the only thing more dangerous than the work is being left without it. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. subheadline: The war is wreaking havoc on the illicit, yet vital, trade of importing fuel from Iran into Pakistan's Balochistan province

headline: Iranian press review: Tehran says it will no longer wait to be attacked
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 13:28 BST | Last update: 6 days 12 hours ago
article_body: Shift to offensive military doctrine in rhetoric Iranian military commanders and politicians have recently underlined a shift in Iran 's military doctrine, moving from a defensive to an offensive strategy against US forces in the Middle East. The shift came with new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointing six military commanders to replace those killed by Israel and the US during the recent war. While some figures had previously mentioned this change in military doctrine, the new appointments have made the topic prominent in local media. On Wednesday, Brigadier General Alireza Sheikh, the deputy commander of the army, explained this new approach towards US forces to the media. He pointed to recent attacks on the bases of Kurdish opposition groups as an example of this strategy. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Trump's political bluffs aim to distract public opinion and disrupt our analysis," Sheikh said. "However, logical thinkers see that Iran can respond proportionally and even act pre-emptively. This shows our doctrine is shifting from purely defensive to deterrence and active action." Previously, Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to the parliament speaker, outlined the new military approach, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' attack on US bases in Jordan on 29 July as an example. The attack came without any preceding US strikes against Iran. "Iran no longer fights the enemy as it did in the past," Mohammadi said regarding the attack. "Launching surprise, fast attacks and targeting sensitive points are part of the country's new war strategy." Mohammadi also dismissed the idea of an unwritten ceasefire between Iran and the US, which some believed was tied to ongoing talks in Oman regarding the management of the Strait of Hormuz. "Over the past week, an impression had formed that due to the ongoing negotiations between Iran and Oman, Iran would not act against the US unless directly fired upon," Mohammadi added. "However, realities on the ground showed this calculation was completely wrong." Pressure mounts to weaponise Strait of Hormuz Ongoing talks between Iran and Oman to create a mechanism for controlling the Strait of Hormuz come amid rising pressure from conservative and ultraconservative groups inside Iran who want to maximise the use of the strait as a new weapon against the US and its allies. On Tuesday, Alireza Zakani, the principlist mayor of Tehran and a former Revolutionary Guard member, emphasised the need to halt any talks with the US, saying that Tehran must use its control over the Strait of Hormuz to advance its policies against Washington and its Arab and European allies. Iran's new Security Council shake-up reveals growing divisions over US deal Read More » "If America wants to benefit from the Strait of Hormuz, it must pay us compensation. If Qatar wants to use this strait, it must release our frozen funds. Hardening access to this vital route will make Europe no longer dare to sanction Iran," Zakani said. The pro-conservative Resalat daily also published a report, headlined “The drawn sword of Hormuz in Iran’s hand”, highlighting conservative demands that the Strait of Hormuz not be returned to the conditions that prevailed before the US and Israeli attacks. According to the daily, closing the strait was a response "proportional to the repeated military aggression of America and the Zionist regime, and the naval blockade imposed on Iran following it". Resalat concluded by stressing the importance of maintaining Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz: "This drawn sword must always remain in Iran's hands so that peace and security are guaranteed not through begging, but through power." 'Echoes' of days before end of Iran-Iraq war Majid Tafreshi, a political analyst and researcher of contemporary historical documents, compared Iran's current political situation to July 1988, when the country accepted UN Resolution 598 to end the war with Iraq . In 1980, Iraq, led by Saddam Hussein and backed by western military and intelligence support, invaded Iran and occupied parts of its oil-rich provinces. Iran, under the leadership of its first Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini, accepted the resolution in 1988. Inside the growing rift between Iran’s dealmakers and ultraconservatives Read More » Making this comparison, Tafreshi criticised political factions that want to continue the war with the US under current conditions. He noted that a similar approach existed during the Iran-Iraq war. He also examined the record of Qassem Soleimani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, who was assassinated in a US strike in Baghdad in 2020. Tafreshi said that portraying Soleimani as someone who only engaged in military conflict contradicts his actual political history. "Even Qassem Soleimani believed in dialogue and negotiation. He was a man of diplomacy and took up arms when necessary. However, some people turned him into a Rambo, Zorro, or Spider-Man figure who only solved problems through war," he added. Economic hardships hit ordinary people While various political factions inside the country debate how to confront the US and Israel and end the "neither war nor peace" situation, the Sazandegi daily has reported rising economic pressure on ordinary people due to the US naval blockade. According to the report , activities at Shahid Rajaee port, one of the main marine import and export terminals, have dropped sharply in recent weeks and the port is "emptier than ever". The daily predicted that the impact of the naval blockade would soon become visible as store shelves ran out of essential goods. Sazandegi also noted that, despite Iran’s extensive access to land borders with neighbouring countries, overland transport is far more costly and time-consuming than shipping by sea. The difference, it said, would further harm the livelihoods of people. The report concluded: "Store shelves are the last place where a supply crisis becomes visible. The first sign must be sought much further away. Somewhere by the sea among cranes, ships, and containers, where, if they do not arrive today, their absence may be seen on people's dinner tables a few months later." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . subheadline: Meanwhile, conservatives demand full control over Hormuz, researcher compares current situation to final days of Iran-Iraq war, and concerns grow over US naval blockade

headline: From autonomy to 'settler colonialism': How India redrew Kashmir's demographic and political landscape
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 9 August 2026 11:02 BST | Last update: 1 week 3 days ago
article_body: Seven years after India revoked the special constitutional status of Indian-administered Kashmir , changes to land ownership, residency laws and governance have continued to reshape the region, which critics have called a part of a multi-pronged strategy to alter Kashmir's demographic and political landscape. On 5 August 2019, India's ruling right-wing nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government revoked Article 370 and Article 35A, which granted Jammu and Kashmir autonomy and constitutional safeguards. What followed was a legal onslaught for a broader restructuring of the contested region, parts of which are held by India, Pakistan and China. As the government of India unilaterally divided the region into multiple Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, it placed the region under direct rule of New Delhi's union government. The Modi-led government in New Delhi said the move was aimed at integrating Kashmir more closely with India, encouraging investment and development, and curbing militancy. However, within months, New Delhi introduced new domicile rules allowing anyone who had lived in the region for 15 years, studied there for seven years or served in certain central government positions to obtain domicile status. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Subsequent amendments also eased restrictions on land purchases. Government figures presented in the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly showed that more than 1.25 million domicile certificates had been issued within two years, including 83,742 to people who had not previously qualified as permanent residents. Residents say that the moves have led to massive disenfranchisement of the native populations, as outsiders have been given free access to the region's resources. 'Erasing historical facts': India orders massive crackdown on books in Kashmir's libraries Read More » "I think what has changed in these seven years is the visible presence of inequality," said Jan, 35, a resident who requested that only her first name be used. "I don't recall Kashmir being so economically unequal before. When you see the much-hyped city centre of Lal Chowk, for example, you get a small glimpse of a colourful metropolis. But the moment you step into the next-door neighbourhood of Maisuma and walk into the lanes of the old city, you encounter real Kashmir: waterlogged roads, people driving rickshaws for a living, stray dogs outnumbering humans and more." She said the changes had become more apparent since 2019. "Before, we had laws that prevented a single person from acquiring land that was more than 12 acres. That kept Kashmir anchored into a socialist character. No one was allowed to build so much as a small hut in agricultural land. Now, it is free for all," she says. "Indian construction firms can tear past our rice fields and apple orchards to construct railway lines and expressways that are completely defacing the Kashmir that we knew as children," she adds. "This infrastructure is meant to serve its military more than it serves us. The poorer lot are especially more defenceless against the onslaught of 'new Kashmir' and the sweeping changes it represents. We are simply getting estranged from our own land." What was Article 370? Article 370 of the Indian constitution was one of the provisions of the pact reached when Kashmir acceded to India following the country's division in 1949. For 70 years, it served as the constitutional connection between the Muslim-majority region and the Union of India. The law barred non-Kashmiris from owning land as a measure to protect the region 's delicate ecology and resources, while regulating jobs, ensuring local employment and providing constitutional guarantees for limited political decision-making. Kashmiris call India's rule settler-colonialism - and we should listen to them Read More » The article operated in conjunction with Article 35A, a legal provision that gives the state assembly of Kashmir the authority to determine who are the “permanent residents” and to prevent outsiders from permanently settling in the region. In 2019, the BJP government unilaterally repealed Article 370, split the region and converted it into two federally governed Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. A new domicile law announced in March 2020 declared anyone who had lived in the area for 15 years, studied there for seven years or worked for the central government in the region eligible for domicile status. In October 2020, another notification rendered even this condition irrelevant for non-agricultural land. Within two years, more than 1.25 million domicile certificates had been issued across the region. According to figures provided by the government to the assembly, more than 83,000 were issued to people who had not previously been state subjects. The authorities in the region say that a domicile certificate was, "for applying for jobs" and did not itself confer land rights or voting rights. The land law changes meant a domicile certificate was not even required to buy most property in the first place. “Since the abrogation of Article 370, land has remained a central point of political and public debate in Kashmir,” said Abu Bakr, 42, a resident of Srinagar, the region's main city. Bakr, who runs a private business and closely follows the region’s politics, said another major government initiative involved opening up land to businesses across the region. "Disempowerment is part of the broader history of imperial control in Kashmir" - Muhammad Junaid, professor “To facilitate investment and improve the ease of doing business, the policy allowed investors greater access to land. Subsequently, the government introduced a series of policy changes affecting land, agriculture, and forest laws,” he said, adding that these steps, presented as reforms, also altered the legal status of many people living in or near forest areas. “In several cases, land occupied by such residents was classified as encroachment, leading to eviction drives. There are many examples of it,” he said. Bakr added that the government's programme to distribute land to homeless families had further reignited the contentious debate over "demographic change", a concern that has shaped Kashmiri political discourse. Restructuring control Prime Minister Narendra Modi defended the abrogation, calling it a historical rectification long overdue. His BJP party in New Delhi said it would help rid the region of a corrupt local political elite, curb militancy, and bring development and private investment, boosting the local economy. India's Kashmir railway is an engineering feat - and an occupation project Read More » In February 2021, a panel of UN special rapporteurs said the revised residency rules had been introduced "without the consultation of the local population", warning that the fast-tracking of domicile certificates for outsiders risked "deteriorating the overall human rights situation of native residents". Ather Zia, a political anthropologist, said the changes should be understood as part of a broader political process. "In my work, I describe this as the iterative temporal dynamic of settler colonialism, where successive changes over a period of time reinforce one another, and cumulatively they are focused on restructuring control over land, political representation, and Indigenous sovereignty, as we see that is what has unfolded," she said. "Settler colonialism as an analytical framework helps explain how changes in legal restructuring, policies of land expropriation, demographic engineering, increasing militarisation, and massive overhaul in how the region is governed illustrate an evolving structure rather than disconnected policies." She added that the cumulative effect had been "extremely transformative for everyday life". "There is heightened uncertainty and deep fear over land; political representation has diminished; journalism, activism, and civil society activity are curbed." Political map redrawn Alongside land reforms, New Delhi redrew electoral boundaries for the first time since 1995. The Delimitation Commission increased the number of assembly seats from 83 to 90, allocating five of the six additional constituencies to the Hindu-majority Jammu region and only one to the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley. The commission also merged geographically disconnected areas across mountain ranges into single parliamentary constituencies, a restructuring designed to artificially shift political power towards New Delhi's allies. While a local assembly election eventually led to the formation of an elected state government, the newly formed administration remains severely hamstrung, stripped of statehood and lacking primary legislative and administrative powers, which are handled by New Delhi. How India is implementing the 'Israel model' in Kashmir Read More » Far from delivering the promised economic surge or an end to insurgency, the situation remains volatile. In May 2025, suspected militants opened fire in Pahalgam’s Baisaran Valley, killing 26 tourists in one of the deadliest civilian attacks in years. Last month, a police official was shot dead on security duty in Anantnag's Lal Chowk. The killing was followed by a crackdown that led to the detention of over 3,500 people across the region. “We are plagued by high rates of unemployment among youth; they are going towards drugs,” said Muhammad Amin, 55, a resident. The unemployment in Kashmir still stands at about 6.7 percent, roughly double the rate in India. There has also been a systematic attempt by the government to oppress intellectuals through censorship even in school books. ‘Total political disempowerment’ While New Delhi maintains the constitutional changes have improved governance, investment and integration, critics argue they have fundamentally altered Kashmir's political, legal and demographic landscape. Seven years after Article 370 was repealed, those competing narratives continue to define the debate over the region's future. Muhammad Junaid, who teaches at Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts, told Middle East Eye that the post-2019 changes were designed as a strategy aimed at the total political disempowerment of Kashmiris as a people. “To bring Kashmir to a level where people of Kashmir would be compelled to demand (or not even demand at all) things that had already once existed rather than seek their historical political rights as a people," he said. "This disempowerment is part of the broader history of imperial control in Kashmir." Junaid said that the history of such a process "in other places and times tells us that the situation in Kashmir resembles many aspects of settler colonialism". "The impacts of the 2019 events are gradually unfolding… as people are being governed by imperial bureaucrats as imperial wards with no say in their own administration," Junaid said. headline: Turkey backs Saudi-led maritime defence coalition in Red Sea
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 11:12 BST | Last update: 6 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Turkey confirmed on Thursday for the first time that it had joined efforts to establish a multinational maritime defence coalition aimed at ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea. The announcement signals increased cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Ankara after the signing of a trilateral pact between the states and Pakistan in Mecca last week. “At the invitation of Saudi Arabia, a technical meeting was held in Riyadh on 28 July to ensure freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, followed by a meeting of the chiefs of general staff on 30 July 2026,” the Turkish Ministry of National Defence said in a statement. The ministry added that Turkey was participating in another coordination meeting on the establishment of the maritime defence coalition in Jeddah on Thursday. “Work continues with the Saudi Arabian authorities to reduce tensions in the Gulf region and ensure the uninterrupted flow of international trade,” the statement said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a defence pact last week committing the three countries to each other’s security, including collective security obligations. Several Ankara-based sources who spoke to Middle East Eye said they believed the Red Sea coalition would be the first area in which the alliance between Turkey and Saudi Arabia would deepen. Saudi Arabia announced last month that it had established a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea. The move followed the Houthis’ declaration on 20 July that they had imposed a maritime blockade on the kingdom, disrupting oil shipments diverted to the Red Sea following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The alliance reportedly includes Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, Bahrain , Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt , Jordan , Kuwait , Qatar , Somalia and Yemen . It will be headquartered in Riyadh. headline: 'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance
author: Sean Mathews
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 22:13 BST | Last update: 6 days 2 hours ago
article_body: This summer, a senior UAE diplomat, Lanna Nusseibeh, held consultations with a US ally in Europe. The meeting was unremarkable but informative because of the impression the European country's officials walked away with. “The UAE is totally aligned with Israel. It’s crystal clear that the partnership has no limits,” a European official who was in the meeting told Middle East Eye. That clarity contrasts with the questions swirling in corridors of power - from the US to Asia - about the Mecca Agreement, which unites Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan under a mutual defence pact that many see as rivalling the UAE-Israel partnership . Western and Arab officials are still trying to decipher just how aligned Saudi Arabia , Pakistan and Turkey are, let alone whether they can back each other up in a hot conflict. For example, no sooner had the ink on the Mecca pact dried than the Houthis in Yemen attacked Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery. Pakistan and Turkey did not come to Riyadh’s defence against the Iran-aligned group. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In contrast, when the UAE came under attack from Iranian drones and missiles earlier this year, Israel dispatched Iron Dome air defence batteries to the Gulf state. Abu Dhabi also joined Israel in launching hundreds of strikes on Iran. “Israel did the UAE a big solid during the war. Abu Dhabi is not going to forget that,” a US official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity. But there are key differences between the two blocs. Despite the UAE and Israel’s military cooperation, their relations are still kept behind closed doors. "At first glance, the UAE-Israel bloc delivers more tangible gains for both parties, but the Mecca pact may ultimately resonate more broadly and less transactionally,” Theodore Singer, a former US intelligence officer, told Middle East Eye. 'The Mecca club can be expanded' When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that he visited the UAE at the height of the war on Iran, Abu Dhabi moved to deny the official statement. To many, that awkward diplomacy underscored just how unpopular the alliance remains outside Israeli and American circles. 'The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it” - Ayham Kamel, geopolitical analyst In contrast, the Mecca pact was celebrated in public. It was announced that Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan joined together for Friday prayer in the holiest city in Islam. The UAE and Israel have cooperated for decades. Their ties were given a public cloak in 2020 when Abu Dhabi officially recognised Israel under the Abraham Accords brokered by the US. They are united by their animosity towards Iran on one side and the Muslim Brotherhood on the other. Abu Dhabi’s escalating rivalry with Saudi Arabia, which has refused to recognise Israel, could give the two another point of agreement. The Abraham Accords have also solidified support in Washington for the UAE’s ruling Al-Nahyan family, even as the Emirates has hedged against the US with countries like China. But some analysts say the alliance between the UAE and Israel lacks depth. In some ways, the Mecca pact is its foil. “The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it,” Ayham Kamel, a geopolitical advisor on the Middle East, told MEE, referring to the Abraham Accords. “The Mecca pact’s foundation is military, but it carries a lot of political meaning,” Kamel added, noting the agreement’s supposed foundation on a Nato-like Article 5 defence commitment. A lack of strategic depth is actually a physical reality for Israel and the UAE. The latter is expanding a military base in Somaliland that some officials in the Horn of Africa tell MEE could be used by Israel, but Somaliland is recognised only by Israel. Israel enjoys especially close ties with Greece . Both Israel and the UAE have growing military and economic ties with India and Ethiopia. But there are only one million Emirati nationals and 10.2 million Israelis. Few of their neighbours want to partner with Israel. Distrust of Israel has only grown in the wider Muslim world as a result of Israel's war on Gaza, which the United Nations and dozens of human rights groups have deemed a genocide . “The UAE-Israeli cooperation is more agile and gets things done. The Mecca pact is going to move slowly and take time, but it has a public support base,” Kamel told MEE. “And the club can be expanded”. On paper, at least, the Mecca pact is formidable. 'Different threat perceptions' Turkey boasts the second-largest army in Nato, Saudi Arabia is the Arab world’s only G-20 economy, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim country. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have effectively been allies for decades. The kingdom provided financial support to Islamabad as it was acquiring a nuclear weapon. Pakistani pilots and officers have long filled the ranks of the kingdom’s military. In return, the Gulf state has provided a financial lifeline to Islamabad. But the two face different threats. UAE and Israel established fund for joint defence acquisition, sources say Read More » Saudi Arabia generally sees Iran as a more serious threat. In 2015, Saudi Arabia allied with the UAE to fight against the Houthis in Yemen. Pakistan decided against military involvement. Its more cordial ties to Tehran have positioned it as a mediator. Meanwhile, until a few years ago, Turkey and Saudi Arabia were at loggerheads over the Muslim Brotherhood. In Egypt, Saudi Arabia backed Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who came to power in a coup that overthrew Egypt’s late president, Mohamed Morsi, who was democratically elected, and an ally of Erdogan Ties between Riyadh and Ankara hit rock bottom in 2019 when Turkey leaked audio tapes exposing the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi at Saudi Arabia's embassy in Ankara. It is only recently that Turkey and Saudi Arabia have converged in hotspots like Syria and Sudan. “The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey alignment is more complex, given that each operates in different regional environments and their perceptions of threat also differ considerably. It will take a lot of energy, effort and political will for the three states to find a way of working together and finding interoperability,” Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow and Gulf expert at Chatham House, told MEE. The war on Iran has only deepened ties between Israel and the UAE. MEE revealed in May that the two countries established a joint fund for defence acquisitions. Quilliam called the Israeli-UAE bloc “more actionable”. “The relationship has had time to bed in and has passed through many tests since the Abraham Accords were signed, and we have seen the two countries draw closer since the Israel-US war against Iran started,” he added. Which alliance has better interoperability? Turkey said on Thursday that its new allies will hold ‌joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation. The latter is a key goal for Ankara, which is pitching its drones and other weapons systems across the Middle East. The US and Turkey are Nato allies, while Saudi Arabia has long relied on the US as its main weapons supplier. Pakistan and Turkey have co-produced small warships, known as corvettes, as well as the Kaan fighter jet. They are working to produce Turkish anti-tank missiles. Saudi Arabia wants a local defence industry. 'The UAE has primarily US-systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems' - Elizabeth Dent, Washington Institute for Near East Studies But deep integration could pose a challenge. Pakistan’s main military supplier is China. Turkey wants to sell the Kaan fighter jet it is developing to Saudi Arabia, but the kingdom is eyeing the F-35. US officials tell MEE that Riyadh is unlikely to buy both. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia cannot match the intensity of Israel's defence cooperation with the US. The former’s military advantage is written into US law. Israel is openly lobbying against Saudi Arabia acquiring F-35s. “The Israelis have a broad defence industrial base, vast intelligence apparatus and battle-proven air and missile defence that is integrated via the US-led regional security order," Elizabeth Dent, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and a former Pentagon official focused on the Gulf, told MEE. “The UAE has primarily US systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems, and have the money and regional prowess,” she added. Still, some analysts say that the very fact that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have publicly codified their agreement gives it room to grow, potentially in ways the UAE-Israel alliance is unable to. The Mecca pact "contains a lot more strategic depth and binding commitment on mutual defence which could ultimately provide a more credible deterrent,” Dent said. “But the countries aren’t already integrated, so they have a long way to go”. headline: In Christian village of Taybeh, Israeli military order fails to stop settler violence
author: Fayha Shalash
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 12:48 BST | Last update: 6 days 12 hours ago
article_body: The residents of Taybeh, a village east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank , continue to face settler attacks despite an Israeli military order declaring the surrounding area a closed military zone. Local residents documented fresh settler attacks on several families east of Taybeh on Tuesday 11 August, including the Naif al-Kaabneh family, who have been subjected to violent assaults in recent days, despite the decision to close off the area under the pretext of protecting Palestinians . Taybeh is a predominantly Christian Palestinian village in the West Bank, and its residents rely on agriculture, olive groves and olive oil production, among other sources of income. In recent weeks, residents and solidarity activists say settler attacks have continued and escalated. These include settlers approaching homes and agricultural land, damaging property, and disrupting water and electricity supplies, while residents face increasing difficulty accessing their land. On Monday the Israeli army declared Taybeh, along with the southern village of Rammun, a closed military zone, saying the move was intended to prevent Israelis and settlers from entering the area. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters But residents say the order has so far done little to change the reality on the ground. While the army says the closure is meant to keep settlers out, residents and activists continue to report attacks and harassment. The measure has also raised concerns that the restrictions could make it harder for journalists, international activists and human rights observers to reach the area and document what is happening. 'We are subjected to the harshest attacks and cannot even raise our hands against them' – Naif al-Kaabneh, Bedouin resident Naif al-Kaabneh, a resident of the Bedouin community east of Taybeh, told Middle East Eye that settler attacks are relentless and almost daily. He explained that a new settlement outpost had been established on land where a Bedouin community, including his relatives, had previously lived. Settlers had since expelled them, he said, forcing them to flee under sustained attack. "They remove the fence we put up around our homes, steal our sheep, and bring in their own cattle. If we try to defend ourselves, we are arrested by the Israeli army," he said. Twenty people live in the community, including Naif's family and his brother's family. They say they endure daily hardship under the constant threat of settlers seeking to displace them and seize their land. "We hope someone will help us. We are subjected to the harshest attacks and cannot even raise our hands against them. We want anyone to amplify our voice to the world; our lives have become miserable," he added. 'We want to live in peace' With the escalation of attacks, residents of Taybeh say the threat is no longer limited to assaults on homes and property, but now extends to their access to agricultural land. Father Jack Abed, parish priest of Taybeh's Melkite church, said the village has been suffering attacks by settlers, particularly young people. "They attack our village, and we haven't been allowed to reach our olive trees in peace for three years," he said. 'They attack our village, and we haven't been allowed to reach our olive trees in peace for three years' – Father Jack Abed, parish priest Abed said olive trees and olive oil are an important source of income for the village, and called for an end to settler attacks. "We want to live in peace. Leave us living in peace. Throw out the illegal settlers who are attacking us, putting their hands on our land and forbidding us to reach our land to cultivate the olive trees." He also expressed concern over the order declaring Taybeh and Rammun a closed military area. "We ask ourselves, and we ask the Israeli army: this closure, what does it mean? Because if it's forbidden for Israelis to get into this area, why are the settlers still there?" He said the closure had, in effect, given settlers free rein while making it harder for human rights activists to reach the area and defend residents' rights. 'Protective presence' The testimonies are not limited to residents of Taybeh. International solidarity activists accompany families in the village as part of what is known as a "protective presence". Avital, an activist who visits Taybeh weekly, told Middle East Eye that in recent weeks she has witnessed an escalation in settler attacks on one family and their property. She said settlers come to the family's home every day, breaking down the fence and bringing their herds – sheep and goats – into the compound. Israel pursuing ‘undeclared annexation’ of West Bank, Peace Now says Read More » On the morning she spoke to Middle East Eye, she said, settlers had damaged several things at the family's home. "They broke a camera, they tore a cable for the electricity, they broke the hose for the water, so they spilled all the water. They're very, very intimidating and very violent," she said. She added that activists had also been beaten in previous incidents, and that while Israeli police were called after the latest incident, they did not always respond. The continued reports from Taybeh come amid a wider escalation in settler violence across the West Bank. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) recorded more than 1,000 settler attacks causing injury or property damage in the first half of 2026, affecting more than 230 Palestinian communities. By early July, Ocha reported that more than 2,200 Palestinians had been displaced in the West Bank since the start of the year – an average of around 10 people a day – as a result of settler attacks and home demolitions carried out under the pretext of a lack of Israeli-issued building permits. It said settler attacks and related restrictions had become the primary driver of displacement in the West Bank during 2026. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: What next for Nigel Farage after beating Count Binface to become MP once more?
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 11:35 BST | Last update: 5 days 13 hours ago
article_body: This time last year, Nigel Farage was the man of the hour in British politics. His party, Reform UK, was dominating in the polls, Farage and his colleagues were effectively shaping the national conversation - with Keir Starmer's government in reactive mode - and many commentators strongly argued that a Reform government was inevitable. Today the situation is quite different. The Reform leader's very political future hangs in the balance as a result of a parliamentary investigation into a gift of £5m ($6.74m), which Farage had received from Thailand-based cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne and didn't disclose. It was because of this that Farage resigned as MP for the seaside town of Clacton last month in order to trigger a by-election. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In the early hours of Friday, it emerged he had won the by-election with 22,239 votes, a 1,000-vote increase on his 2024 majority, and on a lower turnout. But what exactly has this achieved? "Let me be absolutely clear: I have done nothing wrong," Farage declared when he resigned. "I have decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions." But the contest swiftly descended into farce after all the mainstream parties decided to boycott it. In the end, there were 34 candidates standing - an eclectic array of independents, small parties and joke candidates, including three from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party. Farage's main rival ended up being a man dressed as a bin, who says he is an intergalactic space warrior and calls himself Count Binface. He won a remarkable 9,455 votes (26.9 percent of the vote share to Farage's 63.3 percent), an unusually good result for a joke candidate. Hollow victory This meant that Farage's victory rings hollow. He labelled Binface the "establishment candidate", but this is unlikely to prove a convincing narrative to the general public. Speaking at the vote count, Binface responded to Farage's accusation by suggesting that "someone [Farage] who has been an MP, been an MEP, who was one of the chief architects of Brexit and one of the dominant figures in British politics over the last 20 years, and is reputedly a member of the East India gentleman's club , which apparently does not admit women - I would say that's arguably slightly more establishment than a lone wolf space warrior with a Ceefax fixation. "But you know what? It's up to you." From 'absolute monarchy' to dear friend: How Nigel Farage and Reform learned to love the UAE Read More » Farage himself was absent from the count. Perhaps he was unkeen on being photographed next to Binface. He cited police advice about a "campaign to disrupt" the result, but acting returning officer Ian Davidson said it was Farage's personal decision "whether or not to attend". Instead, the Reform leader was at "Farage Fest", a celebration on a farm on Clacton's outskirts, which included festival tents and a ferris wheel. He declared a "resounding victory" and said that "the result in Clacton speaks for itself". Is it really a resounding victory? The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is defining the national conversation. Labour is enjoying a healthy bounce in the polls. There are even whispers that Burnham could call a snap general election in the autumn if the polling continues to look good. Farage is no longer the one setting the tone of the national discourse and the terms of the debate. He appears to be very much on the back foot. He will need something more than this win if he wants to restore the strength and relevance of Reform's platform of national renewal and mass deportations. But now Farage is an MP again, the parliamentary investigation into his £5m gift has resumed and hangs over his head once more. Whether he survives this politically remains to be seen. Count Binface, meanwhile, has declared victory: "I came first in the Clacton by-election! Of the candidates who bothered to turn up for the results." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Palestinians in West Bank village remain under Israeli settler siege for sixth day
author: Fayha Shalash
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 12:45 BST | Last update: 5 days 12 hours ago
article_body: Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra have remained under siege by Israeli settlers for a sixth day, despite an Israeli army operation that was supposedly launched to remove the settlers. Israeli activists attempting to deliver food to the families on Friday were stopped by Israeli forces, according to local media reports. The siege began on Sunday, when a group of settlers surrounded three homes on a hilltop in Qusra, near Nablus. They erected tents at the entrances in what residents said appeared to be an attempt to force the families out and take control of their homes. Residents said the settlers had cut off water and electricity to some of the properties, leaving families, including children, trapped inside and struggling to obtain food and medicine. When the families called the Israeli army for help, soldiers arrived but, according to footage online, were seen drinking and praying with the settlers rather than removing them. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters After the incident attracted international attention, the Israeli army said it had launched an operation to remove the settlers and declared the village a closed military zone. But the settlers have not been removed, and no arrests have been reported. Footage shows Israeli settlers surrounding a Palestinian family’s house, breaking down a stone barrier in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank. This comes amid a surge in deadly settler violence across the occupied West Bank. pic.twitter.com/UFAWGi4JZ0 — Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) August 12, 2026 Instead, Israeli forces deployed large numbers of troops to the village, forcing about 20 Palestinian families from their homes and taking over several properties, which were converted into military positions. The army said the deployment was intended to prevent clashes between Palestinian residents and settlers. Israeli forces later withdrew from some of the homes, allowing families to return. Constant attacks Qusay Abu Rida, who is sheltering in one of the besieged homes, said settlers had repeatedly targeted the property for months. The house was built in 2023 and belongs to his brother, who lives in the United States. During previous attacks, settlers broke through the gate, damaged security cameras and stole belongings from outside the house. This situation forced Abu Rida and his family to move into the house four months ago to protect it. During this time, they have faced numerous forms of harassment aimed at forcing them to leave. “They would constantly come into the yard, shouting and vandalising things. Then, on Sunday, they came and erected a tent directly in front of the house, cutting off our electricity and water,” he told Middle East Eye. 'The settlers are in control': How the West Bank is being ethnically cleansed Read More » Two other homes have also been surrounded by settlers. According to Abu Rida, the soldiers in the area have made no real attempt to remove the settlers. Instead, they placed further restrictions on the besieged families. “The soldiers forcibly evicted us from my house and my neighbour Yousef’s house and moved us to his brother Rizq’s house. They cut off all our essential supplies and prevented us from leaving, even to collect necessities from our homes,” he said. On Thursday evening, Israeli forces withdrew from Abu Rida’s home after causing damage inside. Security-camera footage documenting the settlers' siege was also reportedly destroyed by the soldiers, who dismantled the settlers’ tent but remained in the area. The tents have since been erected again. Abu Rida said the treatment of the families echoed what happened to the al-Tubasi family in nearby Jalud last month, where settlers repeatedly attacked the family home until its residents were forced to leave. The settlers then took control of the property, he said, in full view of Israeli forces. Homes left damaged On Thursday morning, more than 1,000 Israeli soldiers entered Qusra, according to local media reports. Abdul-Azim Wadi, head of the village council, said the military liaison had informed local authorities that troops intended to seize 16 homes. In the end, eight were taken after their residents were ordered out. Wadi said the army did not explain the seizures, telling residents simply: “Leave immediately. This house is under our control.” Some of the seized properties were later vacated by the soldiers, but residents returned to find extensive damage. “In one house, they stole $1,500 and destroyed all the furniture,” Wadi told MEE. “In another, they stole some of the contents.” He said each home was entered by dozens of soldiers. In some properties, troops wrote “We will return” on the walls. Fears of wider control The Ras al-Ain area, where the Abu Rida and Hassan family homes are located, has faced a series of settler attacks since December. Residents say the attacks are aimed at forcing them from their homes and taking control of the land. Hani Odeh, an activist in Qusra, said the situation was “heartbreaking”, with settlers and soldiers taking turns putting pressure on residents to leave. Northern Qusra is now the only part of the village where residents can expand, he said. The other three areas have been taken over by Israeli forces and settlers, with Palestinians barred from accessing them. “Now they even want to control the northern part because it overlooks five villages south of Nablus, including Jalud and Awarta,” Odeh said. “It is classified as Area B, and the nearest settlement activity was at least 15km away.” He said the encroachment began months ago, when a settler started grazing livestock in the area. Other settlers later joined him and began attacking Palestinian homes, apparently seeking to drive residents out. 'The soldiers do not have the authority to remove the settlers; they only oppress us' - Hani Odeh, Qusra-based activist During the siege of the three homes, settlers and soldiers prevented supplies from reaching those trapped inside, Odeh said. Residents even tried to bring food in an ambulance, but soldiers stopped and turned it back. “This whole situation is worrying all the residents of Qusra,” he said. “We don’t know where the settlers will go next after attacking homes in an area classified as Area B. The soldiers do not have the authority to remove the settlers; they only oppress us.” Under the 1995 Oslo Accords, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C as a temporary administrative arrangement that remains in place. Area A is under full Palestinian Authority control for civil administration and internal security and includes major Palestinian cities. Area B is under Palestinian civil administration, while security responsibilities are shared with Israel. It includes smaller towns and rural villages. Despite the accords, Israeli forces have operated inside Areas A and B for years. Area C, which accounts for about 60 percent of the West Bank, is under full Israeli civil and security control. Most Israeli settlements and military bases have traditionally been located in Area C, built on Palestinian land. In recent years, however, settlers have increasingly expanded their attacks and sought to establish a presence in Area B. Settler violence Qusra has a long history of settler attacks, and the latest incidents come amid a sharp rise in violence across the occupied West Bank. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs ( Ocha ) said it had documented more than 1,330 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across 250 Palestinian communities since the beginning of 2026, as of 20 July. The incidents amounted to more than six attacks a day. At least 18 people have been killed and 880 more wounded during settler attacks in 2026. More than 2,300 Palestinians had also been displaced in 2026 as a result of settler attacks and related access restrictions, according to Ocha. Around 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem across roughly 300 settlements and outposts. The settlements are regarded as illegal under international law, according to the International Court of Justice. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved.
