headline: How the Mecca Agreement aims to manage US separation from Middle East
author: Ilya Roubanis
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 21:17 BST | Last update: 6 days 3 hours ago
article_body: The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia , Pakistan , and Turkey was unexpected but hardly surprising. Some have framed it as a Sunni alliance, with the role of the House of Saud as custodians of the two holy cities (Mecca and Medina), Pakistan as a nuclear-armed South Asian Islamic Republic, and Turkey’s Europe-adjacent muscular strand of political Islam. However, this agreement has little to do with religious sectarianism. The Mecca partners have far-reaching industrial, military, and diplomatic ties. The agreement, or the sum of already functioning bilateral partnerships, is not an alliance with a single command structure. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August by Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, attempts to consolidate three strong bilateral relationships into a single collective defence framework. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia concluded a Mutual Defence Agreement on 17 September 2025. At the time, it was speculated that this would provide Riyadh with a nuclear defence umbrella, although this point remains intentionally ambiguous. The Mecca pact adds a Turkish annex. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “It was about time that regional agency takes shape,” says the Bahraini analyst, Abdullah Aljunaid. “Put it this way: it’s not Islamic. It’s not about containing Iran either. It is there to prove that the region can produce its own security. You have three major players within the region: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. What you need to look out for now is the geographical gaps between those three domains, all the way up to Syria.” The militaries of all three states have deep ties. Islamabad and Ankara have a longstanding defence partnership. It is no secret that the Turkish industrial complex makes full use of Pakistani human resources in research and development: the Kaan fifth-generation fighter project employs about 200 Pakistani engineers. Riyadh has relied on Pakistani soldiers and pilots for decades, funded Islamabad’s nuclear programme, and has provided financial breathing space to Pakistan’s fragile economy. 'Put it this way: it’s not Islamic. It’s not about containing Iran either. It is there to prove that the region can produce its own security' - Abdullah Aljunaid, Bahraini analyst Turkey is not only a supplier of arms to Pakistan but has modular input in strategic platforms such as the JF-17 Block III multirole jet fighter, which uses an ASLPOD targeting pod and can be fitted with a MURAD AESA radar and Bozdogan short-range air-to-air missiles. Over the last five years, Riyadh and Ankara have been forging a common worldview. As noted by Aljenaid, Saudi-Turkish relations gained strategic depth in Syria, where cooperation was hailed by Washington. At present, the partnership is gaining strategic significance, as Riyadh sees Ankara as a strategic partner in fulfilling the kingdom’s 2030 Vision, which calls for the localisation of 50 percent of total military expenditure, focusing on armed vehicles, missiles, loitering munitions, and drones. In this context, Riyadh has found that Turkish companies such as Baykar and Aselsan are more willing to engage in technology transfer, joint production, and research. In sum, while this agreement is not an alliance, it is not shallow. However, turning three bilateral partnerships into a single alliance is no simple matter. Why now? According to Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, the Mecca Agreement was negotiated over two years. Its scope predates the us-israeli war on Iran . However, the timing of the agreement certainly relates to the events unfolding around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. American security guarantees lost much of their thrust during the Hormuz crisis. As noted by former US ambassador to Qatar Patrick Theros, Washington’s attack on Iran turned the American umbrella into a liability. What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East Read More » Washington was unable or did not prioritise air defence cover for its partners in the Gulf, creating an additional challenge to the region’s security architecture. "The Saudis have understood that the Abraham Accords have been a security guarantee for Israel, not the kingdom,” notes Dr Yeghia Tashjian, of the Issam Fares Institute at the American University of Beirut. The conclusion is that the Gulf’s defence architecture needs foundations in the region. In that respect, Qatar invested in its partnership with Turkey even before the 2025 Israeli raid on Doha. Riyadh and Abu Dhabi followed two distinct routes: the Emiratis doubled down in their partnership with Israel, with Israel installing the outward layers of its Iron Dome architecture in the Gulf. Riyadh turned to its historical security partner, Pakistan, while incrementally building on its partnership with Turkey. Destructive ambiguity The question is: to what end does this agreement go? According to the foremost expert in Turkish-Israeli relations at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, Dr Gallia Linderstrauss, while this pact is framed as exclusively defensive, it is meant to convey a message to Iran and Israel, perhaps also the UAE. 'Slowly and gradually, in the next one-two-three years, we will see America reducing its presence in the Gulf, and concentrating in the South China Sea' - Air Marshal (Retd) Saeed Khan The lack of clarity is whether this agreement is in fact an alliance. This begs testing, a process that can be destructive. An agreement is a statement of agency. An alliance is a joint perception of national security threats and implies unified command. We are nowhere closer to a regional alliance since 7 August. Pakistani troops and pilots have repeatedly mobilised in Yemen under the Saudi banner. It is doubtful they would take action under a Pakistani banner and challenge the Emiratis head-on. The withdrawal of more than $3.5bn of Emirati deposits from the Central Bank of Pakistan in April 2026 was a warning signal that Islamabad’s loyalty to Riyadh may come at a tangible cost. The deployment of Pakistanis is not the same as the mobilisation of Pakistan. Islamabad has priorities, and its ultimate loyalty lies with Riyadh; still, Islamabad will strive to avoid a head-on collision. When it comes to Iran, Islamabad also has priorities. As the Air Marshal (Retd) Saeed Muhammad Khan and former Pakistani ambassador to Syria underscores, Pakistan shares an extensive and rather unstable border with Iran, facing the common challenge of Baloch separatism. “We have over 1,000km border with them and the common threat of the Baloch. Slowly and gradually, in the next one-two-three years, we will see America reducing its presence in the Gulf and concentrating in the South China Sea. Things could change dramatically,” Khan said. Iran says it is not concerned by new 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement' Read More » Islamabad has little appetite for a direct confrontation with Tehran. Similarly, it is doubtful that Ankara would take on the challenge of deploying in Yemen, risking a direct conflict with Tehran, with which it shares a Kurdish challenge. Even Riyadh would rather avoid feeding Shia-Sunni sectarianism. This regional reluctance to feed sectarianism has been “battle-tested” during successive US-Israeli campaigns against Iran. Will these three powers mobilise together against common threats? Under current circumstances, foes may be tempted to test this resolve. That can be dangerous. There are common challenges, not least in the Red Sea. Turkey’s Turksom Camp in Mogadishu is a major anchor for its power projection in the region. Pakistan is complementing this presence, signing a military cooperation agreement with Somalia that facilitates the landing of an expeditionary force. At the same time, Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025; the United Arab Emirates is known to use the infrastructure of Bosaso port and airport for logistical purposes in its engagement in the Sudanese conflict. At times, there is a clear polarisation between status quo and revisionism, but it's never as neat as in the case of Nato. Whether a common worldview translates into joint mobilisation is a question that depends on the convergence of several contextual variables. All parties have a range of interests. Turkish-Emirati military-industrial cooperation is strong and growing. Pakistan still depends on remittance flows from 1.6 million Pakistanis residing in the UAE. One should not expect Saudi Arabia to punish India for supplying Israel with military equipment when the need arises, as military analyst Kamal Alam notes. Where do we go now The Mecca agreement presents an ambiguous message. The three defence partnerships framed by the agreement remain distinct and compartmentalised. What is simmering is a polarisation between the status quo and revisionist powers. In Ankara, Manama, Riyadh, and Beirut, the Emirati-Israeli alliance is seen as seeking to revise the security status quo, while Iran is seen as seeking to revise the status quo in the Strait of Hormuz. This polarisation is problematic, not least for Israel, which must also manage the ambiguity of the American commitment to the region. 'From an Israeli perspective, normalisation between Israel and Saudi Arabia, if not harder, is at least a more distant reality' - Gallia Lindenstrauss, Institute for National Security Studies Politics in this sense matters, and elections could make a difference. According to Dr Gallia Lindenstrauss, expanding the Abraham Accords to include Saudi Arabia is now a greater challenge. “From an Israeli perspective, normalisation between Israel and Saudi Arabia, if not harder, is at least a more distant reality. That is of concern because this is something that was a priority for Netanyahu.” Whether by reference to Israel’s de facto security zones in Lebanon and Syria, or Kurdish-controlled regions in Iraq and Iran, what unites the Mecca signatories is a commitment to the status quo. “All three signatories have backed central state authority where the UAE has backed sub-state actors: the Sudanese army against the RSF, Yemen’s recognised government against the STC, Somalia’s territorial integrity against Somaliland’s recognition," Toga of the Centre for Iranian Studies tells MEE. "Riyadh no longer faces that network alone, and after the Yemen confrontation of late 2025, that is a meaningful change. But I would not overstate it.” This observation is the point of departure, a foundational consensus among analysts in Islamabad, Ankara, and the Gulf. In that respect, the Mecca Agreement is a statement of intent to shield the territorial status quo even as the US withdraws from the region. A bigger development may be further Chinese mediation. As noted by analyst Aljunaid, China is well positioned to broker an understanding between Iran and the Mecca signatories. The US is no longer seen as having convening power. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Iran attacks US failures as scepticism grows over Israeli role in Trump 'assassination plot'
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 12:02 BST | Last update: 6 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Iran has accused the US of allowing faulty intelligence to drive it into war, as new reports revealed that CIA analysts doubted an Israeli warning that triggered a secret security operation during President Donald Trump’s visit to Turkey . Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday that Washington “has long miscalculated due to intelligence failures”, including when it launched its war on Iran. He said US actions in the Strait of Hormuz represented “an even bigger miscalculation”. “Worse than fake news is fake intelligence,” Araghchi wrote on X. His comments came as The Washington Post confirmed earlier reporting by Middle East Eye that Turkish officials viewed an Israeli warning about an Iranian plot to assassinate Trump during last month’s Nato summit in Ankara as a ruse designed to undermine negotiations with Tehran. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Israel passed the intelligence to the CIA, but US analysts found it unconvincing and warned administration officials about its low credibility, the newspaper reported. The warning prompted security officials to fly Trump out of Turkey aboard an alternative military aircraft after he secretly switched planes on the tarmac in Ankara. Israel passed the intelligence to the CIA, but US analysts found it unconvincing and warned administration officials about its low credibility... Trump confirmed the operation on Tuesday, saying he had followed the instructions of his security team. The dispute over Israeli intelligence comes alongside continuing and competing declarations about control of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes. Hossein Taeb, commander of the Basij paramilitary unit, an affiliate of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said the waterway was “under Iran’s control and management”. “Today you see that the Strait of Hormuz is under the management and control of the Islamic Republic, and our country continues on its path in complete security,” Taeb said, according to Iran’s Fars news agency. This US Navy handout photograph released on 4 August shows an F-18 Super Hornet launching on the USS Abraham Lincoln on 31 July (US Navy/AFP) “The Americans saw the power of the Islamic revolution,” he added. His comments came a day after Trump claimed that the US had “total control” of the strategic waterway. 'The hypocrisy is blatant and embarrassing' Separately, Araghchi also attacked France and other Western governments for condemning Iran’s treatment of protesters while continuing to support Israel despite its genocide in Gaza and attacks across the Middle East. “Countries like France should stop lecturing the world about ‘human rights’ and international law. The hypocrisy is blatant and embarrassing,” he wrote. “Your backing of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and aggression against Iran, has destroyed whatever moral high ground you imagined you had.” Meanwhile, Democratic US Senator Richard Blumenthal demanded answers from War Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Navy over deteriorating conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent more than 250 days at sea. Turkey suspects Israel fabricated Trump Air Force One assassination plot to derail US-Iran deal Read More » “The Trump Admin must explain what they are doing to support sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln who have been continuously at sea for nearly 7 months,” he wrote on X. "Widespread reports of supply shortages, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health & more demand immediate attention.” Washington diverted the aircraft carrier from exercises in the South China Sea to the Middle East in late January as it built up forces before launching the war on Iran. Since then, US military families and members of Congress have raised concerns over worsening mental health conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a prolonged deployment linked to the war on Iran. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported that several sailors had attempted to jump overboard as difficult conditions and psychological pressure pushed the crew towards breaking point. The carrier has entered its ninth month at sea. Its crew has spent 250 consecutive days without reaching land, marking the longest uninterrupted deployment by a modern aircraft carrier. Stars and Stripes reported that one woman told officials her husband had sent her a message that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Tucker Carlson says Israel pushed him to report false allegations against Hunter Biden
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 21:31 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Conservative US commentator Tucker Carlson said Israeli "agents" close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed him to falsely report that Hunter Biden’s leaked laptop material showed him abusing minors. "The claim that there was material involving the abuse of minors on the computer came from the Israelis," Carlson said in an interview aired on Monday with Hunter, former US President Joe Biden's son. "I'm just telling you that they came to me with it, and that's how I know it.” Carlson’s claim dates back to 2020 when he was a presenter at the right-wing cable news network Fox and pushed allegations that Hunter was involved in corrupt business dealings with Ukraine when his father was vice president. The younger Biden’s laptop story emerged in the weeks before the 2020 US election, which President Biden went on to win against President Donald Trump. The story started with John Paul Mac Isaac, a computer repair shop owner in Wilmington, Delaware, who said Hunter left a damaged Apple computer and an external hard drive at his shop in April 2019. The FBI obtained possession of the laptop in December 2019. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In October 2020, The New York Post reported on emails contained in the laptop that detailed the younger Biden’s business dealings with Burisma, a Ukrainian energy company whose board Hunter sat on. Other personal information obtained from the laptop and hard drive included videos of Hunter smoking crack, having sex and soliciting female prostitutes. Photos and videos of Hunter's drug- and alcohol fuelled rendezvous with prostitutes circled online during the early years of his father's presidency and were reported on regularly by Fox and The New York Post. Carlson said that the false allegation about abuse of minors was a product of Israel’s misinformation campaign and was falsely attributed by former US intelligence officials to Russian propaganda. Tucker Carlson interrogated in Israel, has passport seized after interviewing US ambassador Read More » “They (Israel) were behind it," Carlson said. ”I felt like everybody in Washington knew it, but there was so much pressure not to criticise Israel in any way that they just said, 'It's the Russians, it's the Russians'.” "Maybe the Russians had a hand in it, but it was the Israelis who were pushing that fact," Carlson said. ”Fact, I mean literally [pushing it] to me.” There is no evidence that Hunter abused minors. The former US president's son has long acknowledged the videos, texts and photos showing him engaging in drug and sex acts. For his part, Carlson acknowledged not sharing the Israeli angle when he was covering the story for Fox News. Hunter said that he didn’t have confirmation of who was behind his laptop leak, but said several parties were behind the dissemination of the laptop's material, including Russians, domestic US opponents of his father, and a "Netanyahu operation centre, the Israeli side”. Hunter joined Carlson in criticising Netanyahu. "If pointing out that Benjamin Netanyahu is evil incarnate is antisemitic, then I don't know what to tell people anymore," Hunter said. headline: UK withholds information on Israeli firm accused of targeting Scottish first minister in elections
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 13:43 BST | Last update: 6 days 11 hours ago
article_body: The British government has refused to publish any information it holds on an Israeli firm suspected of interfering in the Scottish parliament elections, on the grounds that doing so may "prejudice relations between the United Kingdom and any other state". In June, the French disinformation watchdog Viginum accused Israeli cyber firm BlackCore of meddling in elections in New York City and Scotland , as well as in France ’s local elections. Viginum chief Marc-Antoine Brillant said investigations had led the watchdog to suspect BlackCore of being "used to carry out foreign digital interference operations in other countries or regions, such as Angola, Togo, the elections in Scotland, and the 2025 ​municipal election in New York". However, he said, it was unclear who had commissioned the Israeli company to carry out the operations. The watchdog said BlackCore-linked accounts specifically targeted Scottish First Minister John Swinney. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The National newspaper reported this week that it submitted two Freedom of Information (FOI) requests to the UK and Scottish governments for the release of "any correspondence (including emails and letters) mentioning the French government agency Viginum and discussing its findings regarding alleged Israeli-linked influence operations (and the firm BlackCore) affecting Scotland or Scottish elections". According to The National, the UK Cabinet Office replied that the FOI request "relates to information that must not to be disclosed in order to safeguard national security". The Cabinet Office said: "We have weighed these public interests against a very strong public interest in safeguarding national security. It is important that this sensitive information is protected, as disclosure of information would damage national security. This interest could only be overridden in exceptional circumstances. "Taking into account all the circumstances of this case, we have determined that the balance of the public interest favours withholding this information." Israeli firm BlackCore meddled in US and Scottish elections, French watchdog says Read More » The Scottish government, meanwhile, withheld some information on national security grounds, but published other documents showing officials discussing how to respond to the French government report. They include the principal private secretary to the Scottish first minister saying: "I have shared this with FM - anticipating that he will want to understand more about this report, what we/UKG and security apparatus know/knew about it, and what actions remedial and future / proactive are being taken." Swinney, the first minister, leads the Scottish National Party (SNP), which has been heavily critical of Israel's actions in Gaza. Swinney himself accused Israel of committing genocide in August 2025. "It’s quite clear that there is a genocide in Palestine - it can’t be disputed," he said. "I have seen reports of terrible atrocities which have the character of being genocide. I’ve expressed that and obviously it’s not reached all those individuals, but that’s my feeling." headline: Exclusive: UK to announce raft of new policies on Israel including settlement goods ban
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 16:40 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Since Andy Burnham became prime minister, there has been a serious shift in approach to British foreign policy. But so far none of it has been made public, beyond a change in the rhetoric of government ministers. This is set to change after parliament's summer recess. The government is poised to announce a raft of new policies in September, multiple Whitehall and civil society sources told Middle East Eye. These policies are still under discussion, but are set to include a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in particular is pushing for stronger measures and has been consulting a range of civil society organisations, MEE understands. Sources said discussions are underway in the Foreign Office over whether the measures will involve legal sanctions for companies and organisations that have business or other links with settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. This comes as the Charity Commission, the UK's charity regulator, is investigating several British charities accused of sending money to settlements. The former prime minister, Keir Starmer, said in June that "no UK charity should be supporting [settlements]" but declined to say the government would ban charitable donations to them. By contrast, Burnham's government is exploring doing so. The Foreign Office is looking at imposing new sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in the settler movement in the occupied West Bank, sources with knowledge of the matter said. There have also been internal discussions on potential sanctions on more Israeli ministers, after far-right ministers Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were sanctioned last year. Arms sales under consideration Another key issue under consideration is arms sales. In September 2024, the newly elected Starmer government suspended around 30 export licences for UK-made arms after assessing there was a "clear risk" the items could be used in Gaza in serious violations of international humanitarian law. The licensing of UK-made F-35 components exported directly to Israel was suspended. Significantly, however, parts sent to a global F-35 programme spare parts pool that could end up in Israel were exempted. UK-made F-35 components make up 15 percent of every F-35, one of the world's most sophisticated fighter jets, which Israel used extensively in its campaign in Gaza, as well as in Lebanon and Iran. Exclusive: Britain mulls ban on Israeli settlement goods Read More » The Starmer government argued that there was no way the UK could unilaterally halt the export of UK-made parts without impacting the worldwide fleet of F-35s and threatening global peace and security. Starmer also green-lit $169m in military goods to Israel. These included 8,630 separate munitions exports in the category of “bombs, grenades, torpedoes, mines, missiles and other similar munitions”. Banning the export of these military goods is now under discussion, although no concrete decisions have been made. A Foreign Office spokesperson told MEE on Wednesday: "Settlements are illegal under international law, undermine the viability of a two-state solution and fuel insecurity for both Palestinians and Israelis. "We have given clear advice to UK businesses that they should not engage in economic activity in illegal settlements and warn them of the reputational and potentially legal consequences of any such activities." The UK's slow journey towards a ban Shortly before he became prime minister in July, Burnham set the tone by apologising for the Starmer leadership's early support for Israel's war on Gaza and refusal to back a ceasefire in 2023 and early 2024. Since then he has come under significant pressure from Labour backbenchers to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements and take other strong positions on issues in the Middle East. MEE reported in November last year that Foreign Office ministers privately accepted that a ban on settlement goods was desirable. Discussions on how to implement a ban began in the final months of Starmer's premiership. Labour Friends of Israel defends major West Bank settlement blocs Read More » Then-Middle East minister Hamish Falconer confirmed in early July that the UK was considering the "technical difficulties" of implementing a ban and discussing the issue with allies in the European Union. The Netherlands and Spain have already imposed a ban, and Ireland is currently implementing one. Sources said Burnham has been keen to have the early weeks of his premiership defined by his domestic policies. But he confirmed last month he is considering "further measures to deter unacceptable violence" in the occupied West Bank. Labour Friends of Israel (LFI), a lobby group within the Labour Party, published a report earlier this month apparently justifying some illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestine and urging the British government not to ban goods produced by them. LFI is a group within the Labour Party believed to count more than 70 MPs as affiliates, although it no longer keeps a public list. The report argued that "a boycott of all trade with settlements is practically and politically impossible". It said a full boycott would "impact all Israeli businesses operating in the settlement blocs, as well as East Jerusalem and the Old City". In opposition, Labour called for a ban on the import of settlement goods, with the then shadow foreign secretary, Lisa Nandy, saying in June 2020 that the move would require "courage that so far ministers have not been willing to show". Polling of Labour members earlier this year showed that a staggering 87 percent support a ban on trade with Israeli settlements, with only six percent opposing it. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: 'This isn't the Britain I grew up in': The activists raided by police over Palestine Action videos
author: Katherine Hearst
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 13:38 BST | Last update: 6 days 13 hours ago
article_body: Marji Mansfield, a 70-year-old grandmother of seven, has been waiting for British counterterrorism police to show up at her door. The anxiety sharpens between five and seven in the morning, when police usually conduct dawn raids, particularly if she has her grandchildren stay overnight. “It’s been really, really quite scary not knowing when there's going to be the knock at the door,” Mansfield told Middle East Eye. “This isn't the Britain that I thought I grew up in at all. We've been scared enough to go and sleep elsewhere.” Mansfield is among scores of activists, many of them elderly, who are awaiting dawn raids from counterterrorism police after publishing videos of themselves inviting support for the banned direct action group Palestine Action . New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Since the government proscribed the organisation in July 2025, over 3,000 people have been arrested under the Terrorism Act for participating in silent vigils in support of Palestine Action. But in June, after the Court of Appeal quashed a High Court ruling and found the ban to be lawful, Defend Our Juries (DOJ) - the group helming the campaign to reverse the ban - called for an "escalation" in activism. This involved activists inviting support for the group rather than simply expressing support, an offence that can carry a 14-year sentence under Section 12 of the Terrorism Act. So far, most activists have been arrested under the lesser charge of Section 13. Mansfield and around 100 others responded to the call from DOJ, uploading videos of themselves declaring: “Saving lives is not terrorism, I support Palestine Action, and I think you should too”. Subsequently, some 19 people, many of them retired, have been raided by counterterrorism police across the UK , including in London, the West Midlands, Somerset, Wales, Cornwall and Scotland. They told MEE that police searched their entire homes, confiscating personal devices - as well as items bearing the Palestinian flag - and rifled through personal diaries. Two people reported being handcuffed, despite police policy stipulating that officers may only use the restraint when they have “objective grounds” for believing it is necessary, including “where an officer reasonably believes that without handcuffs the subject may escape, attempt to escape or cause harm to themselves or others”. So far, those who haven’t been raided, like Mansfield, are crippled by the anxiety of the prospect. According to Mansfield, many activists have reported being unable to sleep, while others, who have sick partners, have said that they feel unable to go out for fear the police will arrive in their absence. “It really impacts people's lives. It causes great fear and anxiety,” Mansfield said. Middle East Eye contacted the UK's Counter Terrorism Police for comment but received no response by the time of publication. ‘I just had my shorts on’ At around 7.30am one late July morning, former government worker Asghar Ahmad, 63, opened his door in the town of Telford in Shropshire to find about a dozen police officers, a police van and four police cars parked outside his home. “I just had my shorts on, but that was it,” Ahmad told MEE. “I wasn't challenging anything because I knew what they were going to do. They were going to go through the whole house. 'I spent 38 years working for the government on their IT systems. I’ve got to a point in my life where I can see things for what they are' - Asghar Ahmad, activist “I said: 'Can I just go and get some clothes on?' An officer followed me upstairs. He was present all the time.” Ahmad was then handcuffed and driven to the local police station. While he was gone, the remaining officers searched the house, confiscating all of his devices. “They went through every single room,” Ahmad said. When he was interviewed later that day in the presence of his solicitor, the police presented him with all the items they had removed from the house. These included laptops, old phones, hard drives, scraps of paper and “anything that was remotely Palestinian”, like flags and bracelets. He was released at 5pm that day, with no charges. “I spent 38 years working for the government on their IT systems,” Ahmad said. “I’ve got to a point in my life where I can see things for what they are. “I was too busy, like most people are with their lives, just trying to build a family. “Once I finished work, I realised I could do things without fear of losing my job or my income,” Ahmad said, describing the strength he now feels to speak out on issues he cares about. Ahmad, who is spending his retirement doing volunteer work in his community, said he’s “got nothing to hide”. “If they want to put pensioners in prison, it will not go down well,” he said. ‘A bit creepy’ Paul Graves-Brown, a 64-year-old semi-retired archaeologist in Carmarthenshire, said that some 20 police officers searched his home over a period of six and a half hours. He said they even searched his wife’s underwear drawer and leafed through the diary she kept as a teenager. “They left the diary on the top, highlighting the fact that they've been looking through a teenage girl’s diary, which is a bit creepy,” he said. Graves-Brown was held at the local police station from 8am and released at 4pm that day with no charge. 'They left the diary on the top, highlighting the fact that they've been looking through a teenage girl’s diary' - Paul Gravesbrown, archaeologist “Being raided is quite traumatic, it’s one of those things which hangs around in your mind,” he told MEE. “Our house was burgled just before the first lockdown, so it’s a similar sort of experience - total strangers wandering around your house.” Thirty-year-old Allie, a bartender based in Staffordshire who spoke using an alias, was arrested shortly after she came home from a shift at the pub. She was woken by a series of bangs on her door at around 1am. “I opened the door and I think the first thing I said was, ‘Oh my God, you actually came’,” Allie told MEE. Both Allie and Ahmad said that the officers asked for the pin numbers to unlock their devices. Under Section 49 of the Investigatory Powers Act, police should make these requests in writing. Allie recalled that she had said as she was being handcuffed: “This is a bit much for what this is, isn’t it?” The police then asked her to sign a document stating that she had made this comment during her arrest. She was then driven to Oldbury police station, near Birmingham, where she was held for about eight to nine hours, and released with no charge. “I think the worst thing for me is that it really shatters any sense of personal safety,” Allie said. “You go through life with a belief in the systems that are there to protect you. This is such a heinous overreach and abuse of those systems. I don't think that I'll ever be able to fully reconcile myself with it. It's like having to reconstruct a new reality,” she said. headline: Ein al-Auja: How settler attacks and water diversion erased a Palestinian community
author: Majd Jawad
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 12:53 BST | Last update: 6 days 6 hours ago
article_body: Haitham Rashaidh was among the last to leave his home near Ein al-Auja, a natural spring and waterfall north of Jericho in the occupied West Bank. His family packed up their tents and heaped all their belongings onto a tractor, and then began the two-hour journey across difficult terrain towards al-Balqa, a sparsely populated area of the Jordan Valley, where they set up camp alongside their displaced neighbours. Leaving Ein al-Auja felt like losing a part of themselves, Rashaidh explained mournfully. Water once flowed here in a torrent, estimated at thousands of cubic metres daily - yet today, the ground is parched, the spring that once supported a Bedouin community of more than 100 families reduced to a trickle. Palestinians used to treasure Ein al-Auja as an oasis of calm in a region under siege. But Israel ’s diversion of water, alongside continuing settler attacks, ultimately made life in the community untenable. “We did not leave the first time they tried to push us out,” Rashaidh told Middle East Eye. “We came back, rebuilt what we could, and tried to continue our lives. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “But it didn’t stop,” he said. “Every time we returned, the pressure came back stronger: more restrictions, more attacks, less access to water.” This past January, having reached their breaking point, Rashaidh’s family uprooted their lives to Balqa, a tiny Bedouin encampment with no public services. It takes more than two hours to reach the nearest city centre from here, and Rashaidh acknowledges with visible sorrow that his children are no longer able to attend school. The predicament facing his community has escalated sharply over the last couple of years, since the events of 7 October 2023 began redefining Palestinian life across the occupied territories. 'In the end, it wasn't one incident that forced us out, but the repetition of everything, over and over again - until staying became impossible' - Haitham Rashaidh, displaced resident Before the Gaza war , forced displacement from the Ein al-Auja area had been minimal, with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) recording only two settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage between 2017 and 2023. But since early 2024, several new illegal Israeli settlement outposts have been established in the area - and the attacks have consequently ramped up, with at least 38 documented cases last year. “Access to water has been especially compromised; settlers believed to be from these settlement outposts have repeatedly cut or damaged water pipes connected to [Ein al-Auja] spring, blocked access roads used for water collection and delivery, emptied households’ water tanks, and intimidated or assaulted residents and herders attempting to collect water, severely undermining livelihoods,” Ocha noted in a January report. In one documented case earlier this year, 26 families, comprising 124 people, were forcibly displaced amid ongoing violence by armed settlers and Israeli troops. “It felt like they were testing how long we could endure,” Rashaidh said. “In the end, it wasn’t one incident that forced us out, but the repetition of everything, over and over again - until staying became impossible.” Sustained decline The dramatic and sustained decline of Ein al-Auja spring in recent years mirrors the disappearance of the surrounding Palestinian community. Its water flow, historically estimated at more than 1,000 cubic metres per hour - and potentially double that in rainy seasons - has dropped by 50 to 70 percent in recent years, and sometimes runs entirely dry, according to Ayman Abu Zaher, an environmental researcher who monitors the local water system. As one of the region’s most historically significant springs, Ein al-Auja has come under increasing pressure from both climate change and from wells drilled nearby, Abu Zaher told MEE. In dry years, reduced groundwater recharge, combined with intensive pumping, has limited the spring’s flow. The region’s hydrogeology is composed of two main groundwater layers, Abu Zaher explained: a shallow aquifer, typically accessed through wells ranging from 70-100 metres in depth, and a much deeper aquifer that feeds Ein al-Auja spring. Historically, three state-managed wells in the Ein al-Auja area extended 500-600 metres underground - but over the past three decades, Israeli authorities deepened them to nearly 1,000 metres, and added a fourth, Abu Zaher said. Collectively, he estimates that these wells extract between four and six million cubic metres of water annually from the deep aquifer that feeds Ein al-Auja spring. This water is then diverted to Israeli settlements, instead of supplying nearby Palestinian communities. The imbalance is reinforced by the limited capacity of Palestinian-controlled water sources in the same area. Abu Zaher estimates that there are about a dozen Palestinian wells locally, but they are “shallow and insufficient”. “The water they produce is not enough for agriculture and is increasingly unsuitable for irrigation, which pushes the area towards a trajectory of desertification,” he said. Whereas irrigated orchards and cultivated fields once covered more than 30,000 dunums (3,000 hectares) in the Ein al-Auja area, only around 3,000 dunums remain actively irrigated today, Abu Zaher said. 'We used to have water close to us. Today, every litre has become a struggle' - Naifa Zaied, displaced resident For families who have been displaced from their homes and now live in tents in nearby areas such as Balqa, this transformation is not abstract; it is deeply embedded in the routines of everyday survival. Among those most affected are women, who often bear the responsibility of securing water for their households. When they lived next to Ein al-Auja, they could fill their small plastic containers at the waterfall, quickly gathering enough for a single day’s needs. Now, they must walk several kilometres under the scorching sun in search of water tankers or distribution points, often returning home with empty containers when supplies are unavailable or Israeli forces turn them away. Water rationing has become part of their daily reality. “We were forced to buy large quantities of water due to the shortage in the spring,” Naifa Zaied, who was displaced to Balqa early this year, told MEE. “But in the last year, the army even prevented us from buying it. Water tankers were barred from reaching us.” Water shortages have affected nearly every aspect of life, she said, with families rationing water for drinking, cooking, washing, and caring for livestock. “We used to have water close to us. Today, every litre has become a struggle,” she said. “Sometimes we wait for water tankers that never arrive, and we are forced to save water for drinking before anything else.” 'We are cut off' The devastating impacts of the water crisis extend to local wildlife and pastoral communities across the Jordan Valley, where Palestinians have reported widespread livestock losses amid repeated settler attacks, theft and confiscation. Movement restrictions and a loss of grazing access have worsened their plight. In one of the largest recent incidents, residents of the Ein al-Auja area reported that Israeli settlers stole around 1,500 sheep and goats during a raid on the community early last year, dealing a massive blow to local herding families. The following day, dozens of animal carcasses were found in the area. The decimation of their traditional livelihoods has left many Bedouins with no choice but to seek jobs in nearby Israeli settlements, or to take on seasonal, low-paid work within the Israeli economy. The land that once sustained them is now accessible only as a site of labour, with no job protections or employment rights. Haitham Rashaidh and his family are pictured in al-Balqa, where they have lived since their displacement from the Ein al-Auja area, near Jericho, on 10 April 2026 (MEE/Majd Jawad) In Rashaidh’s case, before the family’s displacement, his primary livelihood was agriculture and livestock. Today, he works as a labourer on a date palm farm near Balqa. “It is a highly risky environment, without work permits, and many of us are injured or arrested while going to or returning from work,” he said, noting that the commute to work is shaped by dangerous checkpoints, surveillance and the ever-present threat of arrest. The fragmentation of this community, like many others across the occupied West Bank, has also contributed to the weakening of social support networks. “Everything has become far. Even reaching basic services takes hours now,” one displaced resident living in Balqa told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of Israeli reprisals. “We are cut off from the places we used to depend on.” A displaced parent from Balqa, who also requested anonymity, highlighted the impacts on education: “My children used to walk to school easily. Now they wake up very early, and still sometimes cannot arrive, because the road is long and unsafe. “Some days, they simply stay home.” Tourists under siege Back in Ein al-Auja, where the cascading waterfall and surrounding mountain trails have long made it a natural attraction for visitors from within Palestine and beyond, it is not just locals who fear settler violence. Tourists have been targeted, too. In January 2023, an international group of hikers - including American, Italian and French tourists - were confronted by a group of armed settlers, who reportedly attacked them with clubs and pepper spray. ‘Policy to displace us’: How settler attacks are drying up the West Bank Read More » “We were pushed back towards the hills and essentially surrounded,” one Palestinian participant told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of Israeli repercussions. “We were beaten. Two women were injured, one Italian and one Palestinian, while the rest of the group tried to reach a safer distance.” It took hours for Israeli forces to arrive to secure the group’s exit, according to the Palestinian participant. Such incidents further chill an industry that has been deeply affected by the ongoing conflict. Tourism across the occupied West Bank took a significant hit after the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023, with official data showing millions of dollars in lost revenue as visitor numbers have plummeted . On weekends, the roads that once carried families, tour buses, and groups of hikers towards the Jordan Valley’s springs are noticeably emptier. Vendors who used to set up plastic chairs and tea stands along the way speak of long hours with no customers. “We used to wait for buses coming from the northern and southern West Bank every weekend, but now traffic has become almost nonexistent,” Muhammad Taha, a vendor from Jericho, told MEE. Today, he and his colleagues watch the landscape instead of serving it. Court battle Meanwhile, for the families forced to flee the Ein al-Auja area, a court battle has become their last hope. In a final attempt to halt their displacement, residents last year petitioned the High Court, calling on Israeli authorities to dismantle the illegal outposts encroaching on their land and to facilitate their return home. “We called for judicial intervention to stop the effective disappearance of our communities under settler violence and the expansion of surrounding pastoral outposts,” Hassan Mleihat, the general supervisor of al-Baidar, a local organisation that advocates for Bedouin rights, told MEE. In arguments before the court, the state denied the existence of any formal evacuation orders, arguing that there was no government policy in place to prevent residents from returning - despite the realities on the ground, which many Palestinians fear have made their expulsion irreversible. Residents displaced to al-Balqa are cut off from basic services (MEE/Majd Jawad) This past February, the court ordered Israeli authorities to help families return to their homes around Ein al-Auja spring, and to report back within 60 days on the actions it was taking to ensure their security. By April, with the deadline unmet, the petitioners asked the high court to compel the state to carry out its obligations. The state is still contesting the requirements, telling the court that there is no basis to station a permanent security force in the area. This case is by no means unique. Palestinian petitions demanding the prevention of evictions or the dismantling of outposts are rejected or stalled in Israeli courts as a matter of routine, with the state granted broad discretion over land management, even when long-term residents are proven to have lived there for decades. And by the time the Ein al-Auja case reached the court, the last families had already left. 'We defended our land alone, and we lost our land, our livestock and our water. If we do not stand together, we will all lose' - Haitham Rashaidh, displaced resident Back in Balqa, Rashaidh cites the importance of regional and global solidarity in the face of an ever-present and growing settler threat. “No one leaves their land willingly, and that is one of the hardest things in life,” he said. “But to stand alone is not enough. We defended our land alone, and we lost our land, our livestock and our water. If we do not stand together, we will all lose.” Resorting to the courts was not a strategic choice, Mleihat said, but rather a last-ditch attempt to assert the rights of Palestinians in the face of a rapidly changing reality outside the courtroom, where “the place had already been emptied”. Indeed, Ein al-Auja is no longer what it once was. The spring that flowed abundantly in years past has been reduced to intermittent streams of water. The soil is dry and cracked. The trees are fewer. The air is quieter. There are no children’s voices, no herds moving. Only the wind, passing through a place that was once alive. headline: Exclusive: UK Charity Commission criticises synagogue for hosting Great Israeli Real Estate Event
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 12:32 BST | Last update: 6 days 9 hours ago
article_body: The UK 's Charity Commission has criticised trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue in London for hosting a real estate event that promoted properties in illegal Israeli settlements in June, Middle East Eye can reveal. The charity regulator has also decided to review a recent decision to close a compliance case on the charity. The commission told MEE that "should any further concerns about the charity arise we will consider escalating our regulatory engagement". MEE understands that this internal review will be conducted by a senior officer in the commission. On 15 June MEE reported that properties in illegal Israeli settlements were advertised at the Great Israeli Real Estate Event. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The event's organisers later admitted properties in Israeli settlements were promoted at the synagogue, saying it happened "by mistake". A Charity Commission spokesperson told MEE: "We share concerns about the potential impact, including on public trust and confidence, of registered charities being seen to actively assist in the development or expansion of illegal settlements in Palestine. We are also clear that charity premises must not be misused. "Our initial compliance case found that despite their own misgivings about the event, and an organisation-wide decision to not permit it in their premises, the charity’s trustees allowed it to go ahead in one of its synagogues and did not put in place sufficient checks and controls to make sure the terms of that booking were kept." The spokesperson added: "The Commission is critical of the charity’s trustees for both decisions and have warned them to fix ongoing weaknesses in its governance. "While we cannot make decisions for trustees, we have set out clear expectations for where improvement is necessary to prevent any repeat of a similar a serious incident in the future. "That expectation stands while we carry out a review of our initial decision. Should any further concerns about the charity arise we will consider escalating our regulatory engagement." The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP), a UK-based legal group, had submitted a formal complaint to Britain's charity regulator on 15 June, requesting that it "open an urgent regulatory compliance case into Edgware United Synagogue" in connection to the event on 14 June. The complaint said it concerned "the use of charitable premises and charitable resources to facilitate a commercial event promoting property located in Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory (“oPt”) notwithstanding extensive public concern, legal warnings, media scrutiny and direct notification of serious legal, regulatory and reputational issues arising from the underlying activities." The complaint added that "charitable premises and charitable resources were made available for a commercial exhibition at which properties located in illegal Israeli settlements in occupied territory were promoted and marketed. "The trustees thereby permitted the charity’s facilities and reputation to be associated with, and used in support of, illegal activities which had already been identified as giving rise to significant legal, regulatory and reputational concerns." The Charity Commission responded to the complaint on 28 July. Its response, seen by MEE, said "we considered the concerns highlighted in the complaint, reviewed the available evidence, and engaged with the Charity's trustees. "Following our engagement, the Commission provided the trustees with regulatory advice and guidance under section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011." Section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011 gives the commission the power to issue formal regulatory advice to trustees of charities. "The trustees are expected to take account of and act on this advice going forward," the commission said. "The Commission has now closed its case into the Charity. Thank you for bringing these matters to our attention." 'Charities cannot ignore credible legal concerns' An ICJP spokesperson told MEE: "We welcome the Charity Commission's decision to review our complaint, but it is now crucial that such a review must meaningfully engage with the evidence we submitted, reconsider whether regulatory advice alone was an adequate response, and result in robust regulatory action where breaches or misconduct are identified. "The Commission's role is not simply to issue guidance after the fact, but to ensure that charities comply with their legal obligations and that the charitable sector is not used to facilitate or promote activity connected to illegal settlements." Exclusive: Illegal settlements promoted in London at Great Israeli Real Estate Event Read More » MEE has contacted the Edgware United Synagogue for comment. Then-Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper said in June that ministers had asked the Advertising Standards Authority to investigate the Great Israeli Real Estate Event. Harey Zahav developers participated in the event, promoting Kfar Eldad , an illegal West Bank settlement south of Bethlehem, and Teneh Omarim , another illegal settlement near Hebron. Tivuch Shelly, a major Israeli real estate agency, advertised property in Ma'ale Adummim – an occupied West Bank settlement – in a brochure at the event, describing an "exciting new project just 10 minutes from Jerusalem!". Jerusalem Real Estate, meanwhile, advertised projects in French Hill and Ramat Eshkol , illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem, in a brochure. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Palestinians reject Hamas disarmament before full Israeli withdrawal, poll finds
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 16:00 BST | Last update: 6 days 9 hours ago
article_body: More than 70 percent of Palestinians oppose Hamas disarming before Israel completely withdraws from the Gaza Strip, according to a new survey. The poll found that 72 percent believe Israel would resume its genocide in Gaza and refuse to withdraw fully if Hamas surrendered its weapons. The Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research published the findings on Wednesday, offering a detailed picture of Palestinian attitudes towards the future of Gaza, their political leadership and the prospect of Palestinian statehood. Even after Hamas accepted a proposal from Nickolay Mladenov, head of the US-backed "Board of Peace", 40 percent of respondents expect “the current situation to continue, with some continued killings”. Israel has rejected the US proposal. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Another 30 percent expect calm to prevail, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to take control and reconstruction to begin. Palestinians reject failed leadership Opposition to disarmament, however, does not translate into satisfaction with the Palestinian political establishment. The survey found that 79 percent want Palestinian Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas to resign. Support for his departure has remained between 79 and 89 percent during the past three years. Why the position of Palestinian health workers in Israel has grown increasingly precarious Read More » Meanwhile, 83 percent believe corruption exists within PA institutions, while 65 percent regard the authority as a burden rather than a national achievement. Marwan Barghouti, the prominent Palestinian leader who has been imprisoned by Israel for more than two decades, remains the preferred successor to Abbas. He received the support of 39 percent of respondents, followed by Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya with 16 percent, Mohammed Dahlan with 15 percent and Mustafa Barghouti with 6 percent. Among likely voters in a hypothetical presidential election, Marwan Barghouti would secure 54 percent, compared with 26 percent for Hayya and just 14 percent for Abbas. The findings also reflect the insecurity Palestinians experience under Israeli occupation and war. Seventy-six percent said they and their families feel unsafe, while only 23 percent said they feel safe. Little trust in US-backed Gaza plan Only 24 percent trust the Board of Peace overseeing the Trump administration’s Gaza plan, while 66 percent distrust it. In the occupied West Bank, 87 percent fear that Israel’s expanding settlements and outposts could cost them their homes or land. Palestinians also remain sceptical that removing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would produce meaningful change. While 34 percent believe Israeli policy would remain unchanged under an opposition government, 33 percent expect it to worsen and 28 percent believe it would improve. Despite the vast destruction of Gaza and accelerating Israeli annexation in the West Bank, 43 percent said the Palestinian people’s highest priority should remain securing a full Israeli withdrawal to the 1967 borders and establishing a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital. headline: ‘They’re all catastrophic’: The paediatric war wounds Dr Abu Sittah tries to heal in Lebanon
author: Gergana Krasteva
publication_date: Published date: 14 August 2026 07:52 BST | Last update: 5 days 15 hours ago
article_body: In his Beirut office, Dr Ghassan Abu Sittah is going over his operating list for the weekend: 11 children in total, with life-altering injuries from Israel ’s wars on Lebanon and Gaza . “There are two siblings who have shrapnel from the 2024 war that is now causing medical problems,” the prominent British-Palestinian plastic and reconstructive surgeon told Middle East Eye. “A boy with a partial amputation of his foot that needs reconstruction, from this war, and another boy with an amputation.” Dr Abu Sittah hopes to finish the stump so that the patient can begin prosthetic rehabilitation. Another boy with an elbow injury needs a prolonged reconstructive procedure to salvage his elbow joint. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “And so on, they are all like that… catastrophic,” the surgeon added. One of his patients is Fatima, 12, the youngest of three sisters who survived an Israeli strike on their house in the small mountain village of Libbaya, in the Bekaa Valley, on 7 March. The body of their fourth sister was blown to pieces in the attack, while their mother was seriously injured and later succumbed to her wounds in hospital. Fatima has already undergone multiple surgeries on her foot and jaw, which was dislocated in the blast. She also lost an eye. Now Abu Sittah must extract more shrapnel from her face and back to avoid further infection. Life‑altering war wounds Days earlier, MEE met with Fatima, her older sisters Malak, 16, and Kawthar, 14, in their hotel in the neighbourhood of Hamra, in the Lebanese capital, where they have been living while undergoing treatment at the American University of Beirut Medical Centre (AUBMC). Inside the two-bedroom apartment, the fragrant aroma of caramelised onion filled the air. Their father, Hassan, 60, was cooking moudardara, a Lebanese dish made of green lentils and rice. ‘It was like something was eating off her body because of all the shrapnel’ – Hassan, father of wounded children Still in their pyjamas, the three girls were sitting together making blue and pink beaded bracelets and phone straps, which they hoped to sell, while eating a bag of BBQ-flavoured crisps – their favourite snack. On the balcony, folded against the wall, was a wheelchair. Until recently, all three sisters needed it. Malak, the eldest, instinctively pulled down her lavender nightdress to hide the extensive burns covering her legs before her father gently reassured her that there was nothing to be ashamed of. The teenager suffered catastrophic wounds – that is, ones that have serious, long-term consequences, often causing permanent disfigurement, disability or loss of independence – including a traumatic brain injury, and multiple fractures. Months of physiotherapy have helped her regain some independence. “I can now go to the bathroom on my own, so I have improved a lot,” said Malak, who spent weeks in intensive care following the Israeli strike. Malak and her father Hassan in their hotel room in Beirut, Lebanon, on 13 July 2026 (Gergana Krasteva/MEE) Kawthar can now also move more freely with the help of a walker. A finger on her right hand and her left leg are still held in place by a rigid external frame and metal pins driven through the skin and into the bone. A scar also stretches across half her face. “All three have progressed a lot, but they still have a long road ahead and it can take a long time,” Hassan said. He explained that each girl faces different challenges. “Kawthar’s leg still needs great improvement. And Malak, only her left arm and face were not injured. She still has a lot of bruising from the needles. And her back still has a lot of injuries. “For two and a half months, someone had to help her move because of all the broken bones in her back. It was very difficult. We always had to turn her on her sides as she was going through a lot of pain. Her skin was all shredded,” he said. The father explained that doctors had to transplant skin from the back of her leg to the front, and because her thigh bone was missing, she required a graft. “Fatima still has to have her eye, teeth and foot fixed. She suffered a lot of infections, which is normal because the wounds were exposed,” he added. “It was like something was eating off her body because of all the shrapnel.” None of the girls wished to discuss the weeks they spent in hospital. ‘Wars keep happening’ However, giggles filled the room when Hassan talked playfully about their different personalities. As the eldest daughter, Malak is naturally more responsible and sympathetic than her siblings, while Kawthar is pensive and stubborn. Fatima was described as “very rambunctious”. For a moment, the apartment felt like any other family home – three sisters making bracelets together, eating crisps and teasing one another, while their father was telling anecdotes about their life before the war. ‘We used to love our lives before […] ​​We will certainly go back, carry on, and love life. But, of course, things won’t be the same as before’ – Malak, wounded child Then Hassan began to talk about the day he found his daughters among the mountain of rubble that their home was reduced to. Their smiles quickly vanished. His youngest, Zainab, was missing, and her remains were never recovered. On the mantelpiece behind the girls’ beds was a portrait of the child, the frame decorated with blooming flowers. “There is no point in a nice picture,” the father said, angrily. “People tell me that my daughter is in heaven. I want her here, with me, not in heaven. I raised her for 10 years.” Hassan said his brother was killed the same way during the 1982 war, when Israel unleashed a major military invasion of southern Lebanon – a painful family memory that has resurfaced with the death of his daughter. Past and present are separated by 44 years, but not by much else, and he is still grappling with making sense of this multigenerational tragedy. A history of Israel’s invasions of Lebanon Read More » The family had spent years building a life in the village. Hassan’s dream was to build four apartments, stacked on top of each other, for his daughters to always be close to one another. Reflecting on his life, the father told MEE he never once considered leaving his homeland, until the fatal attack. “Kawthar said no. She doesn’t want to live elsewhere,” he said. “It is nice in Lebanon, but you need a future. And wars keep happening. I am 60, so I have lived my life. I don’t know how long I have left.” Malak, Kawthar and Fatima are yearning to leave Beirut and return to the Bekaa Valley to see their friends, even though life will be vastly different from what they recall. Israeli hostilities and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon and Israeli officials have repeatedly said the military will not withdraw from land it has occupied during the offensive. “We used to love our lives before,” the eldest said, with a weight in her voice that did not match someone so young in life. “We were all good students in school… ​​We will certainly go back, carry on, and love life. But, of course, things won’t be the same as before,” she added. “We want to be a support system to each other and want to go back and divide the work in the house and be like our mum would want us to be.” Children face years of surgery The three sisters are among the over 400 children in Lebanon that have been treated by the Ghassan Abu Sittah Children’s Fund, established by the surgeon in January 2024 to help provide medical treatment in Gaza and Lebanon. For decades, Abu Sittah, who has his main residence in London, has operated under fire, while treating the youngest, most fragile victims of war during the First Intifada in Gaza, the Gulf War, in Yemen and Syria . ‘Being a spectator is probably the worst thing that you can do when you are watching this horror unfold’ - Dr Ghassan Abu Sittah, surgeon The scenes in Lebanon – and the paediatric cases – he says are “almost identical” to what he witnessed in Gaza at the onset of Israel’s genocidal war in 2023. Israel has killed more than 73,300 Palestinians in Gaza since 7 October 2023 – including more than 1,250 after a ceasefire was announced in October – with thousands believed to be dead under the rubble; and more than 4,330 people have been killed in Lebanon since 2 March. Combined, the Gaza and Lebanon fronts have seen over 185,000 people wounded by Israel. “These children were wounded when Israel bombed their homes… so all of their injuries are either a direct result of the blast wave – shrapnel injuries, burns and tearing of tissue – or they were pulled under the rubble and they have crush injuries,” Abu Sittah told MEE. “And you rarely get a child with a single injury. It is usually a head injury and a fracture and a burn and other things, and they are all severe.” All of his patients have suffered “life-altering” injuries, leaving them with permanent disability or deformity. He estimated that around 80 percent required intensive care. Saving a child’s life is only the first stage. His work then turns to reconstruction. On average, Abu Sittah says that children will require 12 to 16 surgeries until they reach adulthood. Palestinian doctor Ghassan Abu Sittah wins misconduct case Read More » “As a child grows, we need to re-intervene because their body increases in size disproportionately. Scarred and injured parts of the body do not increase in size at the same rate,” he explained. Despite the US-brokered ceasefire on 16 April, the scale of injuries confronting medical teams in Lebanon, where the healthcare system is heavily privatised and under severe strain, has continued to grow. For children like Malak, Kawthar and Fatima, a ceasefire cannot erase what has already happened, nor does it necessarily mean that danger has disappeared. Abu Sittah says the cumulative effect of working amid such suffering is hard to process. “I deal with it by seeing it within the bigger picture and by being grateful that I have ended up in a junction in my life that I am able to not feel paralysed and not feel like a spectator,” he added. “Being a spectator is probably the worst thing that you can do when you are watching this horror unfold.” Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Pentagon tells Congress US killed 153 civilians in Yemen air strikes
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 20:18 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: The US killed and wounded hundreds of Yemeni civilians during its attacks on the country last year, according to an internal US Department of War assessment shared with Congress. The US killed 153 civilians and wounded 243, the Pentagon said in a 12-page report that was sent to the Senate Armed Services Committee on Monday and reported by several news sites in the US. US President Donald Trump ordered the American military to begin bombing the Houthis in March 2025. The attacks came in response to Houthi strikes on vessels in the Red Sea, which the group said were in solidarity with besieged Palestinians in Gaza. The report detailed several specific strikes that the Pentagon said “more likely than not” caused civilian deaths and injuries. The report noted a 6 April attack on Sanaa that killed five civilians and wounded 25 others. The report also noted a 17 April US attack on Hodeidah that killed at least 80 civilians. In a June report, Human Rights Watch said the attack should be investigated as a war crime. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters “The US government’s decision to strike Ras Issa Port, a critical entry point for aid in Yemen, while hundreds of workers were present demonstrates a callous disregard for civilians’ lives,” Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch, said. A US air strike at the end of April also killed at least 68 African migrants in Yemen 's northwestern province of Saada. Saudi Arabia mulls military escalation in response to Houthi threats Read More » The report said that there are 15 incidents related to the air strikes that are under review by the Pentagon. The Trump administration’s decision to attack the Houthis was overshadowed initially by the SignalGate leaks. Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg was mistakenly added to a Signal group chat that included 19 senior US officials planning the military campaign, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, United Nations ambassador Mike Waltz, and envoy Steve Witkoff. The chat offered a rare window into the Trump administration’s planning for the attacks and deliberations, which focused on complaining about Europe and Egypt not remunerating Washington. The Houthis endured more than 1,000 US strikes. The campaign was called off in May 2025 before Trump visited the Gulf. Middle East Eye revealed that Saudi Arabia pressed the US to end the attacks before the president’s visit. Several regional officials told MEE that the US’s campaign did serious damage to the Houthis' military arsenal, but the impact proved fleeting. The group has resumed its attacks in the Red Sea and expanded them to target Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved.
