headline: US rights groups sue Trump administration over ICC sanctions
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 21:49 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday for its sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). In a statement, the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute called the sanctions "blatantly illegal". They said they are being forced "to curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of... First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act", given that anyone who appears to associate with ICC cases or officials could now face legal repercussions. Just days after he assumed power in late January 2025, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order to sanction the ICC over its investigations into top Israeli officials. British barrister Karim Khan, who was the ICC's chief prosecutor, was the only person named as a sanctioned individual. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters He has since been removed through a member states' vote, albeit due to sexual assault allegations. Khan has denied them. The executive order followed a White House visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023. Netanyahu and his then defence minister, Yoav Gallant, were issued arrest warrants in November 2024, alongside three Hamas leaders, who have since been killed by Israel. All non-US individuals and their family members who assist in ICC investigations of US citizens or allies fall under the sanctions order. Their assets are frozen, they cannot use the international banking system, and they cannot enter the US. This is not the first lawsuit in response to US sanctions. In July, advocates for Palestinian rights in the US filed a lawsuit in a New York City federal court, seeking an injunction to stop the Trump administration's enforcement of sanctions against groups or individuals liaising with the ICC. Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, as well as the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), said they felt compelled to immediately go to court after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in an opinion piece that the US was willing to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick". 'No basis in fact' The lawsuit insists that Trump's powers to sanction the ICC "are based on a pseudo national emergency that has no basis in fact", the groups said on Tuesday. ICC states decision on Karim Khan ‘inherently political’, says leading criminal law expert Read More » "The sanctions have stopped the four plaintiff organizations from continuing or undertaking activities like representing victims of war crimes as legal counsel, making legal and policy submissions to the ICC, and collaborating with the sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups to undertake litigation, coordinate advocacy campaigns, research human rights violations, or provide humanitarian aid," the statement said. Last year the Trump administration also sanctioned several Palestinian human rights organisations, many of which receive legal and financial support from US experts and donors. It also sanctioned officials in the Palestinian Authority (PA) and Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) over their work taking Israel to international courts. According to the State Department, the unnamed officials were “undermining the prospects for peace”. In his executive order, Trump said the ICC has "engaged in illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel". The US and Israel are not state parties to the Rome Statute, which is the treaty that established the ICC in The Hague in 2002. Both states have opposed the court’s investigation into alleged Israeli crimes in Palestine , launched by the ICC’s previous prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, in 2021. The court’s jurisdiction was based on the accession of the State of Palestine to the Rome Statute in 2015. That means the court can investigate Israeli individuals for crimes committed in occupied Palestine, which includes the Gaza Strip, the West Bank and East Jerusalem. But Israel and the US have challenged the court’s jurisdiction, saying they do not recognise Palestine as a state, and that Israel is best placed to investigate itself under the principle of complementarity as set out in Article 17 of the Rome Statute. Trump’s order reiterated this view and described the arrest warrants as an abuse of power. Dismantling the ICC Last month, Rubio said the Trump administration is working to "dismantle the [International Criminal Court] brick by brick". “The ICC’s interfering with American military and law enforcement operations isn’t just only a grave overreach of its purported authorities. It would mean the death of the US as a sovereign and independent nation,” Rubio wrote in an opinion article published by The Wall Street Journal. He said that Americans likely don't know the names of the judges, prosecutors or presidents of the international court, and that they "shouldn't have to", while accusing the ICC of waging a war against the US. 'Textbook infringement': Palestine advocacy groups sue for immediate halt to Trump's ICC sanctions Read More » Rubio’s criticism noted "bipartisan" opposition to the court, which was founded in 2002 in response to genocides and atrocities in war zones such as Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia. Rubio made no direct mention of the outstanding arrest warrant issued for Netanyahu and Gallant in his article. The European Union warned earlier this year that Trump's order has the potential to seriously affect the ICC's work in all investigations, not just on Palestine. The court is currently investigating alleged crimes in 16 situations , including Darfur, Ukraine, Venezuela, Afghanistan, and Myanmar. But also last month, the new Venezuelan government - effectively run by Rubio himself from afar - withdrew from the ICC. In a post on X , the US State Department hailed the move as marking a "partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC". It pointed to an investigation by the court into former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, who was abducted from the South American country during a US military assault in January 2026, saying it had produced "no result". "The ICC has instead wasted its resources on investigating and charging persons from countries that have competent, independent judicial systems and which never submitted to the jurisdiction of the court," the statement read. "This is blatant overreach, political bias and selective enforcement," it said, adding that the court is "neither credible, independent, nor legitimate". Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Libya reels from assassination, oil strikes and central bank turmoil
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 12:24 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Libya was plunged into fresh turmoil this week after a car bomb killed eastern military intelligence chief Fawzi al-Mansouri in Benghazi, drone attacks struck the country’s largest operational oil refinery and the central bank governor resigned from his post. Mansouri, the military intelligence chief for forces controlling eastern Libya, was leaving a mosque on Monday night when an explosive device attached to his vehicle detonated, the Libyan National Army (LNA) said on Tuesday. Khaled Haftar , the son of the LNA renegade commander Khalifa Haftar who controls eastern Libya, said authorities had opened an investigation, adding that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic". "Terrorism is a project targeting the entire region, not just Libya," the statement added. While no group has taken responsibility for the attack, Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, told Middle East Eye that "it is a reminder that security in eastern Libya remains fragile despite the domination of Khalifa Haftar’s LNA”. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The killing also challenges the Haftar family’s efforts to present eastern Libya as stable after years of conflict. The LNA said it would "not cease fighting terrorism and will continue our struggle for the stability and security of Libya, as well as for the unification of its institutions". 'Drone attacks on oil infrastructure in Zawiya, a car bomb assassination in Benghazi and the resignation of one of Libya’s top officials underline how quickly Libya’s fragile political and security situation can deteriorate' - Hamish Kinnear, analyst The assassination came as emergency crews fought a major fire at the Zawiya oil refinery, west of Tripoli, following a drone attack on Monday evening. It was the third strike on the facility in two days. Libya’s National Oil Corporation said a drone directly struck a tank holding about 4.5 million litres of fuel. The resulting fire caused the tank to collapse and prompted the company to warn that further attacks could force it to suspend operations. Emergency services reported no serious injuries, although medics treated several people for smoke inhalation. Zawiya is Libya’s largest operational refinery and can process 120,000 barrels of oil per day. “No group has claimed responsibility for the drone strikes, but they came amid an armed confrontation between rival militias in Zawiya and are likely intended as pressure on the Government of National Unity headed by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid al-Dbeibah,” Kinnear said. The turmoil deepened after a letter attributed to Central Bank of Libya Governor Naji Issa circulated widely on social media and local news outlets. 'We've run out of earthly solutions': Inside Libya's electricity crisis Read More » Addressed to the heads of the House of Representatives and High State Council, the letter said Issa would not remain in his post. He declined to explain his decision, citing the “sensitivity” of the reasons. “Drone attacks on oil infrastructure in Zawiya, a car bomb assassination in Benghazi and the resignation of one of Libya’s top officials [in a space of 24 hours] underline how quickly Libya’s fragile political and security situation can deteriorate,” said Kinnear. Libya remains divided between the internationally recognised government in Tripoli and an eastern administration backed by Haftar. The hydrocarbon-rich country produces more than 1.3 million barrels of oil per day but continues to suffer prolonged electricity cuts. Blackouts have triggered protests in Tripoli, Zawiya, Misrata and other cities, where demonstrators have demanded reliable power and called for Dbeibah to resign. “Libya’s energy infrastructure often becomes the target in these confrontations, as it is the easiest means by which pressure can be placed on political leaders and concessions demanded,” Kinnear said. headline: Palestinian students and staff sue Columbia University over discrimination
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 19:01 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: A group of current and former Palestinian students and staff have sued Columbia University, accusing the Ivy League school of discriminating against Palestinians and targeting pro-Palestinian activism on campus. The lawsuit, filed in New York State Supreme Court this week, alleges that Columbia subjected Palestinian students, faculty and staff to unequal treatment following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023 and the ensuing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza perpetrated by Israel. According to the complaint , Columbia "actively participated in and amplified" what the plaintiffs describe as racially, ethnically and politically motivated targeting of Palestinians. Mahmoud Khalil, the Palestinian activist and former Columbia graduate student, also highlighted the lawsuit on X, saying Palestinian students were suing the university over alleged discrimination in its response to the protests in support of Palestinians and Gaza. Proud of my fellow Palestinian students and faculty suing @Columbia for its abhorrent discrimination against Palestinians and anyone who stands with us. Columbia chose to reward those who attacked us and to silence its own community while Israel bombed and starved Gaza. We will… https://t.co/XPtRQusYFJ — Mahmoud Khalil | محمود خليل (@mahmoudkhalel) August 10, 2026 The plaintiffs say the university failed to adequately protect Palestinian members of its community from harassment while subjecting pro-Palestinian activists to "unfair and biased disciplinary hearings". New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Columbia declined to comment on the pending litigation, according to local media, and did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Among the allegations is that Columbia hired private investigators to surveil students involved in the March 2024 "Resistance 101" event. Six students were subsequently suspended and evicted from university housing, according to the lawsuit. The filing also accuses the university of failing to adequately respond to alleged physical attacks against Palestinians, including incidents in which students had their keffiyehs forcibly removed and the January 2024 spraying of a foul-smelling substance at a pro-Palestinian demonstration. The lawsuit also challenges Columbia's decision to call New York City police onto campus to dismantle pro-Palestinian protest encampments and arrest demonstrators in 2024. The plaintiffs include lecturer and former anthropology student Hadeel Assali; former lecturer Bahia Munem; PhD student Mahdi Sabbagh; 2025 graduate and former student organiser Maryam Alwan; and Layla Saliba, who graduated from Columbia's School of Social Work in 2025. Saliba was among Palestinian students who had previously accused Columbia of discrimination in a federal civil rights complaint filed in 2024. At the time, she said Palestinian students were being treated poorly and called on the university to recognise anti-Palestinian racism. Columbia under pressure The case comes after years of controversy over Columbia's handling of protests against Israel's war on Gaza. Columbia University student workers’ union withdraws Israel divestment demand Read More » In July 2025, Columbia reached a deal with the Trump administration to resolve federal investigations into alleged violations of anti-discrimination law and restore federal research funding that had been frozen by the government. Under the agreement, the university agreed to pay $200m to the US government and another $21m to settle Equal Employment Opportunity Commission investigations concerning allegations of antisemitism against Jewish employees. Columbia did not admit wrongdoing or agree with the government's conclusion that it had violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. The university also settled a separate lawsuit brought by Jewish plaintiffs in February 2026 alleging that Columbia had failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from antisemitism. Palestinian activists and free-speech groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly accused Columbia of disproportionately punishing opposition to Israel. Reuters reported that students have faced arrests, suspensions, expulsions and degree revocations during the university's crackdown on pro-Palestinian protests. The new lawsuit seeks monetary damages under New York City's Human Rights Law, which prohibits discrimination and harassment on grounds including race and national origin. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Turkey's cross party Kurdish peace coalition makes history with PKK clemency law
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 12:07 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: It would have been unimaginable three years ago to see lawmakers from Turkey's ruling coalition pose in parliament alongside pro-Kurdish MPs and other opposition politicians after voting to grant partial clemency to members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). But that's exactly what has happened after a historic vote. For the first time in Turkey's modern history, the government introduced legislation establishing a framework for resolving its conflict with the PKK - and potentially ending nearly four decades of fighting. The PKK has waged a guerrilla campaign against the Turkish state since the early 1980s, resulting in the deaths of thousands of civilians and members of the security forces. The group initially sought independence and later greater autonomy for Turkey's Kurds. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Following two years of negotiations with imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan, the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and its coalition partner, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), led by Devlet Bahceli, decided to pursue an end to the conflict. The process was set in motion by Bahceli in a speech in October 2024, when he emerged as an unprecedented advocate for peace. His address was startling not only because he said he would tolerate Ocalan appearing before parliament, after having repeatedly called for his execution, but also because Bahceli's MHP, a right-wing Turkish nationalist party, had long been among the strongest opponents of everything the PKK represented. After months of work by a parliamentary committee addressing the Kurdish question, as well as hours of negotiations with Ocalan, PKK commanders in northern Iraq's Qandil Mountains and leaders in exile in Europe, the legislation was introduced in parliament last week. It was quickly ratified on Monday. Ahmet Davutoglu, former PM turned Erdogan critic, ends political career Read More » The law allows former PKK members who did not commit violent crimes, such as intentional homicide, to receive pardons. It also permits prisoners convicted of nonviolent offenses to be released. The most surprising aspect of the episode was not that parliament approved the law, but the breadth of the alliance supporting it. Alongside the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and the MHP, the legislation was supported by the secularist Republican People's Party (CHP); smaller right-wing and Islamist parties such as the New Welfare Party, or Yeniden Refah; the Felicity Party, or Saadet; and the liberal Democracy and Progress Party, known as DEVA. The Free Cause Party, or Huda Par - an Islamist Kurdish party and an opponent of the PKK - also voted in favour. Socialists in the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) and several smaller left-wing parties also supported the measure. Limited CHP opposition Imprisoned Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu backed the legislation in a statement, while New Party, or Yeni Parti Chairman Ozgur Ozel, who now represents the main opposition inside the country after breaking away from the CHP, publicly expressed his support. The parties supporting the law have differing concerns and reservations. Ozel allowed New Party lawmakers to vote according to their own judgement, and many opposed the legislation. Nevertheless, the broad coalition produced an unprecedented level of parliamentary support, with 468 of parliament's 592 members voting in favour. Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu in shouting match with judge as trial begins Read More » In his parliamentary address, Ozel said he would support the law despite the government's crackdown on opposition mayors across the country and its support for an effort to remove him from the CHP leadership. "We have the greatest right to say no to this law. But we are also the ones who will not put this right before peace," he said in parliament on Monday. "We have not, and will not, put our anger before the future of the nation." Ozel added that his party would not stand in the way of peace. "We will pave the way for peace so that another mother does not have to embrace her son's coffin," he said. Under the legislation, the PKK would first be required to lay down its weapons and demonstrate to Turkish authorities that it was upholding its side of the agreement. The PKK and its affiliated groups would also be expected to end illicit activities, including the smuggling of counterfeit goods and drugs. The repatriation of PKK members who did not commit violent crimes could then begin in September, initiating a six-month implementation period. Former PKK members who failed to apply within the specified timeframe would no longer be eligible to benefit from the law. Turkish intelligence would monitor the process and prepare a report confirming that the PKK had disarmed. The report would then be submitted to the National Security Council, formally initiating the next stage of the process. The law would cover PKK members in all locations, including Europe. Potential sentences based solely on PKK membership would automatically be dropped on the grounds that their membership ended when the organisation dissolved, paving the way for former members to return to Turkey. It remains unclear which components of the PKK - whether based in Europe, Iraq, Syria or the organisation's headquarters in the Qandil Mountains - would seek to take advantage of the law. Some convicted PKK members who have already served 25 years in prison could also qualify for relief and become eligible for release. The legislation would not grant Ocalan a formal role. However, once the law is enacted and implemented, officials expect him to receive greater freedom in his living arrangements on Imrali Island. This could include more comfortable accommodations and increased access to journalists and opinion leaders, enabling him to communicate more effectively with the public. During his speech, Ozel also warned that resolving the Kurdish question could pave the way for a new alliance between Erdogan and the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), potentially enabling Erdogan to seek another term. Although Erdogan is serving his second term, a provision in the constitution would allow him to run again if parliament voted to hold early elections. With the support of DEM and several smaller parties, Erdogan's AKP could potentially secure the parliamentary majority required to call an early election in 2028. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . subheadline: Landmark legislation granting limited clemency to PKK members wins unprecedented support across the political spectrum, opening a path to ending four decades of conflict

headline: Polls open in crunch Clacton contest between Reform's Nigel Farage and Count Binface
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 13 August 2026 09:46 BST | Last update: 6 days 15 hours ago
article_body: Voters are heading to the polls on Thursday in the seaside town of Claton, on England's east coast, to vote in one of the most unusual by-elections in recent British history. The two main candidates are Nigel Farage, the leader of the right-wing Reform UK party, which was until recently dominating in the national polls, and Count Binface , a man dressed as a bin. Farage was elected MP for Clacton in 2024 but resigned last month in order to trigger the by-election. Farage's decision to stand was a response to a controversy over finances. A parliamentary investigation had been launched into a gift of £5m ($6.74m), which Farage had received from Thailand-based cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne and did not disclose. The investigation was suspended when Farage resigned on 7 July but is expected to resume if he re-enters parliament. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Farage has repeatedly insisted the gift, received before he was elected MP, was not linked to his political career. "Let me be absolutely clear: I have done nothing wrong," he said when he resigned. "I have decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions." The next day Farage added : "The media are judging me to be a dishonest person, so it is only fair to say to the voters, 'you judge'." But all the main political parties decided to boycott the by-election, with Labour branding it a "political stunt". How Nigel Farage and Reform fell in love with the UAE Read More » This means that Farage's main rival is Count Binface, a joke candidate who regularly stands in high-profile by-elections around the country. Binface's campaign promises to build "at least one affordable house", "nationalise" the singer Adele and "cut your taxes and raise everyone else's". Three candidates from the Monster Raving Loony Party are also standing, as well as numerous independents and far-right activist Laurence Fox, representing the Reclaim Party, which he leads. In total there are 34 candidates standing. Farage is expected to win by a landslide, but he may face derision if Binface receives more than 5 percent of the vote, which would be highly unusual for a joke candidate. Reform had been leading the national polls for over a year until Andy Burnham succeeded Keir Starmer as prime minister last month. Since then, Labour has enjoyed a bounce in the polls and Reform's leader has been seen as being on the back foot. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt's inclusion in Mecca agreement, sources say
author: Faisal Edroos
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 17:00 UTC | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt joining the security pact signed with Turkey and Pakistan last week, despite Ankara's push for Cairo to be included, three Saudi sources familiar with the discussions told Middle East Eye. One of the sources, a former senior adviser to the Saudi monarchy, said Riyadh did not want Egypt to join the agreement "at least for now". All three sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the issue, said the Saudi position was driven by a growing frustration with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's government and a belief in Riyadh that Egypt no longer offered the strategic or military value it once did. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which was signed in the Holy Muslim city of Mecca on Friday, commits Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to regard an armed attack against any one of the three countries as an attack against all three. Saudi officials have described it as a mechanism to strengthen joint defence capabilities, despite the agreement being vague on operational mechanisms, specific triggers, and how joint military assistance would actually be executed in a crisis. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters According to the sources, the Saudi decision to oppose Egypt's entry was due to simmering tensions between Riyadh and Cairo. They said the kingdom was the biggest financial supporter of Sisi's government after he seized power in a 2013 coup, initially spending around $25b to shore up Cairo's flagging economy, but Riyadh had become frustrated by what it regards as a lack of reciprocal support on key security issues. One of the sources pointed to Egypt's "minimal and unreliable" role in Saudi Arabia's lengthy war with Yemen's Houthis and its position during the US and Israeli war on Iran . They also cited growing unease over Cairo's "subordination" to the United Arab Emirates, specifically after the fallout between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi over the latter's support for Southern Yemeni separatist groups that "threaten Saudi's national security and interests". 'Egypt has always been a dependent on us, on the US, and it does not give back, it just takes and takes with no return' - Former senior adviser to the Saudi monarchy Two of the sources noted that while Egypt sent air defence systems and fighter jets to Abu Dhabi in response to Iranian attacks, and Sisi visited UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed more than once during the war, no such steps were taken towards Saudi Arabia. They concluded that Riyadh had become increasingly alarmed by Sisi's alignment with Abu Dhabi. The sources said this was also due to Riyadh seeing several Emirati policies as running against Egypt's own strategic interests. These include the UAE’s involvement in Somaliland, its strategic relationship with Israel, its support for Ethiopia during disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and its backing of the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. One of the sources said that Cairo's continued engagement with Abu Dhabi had deepened doubts in Riyadh about Egypt's reliability as a strategic partner. Another source described the relationship under Sisi as increasingly one in which Saudi Arabia sees Egypt as "dependent" on Gulf support rather than as a reliable partner. The former senior adviser said Egypt had historically been dependent on the kingdom, the United States and other outside powers while providing little in return. "Egypt has always been a dependent on us, on the US, and it does not give back, it just takes and takes with no return," the adviser said. Turkey wanted Egypt in the pact On Saturday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan suggested that Cairo was a "natural partner" for Ankara and that there was no reason it could not eventually become part of the alliance once technical issues were resolved. Several Turkish sources subsequently told MEE that Ankara had made considerable efforts to include Egypt in the treaty and had formally proposed its participation. However, once it became clear that Cairo was not prepared to join, the other countries decided to proceed without it, according to the Turkish sources. The Saudi sources, however, disputed the suggestion that Egypt itself had rejected the pact. The former senior adviser, who is still close to the country's decision-making, described it as "laughable" to suggest Cairo had decided not to participate. Why Egypt held back from joining Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan's defence pact Read More » "The matter of fact is, Sisi would have been eager to join so he can reap the financial gains of this agreement, as he usually does," the adviser said. The adviser said Saudi decision-makers had serious concerns about Sisi’s loyalty and did not believe he could be trusted in the same way as the Turkish and Pakistani leaderships. "We understand that the Turks wanted Egypt to be included, and understand why," he said. "Maybe in the future, if we see that there is change or improvement." The other sources said that Turkey and Pakistan offered more to the alliance militarily than Egypt. Turkey has an increasingly sophisticated defence industry, while Pakistan has an established weapons manufacturing sector and a large standing military. In contrast, the sources said Egypt's military manufacturing capacity is concentrated heavily on civilian production and does not offer the same level of advanced defence technology. "The role of the military should be to invest in its military manufacturing capabilities, rather than busy itself in investing and managing food factories," one of the sources said. They also questioned the combat readiness and effectiveness of the Egyptian armed forces. The sources said the decision was therefore not simply about Egypt's political alignment but about what Riyadh believes Cairo could tangibly contribute to a new regional security architecture. Egypt's diminishing role The Saudi assessment comes amid a broader debate over Egypt's diminishing role in the region. The Economist reported on Monday that Egypt, which had long presented itself as a pillar of the regional order, had been "sidelined as a mediator and military power". For decades, Egypt was a central military partner for Gulf states, including during the US-led coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991. In contrast to now, where the sources pointed out that Kuwait is now more keen to join the Makkah agreement rather than having the military alliance it once had with Egypt for its protection. But the Saudi sources argued that under Sisi, Egypt had become increasingly dependent on outside financial support while offering less in return on major regional security issues. The former senior adviser said the kingdom regarded its relationships with Ankara, despite being turbulent in recent years, as being more reliable than its relationship with Cairo. Why the Mecca Agreement is a necessary show of force Read More » "The decision makers in the leadership have serious concerns about Sisi's loyalty," the adviser said. "He is simply seen that he cannot be trusted, and rightly so." The adviser contrasted that with Saudi Arabia’s relationships with "the Pakistanis and the Turkish brothers". Saudi social media has also reflected opposition to Egypt's inclusion in the pact, with several accounts supportive of the kingdom’s leadership posting material suggesting Cairo was not wanted in the agreement. The anonymous social media account @Columbuos , widely believed to belong to Saud al-Qahtani, a former senior aide to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is still considered to be close to the young royal, echoed this sentiment. "The door of the alliance is not open to those who only want to address their problems and benefit from it without participating in the same secure mission for the region," he said. "Whoever wants to join must share the same common interests of the three countries. "The era of illusory entitlements, charity, and one-sided giving has passed, and the time of 'my fate alone' has ended, giving way to the phase of 'our single fate'," he added. Despite this, all three sources stressed that the agreement did not necessarily close the door to Egypt joining in the future, but Riyadh’s position was that Cairo should remain on the outside for now. headline: Israel and Venezuela restore diplomatic relations after years of severed ties
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 11 August 2026 22:11 BST | Last update: 1 week 1 day ago
article_body: Israel and Venezuela announced the restoration of official diplomatic relations after 17 years of severed ties in mutual statements published on Tuesday. The rapprochement comes under acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, who has realigned Venezuela towards the US since she took office in January, after the US abduction and imprisonment of then-President Nicolas Maduro. US President Donald Trump has boasted of running Venezuela following the capture of Maduro. In a statement posted on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said that the two countries had "agreed to establish a coordination mechanism that will enable the provision of consular services to citizens of both countries". A similar statement was posted by Venezuela's foreign minister, Felix Plasencia Gonzalez. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Venezuela had long been one of a slim list of non-Muslim majority states with no official relations with Israel. The Bolivarian Republic first severed ties in 2009 under leftist President Hugo Chavez in response to mass civilian casualties during Israel's first major war on Gaza, known in Israel as Operation Cast Lead. Official relations between the two countries remained frozen for decades after Chavez was succeeded by Maduro, who instead deepened Venezuela's diplomatic ties with both the Palestinian Authority and Iran . A wave in Latin America Tuesday's statement comes after months of unofficial ties between the two states since Maduro's abduction by the US. In February, Bloomberg reported that Venezuelan oil had been shipped to Israel for the first time in decades, prompting denials from Venezuela's minister of information. Why is Latin America becoming a breeding ground for 'fanatics of Israel'? Read More » Israel later provided Venezuela with relief and assistance after a devastating double earthquake hit the country in June, killing over 6,000. Statements from both Israel and Venezuela each touted the "importance of the connection between the State of Israel and the Jewish community of Venezuela". There are around 6,000 Jews in Venezuela, according to the World Jewish Congress. Israel has welcomed a wave of support from Latin American states in recent months amid the election of several right-wing leaders across the continent, and in spite of Israel's genocide in Gaza , where over 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Venezuela's announcement comes the same day as neighbouring Colombia recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, territory that is widely regarded as part of Syria under international law. Colombia's new far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced plans to normalise relations with Israel and open a controversial embassy in Jerusalem last month. Last week, the administration of Honduras' right-wing president, Nasry Asfura Zablah, also announced it had returned its ambassador to Israel, having withdrawn the representation amid the genocide in Gaza. Zablah, along with the pro-Israel Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, is of Palestinian descent. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: US strengthens military presence in breakaway Puntland amid battle for Red Sea
author: Victoria Amani Mwaniki Kishoiyian
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 17:58 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: In early August, the commander of US Special Operations Command Africa, Major General Claude Tudor, signed a deal with the president of Somalia’s northeastern, semi-autonomous Puntland State, Saeed Abdullahi Deni. The two agreed to expand the American military base in Bosaso, a port city on the Gulf of Aden. According to a brief statement circulated by the Puntland Government of Somalia, the expansion is essential to “improve operations against terrorism and to help protect maritime security”. “The Puntland state remains committed to fighting terrorism and any threat that could harm the security, stability, and development of Puntland, Somalia, and the Horn of Africa,” the statement reads. The US has previously utilised a United Arab Emirates-built air base in Bosaso primarily for Puntland’s Maritime Police Force (PMPF) , a regional force backed by the UAE to combat piracy and trained, in part, by the notorious US private military contractor Xe, formerly known as Blackwater. Its regional administration and lack of military licensure made the Bosaso Air Base and the PMPF a direct violation of UN Security Council Resolution 1425 and the UN arms embargo on Somalia, prior to the UN Security Council lifting the embargo in late 2023. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters In October, Middle East Eye investigated the Bosaso Air Base, located next to the Bosaso International Airport. It identified military equipment from the UAE, namely “a radar facility, fortified ammunition depots, a dedicated cargo area for IL-76 heavy transport aircraft, a field hospital, a vehicle storage yard that houses dozens of pickup trucks, aircraft hangars and the original hangar of the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF)”. How UAE bases arming Sudan's RSF support US 'grey ops' in Somalia Read More » Much of the weapons and heavy logistical materials in transit from the UAE at Bosaso are destined for Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which have been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces since April 2023 and are accused of committing war crimes and acts of genocide. The expanded US military presence appears closely tied to the widening terrain of the Iran war, as access to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait , the water body uniting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, grows more perilous. It may also suggest Washington’s desire to wage operations against Yemen’s Ansar Allah, commonly known as the Houthis. The deal in Puntland occurred in the wake of the Houthis’ declaration of a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports, a retaliatory measure after Saudi strikes on Yemen’s Sanaa International Airport. Djibouti holds the largest US permanent base in Africa, Camp Lemonnier, but its government is stringent and self-preservational, denying Washington permission to strike Yemen from its base because of concerns that it would endanger its people. Peripheral moves The Puntland deal is legally murky, as it bypasses the US-backed Federal Government of Somalia. Puntland has refused to recognise the federal system after Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud introduced constitutional changes in 2024, concentrating power in Mogadishu. Between June and July, there were at least seven armed clashes between forces of the Federal Government of Somalia and the Puntland administration. US Africa Command (Africom) officials also met with leadership in Jubaland, a federal member state in southern Somalia that doesn’t acknowledge Mogadishu’s authority, in the days before the Puntland government announced the deal. The US still affirms Somalia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty in response to Israel’s formal recognition of Somaliland and Somaliland’s subsequent establishment of a diplomatic mission in Jerusalem - though its negotiations could be seen as provoking divisions in Somalia. New phase in Somali relations At the onset of the War on Terror in 2002, the US began steadily expanding its military presence in Somalia, deploying special operations forces before introducing conventional troops, helicopters, surveillance aircraft, operating outposts, and drones. Egypt deepens Horn of Africa maritime alignment with Somalia MoU Read More » For more than two decades, Africom has conducted drone and air strikes against al-Shabaab leadership and Islamic State affiliates in coordination with the Federal Government of Somalia, while equipping and training the Danab Brigade, the Somali National Army's elite special forces unit that has led many of Mogadishu's ground offensives. In his first term, US President Donald Trump carried out 219 air strikes on Somalia, ostensibly as “counter-terrorism” operations. Since his second inauguration, Trump has presided over an unprecedented escalation of the war in Somalia, striking the country 205 times so far. The expansion of the Bosaso Air Base comes as the Pentagon has delegated operational authority to Africom. During a visit to Africom headquarters in February 2025 , US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a covert directive removing the requirement for White House approval before drone strikes in Somalia. The US ended its financial and logistical support for the UN Support Office in Somalia this July, foreclosing the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia. The decision to negotiate in Puntland signals more than a continuation of America's counterterrorism campaign. Considered alongside Washington’s resignation from multilateral “peacekeeping” missions and the loosening of constraints on Africom, the expanded Bosaso Air Base may be read as the US intensifying its foothold in Somalia while becoming more willing to act within the country’s political fragmentation rather than around or against it. headline: US Senator Fetterman struggles to defend support for Israel as progressives win big
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 21:54 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: The staunchly pro- Israel Democratic Senator John Fetterman has told television host and podcaster Jon Stewart that he would rather lose support in his own party than turn his back on Israel for any reason. The comments are striking because they come at a time when progressive Democrats who are vocal on Palestinian rights are making substantial election gains around the country. On Wednesday, in the key battleground state of Michigan , Abdul El-Sayed beat out a pro-Israel candidate funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, moving one step closer to becoming the first Muslim senator in US history. Even Rahm Emanuel, a former advisor to Barack Obama whose father was part of the Irgun militia that ransacked Palestinian homes and killed their residents in 1948, has acknowledged the Democratic Party needs to move away from unconditional support for Israel. "There are a lot of stories of how I've become increasingly more unpopular with Democrats in my state. And I'm aware of it. But these were all very specific choices," Fetterman told Stewart in an interview recorded on Tuesday. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "I would rather have people know what I happen to believe... My proud standing with Israel through everything after 10/7 has put me at odds more than anything," he added, referencing the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which prompted the nearly three-year-long assault by Israel on Gaza that holocaust experts and the United Nations have labelled a genocide. While many older, centrist Democrats can feel the same, Fetterman has always been an outlier in the party. He has represented the battleground state of Pennsylvania in the Senate since January 2023 and largely votes alongside Democrats, except when it comes to issues related to Israel. Democratic hopeful Rahm Emanuel calls for end to unconditional US aid to Israel Read More » The 56-year-old has voiced his disdain for the widespread college campus protests in 2024 that called for an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza, supported President Donald Trump's war on Iran , and has been entirely immovable on unconditional foreign aid to Israel, which he calls a "special ally". "So for you, you could agree with [Democrats] 90 percent, but Israel is the red line," Stewart told Fetterman. "Absolutely. Israel, for me, like I can't ever turn my back to Israel after where it's at," Fetterman said. "I mean no disrespect on this, but that is not our country," Stewart pushed back. Fetterman responded by referencing growing antisemitism in America. "The Jewish community and Israel are not the same thing, brother man. They're not - that is not the same thing," replied Stewart, who is Jewish, while Fetterman is not. "If I have to pick a side for after 10/7 and after Iran, I'm always going to stand with Israel," the senator said. "I'm always going to vote and support whatever that's necessary to protect themselves and to prosecute Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran too." "If anyone in the Democrat Party is fine with Iran building a nuclear bomb, I disagree with that person," he added. "I think you're caricaturing the issue," Stewart said. "Is there anything you would criticise Israel about?" "No." Talking points Stewart tried to elicit empathy from Fetterman on the more than 22,000 children that have been killed by Israel in Gaza. "It's awful," the senator acknowledged. "Would you say everything Israel is doing is for their own self-defence?" Stewart asked. "Destroying its enemies, yeah," Fetterman replied "Flattening a tiny area and pushing two million people into 30 to 35 to 40 percent of that territory, and having a siege of that area. Is that in their self-defence?" After Michigan upset, Aipac looks to back Republican candidate against Abdul El-Sayed Read More » "People forget that Hamas were just rapists and they were terrorising and killing civilians," Fetterman said. To date, there has been no first-person or direct eyewitness evidence documented by international organisations that rape was committed during the dawn attack on 7 October 2023. When asked if what is happening in Gaza is a genocide, Fetterman said that "by definition", only the Jewish community has "experienced a true, true genocide". "If Israel's goal was to eliminate as many Palestinians as possible, they could have accomplished that a long time ago," the senator declared. "Just because you're killing a group slowly doesn't mean you're not killing a group," Stewart countered. Fetterman explained that the term "Zionist" is now being used as a "slur" among some people in the Democratic Party, and that he himself has been hounded by protesters calling him a "Zio". He then asked why university students were not protesting against the Iranian government for its killing of protesters during a mass uprising earlier this year. "That's because we don't consider Iran an ally. We don't give money to Iran. We don't give billions of dollars a year to Iran. We sanction them," Stewart said. Fetterman pivoted to how much Israel has actually been helping Gaza. "Actually, Hamas has been stealing all of the aid," he said. The former head of the World Food Programme, an American citizen and a Republican, acknowledged last year that there was no evidence that Hamas members were attacking or stealing from the limited aid trucks entering the enclave. Confusion The interview took a bizarre turn at times, when Fetterman seemed to be trying to recall, unsuccessfully, talking points or even structure his answer. He would veer into another topic entirely, almost like he didn't understand the question, rather than trying to evade it. In his final year as lieutenant governor in Pennsylvania - some three months before he beat television personality Mehmet Oz to win the Senate seat in November 2022 - Fetterman suffered a stroke. As he recovered and made public appearances, he seemed incapable of articulating himself in interviews, or indeed in the candidates' debate he had with Oz. Fetterman still ended up winning with 51 percent of the vote. He was sworn into office at the US Capitol in January 2023, and a month later, revealed he had been suffering from depression, leading him to be hospitalised for two months. The announcement was lauded by his colleagues as a brave admission on how men in particular should handle their mental health. During the 75-minute interview with Stewart, about half the time was spent discussing the unpopular state of the Democratic Party establishment, the rising Democratic Socialists who have galvanised voters, and the economic status quo that has turned Americans away from centrist politicians. From Michigan to Missouri: Democratic primaries deliver mixed bag on Israel and Gaza Read More » "Don't you think this new sort of energy and economic populism is a response to that?" Stewart asked. "Well, what is that? Is that socialism... communism?" Fetterman responded, arguing that Democrats with socialist policy platforms cannot defeat Republicans in swing states, which can go either way at elections. "That sounds like a caricature," Stewart fired back. "El-Sayed.. wants to ban corporate money. Wants higher taxes on billionaires for housing and education, Medicare for all. You know, when you say that's communism, that feels like a caricature." "No, no, I never said that," Fetterman said. "I call real communists that are cheering for communism, people like Hassan Piker, for example. You know, he's a big, big influence." "I don't think it's a communist. I think he said he's socialist," Stewart said of the political influencer and Twitch streamer who has backed Sayed and joined him at rallies. "But the point being... capitalism, as it is being practised in America, is increasing inequality and leaving too many people behind," Stewart explained. "I return it back to this idea that AI is transforming the world, whether you like it or not," Fetterman replied, in one of the stranger moments in the discussion. "The second we hinder our own ability to develop these kinds of tools, the Chinese will seize the lead," he continued. When Stewart tried to get him back on track, Fetterman said that while he agrees that money should be taken out of politics in the US - as Sayed and others have campaigned - Piker remains "pro-Hamas", and so Fetterman cannot support the candidates that Piker endorses. "I feel like you're caricaturing people's views if they're critical of Israel. If someone says, 'I think Hamas and Israel are both criminal'... how is that pro-Hamas?" Stewart asked. "What I would say is... our party is starting to elect people that are going to struggle to win in the kinds of places that are going to define who's going to win in [20]28," Fetterman said. "When we live in a very divided country right now, I think the responsibility is to police your own ranks." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: ‘The right to stay’: Italy’s Albanian diaspora sails back to support the Flamingo Revolution
author: Dalia Ismail
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 15:07 BST | Last update: 6 days 18 hours ago
article_body: From the Italian port of Brindisi, activists from Italy’s Albanian diaspora and from Global Sumud Flotilla Italy will set sail for Albania on 20 August, travelling across the Adriatic to join the Flamingo Revolution , the protest movement against luxury developments backed by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The mission is organised by the Italian-Albanian collective Mesdhe (“Mediterranean” in Albanian) and the Albanian pro- Palestine collective Palestina e Lire (“Free Palestine” in Albanian), together with the Italian branch of the Global Sumud Flotilla , an international civil society initiative aimed at breaking Israel 's naval blockade of Gaza and delivering humanitarian aid to the enclave. It will link the two Adriatic shores with a three‑boat flotilla at a moment when activists in Albania are challenging the privatisation of protected land and the growing influence of foreign investors over the country. The action was launched on social media on 8 August, and the choice of date and departure point in Brindisi, in the southern region of Puglia, is deeply symbolic for the organisers. In the 1990s, Puglia became the arrival point for one of the largest mass migrations in recent European history, following the collapse of Albania’s communist regime. On 8 August 1991, the merchant ship Vlora docked in Bari, Puglia’s administrative centre, carrying an estimated 20,000 Albanians in a single journey. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The episode led to one of the most extensive and rapid repatriation operations in Italian history, with more than 17,400 Albanians deported. Migrants in Bari’s Stadio della Vittoria were left without adequate food, water or medical care, hundreds were hospitalised for dehydration, and clashes with police culminated in officers firing shots at refugees trying to escape. That year, tens of thousands more Albanians arrived across southern Italy by sea, particularly in Puglia. ‘The same corruption that forced so many to leave [in 1991] is today selling off our coasts, islands, lagoons and future’ - Mesdhe, flotilla organiser group Now, activists from the Italian-Albanian community say they want to make the journey in reverse. “In 2026, while the Albanian people have been in revolt for 68 days, from Bari we want to leave for Vlora as an organised diaspora,” Mesdhe said in a statement . “Because the same corruption that forced so many to leave [in 1991] is today selling off our coasts, islands, lagoons and future.” The activists will travel towards Vlora, where protests have formed around the so-called “ Flamingo Revolution ”, a protest opposing controversial luxury tourism developments along Albania’s southern coast. At the centre of the dispute is Sazan, a former military island where Kushner’s investment firm, Affinity Partners, is backing plans for a luxury resort valued at around $1.4bn. A separate development linked to Kushner and his partners is planned near Zvernec, within the protected Vjosa-Narta landscape. “The Flamingo Revolution is named after the Narta lagoon, where they want to build a resort,” said the Mesdhe collective and Global Sumud Flotilla Italy on social media. “It is not simply a tourist destination. It is a living ecosystem, home to more than 200 species of migratory birds, including pink flamingos, as well as communities that have lived there for generations.” ‘We want to come back’ For activists, the cause also resonates with the history of migration between the two countries. “I am part of the Albanian diaspora in Italy. And our memory is also made of the sea,” Clara Osma, an Italian-Albanian activist with Mesdhe and Palestina e Lire who organised the mission, told Middle East Eye. ‘I hope Rama resigns’: Why Albania’s Flamingo Revolution isn’t actually about flamingos Read More » “It is the memory of the ships of the 1990s, of the stadiums where Albanians were locked up when they arrived, of deportations and the first systems of administrative detention.” “The diaspora preserves that history,” she said. “And this is where, for me, memory meets what is happening today with the Flamingo Revolution and why we decided to sail. “Because 30 years later, we see another generation of Albanians asking, essentially, for the right to stay, and we want to come back.” For Enton Nazeraj, an Italian-Albanian artist taking part in the mobilisation, the protests have also provided a way of reconnecting with an identity that he says had been fragmented by migration. “As the son of immigrants, I feel at home within the revolution. That is why I am taking part in this action. In the revolution I found my identity,” he told MEE. “As a Puglian, I see the Albanian community, which is the community I grew up with,” said Tony La Piccirella, a Global Sumud Flotilla activist organising the mission. “I was born just before the arrival of the Vlora, so I have never known a Puglia without an Albanian presence. “They are precisely the friends I grew up with.” A common struggle The organisers see the campaign as a protest against land and luxury tourism across the Mediterranean - including in southern Italy. In Puglia, environmental groups and local activists have opposed a planned Four Seasons resort near Ostuni, a project involving the Israeli real-estate company Omnam. ‘The fact that a piece of the Albanian diaspora is returning in support of the Flamingo Revolution, using boats born from solidarity with Palestine, is very powerful’ - Tony La Piccirella, organiser The $115m development plan has faced legal challenges from environmental organisations, while the Puglia regional government has joined the legal proceedings against it, in a case echoing the disputed resort project near Tavolara in Sardinia, opposed on environmental grounds. Italian-Albanian and Global Sumud Flotilla activists say these struggles are connected to the broader question of who controls Mediterranean land and resources. “From Puglia, we see what is happening in Albania and recognise something very close to us,” La Piccirella told MEE. “Touristification and resortisation are already transforming our territory. We want to connect these struggles.” The activists also frame the journey through Palestine as part of a global struggle against the dispossession of peoples. “The same people who finance the oppression of the Palestinian people, planning to build a tourist hub on the rubble of Gaza, are the ones who aim to bury the ecosystems of Sazan Island under a luxury resort,” Mesdhe said in the launch statement . Kushner has played a controversial role in post-war Gaza reconstruction projects, promoting a $25bn plan to redevelop the enclave as a commercial and technology hub. Critics argue the project would facilitate population displacement and erase Palestinian culture. Dua Lipa backs Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ against Kushner-backed resort Read More » La Piccirella said the three boats used for the mission were recovered after being damaged and abandoned following Israeli forces’ attacks on the Global Sumud Flotilla in spring, during which activists were captured. For La Piccirella, their reuse in the journey to Albania gives the boats an additional meaning: vessels of international solidarity, linking the Palestinian cause with the Albanian protest movement. “The fact that a piece of the Albanian diaspora is returning in support of the Flamingo Revolution, using boats born from solidarity with Palestine, is very powerful,” La Piccirella added. For Mesdhe, the journey is ultimately about reversing a historic movement across the Adriatic. “We are returning not as tourists or investors, but as a diaspora organised around the right of people to remain on their land,” the collective said. headline: New oral history project eulogises slain Palestinian journalists via friends' voice notes
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 19:02 BST | Last update: 6 days 9 hours ago
article_body: When Anas al-Sharif was killed in Gaza by an Israeli air strike one year ago, the Reuters news agency ran the headline, "Israel kills Al Jazeera journalist it says was Hamas leader". In 2024, at the height of Israel's genocide in Gaza, Anas had helped Reuters win a Pulitzer Prize for breaking news photography. But the outlet chose to remember the 28-year-old within the scope of Israel's unproven narrative about him - as many other news organisations have done to more than 200 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza since 2023. As of Wednesday, a new project called The Living Record is looking to rectify that by telling the stories of slain Palestinian journalists through the eyes and experiences of their colleagues on the ground. The oral history site launched with eulogies for 40 journalists, with dozens more to come later in the year. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "This project is seriously - and at a mammoth scale - a record of failure," a member of the New York War Crimes editorial collective, which was initiated by the group Writers Against The War On Gaza (Wawog), told Middle East Eye on the condition that they not be named. "[This is] a record of failure of mainstream media, of western media, of international institutions to protect individuals [as governed] by international law." Wawog is behind The Living Record. "What this project does is it asks you to listen to these people speaking to you as if they were your friend, and so that was one of the really big prompts of the project itself," MEE was told. "Often when we spoke to these [Palestinian] journalists, there's a tendency for them to speak in a very formal register because they're accustomed to that being the only way that people would be willing to listen, whether on a live broadcast or in a formal interview where they're anticipating a critique or a challenge - that they must present themselves as sort of indefatigable, impossible to move." "We didn't want that." The result is profound. The voice notes on the site range from journalists who sound broken but steadfast as they recount the relatable, daily habits of their colleagues, to others who speak directly to their slain friends, as if we, the audience, are listening in on a private conversation. Who is a journalist? Many have resigned themselves to becoming "martyrs" at any moment. That's because, according to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate, at least 270 Palestinian media workers have been killed by Israel in Gaza. The Committee to Protect Journalists, however, has a significantly lower count. The mainstream media within the US and Canada have largely defaulted to CPJ for the figures, especially as most choose not to source local organisations or the Palestinian health ministry. In June, CPJ came under fire when it announced it was "conducting a full review of its database of journalists killed during the Israel-Gaza War after militant groups Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad published obituaries identifying as combatants individuals previously listed by CPJ as journalists". As a result, 20 Palestinian journalists were removed from CPJ's count, which now stands at 209 dead. The full review will be completed in the weeks to come, the group said. 'This project is seriously - and at a mammoth scale - a record of failure' - Member of Writers Against The War On Gaza In its emailed statement to MEE at the time, CPJ said it "has not changed its longstanding methodology, which applies to all conflict zones around the world", nor has it "changed the way it classifies journalists". But journalism itself is a "porous" industry, the Wawog member told MEE, especially in the so-called creator economy where thousands of journalists globally are leaving legacy outlets to go independent. "What you find with this project is that these are what we would call maybe 'traditional journalists', but we ask them to define themselves. In that sense, there is really no figure that we're trying to reach, but the archive is ongoing, and the expansion will go beyond just Gaza, and likely into south Lebanon." Wawog, a group made up of writers and creatives, emerged in the weeks following Israel's bombardment of Gaza after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The group has routinely held protests outside, and at times in the lobby of, the New York Times building in the borough of Manhattan. Wawog calls out what it sees as the hypocrisies of the New York Times in its own publication called "The New York War Crimes". Media analysts and human rights groups have repeatedly accused mainstream media of contributing to both the erasure and distortion of Israeli war crimes in Gaza. Several observers have argued that the reporting on what the United Nations and holocaust scholars have called a genocide, as well as the student movement for Palestine in the US, has not merely been inaccurate but has ventured close to journalistic malpractice. Anas al-Sharif Israeli forces assassinated two of Gaza's leading journalists and their colleagues late on Sunday, 10 August 2025, just hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected international condemnation over his plan to occupy the Palestinian enclave. The Al Jazeera Media Network said in a statement that its correspondents Anas and Mohammed Qreiqeh, along with three other colleagues, were deliberately killed when Israeli forces struck their tent outside al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City. Qreiqeh contributed to several publications, including Middle East Eye, before he began working at Al Jazeera. How six months in Israeli jail changed this Palestinian journalist’s life forever Read More » Anas, a father of two, had been stationed outside the hospital's main gate along with cameramen and photojournalists Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal and Mosaab al-Sharif when their tent was attacked. Shortly before his killing, Anas had posted a video on X showing what he called Israel's "intense" missile strikes on the eastern and southern parts of Gaza City. His final video captured the deafening booms of the attacks near where he was. Later, the Israeli military claimed, without providing any evidence, that it killed Anas because he "served as the head of a terrorist cell in the Hamas terrorist organisation". Since Israel launched its war on the enclave in October 2023, it has routinely accused Palestinian journalists in Gaza of being Hamas members, as part of what rights groups say is an effort to discredit their reporting of Israeli abuses. Four months before he was killed, Anas prepared a message to be posted on his social media accounts in the event of his death. "I have lived through pain in all its details, tasted suffering and loss many times, yet I never once hesitated to convey the truth as it is, without distortion or falsification - so that Allah may bear witness against those who stayed silent, those who accepted our killing, those who choked our breath, and whose hearts were unmoved by the scattered remains of our children and women," he wrote. "I entrust you with Palestine - the jewel in the crown of the Muslim world, the heartbeat of every free person in this world," he added. "I entrust you with its people, with its wronged and innocent children who never had the time to dream or live in safety and peace. Their pure bodies were crushed under thousands of tons of Israeli bombs and missiles, torn apart and scattered across the walls." Sharif pleaded: "I urge you not to let chains silence you." headline: Iran's new Security Council shake-up reveals growing divisions over US deal
author: MEE correspondent
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 15:01 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Soon after Iranian negotiators reached a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States in late June to end months of hostilities, Iran 's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) issued a statement endorsing the agreement. The statement was signed by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a former hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) general who had replaced the slain Ali Larijani, a prominent moderate figure who had supported a deal with Washington and was killed in a US- Israeli strike on 17 March. In Iran, the SNSC secretary, who is appointed by the president, does not have a vote on the council. However, Zolghadr was also appointed simultaneously as the supreme leader’s representative on the council, a position that gives him voting authority. Zolghadr’s endorsement caught ultraconservative principlists off guard. Apparently unprepared for his support of the agreement, they subsequently launched repeated verbal attacks against him, including spreading claims that his son lives in Austria. A few days after the SNSC statement, Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s new supreme leader, issued his own statement, making clear that he was “in principle” opposed to the agreement while emphasising that responsibility for the decision should rest with those who negotiated it. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The statement effectively threw the negotiators under the bus, empowering ultraconservatives to intensify their attacks on the agreement, the government, the negotiating team and Zolghadr. According to two sources in the conservative camp, Zolghadr subsequently wrote to Khamenei expressing his dissatisfaction with the supreme leader’s statement. He argued that the details of the agreement had already been presented to Khamenei and offered his resignation. Inside the growing rift between Iran’s dealmakers and ultraconservatives Read More » Khamenei accepted the resignation almost immediately, according to the sources. The resignation was highly unusual: a senior official was resigning explicitly in protest at a decision by the supreme leader. Principlists have publicly claimed that Zolghadr was “removed” because he followed President Masoud Pezeshkian’s position and supported the agreement rather than opposing it. But those claims were contradicted by conversations between Middle East Eye and conservative sources familiar with the episode. According to the sources, Pezeshkian worked hard to persuade Khamenei not to accept the resignation and sought to keep him as secretary because he was broadly aligned with the government’s approach to reaching a deal with Washington. His efforts, however, failed. Khamenei subsequently appointed former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei as his representative to the SNSC. This effectively forced Pezeshkian to appoint Rezaei as secretary, despite the president’s initial resistance to signing off on Rezaei’s appointment until the last minute. A political decision Speaking about the reasons behind Mojtaba Khamenei’s decision to appoint Rezaei, a principlist source told MEE that the role requires more than institutional authority. It also demands strong personal qualities, political credibility, public recognition and established connections with the media and wider society, particularly as the SNSC has increasingly become involved in major political and social debates. The source added that recent US-Israeli assassinations have, among other objectives, sought to eliminate Iran’s strategic decision-makers and weaken the country’s ability to coordinate and make effective decisions. “Against this backdrop, the appointment of Mohsen Rezaei to the SNSC secretariat is an attempt to fill that void and significantly strengthen and enhance the institution’s effectiveness,” he said. Meanwhile, a moderate political source told MEE that, beyond technical considerations, Rezaei’s appointment was more of a political decision. The source said the leader’s choices may have been constrained by the need to appoint someone who would be acceptable, at least to some extent, to Pezeshkian and his administration, rather than a figure such as hardline former nuclear negotiator Saeed Jalili. Who is Mohsen Rezaei? Rezaei, 71, has been involved in the Islamic Republic’s military, security and political establishment for nearly half a century. After the 1979 revolution, he played a role in establishing the IRGC’s intelligence apparatus and, at the age of 27, became commander of the IRGC. He remained in the position for 16 years, spending virtually the entire Iran-Iraq War at the helm of the Revolutionary Guard. War on Iran: What is Tehran's 'shadow fleet' really and how does it work? Read More » In the mid-1980s, Rezaei became involved in secret contacts with the United States during the Iran-Contra affair, in which Iran received American weapons while proceeds from the arms sales were diverted to support the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Former Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani once told local media that his nephew, Ali Hashemi, a key intermediary in contacts with the administration of then-US President Ronald Reagan, had informed him and, subsequently, Rezaei about meetings with American officials. According to Hashemi’s account, Rezaei told him: “Keep going. We need weapons.” Hashemi also recalled: “I went to see Mr Rezaei... He told me, ‘Just connect your contacts to the people I introduce you to so that the process can continue.’” He later said that, following the second round of negotiations, Rezaei told him that Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini was “aware” of the talks. As the secret contacts continued, Hashemi and two IRGC officials travelled to Washington for clandestine negotiations. In the 1990s, Rezaei’s eldest son moved to the US, where he sought asylum and later became a critic of the Islamic Republic. He eventually returned to Iran but died years later under suspicious circumstances in a hotel in Dubai. By the late 1990s, Rezaei was seeking to move beyond his military background and establish a more prominent political and managerial role. He studied economics at the University of Tehran, pursued a doctorate and increasingly focused his work at the Expediency Discernment Council on issues including macroeconomics, national planning and the establishment's broader policy priorities. Rezaei has repeatedly run for president but never won. In September 2021, the late President Ebrahim Raisi appointed him vice president for economic affairs and secretary of the Supreme Economic Coordination Council of the Heads of the Three Branches of Government. Rezaei resigned as vice president for economic affairs in June 2023, while Raisi agreed to allow him to retain his position as secretary of the economic coordination council. A hardline pragmatist On 6 April, Rezaei said that the US naval blockade was “vulnerable” and amounted to little more than psychological warfare, adding that it would not affect Iran’s negotiating position. “I do not personally support extending the ceasefire. It should happen only if a final agreement is reached and our rights are secured,” he said. Turkey suspects Israel fabricated Trump Air Force One assassination plot to derail US-Iran deal Read More » He also argued that the US had no clear plan to end the war, saying Washington tries one strategy, fails and then moves on to another. One possibility, he said, was that the US was coming to terms with defeat. Another, he suggested, was that Trump could damage the US's standing so severely that he would ultimately be removed from office. On 7 July, Rezaei said: “Those opposed to negotiations should wait. The Americans themselves will derail these talks.” Despite Rezaei’s increasingly hardline public rhetoric, a senior political source familiar with his thinking told MEE that he has personally been more of a pragmatist and has favoured restoring relations with the US and ending the conflict. The source, however, said that Rezaei’s political calculations and his determination to remain in the power structure have repeatedly led him to “go with the flow” and adapt his positions to changing circumstances. The source described this as one of the defining characteristics of Rezaei’s political personality. He added that it would soon become clear whether his harsh rhetoric reflected genuine opposition to negotiations or was simply a political strategy directed at the negotiators because he was not at the centre of power.
