headline: Colombia sides with Morocco over Western Sahara as it aligns with Israeli foreign policy
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 12 August 2026 15:11 BST | Last update: 1 week ago
article_body: Colombia’s newly elected far-right government has recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, beginning its presidency with a raft of decisions that align Bogota with the foreign policy priorities of Israel and the United States. Vice President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar announced the reversal after holding talks with Moroccan officials. Escobar, in a post on X, said that Colombia “recognizes Morocco's sovereignty over its Sahara”. Bogota also withdrew its recognition of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and froze diplomatic relations with the territory’s independence movement, reversing former President Gustavo Petro’s restoration of ties in 2022. Morocco has controlled most of Western Sahara since Spain withdrew from the territory in 1975. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The United Nations continues to classify it as a non-self-governing territory and supports the Sahrawi people’s right to determine their future. US President Donald Trump recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in 2020 in exchange for Rabat establishing formal relations with Israel. Colombia has now adopted the territorial settlement produced by that deal, making its decision part of a wider turn towards Washington and Israel and a sharp break from the foreign policy of former Colombian President Gustavo Petro. Petro fiercely opposed Israel’s war on Gaza, calling it a “genocide” and a “crime against humanity”. His government severed diplomatic relations with Israel in May 2024 and backed international legal efforts to hold Israeli officials accountable. In contrast, the new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella gathered members of his incoming government for a Christian retreat before taking power. Kneeling during the gathering, he said: “To build a great nation, we must put God at the centre of every decision.” Colombia recognises Israeli sovereignty over Golan Heights Read More » His government’s first foreign policy decisions have seemingly placed Israeli and US interests at the centre. On Monday, as rescuers searched through rubble after Colombia’s deadliest earthquake in more than a decade, Bogota recognised Israel’s annexation of the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. The magnitude 7.4 earthquake killed at least 250 people, injured more than 2,500 and left thousands missing. On the same day, the foreign ministry found time to declare Israeli control of occupied Syrian land essential to Israel’s security. Colombia joined the US as the only countries in the world to recognise Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights. Israel seized most of the territory from Syria in 1967 and imposed its laws there in 1981. United Nations Security Council Resolution 497 declared that decision “null and void and without international legal effect”. Syria sent formal letters of protest to the UN secretary-general and Security Council on Wednesday. Turkey , Saudi Arabia , Qatar , Kuwait , Iraq , Palestine and Oman also condemned Bogota’s decision. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Exclusive: ICC judges order Taliban case split from Afghanistan probe that covers US troops
author: Sondos Asem
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 12:51 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ordered prosecutors to open a standalone investigation into allegations of gender persecution by the Taliban, separating it from the court's long-running Afghanistan war crimes probe that covered US nationals, Middle East Eye can reveal. According to court documents obtained by MEE through independent sources, a three-judge panel in pre-trial chamber II issued the request to the Office of the Prosecutor in mid-July. If prosecutors proceed, the Taliban investigation will effectively be split from a broader Afghanistan inquiry looking into alleged war crimes committed since 2003 by Afghan National Security Forces, the US military and CIA personnel, in addition to the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province (IS-K) group. The move is likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies. The chamber's communication came days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to "dismantle the ICC, brick by brick", in remarks referencing the court's 2020 decision authorising an investigation into alleged crimes committed in Afghanistan. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Since February 2025, the US has imposed retaliatory financial and visa sanctions on court officials in connection with the Afghanistan and Palestine investigations, citing efforts to prosecute nationals or allies of the US. ​​The first target was Karim Khan , the former prosecutor of the ICC, who was controversially removed by member states last month after an 18-month long misconduct probe. Rubio says US will dismantle ICC 'brick by brick' Read More » Also targeted were eight judges, three of whom - Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Luz Ibanez - were members of the 2020 Appeals Chamber that authorised the Afghanistan investigation. The sanctions came despite the decision by Khan in 2021 to deprioritise the strand of the Afghanistan probe concerning US military and CIA personnel, as well as former Afghan government forces, in order to focus the investigation on the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province. The ICC already issued arrest warrants a year ago for Supreme Leader of the Taliban Hibatullah Akhundzada and Abdul Hakim Haqqani, the group's Chief Justice, for the crime against humanity of gender persecution. The applications were prepared by a team of lawyers under the leadership of Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan, who oversees the Afghanistan investigation, and Special Adviser on Gender Crimes Professor Lisa Davis, who authored the office’s policy on gender-based crimes. The deputy prosecutor has been among those sanctioned by the US government over the past year, while Davis has filed and won a court case in New York shielding her from potential punitive measures by the administration. MEE reported in December that diplomats at the ICC's annual Assembly of States Parties meeting in The Hague said the Trump administration had pressed the court to drop its investigations into Afghanistan and Palestine as a condition for lifting sanctions. It also demanded states to amend the ICC’s founding treaty - The Rome Statute - to prevent the prosecution of nationals from countries that aren’t members of the court, such as the US and Israel. At the end of its meeting, however, the assembly issued a declaration resisting those demands and rejecting calls to amend the Rome Statute, without naming the US directly. 'Materially different context' The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group. That request was initially rejected by a differently composed pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed. Bensouda was sanctioned by the US government a few months later over alleged attempts to subject Americans to the court's jurisdiction. The probe was suspended later that year after a deferral request from the then Afghan government, and only resumed in late 2022, a decision upheld on appeal in April 2023. In November 2024, six states - Chile, Costa Rica, Spain, France, Luxembourg and Mexico - jointly referred allegations of crimes against women and girls committed since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, asking prosecutors to fold them into the existing Afghanistan investigation. ‘Financial death penalty’: How US sanctions are upending the lives of ICC judges Read More » Weeks later, in January 2025, then-Prosecutor Khan applied for arrest warrants, arguing the gender persecution allegations already fell within the scope of the 2020 authorisation, and the warrants were later issued for Akhundzada and Haqqani. Now, in their latest decision obtained by MEE, the pre-trial chamber II found that the post-2021 conduct by the Taliban is "materially different" from the armed conflict-related violence that defined the original, conflict-nexus investigation authorised in 2020. The judges on the chamber, Rosario Salvatore Aitala (presiding), Sergio Gerardo Ugalde Godinez and Haykel Ben Mahfoudh, directed prosecutors, if they still consider the legal threshold met, to open a wholly separate investigation based on the states' 2024 referral, and to notify the ICC Presidency of that referral, which the decision notes had not yet happened. "The Referral concerns allegations of gender and political persecution through the adoption, implementation and enforcement of discriminatory decrees, policies and restrictions made possible by the Taliban's exercise of de facto governmental authority, rather than conduct allegedly committed by the Taliban as an insurgent armed group during the armed conflict," the judges said. They cited the prosecutor's previous recognition that the conduct of the Taliban after seizing power in August 2021 was not based on armed attacks against the civilian population, but rather the imposition of "discriminatory rules and prohibitions on the population directly" and punishing those "whom they considered did not conform". "The allegations in the Referral therefore arise in a materially different factual and institutional context, involve distinct alleged modes of commission, do not appear to be related to any armed conflict, and concern conduct occurring after the Taliban’s assumption of governmental de facto authority. "In light of the above, the Chamber considers that the conduct identified in the Referral constitutes a sufficiently distinct subset of alleged events that, in the interests of the proper administration of justice and the orderly management of the Court's proceedings, warrants a separate investigation," they said. Dormant investigation The judges also flagged that the original Afghanistan investigation, the one that nominally covers alleged crimes by all parties, has now sat dormant for years, and pointed prosecutors towards a newly available procedure allowing them to formally close the situation record. ICC states decision on Karim Khan ‘inherently political’, says leading criminal law expert Read More » In a footnote, the chamber said: "Considering that more than three years have elapsed since the Chamber authorised the resumption of the investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan and that no proceedings are presently pending in relation to the conduct covered by that authorisation, the Chamber draws the Prosecution’s attention to the recently implemented regulation 66 ter of the Regulations of the Court, which allows the Prosecution to request the closure of a situation record when it does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities in relation thereto." The office of the prosecutor has yet to make a decision on the closure of the original Afghanistan investigation or the opening of a new one. When contacted by MEE, a spokesperson said the office "does not comment on investigations". Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: UK: Dozens of MPs urge Shabana Mahmood not to block evacuation from Gaza
author: Imran Mulla
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 13:20 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: More than 85 British MPs have written to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood expressing concern over reports that the government is blocking the evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza . Labour MP Kim Johnson sent a letter to Mahmood on Thursday which was signed by MPs from across different parties. Last September the Home Office suspended refugee family reunion applications pending the introduction of new, stricter rules, but these have not yet been announced. As a result, families in Gaza who had applied to join an immediate family member in Britain before the suspension have been blocked from doing so. Johnson told Middle East Eye on Thursday: "Family reunification should never be treated as a political bargaining chip. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "For families enduring the horrors of Gaza, it is a lifeline – often the only hope of safety and the chance to hold their loved ones again." She added: "At a time of unimaginable loss and trauma, the very least we should be doing is ensuring those with a legal right to be together are not torn apart by needless Home Office obstruction. We cannot allow bureaucracy to stand in the way of humanity." 'We cannot allow bureaucracy to stand in the way of humanity' – MPs' letter to home secretary Johnson's letter has been signed by dozens of Labour MPs, including Richard Burgon, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis, John McDonnell and Abtisam Mohamed. It has also been signed by Green MPs Sian Berry, Carla Denyer and Hannah Spencer, members of the parliamentary Independent Alliance and some Liberal Democrat and Scottish National Party MPs. The letter says: "Palestinians in the UK have been told by the Foreign Office that they have agreed to evacuate their families from Gaza. "But their lawyers report that the Home Office appear to be refusing to provide the required onward travel assurance and sometimes to be using legal challenges to block these families coming to the UK, in a way that appears to be taking a harsher line with Palestinian families than with refugees from other countries who are applying for family reunification visas." Home Office urged to reinstate family reunification The letter further says that the government's medical evacuation scheme, which commits to bringing 300 children "in need of life saving and life changing medical care" from Gaza to the UK, "still remains unmet". It raises the specific cases of two children from Gaza, 12-year-old Mahmoud Mansi and 15-year-old Obaida Atwan, who were evacuated from Gaza and met former Prime Minister Keir Starmer last December "where he promised to do everything in his power to reunite them with their remaining family back in Gaza". However, "they have heard nothing further in the months since". How Keir Starmer supported Israel throughout its genocide in Gaza Read More » The letter asks the home secretary to "urgently reinstate the family reunification process for Palestinians and work collaboratively with your counterparts in the Foreign Office to evacuate everyone who has been granted permission to come to the UK". It further asks that the Home Office ensures its policy on Palestinians from Gaza "is in line with refugees from other countries who are applying for family reunification visas". MEE has contacted the Home Office for comment. This comes after Andy Burnham apologised for the Starmer government's response to Israel’s genocide in Gaza shortly before he became prime minister last month. “I know many people feel that at the start of Israel’s military action in Gaza, my party didn’t get it right, and I am sorry about that. The response has too often not been good enough. We need to do better,” Burnham said. Burnham said the “unbearable suffering” in Gaza was a “scar on our collective conscience”. He also criticised Israel's ever-expanding occupation of territory in Gaza, adding, “We’ve got to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government.” Britain operated hundreds of surveillance flights over Gaza during Israel's genocide and shared intelligence with Israel, which the government insisted was for "hostage rescue" purposes. The Starmer government imposed a partial arms embargo on Israel in 2024 and recognised Palestinian statehood last September. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: War on Iran: Saudi Arabia warns of imminent attacks by Iraqi groups and Yemen's Houthis
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 12:06 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Saudi Arabia has warned that Iraqi armed groups and Yemen’s Houthis could soon launch coordinated attacks against the kingdom under the supervision of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. A senior Saudi official, speaking anonymously to Reuters late on Thursday, said intelligence gathered by Saudi Arabia, the United States and other countries in the region indicated that civilian and economic sites could be targeted. The potential targets include energy infrastructure, ports and airports. Saudi Arabia had detected the movement of drones and missiles, according to the official, suggesting preparations for attacks from Iraq to the north and Yemen to the south. Riyadh was ready to take all necessary measures against “any aggression” the official added. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The warning comes as Saudi Arabia becomes increasingly entangled in the Israeli-US war on Iran that began on 28 February. Saudi and US forces struck positions belonging to Iran-backed groups in Iraq on 29 July after Riyadh blamed them for drone attacks on its oil facilities. The strikes targeted headquarters used by the Popular Mobilisation Forces, killing more than 20 people and wounding at least 30. Iraqi armed groups vowed to retaliate. However, Hadi al-Amiri, the head of the Badr Organisation, urged them to delay their response. In a video broadcast by Iraqi media, Amiri called on fighters to postpone attacks over what he described as “American-Saudi” aggression and to overlook their wounds for the “sake of Iraq’s highest interests”. Renewed campaign Saudi Arabia has also faced renewed attacks from the Houthis. Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to 'sign defence pact' on Friday Read More » The Yemeni group said it attacked Najran airport on Tuesday as part of a broader campaign against Saudi military, infrastructure and shipping targets. Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis killed at least 17 government soldiers on Thursday during attacks on Saudi-backed deployments in Marib and Hadramout provinces. Some sources have put the government death toll at at least 58. The Houthis have also disrupted Saudi oil exports through their blockade in the Red Sea, further drawing Riyadh into the wider confrontation. Amid the escalating threats, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are expected to sign a joint defence agreement in Mecca on Friday, sources familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye. Neither the Houthis nor Iran immediately responded to the Saudi warning. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Iran: Trump says he'd rather make deal than 'kill people' amid reports of weapons shortages
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 12:40 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday evening that Washington is holding talks with Iran and would prefer an agreement rather than further military action against the country. Speaking during an event in Las Vegas, Trump said the US had been preparing to launch what he described as “the biggest attack since world war two before Iranian officials asked for negotiations. “I would rather make a deal with Iran because I don’t want to kill people,” he added, while reaffirming his commitment that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain nuclear weapons. It came as the Washington Post reported that Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over a critical shortage of munitions during the war on Iran . According to the newspaper, citing sources familiar with the matter, Trump demanded answers during a cabinet meeting last week, after finding out about a deficit in vital weapons, despite his understanding that the issue had been addressed. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The report cited the shortage in munitions as one of the reasons behind Trump's decision to pause large-scale strikes against Iran. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the shortages and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles. The White House denied the report, with press secretary Karoline Leavitt calling it "100 percent fake news", adding that Trump "has the utmost confidence" in Hegseth. "'Leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down" – President Trump on Truth Social The US army has used up nearly 80 percent of its interceptors for a key missile defence system, CNN reported on Wednesday, citing several sources familiar with the matter. According to the report, senior US military officials warned that the Pentagon’s munitions stockpile is "dangerously low", with key air defence systems particularly depleted during the war on Iran. The US military exhausted nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared with pre-war figures. Half of its Patriot interceptors have been used up since the start of the war. One source familiar with recent internal Pentagon reports noted that the army used "virtually all" of its highly accurate long-range, surface-to-air weapons in the same period. Trump hit back against media reports of depleted munitions, insisting that the army had large stockpiles and was expanding manufacturing. "The US has massive amounts of 'munitions', especially of certain types," he said in a post on social media platform Truth Social, adding that "large amounts" are being manufactured and shipped over to the Middle East "as needed". “Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history,” Trump said. He also threatened that "'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down" and wrote that "long term jail sentences will be sought". Fresh wave of Israeli attacks on Lebanon Meanwhile, eight people have been wounded in an Israeli strike on the southern Lebanese town of Burj Shemali, the country's health ministry reported on Thursday. Earlier, Israeli forces escalated attacks on southern Lebanon , with state media reporting a "wide-scale aggression" on the city of Tyre. As a result of the strikes across several areas in the city, four people were wounded and transferred to nearby hospitals. Residents in these areas were also displaced. The fresh wave of attacks comes as Lebanese-Israeli peace talks entered a third day in Rome, in the seventh round of US-brokered negotiations. Israel's army to set up polling stations in occupied Gaza, Lebanon and Syria Read More » Lebanese negotiators are demanding that Israel cease bombardment and withdraw from around 60 villages and towns occupied in its latest onslaught, which began in March. Meanwhile, Israel wants the Lebanese army to dismantle Hezbollah's military infrastructure. Israeli reports have suggested that additional military attacks in Lebanon are being considered, as the army prepares for further escalation. Israel's public broadcaster said that the army's response to what it described as Hezbollah violation "has not ended", with "sensitive operations" likely under way. Channel 12 reported that the army is calling on the political leadership to approve a "stronger and more decisive" response in Lebanon. Elsewhere in the region, a tanker nine nautical miles southeast of the village of Kumzar in Oman reported hearing two explosions while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said early on Thursday. According to the UKMTO advisory, the vessel and its crew were reportedly safe, with no environmental damage indicated. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Court hears Palestine Action defendant suffered from emotional turmoil before Elbit raid
author: Katherine Hearst
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 13:50 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: A British court has heard that a defendant in a Palestine Action trial accused of planning a raid on an Israeli- owned arms factory was suffering from emotional turmoil at the time the coordination of the action was alleged to take place. Representing Julija Brigadirova, lawyer Tom Copeland told the court on Wednesday, that her circumstances around the time she was alleged to be planning the Filton action were marked by mental and emotional distress - including an attempt on her own life. Copeland suggested that the reason Brigadirova appears to be absent from the evidence of the alleged coordination of the Elbit raid in the weeks preceding it, is because “in the context of her life at the time, she may not have been in a place to usefully contribute”. "You may think she had more important things going on," he said. Brigadirova, 33, along with co-defendants Hannah Davidson, 53, Ian Sanders, 47; Aleksandra Herbich, 41; Teuta Hoxha, 30; Sean Middlebrough, 33; and Madeleine Norman, 31, face charges of violent disorder and criminal damage in connection with a break-in to an Elbit Systems plant in Filton, near Bristol, in August 2024. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters William Plastow, 35, was acquitted of violent disorder. He continues to face criminal damage charges. The eight defendants are accused of coordinating the break-in by carrying out reconnaissance and purchasing equipment, but are not alleged to have gone into the factory premises during the raid. They all deny the charges. Representing Brigadirova, barrister Tom Copeland told jurors in his closing remarks on Wednesday that the prosecution's case that she was a “key player” in the action is an “assumption” not “borne out by evidence”. He highlighted that the prosecution had not presented any evidence of financial transactions made by Brigadirova linked to the Filton raid, nor were any messages sent from her signal handles related to planning or organising the action. “If the prosecution is right, perhaps she should be called the invisible coordinator,” Copeland said. “She’s not invisible - you can see her in the flesh in the dock. She is a real human being.” “Or perhaps, the prosecution have got it wrong when it comes to Ms Brigadirova. That is a bigger mistake and one which is unforgivable," he said. Supreme Court will allow appeal hearing over Palestine Action ban Read More » The prosecution pointed to messages between Brigadirova and a friend, Jasmine Cruickshank, in the days before the action. They suggested that a message from Cruickshank to Brigadirova on 24 July asking, “Are you still up for the Bristol van trip next weekend?" evidences the defendants’ knowledge of the Filton site, and that this was Bridagirova's means of travel to the action. Copeland dismissed this as “a nonsense”, pointing out that the prosecution had not called Cruickshank - who had provided a character statement for Brigadirova in which she described her as “part of my family” - as a witness. “They could have asked her how the message came about,” Copeland said. “It didn’t happen. Her statement was read to you unchallenged as agreed evidence. At the same time, the prosecution seeks to use that message against her”. “The idea that she has used her friend as some sort of charade is an assertion, not evidence,” he told jurors. The jury heard that Brigadirova was driven down to Bristol on 4 August by Cruickshank, and later took a selfie upon arrival at Cruickshank's father's house. They also heard that Cruickshank later drove the van back to Manchester, without Brigadirova. ‘Low mood’ Copeland noted that the prosecution had “glossed over” the information about Brigadirova's mental health at the time, describing the defendant as suffering from “low mood”. The court heard that Brigidirova was kept in hospital for four days after the attempt on her life. “Low mood, seriously?” Copeland asked jurors. “This is not the first time it’s happened. It was a serious, genuine attempt to take her own life”. The defendants from left to right: Ian Sanders, Aleksandra Herbich, William Plastow, Hannah Davidson, Teuta Hoxha, Julija Brigadirova, and Madeline Norman (Supplied) He noted Brigadirova's presence at the Airbnb, where activists stayed from 4 August ahead of the action on the morning of the 6 August. “Can you rule out the possibility that at that difficult time in her life, or her going along for the ride, with friends? As a support, but a support for herself more than anything,” Copeland said. Copeland told jurors that the first mention of Brigadirova in the evidence following the raid is a message sent to a contact named Saeed (Feeld), saying “just stayed with friends down south, nothing special”. He explained that ‘Feeld’ is the name of a dating app. “What I cannot tell you is who in this courtroom knew it was a dating app,” adding that he would leave jurors “to speculate on that”. ‘Cooking a lot of pasta’ Representing co-defendant Aleksandra Herbich, barrister Emma Fenn told jurors that her role in the Filton raid was so limited that she handed over her phone to another defendant at the time of the action. She noted that this runs contrary to instructions outlined in the Palestine Action document entitled the "Coordinator’s manual" which stipulates that coordinators “must be contactable at all times”. Fenn said that the evidence shows that Herbich’s role in the raid was primarily limited to purchasing food and cooking. She described Herbich captured on CCTV footage at Paddington Station on 4 August, with “blue hair distinctly on show”, carrying a box “the size and shape of a sushi box". During her time at the Airbnb "safe house" in Bristol prior to the action, Herbich was described by co-defendant Madeline Norman as “cooking a lot of pasta. That’s all I saw her doing”. Fenn emphasised that “cooking doesn’t even come close” to qualifying as an “intentional act” assisting or encouraging the offences of violent disorder and criminal damage. “There is nothing to connect her with tools or weapons,” Fenn said, describing Herbich as “someone doing the cleaning at most and the cooking at least”. ‘Limited interaction’ Representing Plastow, Barrister Andrew Rose told jurors that his client had “limited interaction” with Palestine Action in the months prior to the raid, agreeing to do odd jobs and purchase tools. The prosecution case against Plastow rests on his purchasing of a number of items used in the Filton raid - including rucksacks, protective gear and crowbars - and handing them over to co-defendant Charlotte Head. They argue that this is tantamount to coordinating the action, and assisting with criminal damage to Elbit’s property. When giving evidence on 16 July, Plastow told jurors that he had no knowledge of the Filton site prior to the action, and that the first he had heard of it was via a news item on the morning after the raid. Citing the judge’s directions, Rose urged jurors that they must be sure Plastow supplied the equipment to Head with the intention that "Elbit’s property would be destroyed or damaged in accordance with the plan in which Charlotte Head and others were engaged”. “If he thought the equipment might be used by others including those he handed it over to, in a different type of action involving Elbit that wouldn’t be the plan in which others were engaged,” he said. ‘We just disappeared’: Palestine Action defendant recalls ‘horrifying’ arrest Read More » Rose noted that the equipment list Plastow accessed for the purchase of the items included tools that were not used in the Filton action, including banners and rope. He said that a more detailed, and seemingly more Filton-specific list was not shared with Plastow. Citing Palestine Action guidelines, Rose read: “Everything is on a need-to-know basis, even among trusted people.” “Mr Plastow was not ‘need to know,’ and didn’t want to know,” Rose said. Rose reminded jurors that Plastow had been acquitted of violent disorder charges after Judge Field concluded that there was insufficient evidence that he knew violence would occur at the Filton site. Rose argued that the remaining criminal damage charges against Plastow contain an “inherent, inescapable contradiction”. He said that the prosecution’s case against all eight defendants is that, if they were involved in the Filton plan, they knew that the action would involve criminal damage (count 1) and, if necessary, violent disorder (count 2). “It would be illogical, nonsense in my submission for Mr Plastow to be in the know, with knowledge of the Filton plan of criminal damage, but in complete and utter ignorance of violent disorder,” Rose told jurors. “How could he really be a knowing participant and not be told this key part?” he asked. “It’s ridiculous. The death of count 2 should also spell the death of count 1." Rose, Fenn and Copeland’s closing remarks came as the judge sent jurors out to deliberate on Thursday. The trial continues. If you need support in the UK, then the Samaritans can be contacted at jo@samaritans.org or on 116 123. For the US, please try the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 1-800-273-8255. For other countries, please see befrienders.org . Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters. headline: Why Israel's opposition no longer wants Palestinian parties in government
author: Samah Watad
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 07:31 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Gadi Eisenkot last week became the latest Israeli politician to pledge to form a "Zionist majority" government if he became Israel's next prime minister. The phrase is widely understood as ruling out a coalition with Palestinian Arab parties to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "I prefer to achieve a Zionist majority of 63-64 seats, and if that doesn't happen, to call on the ultra-Orthodox parties to understand the gravity of the moment," Eisenkot, a former general and leader of the Yashar party, said at a security conference organised by Yedioth Ahronoth and the Institute for National Security Studies. "If they don't understand, then it's better to go to new elections," he added. His remarks reflect a broader shift. From Naftali Bennett to Yair Lapid, leaders across the anti-Netanyahu camp have increasingly ruled out forming a government that relies on Palestinian Arab parties, including the United Arab List (Ra'am), whose leader, Mansour Abbas, has repeatedly said he is willing to negotiate with Jewish-majority parties. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The change is striking. Bennett and Lapid defended their partnership with Abbas in the 2021 coalition as a necessary political experiment that ended Netanyahu's 12-year hold on power. Today, the post-7 October reality in Israel has made such cooperation politically costly. Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief challenging Netanyahu? Read More » "This is first and foremost the result of the shift in Israeli public opinion after 7 October," Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst, told Middle East Eye. "Any partnership with a Palestinian Arab party is now presented electorally as a concession on security and identity. Even parties in the political centre fear being portrayed as relying on those who reject the Jewish character of the state." The election, scheduled for 27 October, is widely seen as pivotal for Israel's political future. Polls show an Eisenkot-led bloc running neck and neck with Netanyahu's. Some surveys suggest Eisenkot could win enough seats to govern without Palestinian Arab parties, while others indicate that neither bloc is likely to secure a parliamentary majority without their backing. Taboo returns Palestinian parties represent Palestinian citizens of Israel , the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homeland after Zionist militias displaced around 750,000 people in 1948 to create the state of Israel, an event Palestinians refer to as the Nakba . Today, the community numbers about two million people, accounting for roughly a fifth of Israel's population. After decades of discrimination, Palestinian citizens of Israel established political parties to advocate civil equality, an end to the occupation and recognition of Palestinian national rights. For decades, however, those parties remained on the margins of Israeli politics. Cooperation with governing coalitions was widely viewed as politically toxic by much of the Jewish electorate and many Palestinian citizens alike. That taboo was broken in 2021, when Ra'am became kingmaker, providing the four seats needed for Bennett and Lapid to assemble a razor-thin majority and end Netanyahu's rule after four inconclusive elections. 'Today, the political cost of being seen as close to Palestinian Arab parties has become very high' – Ehab Jabareen, political analyst Since the Hamas-led attacks of October 2023, however, the taboo has largely returned. According to the Israel Democracy Institute's Democracy Index, published in December 2025, 71.5 percent of Jewish Israelis opposed including Arab parties in the next government. A separate 2025 survey by the Institute for National Security Studies found that 57 percent of Israelis opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state under any circumstances, underscoring the hardening of public opinion. "Netanyahu succeeded in turning relations with Palestinian Arab parties into an electoral weapon," Jabareen said, referring to years of campaigning that portrayed cooperation with Palestinian politicians as politically illegitimate. "Today, the political cost of being seen as close to Palestinian Arab parties has become very high." Jabareen believes some parties could still seek the support of Palestinian Arab parties after the election if the parliamentary arithmetic leaves them with no alternative. During the campaign, however, few are willing to signal that possibility. "They keep the back door open, but the front door is locked." Politics of the possible The increasingly hostile political climate towards Palestinian citizens of Israel since October 2023 has also reshaped the strategy of Palestinian parties. For years, Abbas has maintained that Ra'am is willing to negotiate with any coalition capable of replacing Netanyahu, despite repeated declarations from opposition leaders ruling out such cooperation. Mansour Abbas: An icon for supporters of Israeli settler-colonialism Read More » This election cycle, however, he has gone further. Israeli media have reported that Ra'am has reached an agreement in principle with Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former Yesh Atid lawmaker, to include him on the party's electoral list. A Channel 13 poll suggested Segalovich's inclusion could lift Ra'am's projected representation from five seats to an unprecedented seven. Jabareen says Abbas is speaking to three audiences at once: Palestinian voters, the anti-Netanyahu camp and the Israeli establishment. "He wants to tell Palestinian Arab voters that he is still the only one practising the politics of the possible," says Jabareen. "At the same time, he is leaving the anti-Netanyahu camp an exit if it eventually needs the support of non-Zionist parties, while signalling to the Israeli establishment that Ra'am remains a reliable institutional partner." But the strategy also carries risks. "He is signalling a willingness to negotiate with a side that publicly says it has no interest in negotiating with him," Jabareen said. "That creates an image of weakness because the balance of power is not in his favour." Should Palestinians run for the Knesset? For Aida Touma-Sliman, a Knesset member from Hadash, a Palestinian-led party, the refusal of Jewish parties to work with Palestinian parties reflects more than electoral strategy. "The leaders of these parties know the Israeli public does not want any partnership with Palestinian Arab parties after years of incitement," she told MEE. "They lack the courage to present a genuine alternative to the current government's policies. In reality, they also hold Zionist and discriminatory positions." Ahead of Israel's elections, Bennett rejects two-state solution as Eisenkot surges in polls Read More » Touma-Sliman also rejects the idea that joining a governing coalition should be the primary objective of Palestinian parties. "Our presence in the Knesset was never based solely on joining governments," she said. "It is a space for political struggle where we represent our community, expose government policies and defend our people's rights." While she acknowledges that parliament is no longer the only arena for political action, she argues that abandoning it would only weaken Palestinian citizens' influence at a time when, she says, "our political weight is needed to confront fascism, even if that only means preventing the formation of another far-right government". For Jabareen, however, the challenge extends beyond coalition politics. He argues that Palestinian parties have spent too many election campaigns focused on which government they might help form, even as Israel's political landscape has fundamentally changed. "The important question is no longer who will invite us into a coalition," he said. "The real question is how we rebuild Palestinian political power inside Israel over the next decade in a way that makes ignoring us politically costly." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. headline: Hearing set to decide 'terror sentencing' of activists who targeted Barclays
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 16:42 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: A judge has ordered a hearing in which he will decide whether five Palestine Action defendants convicted of criminal damage will be sentenced as terrorists. The five defendants - Brendon O’Hagan, 28, Amanda Kelly, 31, Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31, Mohammed Malik, 28, and Alma Yaniv, 70 - were found guilty in June 2026 of causing £212,000 ($283,000) worth of damage to a Barclays branch in Burnley in August 2024. Following their convictions, presiding Judge Phillip Parry told defence lawyers that he would consider applying a “terrorist connection”, despite jurors not being told about a potential terror sentencing in the case. He then referred the matter to Judge Robert Altham who will decide whether to apply the terror designation at a hearing on 21 August, two weeks ahead of their sentencing on 4 September. In 2018, the court of appeal found that Judge Altham had issued "manifestly excessive" prison sentences to anti-fracking activists for causing public nuisance outside a site near Blackpool. The court ruled that the sentences were inappropriate and that the activists should be freed immediately. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters After the Barclays trial concluded, Judge Parry circulated a ruling made by Justice Johnson , the presiding judge in a recent Palestine Action case in which four activists convicted of criminal damage at an Elbit Systems site in Filton, near Bristol, were sentenced as terrorists despite being convicted of criminal charges. Gross overreach The CPS subsequently argued that the defendants should receive a terror sentencing, despite not mentioning the possibility during the trial. ‘We just disappeared’: Palestine Action defendant recalls ‘horrifying’ arrest Read More » The Barclays action took place prior to the proscription of Palestine Action and is not listed among the three incidents connected to the group which the government classified as terrorism, each allegedly involving over £1m ($1.35m) in damage. Simon Roscoe Blevins , an anti-fracking activist who was handed a 16-month custodial sentence by Altham in 2018, said: "Surely this move to add a terror connection to the sentencing of another direct action case, after no mention before or during trial, is another gross overreach and one he in particular cannot be trusted with?" Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said that it was "shocking" that Altham is deciding whether the terrorist designation will be applied. She added that both in the Filton case and the Barclays case "the jury were under the impression that they were simply deciding whether criminal damage was caused. They were completely unaware that a conviction of criminal damage, would essentially be convicting the defendants of terrorism". Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Houthi missile and drone attacks kill dozens of Yemeni government troops
author: MEE staff
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 12:09 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: At least 38 members of Yemen 's government forces were killed and 29 others were wounded in missile and drone attacks carried out by Houthis on Thursday, according to AFP. The attack marked the deadliest assault on forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government since the 2022 United Nations-brokered truce, military officials have said. The Houthis said the attacks were in retaliation for the "Saudi-backed military buildup", as Yemen's long-running conflict shows signs of intensifying alongside the broader US - Iran confrontation. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group targeted government military positions with ballistic missiles and drones, naming al-Ruwaik, al-Thaniyah and al-Abr as among the areas struck. "We are prepared to confront any escalation," Saree said. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Two medical sources told AFP that at least 38 government troops were killed and 29 others injured in the attacks. According to the report, one missile struck troops during their morning formation at a military camp in the al-Ruwaik area of Marib province, killing and wounding at least 45 personnel. Other attacks targeted military camps in al-Abr and al-Wadiah in Hadramawt province near the border with Saudi Arabia , AFP quoted military sources as saying. Yemen's defence ministry condemned the attacks and said in a statement that its armed forces "will respond to the missile and drone attacks at the appropriate place and time". Renewed conflict The Houthis have stepped up military operations since the outbreak of the US-Iran war earlier this year, ending a period of relative calm that followed the 2022 UN-brokered truce between the group and the Saudi-backed government. The renewed hostilities escalated after the Houthis declared the end of the country's de-escalation phase on 12 July, alleging that Saudi Arabia carried out air strikes on Sanaa International Airport as the group received an Iranian aircraft in the capital, Sanaa. Yemen's Houthis declare blockade on Saudi Arabia, raising Red Sea tensions Read More » Following the development, the group announced a maritime blockade of Saudi ports and launched attack s on Saudi-linked shipping, according to previous statements by the group. Saudi Arabia has utilised Bab el-Mandeb as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked to US-allied vessels since March, following the launch of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February. Last month, the Houthis killed 16 government-aligned troops in an attack south of the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, according to AFP reports. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen's government since seizing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. The group controls Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, while the government holds large areas in the south. The front lines had remained largely static following the 2022 truce, despite its formal expiry. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: Israeli bulldozers uproot West Bank olive trees ahead of harvest season
author: Mojahid Nawahda
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 15:49 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: Israeli bulldozers destroyed scores of olive trees in Palestinian villages near Jenin on Wednesday, as part of an ongoing campaign of uprooting olive groves across the occupied West Bank. The latest operation targeted farmland in the villages of Ajjah and Zububa, near the separation barrier, weeks before Palestinian farmers were due to begin this year's olive harvest. Zaki Jaradat, head of Zububa Village Council, said Israeli forces have uprooted more than 2,950 olive trees across more than 300 dunams of agricultural land since the start of the year. Among those affected is Fuad Yahya Maqalda, whose family has cultivated olive trees on the land for generations. From the rooftop of his home overlooking the family's land, Maqalda watched Israeli bulldozers move through the olive groves, uprooting trees that had stood for generations. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Unable to reach the site, he could only watch as the destruction unfolded below. "We are unable to do anything," he told Middle East Eye. "We cannot understand the intentions behind this uprooting. “The occupation uprooted olive trees that have stood on our land since the time of our grandparents." 'The occupation uprooted olive trees that have stood on our land since the time of our grandparents' - Fuad Yahya Maqalda, Palestinian farmer The timing, he said, made the loss even more painful, with the harvest season only weeks away. “Just as the olive harvest season is approaching, three plots of land that have belonged to our family for generations were targeted. They uprooted 111 olive trees from one plot and another 215 from a second. Every single one of those trees has been removed.” Tareq Ighbariya, spokesperson for the Palestinian Commission Against the Wall and Settlements in Jenin, said the destruction often extends beyond the areas specified in Israeli military orders, with the damage on the ground exceeding official boundaries. “Military orders may specify a certain area for tree uprooting or land clearing, but when they are carried out, the affected area is often much larger,” Ighbariya told MEE. “In some cases, bulldozers enter agricultural land and begin clearing it without any prior military order.” Olive harvest under attack The destruction in Zububa is not an isolated incident. Ighbariya said similar operations have targeted agricultural land elsewhere in the Jenin governorate, where the commission has documented damage to around 300 dunams of farmland in recent months. He warned that the true extent of the destruction may be higher as assessments continue. Why are Israeli settlers destroying the Palestinian olive harvest? Read More » The olive harvest is one of the most important agricultural seasons for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, providing a vital source of income for thousands of families. Beyond its economic importance, the harvest is deeply tied to Palestinian cultural and social life, with many olive groves passed down through generations. The uprooting of trees in Zububa comes as farmers across the occupied West Bank report increasing restrictions and attacks during the olive harvest season, including settler violence, vandalism, crop theft and difficulties accessing farmland, particularly near Israeli settlements and military zones. For many communities, the harvest has become a period of both economic importance and heightened uncertainty, with families fearing they may lose access to their land or face attacks while collecting their crops. headline: The Briton who helped 6,000 Jews move to Israel
author: Melissa Muller
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 09:21 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: A UK -born migration consultant has helped more than 6,000 Jews move to Israel over the past 15 years - much of it while working for an organisation that advertises migration to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and Golan Heights. As the number of illegal Israeli settlements and outposts in the occupied West Bank rises, Israel-linked organisations help Jews from across the world to move there. One of the most prominent organisations that advertises for illegal settlements and helps with Jewish immigration to Israel (also described as Aliyah) is Nefesh B'Nefesh (NBN). Its website lists information pages about various illegal settlements, which include local "community contacts" for those interested in moving there. NBN, for example, promotes the Israeli settlement cluster Gush Etzion, introducing various settlements within it. One of them is Tekoa. NBN promotes it by saying the population grew due to the "opening of a new road which bypasses Arab communities". The Katzrin settlement in the Golan Heights is also advertised . NBN promotes it by saying it is "surrounded by breathtaking views", while omitting the fact that the settlement is located within illegally occupied Syrian territory. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters NBN also promotes the West Bank settlement Elkana as a "well-situated community in the center of Israel", and describes the cluster of illegal settlements Mateh Binyamin as "one of the most beautiful regions in Israel". NBN fails to note that neither lies within Israel's internationally recognised borders. To promote Mateh Binyamin, NBN added a webinar recording from 2021 to its information page, in which US-born settlers advertise to live there. Pioneering effort The page also introduces the settlement Mitzpeh Yericho. "If you want to be part of the pioneering effort to build up Eretz Yisrael [land of Israel], then Mitzpeh Yericho is for you!", NBN says, adding that most families "live in regular houses, while the rest live in temporary housing (mobile homes and eshkubiot [modular concrete units])." Mobile homes are frequently used by settlers to establish new outposts or settlements. NBN also advertises for Shiloh, stating that there are "several construction initiatives" to "expand its borders". In this context, "expanding borders" would mean taking over Palestinian land. 'Israel survives and thrives on Aliyah' - Dov Newmark, consultant How many internationals NBN helped move to illegally occupied territories remains unclear. But the information page for Efrat gives an insight, stating that "thousands of NBN Olim" are living in the illegal settlement. Nevertheless, NBN claims the settlement information pages on its website are "for educational and informational purposes only" and that it "does not endorse, recommend, or promote any specific community". The terminology used by NBN does, however, suggest that the organisation views both the Golan Heights and the West Bank as part of Israel. Nefesh B'Nefesh mainly helps Jews from the USA and Canada migrate to Israel. But it also used to operate in the UK, where the British-born Aliyah-consultant Dov Newmark appears to have run its British business. According to his LinkedIn , he was NBN's "Director of UK Aliyah" from 2009 until 2023. "I was at Nefesh for 15 years. Amazing 15 years. Great organisation", Newmark told the British-Israeli podcaster David Goodwin in May 2024, adding that NBN made Jewish migration to Israel significantly easier: "Nefesh really put all the information together on one site, which was amazing." A Facebook post by Dov Newmark offering Aliyah consultations in London (Screengrab) Newmark says that during those years he helped over 6,000 Jews migrate to Israel. Whether he assisted any of them in moving to illegal settlements remains unclear - neither he nor NBN responded to MEE press inquiries. It also remains unclear until when NBN operated in the UK. Newmark says the organisation pulled out around 2018. But a UK charitable company called Friends of Nefesh B'Nefesh Limited was formally dissolved in July 2024, with NBN listing a UK number on its website until 2021. When contacted by MEE, a spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office reiterated the UK's official position on the illegality of settlements, but did not comment on Newmark's activities in particular. “The UK is clear that settlements are illegal under international law and jeopardise prospects for peace," they said. “We oppose further settlement expansion and strongly advise against conducting any economic and financial activities in illegal Israeli settlements.” 'Make Aliyah easy' Newmark says Aliyah was "always on the cards". Having grown up in northeast London, he was active in Bnei Akiva during his youth. The Zionist Jewish youth organisation sees migration to Israel as the "ultimate expression of its ideology" and sends international Jews on gap year trips in Israel. In 2008, Newmark, his wife and his three children moved to Israel, where they've been living in Modiin since. Rights groups sue France over inaction on financial ties to illegal Israeli settlements Read More » After leaving NBN in 2023, Newmark started his own Aliyah consultancy business, Make Aliyah Easy , to help British Jews move to Israel. His services include Aliyah planning, relocation assistance and post-Aliyah support - all free of charge. Instead of billing his clients, Newmark says he works with English-speaking service providers that pay him commission: "For instance, if you need a shipper, and you use my shipper, I'll get a commission. If you move money from the UK and use my currency converter, I'll get a commission". MEE was unable to identify which service providers the Aliyah-consultant works with and whether any of them operate in occupied territories. To promote his new business, Newmark organised informational webinars in collaboration with the Israeli organisations Yad L'Olim and Olim Paveway . He also ran a webinar with the UK shipping firm Stephen Morris , for which he invited Israeli realtors and experts to speak about the migration process, Israeli property markets and immigration benefits. Newmark moreover held a webinar in collaboration with Raymond James , a London-based investment firm that offers "long-term financial planning advice for those making Aliyah". Neither Newmark's adverts nor his online presence suggest that he helps British Jews move to illegal settlements. Publicly, all the communities he advertises for lie within Israel's internationally recognised borders. But a new collaboration raises questions. Business partnership In June 2026, Newmark announced a partnership with Shivat Zion, an Israeli organisation that - despite lacking registration with the UK Charity Commission - said it launched as "the UK's Only Free Aliyah Support Charity" in 2025. In 2026, Declassified UK revealed that the organisation offered to assist a UK citizen with migration to a settlement, prompting calls for sanctions by two Labour MPs. In response to the report, Shivat Zion uploaded a video of a representative claiming that the organisation works "under Israeli law". He did not address concerns that Shivat Zion helps internationals move to occupied territories and instead said: "If someone has decided on a specific city in Israel, we help them: "If someone has decided on a specific city in Israel, we help them." 'There's always a spike in Aliyah after a conflict' - Dov Newmark, consultant Israel regularly declares settlements in the West Bank as its national territory, thus making them legal under its national law. But this doesn't change the fact that all Israeli settlements in the West Bank - regardless of their legal status in Israel - are considered illegal both under international and British law. Newmark publicly describes his relationship with Shivat Zion as a "partnership". The organisation, however, officially lists the Briton as a Senior Aliyah and Strategic Consultant for the UK on its website. It thus remains unclear whether Newmark is an employee, receives commission or works for Shivat Zion on a freelance basis. It does, however, appear as though Newmark functions as the organisation's primary link to the UK - no other UK Aliyah consultants are listed on Shivat Zion's website. The Aliyah organisation did not respond to an MEE press inquiry about its activities in the UK, its work in occupied territories or its partnership with Newmark. It also failed to take up the opportunity to publicly rule out helping people move to settlements within occupied territories. BBQs on army bases Despite working with organisations that have promoted migration to illegal settlements, Newmark seems proud of his work and eager to continue it. Israeli army 'murdered child' in Gaza and then dumped body on a roadside Read More » "If you think about it, Israel is a country made up of Olim [immigrants]", the Aliyah-consultant told Goodwin. "Israel survives and thrives on Aliyah." Newmark believes the State of Israel should be celebrated because "it didn't come easy". He also told Goodwin that his daughter was serving in the Israeli navy at the time of the interview, while he himself volunteered to help the Israeli army by going to army bases and cooking BBQs for its soldiers. Although the Israeli army has committed well-documented human rights violations and has been accused of perpetrating genocide in Gaza , Newmark says he enjoyed being around soldiers: "You can see the determination in those soldiers to go in there and do what they need to do. They're so positive and the morale is so high, you can't help but be sucked into that positivity." Newmark also believes the war on Gaza may lead to higher levels of Jewish migration to Israel. "There's always a spike in Aliyah after a conflict," he told Goodwin. "And this will be no different. There will be a spike. [...] And I'm excited to help people fulfil and realise their dream of moving and making Aliyah." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. headline: 'We've run out of earthly solutions': Inside Libya's electricity crisis
author: Elis Gjevori
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 15:51 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Earlier this month, Al Robyan, one of Tripoli's most popular seafood restaurants, made an unusual offer: a table laden with seafood in exchange for "some fuel for the generator". "We've run out of earthly solutions," the restaurant wrote on Facebook. The post drew thousands of responses, with some joking that the fuel would cost more than the seafood on offer. Over the summer, Libyans across the country have endured almost daily power outages lasting between six and 10 hours. That might sound unusual for a hydrocarbon-rich country that produces more than 1.3 million barrels of oil a day and has a population of just over 7.5 million. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Since these massive shortages started, every business in Libya has been affected," said Alaeddin Muntasser, a retired businessman in Tripoli, who described the situation as an "electricity disaster". Muntasser told Middle East Eye of one water-bottling plant severely affected by the blackouts. "We had a shortage of drinking water for a couple of weeks. If they can't pump or filter, they can't bottle," he said. "Many small restaurants have shut down; a few who can afford to have a generator to run their ovens managed to open." Meanwhile, people with the worst blackouts lost all the food in their freezers and fridges. 'The electricity crisis is one of those problems that will not go away until Libya's government can implement a longer-term strategy' – Hamish Kinnear, analyst The blackouts have sparked protests in Tripoli, Zawiya, Misrata and elsewhere in Libya. Demonstrators demanding a more reliable electricity supply have also called for the resignation of Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. Libya generates roughly 70 percent of its electricity from natural gas, leaving the power grid highly exposed to falling gas production and disruptions at fields and pipelines. Oil accounts for almost all the remainder. "The electricity crisis and related protests is one of those problems that will not go away until Libya's government can implement a longer-term strategy that ensures a more reliable electricity supply, whether that be through refined fuels or renewable energy sources," Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, told MEE. Kinnear noted that Libya was not alone in facing such problems, "but for citizens of a country with the largest oil reserves and the fifth largest gas reserves in Africa, as well as significant solar power potential, blackouts are a particular source of frustration". A crisis decades in the making The roots of Libya's current electricity crisis go back years. The country has not recovered since it plunged into chaos after a Nato-backed uprising toppled and killed longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. Since then, the country has split, with rival administrations in the west headed by the internationally recognised government of Dbeibah, and in the east backed by forces led by General Khalifa Haftar and foreign governments. Years of underinvestment in the power grid and gas production, combined with this year's heatwave, in which temperatures hit 50C, have all come to a head. "Oil wealth only becomes reliable electricity when institutions can convert it, and Libya's institutions have been fractured for over a decade," said Karim Elgendy, executive director of the Carboun Institute, a think tank focused on Middle East and North Africa energy and climate. "Rival authorities issue competing decisions over the same grid and the utility recovers almost none of its costs. Years of deferred maintenance have left the network running on ageing equipment with no margin for error. So every summer becomes a stress test the grid is not ready for," Elgendy told MEE. Brega oil port in Marsa Brega, 270kms west of the eastern city of Benghazi, on 24 September 2020 (Marsa Al Burayqah/AFP) In January, Egypt and Libya signed a memorandum of understanding to deepen cooperation in the oil and gas sector. In July, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and other Egyptian officials met with senior Libyan officials, including National Oil Corporation chairman Massoud Suleman, to discuss deepening energy ties between the two sides. Following Libya's electricity blackouts throughout July, Tripoli turned in part to Egypt, which boosted electricity export capacity to Libya by approximately 43 percent, reaching 100 megawatts. Despite the apparently sharp rise, the extra supply meets only a fraction of Libya's electricity needs, covering less than a tenth of its recent generation shortfall. Libya also settled outstanding dues to Egypt totalling around $90m. 'A country importing electricity from Egypt is, indirectly, importing Egypt's gas risk' – Karim Elgendy, Carboun Institute On the surface, both sides stand to benefit from deepening energy cooperation. Egypt has a massive appetite for energy, and Libya has significant hydrocarbons sitting under its soil. "The complementarity between the two economies is real: Libya has the hydrocarbons, Egypt has the refining, the generation fleet and the contractors," said Elgendy. "But genuine integration begins when both sides commit to a long-term commercial framework with obligations running both ways." And that shows little sign of happening. Egypt's own electricity needs run on burning gas, and lots of it. Where it once had enough production of its own to meet much of its energy needs, that production has been declining as reserves are depleted. "Egypt's own power system leans heavily on imported gas it does not control, and recent supply interruptions showed how quickly that exposure travels down the chain. A country importing electricity from Egypt is, indirectly, importing Egypt's gas risk," noted Elgendy. In recent years, Egypt has had to turn to Israel . Cairo signed a record $35bn gas deal with Israel in 2025, almost tripling its gas imports from the Israeli Leviathan gas fields and marking the largest export deal in Israel's history. A man waves the Libyan flag during a march to commemorate the 14th anniversary of the uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi in Tajura, Tripoli, on 16 February 2025 (AFP) Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist with the Royal United Services Institute, says the attempts by Libya and Egypt to look to meet each other's energy needs are "not to be taken seriously". Harchaoui is sceptical that energy needs were driving the outreach. "I think it would be very incorrect to say that the electricity situation is the reason for the meeting," he told MEE. "There has been a pattern whereby Tripoli tends to say to Egypt: 'Let's talk. And by the way, I notice you're suffering from energy shortages. Libya has a small population and a lot of energy, Tripoli is happy to help you, Egypt.'" He described it as "more of a diplomatic trick than something really genuine, especially during a summer when Libya itself is grappling with a very serious electricity crisis". Harchaoui says the deeper problem is one that Tripoli has been ignoring for a decade. 'To do a corrupt project, you need more time than to do an honest project, because you have to make sure all the key officials are satisfied with their bribes' – Jalel Harchaoui, RUSI Libya sits on abundant natural gas reserves both onshore and offshore, "but the error that Libya made, and it's a profound error with long-time consequences, is that it hasn't kept up in terms of natural gas production capacity". Gas still accounts for roughly three-quarters of the country's electricity output, yet years have gone by "with no new natural gas project of any significance even being launched". The result, Harchaoui said, is that existing assets have been "shrinking in terms of output", and even a new project greenlit today would take "at least seven or eight years" before producing results. On current trends, he warned, Libya could within a few years be "humiliated to the point of having to import natural gas", a reversal that would undercut any framing of Libya and Egypt as complementary energy partners. Part of the failure is cultural as much as technical, he argued. Libya operates with "the culture of a crude oil-producing country" that "just doesn't think in terms of natural gas" as a priority, even though gas, not oil, is what actually keeps the lights on. Corruption has compounded the delay, not only by diverting money but by slowing decision-making itself. "To do a corrupt project, you need more time than to do an honest project, because you have to make sure all the key officials are satisfied with their bribes," Harchaoui said, alleging that some power plant units installed between 2022 and 2025 were purchased secondhand and passed off as new. Political dynamics have also shaped the outbreaks of anger. Harchaoui pointed to years of unfulfilled promises by the country's prime minister – who has claimed since 2021 to have "resolved" the crisis – as one reason unrest has concentrated in the west, where protest is easier to organise than under Haftar's tighter grip in the east. Blackouts, he stressed, are hitting the east and south too, just less visibly and without the same political cost. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved.
