subheadline: As blackouts spark protests, a decade of fractured governance, underinvestment and corruption has left an oil and gas-rich nation unable to keep its lights on

headline: Netanyahu's ultra-Orthodox alliance shows signs of fracture before crucial election
author: Nadav Rapaport
publication_date: Published date: 6 August 2026 16:14 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago
article_body: For nearly three decades, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has relied on ultra-Orthodox parties as one of the pillars of his political survival. But as Netanyahu gears up to one of his toughest elections in years, his governing alliance is facing unprecedented strain over the long-running dispute about military conscription for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. The row has exposed deep divisions within Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and raised questions about whether the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, two of his most dependable allies since he first became prime minister in 1996, could look elsewhere. "There's disappointment and anger within the ultra-Orthodox public over their situation," Pnina Pfeuffer, director general of the Ultra-Orthodox Public Organisation, a civil society group working within ultra-Orthodox communities, told Middle East Eye. The political future of the ultra-Orthodox parties is so unclear, she adds, that it is no longer "far-fetched" that they could join a government led by Gadi Eisenkot , Netanyahu's fiercest challenger in years. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "Eisenkot is not perceived as anti-ultra-Orthodox," Pfeuffer said, referring to the former military chief's standing among religious voters. Avi-ram Tzoreff, an Israeli historian and human rights activist specialising in Jewish cultural, political and religious history, said the growing divide between Netanyahu's allies and the ultra-Orthodox had opened new political possibilities. "Clearly there's a rift between the ultra-Orthodox and the right," Tzoreff told MEE. Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief challenging Netanyahu? Read More » "The ultra-Orthodox are a political subject that says: 'we will rather die than be drafted'," he added, referring to a common chant heard during anti-conscription protests. "The alliance between the ultra-Orthodox parties and the right is not a given." Instead, Tzoreff argued that an Eisenkot-led bloc could exploit the divisions to dismantle what he described as the Israeli right's "unnatural political alliance" with the ultra-Orthodox. According to Tzoreff, opposition parties hoping to defeat Netanyahu need to rethink their traditional coalition strategy. "Once political relationships are organised around the drafting of the ultra-Orthodox into the military," he said, "it becomes difficult to work toward broadening coalitions." He argued that if the centre-left hopes to win power, "the centre-left needs to think about how to draw the boundaries of the political camp differently." Fractured alliance Since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, the question of military service for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men has become one of the country's most divisive political issues. While hundreds of thousands of reservists have been mobilised for the war, ultra-Orthodox men have historically been exempt from compulsory military service in order to pursue full-time religious studies in yeshivas. The arrangement has long been contentious, but the war has intensified pressure to end the exemption. Netanyahu's coalition has repeatedly failed to pass legislation regulating ultra-Orthodox enlistment, leading to the detention of dozens of young men accused of evading military service and triggering mass protests backed by UTJ and Shas. Settler terrorism is the modern incarnation of the Zionist dream Read More » Last year, ministers from both parties resigned from government posts in protest over the coalition's failure to pass a conscription law, although they continued cooperating with the government on key legislation. The issue has also fuelled divisions within Netanyahu's own Likud party, where several lawmakers viewed efforts to pass a new draft law as an unacceptable concession to the ultra-Orthodox. Knesset member Dan Illouz, who left Likud last month over the issue, told Israeli news outlet Ynet that the right-wing bloc "has become idolatry". According to Illouz, the bloc "undermines our ability to advance right-wing economic and security policy", including ensuring the military has sufficient manpower. Ultra-Orthodox leaders, meanwhile, have increasingly questioned their long-standing partnership with Netanyahu. In May, Rabbi Dov Lando, the spiritual leader of Degel HaTorah, one of the two parties that make up UTJ, declared that "we no longer have trust in Netanyahu", adding that the party was no longer "committed to him". Last month, a senior Degel HaTorah official told Israel's Ma'ariv newspaper that "there's no such thing as a bloc anymore", adding that the party would negotiate with any political camp willing to meet its demands. Deep ideological divisions The dispute over military conscription has exposed more than just tensions within Netanyahu's coalition. It has also highlighted deep ideological divisions over Israel's military campaigns and the role of the state among the ultra-Orthodox leadership. Although Jewish opposition parties broadly agree that ultra-Orthodox men should be drafted into the military, analysts say the debate also reflects sharply different attitudes towards Israel's wars in Gaza and across the region. Those differences were thrown into the spotlight last month when Rabbi Dov Lando, the 96-year-old spiritual leader of Degel HaTorah, launched an unusually scathing attack on the Religious Zionist movement, whose supporters have played a prominent role in Israel's war on Gaza and in the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank. "They wage wars not for the sake of rescue, only for the sake of the state's honour," Lando said, accusing Religious Zionists of being "evil" and murderers. 'The ultra-Orthodox don't perceive the war as their own' - Pnina Pfeuffer, Ultra-Orthodox Public Organisation His remarks drew condemnation from across Israel's political spectrum, including Netanyahu, who said he rejected "the awful remarks". But the comments were consistent with Lando's long-held views. Last year, he said Religious Zionists had "brought physical disasters, not only spiritual ones, upon the Jewish people", adding that Zionist actions had created a situation in which Arabs hated Jews "like never before". Pfeuffer argued that Lando's comments should not be viewed as a direct political challenge to Netanyahu's coalition. "Rabbi Lando is expressing an ethics-based position on the situation, not a political one, and as evidence, he never demanded leaving the government over the war," she told MEE. Instead, she said the remarks reflected a long-standing ultra-Orthodox worldview that distances itself from the state's military ethos. "The ultra-Orthodox don't perceive the war as their own," Pfeuffer said, noting that during the past almost three years "life continued fairly normally" in ultra-Orthodox communities in Israel and the occupied West Bank. The Ben Gvir effect Even without immediate political consequences, Pfeuffer said Lando's intervention was significant because it offered a markedly different vision from the dominant Israeli narrative surrounding the war. "It represents moderation and restraint, which stems from a perception that our place in this land is not guaranteed and that we need to live alongside our enemies," she said. Tzoreff agreed that Lando's remarks reflected a deeply rooted theological position rather than a tactical political intervention. "If you send someone to kill in the name of the honour of the state, you're actually elevating the theological status of the state at the expense of Torah study," he said. "This isn't just a random statement. It was released to the media, and even if it doesn't currently have traction with the public, its purpose was to build traction with the public." Yet Lando's position also sits uneasily alongside a broader shift to the right within parts of Israel's ultra-Orthodox electorate. According to Pfeuffer, National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has made inroads among traditional Shas and UTJ voters, complicating the political calculations of ultra-Orthodox leaders. "Part of Shas's constituency aren't classic Shas voters, they could vote for Ben Gvir or Likud, as they don't live ultra-Orthodox lives. Therefore, Shas needs to show that it is part of the right-wing bloc and with Netanyahu," she said. While she argued Shas remains considerably more committed to Netanyahu's coalition than UTJ, Tzoreff said the party has steadily drifted towards the far right since the death of its founder, Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, in 2013. Shas, he said, has "undergone a process of Ben Gvirization", with hardline religious figures such as the late Rabbi Meir Mazuz assuming greater influence over the party's direction. "Rabbi Ovadia was a wedge against moving rightward," Tzoreff said. Since the revered spiritual leader's death, he argued, Shas has been "struggling to set red lines". "The party's leadership, similar to other parties, doesn't act as leadership, but acts to please public opinion." Tzoreff said the shift extends beyond Shas, pointing to what he described as increasingly close ties between the ultra-Orthodox and Israel's settler movement, as well as the growing adoption of nationalist rhetoric within ultra-Orthodox communities. Furthermore, he cited the strengthening relationship between settlers and ultra-Orthodox communities in the occupied West Bank, together with the increasing embrace of the idea that Torah study itself contributes to Israel's security. "But on the other hand, there's a strong movement against military conscription," he said. For Israel's opposition parties, Tzoreff argued, that contradiction presents an opportunity. "The role of the centre-left is to divide and conquer within the right-wing bloc," he said. Rather than ruling out cooperation with the ultra-Orthodox parties, he said opponents of Netanyahu should consider engaging with them pragmatically. "They need to consider partnership with the UTJ and Shas not out of idealisation of the ultra-Orthodox, but because there's a space that can be played politically." Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: Saudi Arabia's last major oil route comes under Houthi pressure
author: Gaspard Rouffin
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 15:55 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: The Houthis said on Wednesday that they had fired ballistic missiles at the NCC Wafaa , a Saudi oil tanker, off the coast of Yanbu, a major Saudi port city in the northern Red Sea. It is the northernmost attack by the Yemeni group since it began a blockade on Saudi Arabia on 22 July, and analysts warn a shift north towards Egypt and the Suez Canal would lead to increasing economic pressure on the Gulf kingdom. Until now, the Houthis had mostly targeted ships off Yemen's coast, in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. The group accused the Wafaa of violating the blockade and ignoring warning calls before it was struck. Since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Saudi Arabia had kept part of its oil flowing through the alternative route of Bab al-Mandab. But the Houthi blockade on the strait is now limiting that option. Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen analyst, described the move as a “bid to deny the Suez Canal rerouting” – the alternative route Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters Jalal argues that the Houthis are threatening to expand the conflict further north in the Red Sea for two reasons. Externally, he said, the move is intended to strengthen Iran's "bargaining position" over the Strait of Hormuz; internally, it aims to "restore coercive leverage over Riyadh ". Matthew Wright, an analyst at the ship-tracking firm Kpler, told the BBC this week: "In terms of threat to the trade of crude, we're at the worst period that we've been in since this crisis began." The Houthis claim to have hit eight tankers since the blockade was declared, at least five of which were Saudi and one Indian -flagged, the latter sinking near Bab al-Mandab on 4 August. Only four strikes have been independently verified by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO), the international reference for maritime security incidents. The Saudi authorities have not confirmed any of the strikes. Houthi strikes in the Red Sea Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesperson, said on 5 August that at least 29 Saudi vessels had turned away from Bab al-Mandab during the first two weeks of the blockade. Calling the move “blockade for blockade”, Saree said the group would “respond to any escalation with escalation”. ​​​​The attack on 5 August marked the northernmost Houthi strike in the Red Sea since the start of the blockade on 22 July. Satellite imagery by Google. Source: UKMTO and Yemeni media Salah Ali Salah, a security affairs researcher at the Sanaa Centre, told Middle East Eye, “the Houthis are still on an escalatory trajectory”, adding that he did not believe they had “yet deployed the full weight of their maritime capabilities against Saudi Arabia”. While some Saudi vessels are turning away from Bab al-Mandab, such as six tankers that took a significantly longer route around Africa this week, others are switching off their transponders to cross the waterway instead, Bloomberg reported. Saudi oil exports normally account for around 66 percent of Bab al-Mandab traffic, and the Red Sea carries 10 to 12 percent of global trade overall. Ryan Bohl, a senior Mena analyst at RANE, a global risk intelligence company, said it was “unlikely” the Houthis could close off “all traffic” in the northern Red Sea. Instead, they could demonstrate they are a “credible threat” by hitting Egyptian ports and the Suez Canal , forcing the Saudis to “take measures to hide their ships”. This would include “turning off transponders” and paying crews “substantially more”, forcing Saudi shipping companies to “absorb all the war risks associated with such an outcome”. Rerouting through the Suez Canal Rerouting around Africa also forces Saudi tankers to pass through the Suez Canal to reach Yanbu, adding at least four weeks to the journey for Asia-bound ships, the main destination for Saudi crude. That route is itself constrained. Saudi Arabia typically ships using Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) holding around 2 million barrels. But the Suez Canal’s limited depth means it must use Suezmax carriers with a capacity of 1 million barrels, or partially loaded VLCCs. A VLCC carries roughly double the cargo capacity of a tanker capable of passing through the Suez canal. Infographics by Reuters. “If VLCCs have to pass through Suez partially loaded, it will impact how much Saudi is able to get through,” Bohl said. Tankers bound for Asia will need more journeys to deliver the same volume, adding an estimated $1.6m in fuel costs plus a $1m Suez toll fee per transit. Salah said the issue was not “simply whether Saudi Arabia can find another route, but whether it can find one that preserves the same scale, cost and efficiency of its existing export system”. Bohl said the Suez restrictions would be “partially offset by offloading through the Sumed pipeline”, one of the pipelines that now serve as Saudi Arabia’s main contingency for consistent crude deliveries. The Sumed pipeline in Egypt lets tankers offload part of their cargo in deep water before crossing the canal, then reload it on the other side. Increased uncertainty in the northern Red Sea and Suez Canal would complicate Saudi Arabia’s last safe option for strategic oil exports. (Map by MEE; Source: CIA) Growing exports in Yanbu The East-West pipeline, which crosses Saudi Arabia coast to coast, transfers oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea, where the kingdom’s largest refineries are concentrated. It has been especially useful for moving oil east to Yanbu, where the export volumes have more than tripled since the Strait of Hormuz closed, according to Bloomberg data. Some analysts see the Wafaa strike as a possible step towards attacks on non-tanker vessels. Salah said the “greater danger would be the expansion of maritime targeting to non-tanker vessels and imports”. He added the broader danger was “the precedent this creates”. Saudi oil exports through the Gulf have fallen since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with most shipments now departing from Yanbu (Data from Bloomberg) But Bohl argues this is not in the Houthis’ best interest. A “major new offensive” from Saudi Arabia against the Houthis in Yemen, particularly one targeting Hodeidah, their “own critical Red Sea lifeline”, would have severe consequences for the group. If the Houthis did escalate, Bohl said, Saudi Arabia “would face the same kinds of logistical issues that the littoral Gulf Arab states” are currently dealing with under the Strait of Hormuz closure, though Riyadh would likely be better prepared, given its land routes through Jordan and air options. Declining Saudi oil exports The Houthi blockade on Bab al-Mandab has had less of an impact on Saudi oil exports so far than the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Exports through Hormuz have declined sharply since its closure on 4 March, but Saudi Arabia has shifted most departures to the Red Sea instead, making that waterway especially sensitive now. Kpler, a maritime intelligence firm, estimates Bab al-Mandab volumes have increased eightfold, and Yanbu had one of its busiest days on record on 1 August, with five supertankers positioned for loading. Oil infrastructure at Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea port of Yanbu on 4 March 2026 (AFP / Planet Labs) The Houthis targeted Saudi Aramco plants in July, but CEO Amin Nasser said there had been no material operational or financial impact. Aramco reported on Tuesday that second-quarter profits surged 33 percent, driven by higher energy prices from the war on Iran and the Saudi pipelines bypassing Hormuz. According to Bohl, “it remains to be seen whether or not Saudi exports will see a major dip or if this is just downward pressure that they can adjust to”. This week, hopes of an Iran-Oman deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz led Saudi Arabia to cut its main oil price for Asia by 50 cents to $2 a barrel, a sign that Riyadh does not view the Houthi blockade in the Red Sea as a grave threat. Salah said the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz “would certainly ease pressure on global energy markets, but it would not resolve the Houthi problem in the Red Sea”. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . headline: UK: Nearly one in five Prevent referrals had autism, new Home Office figures reveal
author: Areeb Ullah
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 11:26 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Nearly one in five people referred to Britain's controversial Prevent counter-extremism programme had autism recorded as a condition, according to new Home Office figures, raising fresh concerns over the scheme's impact on neurodivergent people. Analysis of the figures show that 1,833 of the 9,957 people referred to Prevent between October 2024 and September 2025 had autism recorded, with 1,199 classified as confirmed cases and a further 634 recorded as suspected. The Home Office data also shows that almost 10,000 people were referred to Prevent in England and Wales during the period - the highest annual total number of referrals since records began in 2015, following a 39 percent increase on the previous year. Overall, 36 percent of the 9,957 individuals referred to Prevent had at least one mental health or neurodiversity condition recorded. Autism was the most commonly recorded neurodiverse condition. Jacob Smith, Freedom of Expression and Belief team leader at Rights and Security International, told Middle East Eye that the increase in referrals of people with autism was "particularly concerning" and reflected longstanding problems with the government's counter-extremism programme. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "We've been aware for a while that autistic people are overrepresented within Prevent, but the fact that it has increased so much over the last year is particularly concerning," Smith told Middle East Eye. "Prevent has, since its inception, been plagued by accusations of bias and discrimination. "It initially targeted Muslim communities and, although the representation of Muslims within Prevent has changed over time, we still see the disproportionate representation of Asian and Black people. We're now seeing that with autistic people as well." The figures also showed: a 20 percent rise in referrals for individuals related to far-right extremism. Asian people continue to be overrepresented in the Prevent programme, making up 18 percent of referrals where ethnicity was recorded - double their proportion of the wider population in England and Wales. Black people are also overrepresented in the Prevent programme - (eight percent of referrals when ethnicity was noted, compared to four percent of the population Despite government warnings that “Islamist extremism” remains the greatest threat facing the UK, referrals categorised under that label have declined to eight percent of all Prevent cases. Smith argued that the programme's referral process relies too heavily on subjective judgement with public sector workers legally obliged to refer anyone to Prevent if they are suspected of terrorism. "Prevent is set up in a very vague way and relies heavily on referrers' gut instincts," he said. "That effectively encourages them to take their biases into account when making decisions, whether intentionally or subconsciously. To me, that's a key reason why we're consistently seeing the overrepresentation of certain groups within Prevent." The Home Office data showed that autism became more prevalent as cases progressed through the Prevent process. Around 23 percent of individuals whose cases were discussed by a Channel panel had autism recorded, rising to 24 percent among those formally adopted into the government's de-radicalisation programme. The figures form part of the Home Office's second statistical release to include mental health and neurodiversity data following the introduction of the Prevent Case Management Tracker (PCMT) in 2024. The department said the new system had improved how such conditions are recorded but warned that the quality of the data is still developing. The Home Office stressed that the figures do not demonstrate a causal relationship between neurodiversity and susceptibility to radicalisation. "It is important to note that these findings describe associations within the data rather than causal relationships," the report said. "The analysis does not indicate that being neurodiverse or having a particular mental health condition increases or decreases the likelihood of progressing through the Prevent or Channel process." Criminalising sterotypes about autistic people But Smith warned that the programme risked reinforcing and criminalising sterotypes about autistic people. "A lot of the language used about autistic people [by Prevent] points to traits that are directly linked to autism - for example, hyperfixation. The implication is that autistic people are more likely to pose a risk because of characteristics associated with their diagnosis." "Instead of addressing the underlying issue, there's a degree of doubling down by relying on autistic people's diagnoses as an explanation," he added. Following an initial screening and assessment, Prevent referrals which are deemed at risk of radicalisation may be passed to a multi-agency "channel panel". These panels are chaired by local authorities and tasked with determining a person’s susceptibility to radicalisation, and whether a tailored package of support is necessary to address the risk. Of the 1,100 referrals taken on as a channel case in the year to September 2025 where ethnicity was known, 835 (76 percent) were white, 159 (14 percent) were Asian, 59 (five percent) were black and 47 (four percent) were "other". Smith said people referred to Prevent could face lasting consequences even when no further action is taken. "As we documented in our 2024 report Caught in the Web , information about Prevent referrals - including referrals that don't go anywhere or are mistaken or malicious - is shared with a wide range of policing bodies, as well as other public authorities, including the security services and immigration authorities," he said. "While much of what happens within Prevent is secret, there is a real risk of long-term consequences for people who are referred, not only in their interactions with the police but also in their interactions with other public services." headline: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan sign defence pact
author: Ragip Soylu
publication_date: Published date: 7 August 2026 07:57 BST | Last update: 1 week 5 days ago
article_body: Turkey , Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a joint defence agreement on Friday, connecting the three largest Muslim countries in the world under one security umbrella for the first time. The deal, which has been under negotiation since last year, creates a significant new trilateral framework amid a deepening regional crisis following Israeli and US attacks on Iran . Saudi analysts have previously said that Riyadh could activate the defence pact it currently has with Pakistan should it enter the Iran war. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the deal in Mecca in a joint ceremony. The leaders, in a joint statement, said that the defence agreement reflects their shared determination to further strengthen their collective security, in the region and beyond. New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "The Agreement aims to bolster collective deterrence against all forms of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack carried out against any one of the three states shall be considered an attack against all of them," the joint statement said. "The Agreement also provides for the development of defense cooperation among the three states in all its dimensions." Saudi Aramco reports bumper profits as it bypasses Strait of Hormuz Read More » “The agreement will change the balance of power in the region,” one Ankara-based source said. “If successfully implemented, the deal will enhance the stability and security of people living in this part of the world.” The sources said the deal would cover all defence cooperation among the three countries. “It will not alter or undermine any other alliance commitments the three countries may have,” the same source added. One Turkish official told Reuters that the agreement was defensive in nature, was not directed against any specific actor, and was open to other regional countries. Former rivals draw closer together The pact would link three of the region’s largest countries, each with unique advantages. Oil-rich Saudi Arabia is the Arab world’s only G20 economy and home to Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam. Pakistan is the Muslim-world’s only nuclear-armed state. Turkey, which straddles Asia and Europe, boasts Nato’s second-largest army. Bab al-Mandeb: US war on Iran gives Houthis new leverage over Saudi Arabia Read More » Both Islamabad and Ankara are emerging as major weapons manufacturers and exporters. Pakistan is historically close to both Saudi Arabia and Turkey, but the latter two countries have not always seen eye-to-eye. Turkey's President Erdogan backed popular protests following the Arab Spring that Riyadh saw as a threat to its monarchical system of governance. A decade ago, Saudi Arabia and the UAE joined forces to battle Turkey in Libya. They also supported Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, a former general whom Erdogan once denounced. But the region’s alliances have whipsawed. Erdogan and Sisi are moving closer amid joint concerns over Israel’s war on Gaza - recognised as a genocide by the United Nations - and broader attacks on Lebanon, Syria and Iran. Saudi Arabia and Turkey began patching up ties around 2021. Copyright © 2014 - 2026 . Middle East Eye. All rights reserved. Only England and Wales jurisdiction apply in all legal matters.
